Tip in the dry rice, stir to coat it in fat, then moisten with hot stock, two parts to one.
Cook 18 minutes covered without ever lifting the lid, then rest ten minutes off the heat.

entrevero-de-pinhao.d: A sautéed mixture of araucaria pine nuts, meats and vegetables. The southern Brazilian araucaria bears seed only after twenty years and only in winter: entrevero is strictly seasonal, from May to August.
s: Boil the pine nuts forty minutes in salted water, then split the shell with a knife while still hot.
Cold, they become impossible to shell without crushing the kernel: they must be opened straight out of the water.
Cut them in two or three, depending on size, and set aside.
Fry the meats separately — belly first, then sausage, then beef — so each browns at its own pace.
Bring everything together with the vegetables and pine nuts, toss five minutes over high heat and serve scalding.

cuca-alema.d: A flat brioche topped with fruit and streusel, inherited from the German settlers of the south. Cuca is the Brazilian corruption of Kuchen; the recipe arrived in 1850 with migrants from Pomerania and the Rhineland and has barely changed.
s: Make a sponge with warm milk, yeast and a little flour, and wait twenty minutes for it to double.
Knead with the remaining flour, eggs, sugar and soft butter for ten minutes, until the dough pulls away.
Spread it in a rectangular tin without working it, and prove an hour under a cloth.
Make the streusel by rubbing flour, sugar and cold butter with your fingertips, never forming a dough.
Lay on the fruit, cover with streusel and bake 40 minutes at 180°C. Eaten warm, with afternoon coffee.

sagu-com-creme.p: Caxias do Sul, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
sagu-com-creme.d: Tapioca pearls cooked in red wine, served with a custard. It is the dessert of the Italian settlers of the Serra Gaúcha, who had vines and not much else: wine here simply replaces water.
s: Soak the tapioca pearls an hour in cold water: without soaking they stay raw at the centre.
Bring the wine, sugar and spices to a tremble, add the drained pearls and stir often.
Allow thirty minutes over low heat. The pearls are ready when only a tiny white dot remains at the centre.
That dot disappears as they cool: waiting for it to go on the heat gives porridge.
Make a custard with the milk, yolks and vanilla, and serve the sagu very cold with the cream alongside.

ovelha-no-buraco.d: A whole sheep cooked twelve hours in a pit dug in the ground. The Campo Mourão festival cooks several hundred each year; the technique comes from the indigenous peoples of Paraná, the sheep arrived with settlers.
s: Dig a pit a metre deep and burn hardwood in it for four hours, until you have a thick bed of coals.
Marinate the sheep twelve hours in white wine, garlic, rosemary and coarse salt.
Wrap it entirely in banana leaves, then in wet hessian, in several tight layers.
Set it on the coals, cover with sheet metal then with all the earth removed, and seal every crack: the least draught makes it flare and burns the meat.
Reopen twelve hours later. The meat falls from the bone by itself; serve with cassava cooked under the same earth.

matambre-recheado.p: Santana do Livramento, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
matambre-recheado.d: The flat muscle between hide and ribs, stuffed, rolled and braised. Its name comes from mata hambre, hunger-killer: it was the cut the gaucho grilled first while butchering, because it cooks quickly.
s: Trim the matambre, removing the outer membrane and excess fat, then flatten it with a mallet to 1.5 cm.
Marinate it overnight in white wine, garlic and parsley: this meat is fibrous and the marinade genuinely tenderises it.
Spread the filling — blanched spinach, carrot batons, peppers, whole hard-boiled eggs lined up along the axis.
Roll tightly with the grain, never across it: rolled the other way, it tears when sliced.
Tie every three centimetres and braise two hours in stock at 160°C. Cool before slicing.

pinhao-na-chapa.p: Gramado, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
pinhao-na-chapa.d: Araucaria pine nuts boiled then griddled, eaten by hand in winter. They are sold in the streets of the Serra during the cold season, in newspaper cones, and the shell is opened with the teeth.
s: Nick the tip of each nut with a knife: without that cut they burst noisily on the griddle.
Boil them forty minutes in heavily salted water — the salt in the water seasons them, since the shell is impermeable afterwards.
Drain them and let them dry ten minutes in the air.
Pass them over a very hot cast-iron plate with a knob of butter, ten minutes, tossing them.
The shell should blacken in places and split slightly. Serve scalding, in paper, to open yourself.

causa-limena.d: A cold terrine of yellow potato purée with chilli, layered with a filling. Peru has more than three thousand potato varieties; causa accepts only the papa amarilla, whose floury flesh works like a dough.
s: Cook the potatoes whole in their skins in salted water, and peel them scalding hot.
Rice them at once: cooled, the starch retrogrades and the purée turns grainy and impossible to smooth.
Work it by hand with the yellow chilli, lime and oil for ten minutes, until it turns elastic like a dough.
Layer it in a ring: purée, chicken in mayonnaise, avocado, purée, pressing at each level.
Chill four hours before unmoulding. Warm, causa collapses the moment the ring comes off.

pachamanca.d: Meats and tubers cooked underground on heated stones, in the Andes. The name comes from Quechua pacha, earth, and manka, pot: the earth itself is the vessel, and the technique predates the Incas.
s: Heat volcanic stones in a wood fire for three hours, until they are white with heat.
Marinate the meats overnight in pounded huacatay, panca chilli, garlic, cumin and chicha.
Huacatay is an Andean black mint with no equivalent: it gives pachamanca its unmistakable scent.
Layer stones, meats, tubers and beans alternately, each layer separated by scalding stones and herbs.
Cover with leaves, wet cloth then earth and cook three hours without ever opening it.

cuy-chactado.d: A whole guinea pig, flattened under a stone and pan-fried. Cuy has been raised in the Andes for five thousand years; it is festive meat, served at baptisms and weddings, and the stone that presses it gives the dish its name.
s: Scald the animal for a minute to remove the hair, gut it and rinse it thoroughly in acidulated water.
Open it flat by splitting the belly and spreading the ribs, then break the leg bones so it lies truly flat.
Marinate two hours in garlic, cumin and panca chilli pounded together.
Flour it with corn flour and fry it in a pan under a heavy flat stone, ten minutes a side.
The stone ensures full contact with the pan: without it the cuy curls and only part of the skin crisps.

arroz-con-pollo-peruano.d: Green rice, coloured with blended coriander, cooked with chicken and beer. The green sets the Peruvian version apart from every other in Latin America: it comes from several bunches of coriander put through a blender, not a herb added at the end.
s: Blend the whole coriander, stems included, with the spinach and a little water, to a deep green purée.
The spinach is only there to fix the colour: without it the green turns khaki as soon as the rice cooks.
Brown the chicken, remove it, then make the aderezo — onion, garlic and yellow chilli melted at length, a good ten minutes.
Add the green purée, beer and stock, bring to the boil and check the salt before adding the rice.
Cook 20 minutes covered with the chicken on top, then rest ten minutes off the heat.

carapulcra.d: A pork stew with dried potato, thickened with peanuts. Papa seca is a pre-Columbian invention: potato boiled, peeled, cut and sun-dried, which keeps it for years and gives it a nutty taste the fresh tuber does not have.
s: Toast the papa seca dry in a pan until it browns slightly, then soak it eight hours.
That prior toasting is what makes carapulcra: without it the dish stays pale and shallow.
Brown the diced pork, set it aside, and make the aderezo of onion, garlic, cumin and panca chilli, fifteen minutes.
Return the meat, add the drained papa seca, wine and stock, and simmer an hour.
Finish with pounded peanuts and a square of dark chocolate, which rounds the chilli's acidity without being tasted.

chuno-cola.d: A thick soup of freeze-dried potato, meat and rice. Chuño is made on the altiplano by exposing potatoes to night frost and day sun for a week, treading them underfoot: the oldest known freeze-drying.
s: Soak the chuño eight hours, changing the water three times: the bitterness must come out, and one change will not do.
Rub it between your hands to remove the remaining black skins, then crush it roughly in a mortar.
Boil the meat two hours, skimming, until it falls from the bone.
Add the chuño, rice and vegetables, and thicken forty minutes, stirring regularly.
The soup should stand on a spoon. Serve with crumbled fresh cheese and oregano crushed between the fingers.

picarones.d: Fried rings of squash and sweet potato dough, drenched in chancaca syrup. They descend from Spanish buñuelos, which Afro-Peruvian cooks remade with local tubers when wheat flour was scarce.
s: Cook the squash and sweet potato in water scented with anise and cinnamon, and mash them hot.
Keep that cooking water: it hydrates the dough, and plain water would give bland picarones.
Mix the yeast, flour and purées and prove two hours — the dough should turn sticky and full of bubbles.
Wet your hand, take a handful of dough and pierce it with your thumb over oil at 180°C, letting it drop.
That gesture makes the picarón, and it takes practice. Drench with chancaca syrup reduced with citrus and spices.

alfajores-peruanos.d: Two very short biscuits joined with manjar blanco and rolled in icing sugar. The name comes from Arabic al-hasú, the stuffed one, which reached Spain with the Moors and America with the Spanish: three continents in one biscuit.
s: The proportion of cornflour makes the alfajor: it develops no gluten and gives that texture that melts without resistance.
Cream the butter and icing sugar at length, then beat in the yolks one at a time and the sifted flours.
Do not knead — gather the dough by hand and rest it an hour in the cold.
Roll to 6 mm, cut out and bake 12 minutes at 170°C: the biscuits should stay pale, barely coloured at the edge.
Cool completely before filling. Warm, they break at the slightest touch.

suspiro-a-la-limena.d: A caramelised milk cream topped with a port meringue. The poet José Gálvez named it in the nineteenth century, calling it soft and light as a woman's sigh; his own wife had invented it.
s: Reduce the two milks over low heat for forty minutes, stirring without pause, until the cream browns and coats the spoon.
Off the heat, beat in the yolks in a stream, whisking — poured into boiling cream they coagulate into lumps.
Divide into glasses and cool completely, at least two hours.
Make a syrup of sugar and port cooked to 118°C, then pour it in a stream onto the whipped whites, whisking without pause.
Whisk until completely cool — the meringue must be firm and glossy. Pipe on top and dust with cinnamon.

pisco-sour.d: A cocktail of pisco, lime and egg white, crowned with a dense foam. Pisco is a grape spirit never aged in wood, distilled once and never cut with water: Peruvian law forbids any addition, even sugar.
s: Squeeze the limes by hand and use the juice within the hour: after that it oxidises and turns frankly bitter.
Begin with a dry shake, without ice, for ten seconds: that is what lifts the egg white and makes the whole foam.
Then add ice and shake hard for fifteen seconds more, until the shaker frosts.
Strain into a chilled glass and let the foam settle for half a minute.
Drop three dashes of bitters onto the foam. They should not be stirred in: their scent is met by the nose, before the first sip.

chicha-morada.d: An infusion of purple corn with fruit and spices, drunk iced and without alcohol. Morado corn takes its colour from anthocyanins, which it concentrates more than any other known plant; it has been grown in the Andes for at least two thousand years.
s: Use the whole cobs, core included: the core carries most of the pigment, and stripping the kernels throws the colour away.
Boil with the pineapple skins, apple cores, cinnamon and cloves for an hour.
Strain without pressing and cool completely before sweetening — hot, the drink always tastes less sweet than it is.
Add the lime only once cold: hot, the acid degrades the pigment and the colour turns brown.
Serve very cold, with diced pineapple and apple. Keeps three days in the refrigerator.

changua.d: A milk soup with a whole poached egg, eaten at breakfast on the altiplano. At 2,600 metres Bogotá mornings are cold all year: changua is a breakfast soup by climatic necessity as much as by tradition.
s: Bring equal parts water and milk to the boil with the sliced spring onions and a good pinch of salt.
The half water is not an economy: pure milk boils over and splits on contact with the egg.
Lower the heat to a tremble, then break the eggs straight into the liquid, keeping them whole.
Poach exactly three minutes: the white should be set and the yolk still entirely runny.
Put the stale bread in the bottom of the bowl, pour the soup and egg over it and scatter coriander and fresh cheese.

oblea.d: Two very thin wafers joined with arequipe and topped to order. They descend from communion hosts, baked in the same kind of flat iron; street vendors now offer half a menu of sweet fillings.
s: Whisk the flour, water, sugar, oil and salt into a very thin batter, looser than a pancake batter.
Strain it and rest it an hour: lumps, invisible raw, leave holes in the wafer.
Pour a thin ladleful onto a scalding flat iron, close it and cook a minute a side.
The wafer should stay white and dry, barely amber at the edges; browned, it turns bitter and brittle.
Stack them flat as they cool, never in a curved pile — they warp as they harden. Fill as you serve.

arequipe.d: Colombia's milk jam, paler and less sweet than Argentine dulce de leche. It is made over an open flame in copper cauldrons, whose ions catalyse the browning: the same milk in a steel pan takes an hour longer and stays paler.
s: Use a wide, heavy pan, in untinned copper if possible: the evaporating surface matters more than the capacity.
Bring the milk and sugar to the boil, stirring until fully dissolved, then add the bicarbonate.
It stops the milk curdling and speeds the Maillard reaction, the one that gives colour and caramel flavour.
Reduce over medium heat for two and a half hours, stirring every five minutes and without pause towards the end.
Stop when a drop on a cold plate holds its shape. Arequipe thickens a great deal more as it cools.

cazabe.d: A dry flatbread of bitter cassava, with no leavening and no fat, that keeps for months. It is the bread of the Taíno that Columbus described on his first voyage; it has scarcely changed since, technique included.
s: Peel and grate the bitter cassava very finely, working in the open air: the fresh pulp gives off hydrocyanic acid.
Press the pulp in a cloth or press until it is frankly dry and crumbly.
That juice is toxic and is thrown away; it is the pressing, not the cooking, that makes bitter cassava edible.
Sieve the pulp to a fine, even semolina, free of lumps.
Spread it in a 5 mm disc on a scalding plate and cook five minutes a side, with no fat. The disc binds itself through the starch.

cuchuco-de-trigo.d: A thick soup of cracked wheat, pork ribs and greens. Cuchuco is wheat broken into coarse fragments, inherited from the cereals brought by the Spanish and adopted by Boyacá farmers as a substitute for Andean corn.
s: Soak the cracked wheat two hours: without soaking it needs an extra hour and cooks unevenly.
Boil the pork ribs an hour and a half, skimming, until they fall from the bone.
Add the drained wheat and cook forty minutes, stirring regularly — it catches the moment you forget it.
Add the potatoes, broad beans and peas, and continue twenty minutes.
Throw in the shredded spinach in the last three minutes only, so it stays green and does not collapse.

viudo-de-pescado.d: River fish steamed on a bed of tubers, in the open air. Viudo means widower: the fish is cooked with no sauce or liquid accompaniment, alone with the vegetables, and fishermen make it on the riverbank in a pot set on three stones.
s: Gut and scale the fish, score them and rub them with lime, garlic and cumin half an hour ahead.
Line the pot with plantain leaves or thick stems: that is what stops the tubers burning, since there is almost no water.
Lay in the tubers and corn in a thick layer, pour in one glass of water only, and cover.
Set the whole fish on top, add the tomato and onion hogao, and seal tightly.
Cook forty minutes without ever lifting the lid: all the cooking is done by the vegetables' own steam.

caldo-de-piedra.d: A fish soup cooked in seconds by a white-hot river stone plunged into a gourd. Among the Chinantec only men prepare it, and the gesture is as old as the village.
s: Heat smooth river stones in a wood fire for two hours, until they glow red.
Cut the fish into large pieces and peel the prawns; on no account cook them in advance.
Divide between gourds the raw fish, prawns, tomato, onion, garlic, chilli and herbs.
Pour in cold salted water to cover, then lower in a scorching stone with wooden tongs.
The water erupts into a boil and cooks everything in thirty seconds. Lift out the stone and serve at once with lime.

tlayuda.d: A large dried tortilla, grilled until it cracks, spread with black bean lard and covered in quesillo. It is folded in two over the coals: eaten flat it is a tlayuda; folded, a late-night clayuda.
s: Cook the black beans with epazote, then mash them and reduce them in the lard into a thick black paste, the asiento.
Grill the cecina and chorizo over the coals and cut them into pieces.
Lay the large tortilla on the grill and spread it with asiento as it heats.
Add the shredded quesillo and let it melt: the tortilla should crisp without burning, about 4 minutes.
Crown with finely shredded cabbage, meat, tomato, avocado and a pasilla chilli salsa. Fold in two and eat by hand.

papadzules.d: Tortillas rolled around hard-boiled egg, cloaked in a green pumpkin-seed sauce with its separated pepita oil. The Maya name is said to mean 'food of the lords'; the dish predates the conquest.
s: Toast the pumpkin seeds dry without letting them brown, then grind them very finely.
Infuse the epazote in half a litre of hot salted water, and strain.
Work the seed powder with this warm water, kneading by hand: the green oil separates and rises. Spoon it off.
Make a tomato sauce with the onion, garlic and whole habanero, and pass it through a sieve.
Dip each tortilla in the seed paste, roll it around chopped hard-boiled egg, cloak with tomato sauce and drizzle over the reserved green oil.

chiles-en-nogada.d: A poblano chilli stuffed with meat and fruit, cloaked in a fresh walnut cream and scattered with pomegranate. Green, white, red: the colours of the flag. It is served only in August and September, when the walnut is milky.
s: Char the poblanos over a flame until the skin blisters, close them in a bag for 10 minutes, then peel and empty them through a slit.
Make the picadillo: fry onion and garlic, add the meats, the tomato, then the diced fruit, raisins, almonds and cinnamon. Cook down for 30 minutes.
Peel the fresh walnuts one by one, removing the thin bitter skin: it is slow, and it is essential.
Blend them with the fresh cheese, cream and sherry, without sugar: the nogada must stay a frank white.
Stuff the chillies, cloak them in cold nogada and scatter pomegranate seeds and parsley. Never reheat.

birria-de-res.d: A beef stew with guajillo chillies and cinnamon, whose red broth is used to dip the tacos. Birria once meant 'worthless thing': the colonists scorned goat, and Mexicans made a masterpiece of it.
s: Toast the chillies dry for 30 seconds a side — no more, or they turn bitter — and soak them for 30 minutes.
Blend them with the tomato, garlic, spices and vinegar into a smooth sauce, and pass it through a sieve.
Rub it over the meat and marinate for 6 hours.
Cook for 3 hours covered, with water halfway up and the bay, until the meat falls apart.
Shred the meat and skim the broth, keeping the red oil from the top: it is what the filled tortillas are fried in before being dipped in the consommé.

machaca-con-huevo.d: Sun-dried beef pounded until fluffy, fried with eggs and a pico de gallo. Machacar means 'to pound': in the northern desert the dried meat was beaten with a stone to tenderise it.
s: Soak the dried beef in warm water for 15 minutes, squeeze it dry, then pound it in a mortar until it falls into strands.
Toast it dry in a very hot pan to rehydrate it and concentrate its flavour.
Add the oil, onion, garlic and serrano chilli, and soften for 4 minutes.
Add the crushed tomato and let it evaporate completely: moisture would make the eggs runny.
Pour in the beaten eggs and scramble over low heat, barely setting them. Serve in flour tortillas.

kak-ik.d: A vivid red Q'eqchi' turkey soup with cobanero chilli and annatto. The name comes from kak, red, and ik, chilli; a Maya ceremonial dish declared Guatemalan national heritage.
s: Cook the jointed turkey for 1 hour in three litres of water with the onion and garlic; keep the broth.
Char the chillies, tomatoes and tomatillos dry on a griddle, until they blacken in patches.
Blend them with the annatto and a ladle of broth, then pass through a fine sieve.
Cook this purée for 20 minutes over low heat, stirring, then stir it into the broth.
Return the turkey, add the coriander and mint ten minutes before the end, and serve with tamalitos or rice.

sopa-de-caracol.d: A Garifuna conch soup with coconut milk, cassava and green plantain. It travelled the world in 1991 on a Banda Blanca song, and many know the chorus without knowing the dish.
s: Beat the conch with a mallet to tenderise it, then cut it into strips and rub it with lime.
Fry the onion, garlic and annatto in the oil, and add the cumin.
Add a litre of water with the cassava, the green plantain broken by hand and the carrot.
Cook for 30 minutes, then pour in the coconut milk and let it steam without boiling.
Add the conch for 8 minutes only: overcooked it turns to rubber. Coriander and lime off the heat.

olla-de-carne.d: A Costa Rican boiled dinner with seven different roots, cooked for three hours on Sundays. The broth is drunk first from a cup, before the meat and vegetables come to the table.
s: Cook the shank on the bone for 2 hours in four litres of water, with the onion and garlic, skimming regularly.
The collagen from the bone is essential: without it the broth stays thin and flat.
Add the roots in order of firmness — cassava, yautía, sweet potato — at twenty-minute intervals.
Finish with the squash, chayote, corn and plantain, which need 20 minutes.
Serve the broth in a cup first, then meat and vegetables in a deep plate, with rice and lime.

tamal-en-cazuela.d: The Cuban tamal freed from its husk: fresh corn and pork cooked together in a pot, like polenta. It was invented out of frank laziness, and nobody in Havana apologises for it.
s: Marinate the diced pork for 2 hours in sour orange, garlic, cumin and oregano.
Render the bacon, sear the pork, then lift it out and make the sofrito: onion, pepper, garlic, tomato, 20 minutes.
Grate the fresh corn and blend it with the maize flour and a litre of water; sieve to remove the fibres.
Pour this cream into the sofrito and cook for 45 minutes over low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon.
Return the pork for the last 20 minutes. The cazuela is ready when the spoon stands up in the middle.

arroz-con-gandules.d: Puerto Rico's national rice, with pigeon peas and sofrito, prized for its caramelised bottom crust, the pegao. Serving rice with no pegao is taken as an admission of clumsiness: it is scraped up and fought over.
s: Render the salt pork and smoked ham in a cast-iron caldero, until they crisp.
Add the sofrito and annatto, and fry for 5 minutes: the fat should turn orange.
Add the tomato sauce, olives, capers and spices, then the drained pigeon peas.
Pour in the rice and water to one centimetre above it, and never stir after that moment.
Let it evaporate uncovered, then cover for 20 minutes over very low heat. Raise the heat for 2 minutes at the end to form the pegao.

soup-joumou.d: A pumpkin and beef soup drunk every 1 January. Under the colony it was forbidden to the enslaved; independence in 1804 made it the symbol of freedom regained, and UNESCO listed it in 2021.
s: Wash the meat with lime, as custom requires, then marinate it for 4 hours in epis.
Cook it for 1 hour with the thyme, cloves and whole chilli; keep the broth.
Boil the pumpkin in pieces until it collapses, then blend it with its water into a smooth cream.
Combine the purée and the broth, add the vegetables in order of firmness and give them 30 minutes.
Add the vermicelli for the last eight minutes. The soup should coat the spoon without being thick.

sancocho-dominicano.d: A thick soup of seven meats and seven root vegetables, served on great occasions. Each meat goes in at its own moment; a cook who adds them all at once is shown the door.
s: Marinate each meat separately in sour orange, garlic and oregano for 2 hours.
Sear them one after another in the pot, starting with the goat and beef, which take longest.
Add five litres of water and simmer for 1 hour before adding pork, chicken and sausage.
Add the roots in order of firmness: yam, yautía, cassava, then plantain and squash.
Crush a little squash and plantain against the side to thicken the soup. Serve with white rice and avocado.

pelau.p: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
pelau.d: Chicken caramelised in burnt sugar, then cooked with rice, pigeon peas and coconut milk. The sugar must blacken and smoke before the meat goes in: the gesture that defines the whole dish.
s: Marinate the chicken for 4 hours in green seasoning, the Trinidadian herb and garlic paste.
Heat the oil and brown sugar in a heavy pot, without stirring, until the caramel smokes and blackens.
Drop the chicken in at once and stir to coat: it should take on a mahogany colour.
Add onion, carrot, squash, pigeon peas, thyme and ketchup, then the rinsed rice.
Pour in the coconut milk and water to one centimetre above the rice, set the whole chilli on top, cover and cook for 25 minutes.

bokit.d: A flatbread fried until it puffs, split and filled like a sandwich. It descends from the North American johnny cake by way of the English-speaking Caribbean; the name is said to come from bake it, and it is now sold from vans along the roads.
s: Knead the flour, baking powder, salt and water for five minutes only: overworked, the dough turns elastic and stops puffing.
Rest it an hour under a damp cloth, so the gluten relaxes.
Roll discs 15 cm across and 5 mm thick, evenly: uneven thickness gives a bread that puffs on one side only.
Slide into oil at 180°C; the disc should rise and balloon within seconds, spoon oil over it.
Drain, split it horizontally and fill with flaked salt cod, salad and chilli.

matoutou-de-crabes.d: Rice with land crabs, the obligatory Easter Monday dish in the French Antilles. The crabs are caught alive during Lent and fattened for several weeks on chilli and coconut in cages, to purge their flesh.
s: Scald the live crabs for a minute, then scrub them at length under water and remove the gills and sand sac.
Crack the claws with the back of a knife so the broth penetrates and the meat can be eaten without tools.
Marinate them two hours in lime, crushed garlic and chilli, in a non-metallic dish.
Fry the aromatics, add the crabs and let them give up their water for twenty minutes, covered.
Tip the dry rice over them, moisten with one and a half times its volume and cook 20 minutes without stirring. Eaten with the hands.

tourment-damour.d: A small tartlet of coconut jam covered with sponge. The women of Les Saintes made them for the return of fishermen gone several days: the torment was the waiting, and the cake the reward for coming home.
s: Rub the flour and cold butter together with your fingertips, bind with iced water and rest an hour in the cold.
Cook the grated coconut with the sugar, vanilla and a little water for twenty minutes, until the jam pulls from the base.
Scent it with rum off the heat, never during cooking: the alcohol would flash off and leave nothing.
Line tartlet tins, fill only two-thirds with jam — it swells and would overflow.
Cover with a spoonful of sponge batter and bake 30 minutes at 180°C, until the top browns and domes.

sorbet-coco-guadeloupe.d: Coconut ice churned by hand in a wooden bucket packed with crushed ice. Vendors make it in front of you on the beach, turning the crank for twenty minutes: the grainy texture that results is precisely the point.
s: Infuse the split vanilla and cinnamon in hot milk for half an hour, then cool completely.
Mix with the coconut milk, grated coconut and sugar, and taste: it should seem slightly too sweet, cold dulls perception by a third.
Pour into the inner bucket and pack it in crushed ice mixed with coarse salt.
The salt lowers the melting point of the ice to -18°C: without it the ice melts at zero and nothing sets.
Turn the crank without pause for twenty minutes, scraping the sides. Serve at once, it does not keep.

dombres-aux-ouassous.d: Small flour dumplings poached in a sauce of river crayfish. The ouassou takes its name from king of the springs; it is a large freshwater prawn that climbs the rivers of Basse-Terre and is caught in traps.
s: Knead the flour, salt and water to a firm dough, then rest it thirty minutes.
Roll marble-sized balls between your palms; any larger and they stay raw at the centre.
Fry the aromatics, add the shelled ouassous, tomato and water, and bring to a tremble.
Drop the dombrés into simmering liquid, never boiling: at a hard boil they disintegrate and cloud the sauce.
Twenty minutes' cooking, they rise to the surface when done. Adjust with lime and chilli.

bebele.d: The emblematic dish of Marie-Galante: tripe, green bananas, breadfruit and dumplings in one broth. It is made for great occasions and simmers a whole morning; the name is said to come from a West African word for a mixture.
s: Clean the tripe with lime and coarse salt, rubbing, then rinse it and blanch it twenty minutes.
Throw away that first water: it carries off the strong smell, and keeping it would spoil the whole broth.
Cook the tripe two hours with the pork tail, garlic, thyme and cloves.
Add the peeled green bananas and breadfruit in large pieces, and continue forty minutes.
Finish with hand-rolled dumplings, twenty minutes at a tremble. The broth should be thick and cloudy.

gratin-de-christophine.d: A chayote gratin with béchamel, mild and faintly sweet. The chayote came from Mexico with the Spanish; its very neutral flavour makes it a perfect vehicle for béchamel, and it is the Sunday gratin of the Antilles.
s: Boil the chayotes whole in salted water for thirty minutes, until a knife passes through without resistance.
Halve them, remove the flat central stone and scoop out the flesh without piercing the skin.
Drain that flesh in a sieve for a quarter hour, pressing: chayote is very watery and would soak the gratin.
Make a thick béchamel, well nutmegged, and mix it with the crushed flesh and softened onion.
Fill the half shells, cover with gruyère and breadcrumbs and bake 25 minutes at 200°C.

feroce-davocat.d: A purée of avocado, grilled salt cod and cassava flour, fiercely spiced. That is where the name comes from: fierce as the chilli, and the cassava flour absorbs enough fat that it can be rolled into balls and eaten with the hands.
s: Desalt the cod twelve hours, changing the water three times, then grill it over a flame or in the oven until it colours.
The grilling is not optional: it gives the féroce its smoky taste, and merely poached cod makes it bland.
Flake it finely, removing skin and bones.
Crush the avocados with a fork with lime, crushed garlic and plenty of chilli — never in a blender, the texture must stay coarse.
Work in the cassava flour little by little until the mass rolls into balls that hold in the hand.

flan-coco-antillais.d: A coconut-milk flan with caramel, baked in a water bath. It owes the caramel to the Spanish flan and the coconut and local vanilla to Antillean cooking; it is served chilled, which its coconut fat allows without hardening.
s: Make a dry caramel with the sugar, no water and no spoon: tilt the pan, never stir.
Pour it scalding into the mould and swirl it at once — ten seconds cold and it no longer spreads.
Beat the whole eggs without frothing them: bubbles would rise and pit the flan's surface.
Mix the coconut milk, condensed milk, scraped vanilla and rum, then strain to remove the chalazae.
Bake in a water bath 60 minutes at 160°C; the flan should still tremble at the centre. Chill twelve hours before turning out.

chiquetaille-de-morue.d: Salt cod grilled then torn by hand, marinated with onion, lime and chilli. Chiquetailler means to tear to pieces in Creole: the fish is pulled apart with the fingers and never cut, the fibres having to stay long.
s: Desalt the cod twelve hours, changing the water four times, and taste a fragment before going further.
Grill it over coals or under a grill until the skin blackens in places and the flesh cracks.
Tear it into long threads with your fingers, removing skin and bones as you go.
Slice the onions very thinly and salt them for ten minutes before rinsing — raw, they overpower everything.
Mix everything with oil, lime and chilli, and marinate two hours in the cold. Served cold, on bread.

lambi-martiniquais.d: The great Caribbean mollusc, long simmered until tender. Conch is now protected and its fishing regulated: it grows slowly, and Antillean reefs were nearly emptied of it in the 1980s.
s: Beat the flesh with a mallet until visibly tenderised: it is a very dense muscle, and without this two hours' cooking will not do.
Rub it with lime and coarse salt to remove the mucus, then rinse thoroughly.
Cut into even pieces and blanch them ten minutes; discard that water.
Fry the aromatics, return the conch, moisten with white wine and water, and simmer two hours covered.
Test with a fork before serving: depending on the animal's age, another thirty minutes is sometimes needed.

ti-punch.d: Agricultural rum, cane sugar and a twist of lime, with no ice and no water. Martinique's rhum agricole is distilled from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, the only rum in the world with an AOC, granted in 1996.
s: Use a white rhum agricole at 50 or 55 degrees: a molasses rum gives a heavy, sweet drink, something else entirely.
Cut a piece of lime peel with a little flesh, never a whole slice — the juice would make the punch sour.
Barely crush the peel against the bottom of the glass with the lélé stick, to release the oils without bitterness.
Pour in the cane syrup then the rum, and stir slowly for a few seconds.
Add no ice: it would dilute and chill the rum, whose aromas only open at room temperature.

planteur-martiniquais.d: A fruit-juice punch, long macerated with rum and spices. The Caribbean mnemonic runs: one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak — the proportions are still remembered that way.
s: Use pressed juices or at least ones with no added sugar: commercial nectars unbalance everything and make the punch cloying.
Infuse the cinnamon, split vanilla and grated nutmeg in the rum for twenty-four hours.
This prior infusion changes everything: added at the last moment, spices stay on the surface and scent nothing.
Mix the juices, cane syrup and infused rum, and taste before adjusting the acidity with lime.
Rest in the cold at least six hours. Serve over ice, with fresh grated nutmeg.

blanc-manger-coco.d: A coconut cream set with agar or gelatine, turned out as a ring. Blancmange is a medieval European dessert that the Antilles remade with coconut milk: the Creole version has entirely displaced the almond original.
s: Heat the coconut milk with the split vanilla and cinnamon without ever boiling it: boiled, it splits and releases its oil.
Slake the agar in a little cold milk before adding it, or it forms grains that never dissolve.
Bring to a tremble for exactly one minute: agar needs 90°C to activate, but no more.
Add the condensed milk and rum off the heat, and strain.
Pour into a wetted ring mould and chill four hours. Agar sets at room temperature, but cold refines the texture.

accras-de-crevettes.d: Fritters of chopped shrimp, more delicate than the salt-cod kind. The word accra comes from the Yoruba akara, a West African bean fritter; the crossing replaced the bean with flour and fish.
s: Shell the shrimp and chop them coarsely by knife: blended, they release their water and the batter goes thin.
Make the batter with flour, eggs, milk and baking powder, and rest it an hour — resting gives light fritters.
Fold in the shrimp, chopped herbs and chilli just before frying, never in advance.
Heat the oil to exactly 175°C: hotter, the outside browns before the centre cooks.
Drop by teaspoonfuls and fry three minutes, turning once. Drain on paper and serve scalding.

boudin-creole.d: A blood sausage with soaked bread, heavily seasoned with chilli and herbs. It is eaten as an appetiser with accras, cut into short lengths, and together they form the obligatory opening of any Antillean meal.
s: Beat the blood as soon as it is collected and strain it through muslin to remove clots — a single clot will burst the casing.
Soak the stale bread in the milk, press it out and crumble it.
Chop the onions, chives, garlic, thyme and chilli very finely: Creole boudin is marked by the quantity of herbs, almost as much as blood.
Mix everything, taste by frying a spoonful, and adjust before filling.
Fill the casings only three-quarters full and poach at 80°C for twenty minutes, never letting it boil.

pimentade-de-poisson.d: A fish court-bouillon with annatto and chilli, deeply red. Annatto comes from Amerindian urucum, a seed whose pulp colours with almost no flavour; the Wayana painted their bodies with it long before it entered the kitchen.
s: Marinate the fish steaks half an hour in lime, garlic and salt.
Infuse the annatto in hot oil over low heat for five minutes, then strain: the oil turns bright orange and it is the oil that colours, not the seed.
Do not let the annatto burn — a few seconds too long and it turns bitter brown.
Fry onions, tomatoes and chilli in the coloured oil, and moisten with boiling water.
Poach the fish ten minutes in this simmering broth, without stirring. Serve with white rice.

riz-colle-guyanais.d: Rice cooked with red beans and coconut milk until the grains bind together. It is made throughout the Caribbean under different names; in Guiana it accompanies smoked fish and is served at All Saints.
s: Soak the red beans overnight, then cook them an hour in their water with the thyme and cloves.
Keep that cooking water: it gives the rice its brown colour and its flavour, and throwing it away is the commonest mistake.
Render the bacon, add onions and garlic, then the rice, pearled for two minutes.
Moisten with the bean water made up with coconut milk, add the beans and the whole unpierced chilli.
Cook 20 minutes covered over very low heat, without stirring. Remove the chilli before serving.

couac.d: A semolina of bitter cassava, grated, pressed then toasted, the staple of Amerindian Guiana. Bitter cassava is toxic raw: the traditional woven press, the couleuvre, squeezes out the cyanogenic juice before cooking.
s: Peel and grate the bitter cassava very finely — grating releases the enzymes that destroy the cyanogenic compounds.
Pack the pulp into the couleuvre, a long tube of flexible basketry, and hang it, pulling downwards.
The tube lengthens and tightens, and the toxic juice runs out: let it press for several hours, until the pulp is dry.
Sieve the pulp to aerate it, then toast it on a scalding plate, stirring without pause, for a full hour.
Couac is ready when golden, dry and crisp. It keeps for months and is eaten with everything.

wassai-bowl.d: The pulp of wassaï, Guiana's açaí, served savoury with couac and fish. Wassaï is picked from a twenty-metre palm climbed barefoot with a liana loop; the pulp oxidises within hours and must be worked the same day.
s: Soak the wassaï berries in warm water for half an hour: the pulp is a thin film around a large stone and will not come away cold.
Rub them by hand in the water until the pulp releases, then strain and discard the stones.
Do not sweeten: in Guiana wassaï is savoury, and serving it as a frozen dessert is a foreign habit.
Flake the smoked fish and mix it with the chives and chilli.
Serve the pulp barely cool, with the fish and couac to dust over it yourself.

kalawang.d: A Wayãpi fish soup with reduced cassava juice, brown and thick. The bitter cassava juice, toxic raw, becomes harmless after long boiling: reduced for hours it gives a dark, smoky sauce also known as black tucupi.
s: Collect the pressed juice of bitter cassava and let it settle: the starch falls to the bottom and is kept separately.
Boil the juice uncovered for at least two hours — that prolonged boiling is what makes it edible, and there is no shortcut.
It reduces by half, browns and takes on a syrupy body and a smoky taste.
Add the whole chillies and give it another twenty minutes, then the fish in pieces.
Ten minutes' poaching is enough. Serve with couac, dipped into the sauce.

punch-coco-guyanais.d: A creamy liqueur of coconut milk, condensed milk and rum, served iced at Christmas. Every Guianese family has its own proportions and keeps them; bottles are exchanged as gifts throughout December.
s: Warm the coconut milk gently with the split vanilla and cinnamon, without boiling, then infuse for an hour.
Strain and whisk into the condensed and evaporated milks, until perfectly smooth.
Cool completely before adding the rum: poured into hot liquid it partly evaporates and the punch loses its strength.
Add grated nutmeg and a twist of lime, and bottle.
Rest a week in the cold, shaking daily. It keeps for months and improves.

samoussas-reunionnais.d: Small fried triangles with a spiced filling, the island's universal appetiser. They arrived with nineteenth-century Indian indentured workers but have shrunk considerably: the Réunion samosa is a single mouthful, against three or four for the Indian.
s: Knead a firm dough, roll it very thin and cut 5 cm strips; oil them and stack them before briefly cooking them dry.
This pre-cooking of the strips is what gives the fineness: fried raw, they thicken and turn brittle.
Fry the meat with onion, garlic, ginger and spices until dry — a wet filling unsticks the pastry in the fryer.
Fold into triangles by turning the strip on itself, and seal with a flour-and-water paste.
Fry at 170°C for three minutes, until evenly golden. Eaten scalding.

bonbon-piment.d: Fritters of Cape peas or lentils, sharply spiced, sold at the open-air market. They descend from the Indian vada and are eaten warm, often slipped into a roll, while waiting for a meal.
s: Soak the peas twelve hours: they should snap cleanly under a nail without being soft.
Drain them perfectly and grind them without adding water — this is the crucial point, water stops the paste holding.
The paste must stay grainy: too smooth, and the fritters turn compact instead of airy.
Mix in the spices, onion, garlic and finely chopped chilli, and rest an hour.
Shape balls with a spoon and fry at 170°C for four minutes, until they rise and colour.

achards-de-legumes.d: Vegetables cut into fine batons, blanched and preserved in turmeric oil. The word comes from Persian achar by way of India; on Réunion achard is not a condiment but an entrée in its own right, served in bowls.
s: Cut all the vegetables into batons of the same thickness, fine as matchsticks, so they cook at the same rate.
Blanch them barely thirty seconds in boiling salted water, then plunge them straight into iced water.
This thermal shock fixes the colour and the crunch; without it, achard goes soft within a day.
Drain and dry very thoroughly on a cloth — the least residual water will turn the preparation.
Heat the oil with the turmeric, garlic and ginger, pour it over the vegetables, add the vinegar and macerate overnight.

gateau-patate-douce.d: A dense sweet potato cake without flour, scented with Bourbon vanilla. It is the cake of the inland cirques, where sweet potato grows well and flour was costly; it keeps for days and travels well on a hike.
s: Cook the potatoes whole in their skins, in the oven or steamed: boiled peeled, they take on water and the cake will not set.
Peel them hot and mash them with a ricer, never a blender, which would make the flesh elastic.
Mix in the melted butter, sugar, yolks, scraped vanilla, rum and coconut milk.
Whip the whites and fold them in gently: it is the only thing that lightens a flourless cake.
Bake an hour at 170°C. The cake should stay moist at the centre; it firms as it cools.

rhum-arrange.d: Rum macerated for months with fruit, spices or bark. Every Réunion family keeps its demijohns and its recipes; faham, an orchid endemic to the highlands, gives the most sought-after and hardest to find arrangé.
s: Use a traditional white rum of at least 49 degrees: below that, the maceration clouds and the fruit ferments instead of infusing.
Split the vanilla pods lengthways and scrape them only half out, so the scent releases slowly.
Peel and cut the fruit into large pieces; finely diced, it disintegrates and clouds the arrangé.
Fill the demijohn, cover with rum and add the cane syrup, then seal tightly.
Macerate at least three months away from light, turning the jar weekly. A year is better.

rougail-morue.d: Flaked salt cod stewed with tomato, onion and turmeric. Salt cod reached Réunion on the ships of the Compagnie des Indes, loaded in Newfoundland: a North Atlantic fish that became one of the most Creole dishes there is.
s: Desalt the cod twelve hours, changing the water four times, then poach it ten minutes and flake it.
Fry it alone in hot oil until it browns in places — that colouring is what separates a good rougail from a bland dish.
Melt the onions at length, a good ten minutes, until they turn golden and sweeten.
Add garlic, ginger, turmeric and crushed tomatoes, and reduce twenty minutes uncovered.
Return the cod, fold it in without crushing and give it ten more minutes. Serve with rice and pulses.

carry-bichiques.d: Goby fry caught at river mouths, stewed as a curry. They are called Réunion's caviar: they run only on certain moons, a few weeks a year, and fetch prices above lobster.
s: Rinse the bichiques in clear water with extreme gentleness: they are two-centimetre fry that crush between the fingers.
Do not gut or behead them — they are eaten whole, and that is the whole point.
Make the base massalé: melted onions, garlic, ginger, turmeric and tomatoes, reduced for twenty minutes.
Add the bichiques all at once and do not stir at all; shake the pan if you must.
Five minutes is enough. Overcooked, they collapse into mush and the dish loses its reason to exist.

rougail-dakatine.d: A condiment of peanut paste, tomato and chilli, served alongside the main dish. Dakatine is a peanut butter brand that became a common noun on Réunion, as hoover did elsewhere: no one calls it anything else now.
s: Use unsweetened peanut paste: sweetened peanut butters give a cloying condiment that goes with nothing.
Pound the chilli, salt and ginger in a mortar to a smooth paste — the order matters, the salt acts as an abrasive.
Add the garlic then the onion, continuing to pound, and finally the seeded tomatoes.
Work in the peanut paste little by little, loosening with warm water to the consistency of a thick cream.
Adjust with lime and rest an hour. Served cold, in small quantity, beside a curry.

massale-cabri.d: Goat stewed with massalé, a blend of spices toasted and ground to order. Réunion massalé differs from curry in the toasted coriander that dominates it, and each family has its own ground at the neighbourhood mill.
s: Dry-toast the coriander, cumin, fennel and mustard seeds until they crackle and fill the room, then grind them.
The toasting is what makes massalé: the same spices untoasted give an ordinary curry.
Marinate the goat two hours with half the massalé and the crushed garlic and ginger.
Brown the meat, add the softened onions, the rest of the massalé and the tomatoes, then moisten to cover.
Simmer an hour and a half covered, very gently. Serve with rice, pulses and rougail.

mataba.d: Cassava leaves pounded and stewed in coconut milk, the everyday dish of Mayotte. As in Brazil and central Africa, the pounding and long cooking are what make the leaf edible: raw, it is toxic.
s: Remove the stems and tough ribs, then pound the leaves in a mortar to a uniform green paste.
The pounding is not just texture: it ruptures the cells and releases the enzyme that neutralises the cyanogenic compounds during cooking.
Boil the paste in water for a good hour, skimming, before adding anything else.
Add the desalted dried fish, tomatoes and coconut milk, and give it another thirty minutes.
Mataba is ready when it coats the spoon and has lost all bitterness. Serve with rice.

pilao-mahorais.d: Rice scented with spices and meat, served at Mahoran grand weddings. The manzaraka, the traditional wedding, lasts several days and pilao is cooked there in hundred-litre pots, for whole villages.
s: Brown the sliced onions at great length in the oil, twenty minutes, until they are frankly brown.
That deep caramelisation gives pilao its colour and depth; pale gold onions give a pallid, flat rice.
Add the whole spices and let them crackle thirty seconds before the meat goes in.
Brown the chicken, moisten, cook forty minutes, then remove the meat and measure the broth.
Cook the rice in that broth, one and a half parts to one, twenty minutes covered, with the meat replaced on top.

mkatra-foutra.d: A flatbread with coconut milk, cooked in a pan and scattered with sesame. It accompanies morning tea and is torn by hand; its dough contains rice semolina, which gives a particular grain no wheat flour reproduces.
s: Slake the yeast in warm coconut milk with the sugar and wait fifteen minutes for it to froth.
Mix the two flours and pour in the liquid, whisking: the batter should stay pourable, like a thick pancake batter.
Let it rise an hour and a half somewhere warm, untouched — it covers itself in bubbles.
Pour a ladleful into a buttered pan over low heat, cover and cook eight minutes without turning.
Scatter sesame during cooking. The underside should brown, the top stay pale and honeycombed.

mkatra-sinia.d: A rice cake with coconut milk baked in a large round dish, the sinia. It is made for religious feasts and cut into diamonds; the batter ferments overnight, which gives it a slight acidity and a very open crumb.
s: Slake the rice flour in warm coconut milk with the yeast and sugar, and whisk to a smooth batter.
Ferment eight hours covered at room temperature: that long fermentation gives the flavour, and shortening it gives a flat, dull cake.
Add the beaten eggs, crushed cardamom and vanilla just before baking.
Pour into a large buttered dish, three centimetres deep, and scatter with sesame.
Bake 40 minutes at 180°C. It should be golden and dry on the surface, moist at the centre. Cut into diamonds.

brochettes-de-zebu.d: Cubes of zebu marinated in spices and grilled over charcoal, sold in the evening at the market. Mahoran zebu roams free and its meat is firm and lean: the long marinade is not a refinement but a necessity.
s: Cut the meat into two-centimetre cubes across the grain: with the grain, zebu stays tough even marinated.
Pound the garlic, ginger, chilli and spices with the lime and oil to a paste.
Marinate at least two hours, four for preference, massaging the meat to help it penetrate.
Thread onto skewers, packing the pieces close — spaced out, they dry instead of staying juicy.
Grill over hot coals, three minutes a side, brushing with marinade at each turn.

kakamkou.d: Fish stewed in coconut milk with green bananas and cassava. It is the dish of Mayotte's west coast, where the pirogues come in late morning: the fish is cooked within an hour of landing.
s: Peel the green bananas under water and oil your hands: their latex stains the skin a brown that lasts days.
Cook the bananas and cassava twenty minutes in salted water before adding anything else — they take far longer than the fish.
Fry onion, garlic, ginger and tomato, then pour in the coconut milk.
Never let it boil: at a rolling boil it splits and the oil rises to the surface.
Add the fish steaks and poach ten minutes at a tremble. Lime as you serve.

morue-a-la-saint-pierraise.d: Desalted cod baked with cream, potatoes and onions. The archipelago lived on cod for four centuries; the Canadian moratorium of 1992 ended industrial fishing, and the recipe has become a memory as much as a dish.
s: Desalt the cod twenty-four hours in the refrigerator, skin up, changing the water five times.
Skin up is not a detail: salt sinks, and laid the other way the cod desalts far more slowly.
Poach it ten minutes in bay-scented milk, then flake it into large pieces.
Melt the onions in butter without colouring them and half-cook the sliced potatoes.
Build in layers, coat with cream, cover with gruyère and bake 35 minutes at 190°C.

beignets-de-moules.p: Île aux Marins, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon
beignets-de-moules.d: Archipelago mussels coated in batter and fried, served as an appetiser. Saint-Pierre mussels grow in water at six degrees: they grow slowly and their flesh is denser and more briny than that of temperate Atlantic mussels.
s: Open the mussels in white wine with the shallots, barely two minutes, and take them out as soon as they gape.
Shell them and cool them on a cloth: damp, they make the batter slide off and the fritter comes out bare.
Make a beer batter and rest it an hour — the gas in the beer makes it light and crisp.
Add no salt: the mussels bring enough, and salted batter dries out in the fryer.
Dip and fry at 180°C for two minutes, until the fritters rise and colour. Serve with lemon.

pua-roti-tahitien.n: Pua roti in the Tahitian oven
pua-roti-tahitien.d: A whole pig cooked in the ahima'a, the Tahitian earth oven, on scalding volcanic stones. Porous volcanic rock holds heat for hours without shattering; any other stone would explode from the trapped steam.
s: Dig a metre-deep pit, fill it with wood and volcanic stones, and let it burn for three hours.
The stones must glow red: it is their stored heat that cooks, the fire being out before the food goes in.
Rub the pig with salt, garlic and ginger, and leave it overnight.
Spread banana leaves on the stones, lay in the pig and the root vegetables, cover with leaves then wet sacking and earth.
Four hours later, open it. The meat falls apart by itself; serve with fresh coconut milk.

firifiri.d: A figure-of-eight doughnut with coconut milk, sold at dawn in the markets. The shape is not decorative: it doubles the length of crust for the same quantity of dough, and the doughnut cooks faster and more evenly.
s: Slake the yeast in warm coconut milk with a spoonful of sugar and wait for it to froth.
Knead with the flour, eggs, butter and vanilla for ten minutes, until the dough turns supple and stops sticking.
Rise for an hour and a half, then roll twenty-centimetre ropes and cross them into figures of eight.
Prove a second time for thirty minutes on the floured worktop, without handling them afterwards.
Fry at 170°C, two minutes a side. Roll them warm in sugar and eat them within the hour.

poe-tarua.d: A pudding of fruit and cassava starch, cooked in leaves and topped with coconut milk. Poe varies with the season's fruit — banana, papaya, pumpkin, taro — and is eaten warm, with a spoon, doused in coconut milk pressed the same day.
s: Boil the taro until it crushes, and handle it with gloves: raw, it strongly irritates the skin.
Mash it with the ripe bananas and sugar, to a thick, lump-free purée.
Work in the cassava starch little by little: it is what sets the poe, and there must be enough for the paste to hold on a spoon.
Spread on banana leaves passed through a flame and cook an hour, steamed or in a low oven.
Cool to warm, cut into squares and top with fresh coconut milk, never heated.

chevrettes-vanille.d: Freshwater prawns in coconut cream with Tahitian vanilla. Vanilla tahitensis is not the same species as Madagascar vanilla: more floral and less woody, it stands up to savoury dishes where the other overwhelms them.
s: Shell the prawns keeping the heads and shells, and fry them separately to draw a stock.
Split the vanilla pods and scrape out the seeds; infuse the empty pods in the stock for twenty minutes.
Sweat the shallots in butter, deglaze with white wine and add the strained stock, then reduce by half.
Pour in the coconut milk and cream, add the vanilla seeds and thicken ten minutes without boiling.
Drop the prawns into the sauce and give them exactly three minutes. Beyond that they turn rubbery.

salade-de-benitiers.d: Raw giant clam cut fine, marinated in lime and coconut milk. The giant clam lives in symbiosis with algae lodged in its mantle: it draws part of its food from them, like a coral.
s: Use only live clam bought the same day: raw, it forgives no approximation of freshness.
Detach the muscle and remove the coloured mantle, firmer and bitter, then rinse in seawater or salted water.
Cut into very thin slices across the grain — thick, they stay rubbery however long they marinate.
Marinate twenty minutes in lime alone, until the flesh whitens and firms.
Then add the coconut milk and vegetables, and serve at once. Marinated longer, the flesh hardens.

cerf-saute-caledonien.d: Rusa deer stewed in wine with aromatics, the dish of the Caledonian bush settlers. Rusa deer were introduced from Java in 1870 and multiplied until they became a pest: hunting them is a service to the bush as much as a pleasure at table.
s: Marinate the venison twenty-four hours in red wine with the carrots, onions and juniper.
Drain and blot the meat thoroughly: wet, it boils instead of browning and the sauce stays grey.
Sear it in small batches in the rendered bacon fat, then dust with flour and cook it two minutes.
Moisten with the strained marinade, boiled and skimmed beforehand — unboiled, it gives a raw, harsh taste.
Simmer an hour and a half covered. Serve with sweet potatoes mashed with butter.

gateau-de-manioc-caledonien.d: A dense cake of grated cassava with coconut milk, slowly baked. It is made in the Loyalty Islands tribes for customary feasts and shared in thick slices; with no flour and no raising agent, it holds together entirely on cassava starch.
s: Peel the cassava and remove the woody central thread, which stays hard however long it cooks.
Grate it finely and press it in a cloth to extract the water — but keep that water for an hour.
The starch settles at the bottom; pour off the clear water and recover the white deposit, which goes back into the batter: it is what binds the cake.
Mix cassava, starch, coconut milk, sugar, eggs and melted butter, and pour into a buttered tin.
Bake 70 minutes at 170°C. It should be golden and firm; it slices better the next day.

kava-wallisien.d: A drink of pounded pepper root steeped in cold water, taken at customary ceremonies. Kava is not alcoholic: its kavalactones act on the nervous system and numb the mouth, without ever slurring speech.
s: Use dried root from a plant at least four years old: younger, it holds few kavalactones and the effect is nil.
Pound it at length in a mortar to a coarse, fibrous powder.
Wrap it in a tight-woven cloth and knead it in cold water, squeezing and releasing, for a good quarter hour.
Never use hot water: heat degrades the kavalactones and leaves only a bitter, inert liquid.
Strain, serve in the ceremonial bowl and drink in one draught. The bowl passes in an order fixed by rank.

faikakai-taro-coco.d: Taro dumplings poached in a coconut caramel. Faikakai is the Sunday and village-feast dessert throughout Polynesia; in the older version the caramel is made with no refined sugar, only reduced coconut cream.
s: Boil the taro forty minutes in salted water and mash it hot, wearing gloves, to a smooth purée.
Work in the cassava starch until the paste rolls without sticking to your palms.
Roll walnut-sized balls: any larger and they stay raw at the centre and break up in the caramel.
Reduce the coconut milk and brown sugar for twenty minutes, stirring, until it browns and coats the spoon.
Poach the dumplings ten minutes in that simmering caramel, uncovered. Serve warm, in the caramel.

accras-de-lambi.d: Fritters of chopped conch, firmer and brinier than the salt-cod kind. Saint Barthélemy was Swedish for almost a century, from 1784 to 1878; its cooking nonetheless stayed entirely Creole, without a trace of Scandinavia.
s: Beat the conch with a mallet then simmer it an hour: raw, it would stay hard as rubber.
Chop it coarsely by knife once cooled — it is a dense muscle that must be felt under the tooth.
Make the batter and rest it an hour, so the flour hydrates completely.
Fold in the conch, herbs and chilli just before frying, and taste the raw batter for salt.
Fry at 175°C for three minutes, turning. Serve scalding, with lime.

court-bouillon-saint-martin.d: Reef fish poached in a tomato broth sharpened with chilli and lime. Grand-Case built a reputation as the Antilles' gastronomic capital on its lolos, beachside shacks where court-bouillon is served on paper plates.
s: Scale and gut the fish, then score it in a lattice on both sides and rub it with lime and garlic.
Marinate half an hour in the cold: beyond that, the lime starts cooking the surface and the flesh falls apart later.
Fry the aromatics and tomato in the oil to a thick sauce, fifteen minutes.
Moisten with boiling water, add the whole unpierced chilli and simmer ten minutes.
Lay the fish in the broth and poach twelve minutes uncovered, without turning it. Serve with rice.

tarte-coco-saint-martin.d: A coconut cream tart scented with nutmeg, served on both sides of the island. Saint Martin has been shared between France and the Netherlands since 1648 with no border ever marked on the ground: the recipe circulates as freely as the residents.
s: Rub the flour, cold butter and a spoonful of sugar together, bind with iced water and rest an hour in the cold.
Line the tin, prick the base and blind bake fifteen minutes with weights — without blind baking, the filling soaks the pastry.
Warm the coconut milk with the vanilla and nutmeg, then pour it onto the sugar-beaten eggs in a stream, whisking.
Add the grated coconut and rum, and rest ten minutes for the coconut to drink the liquid.
Fill and bake 30 minutes at 170°C. The centre should still tremble slightly as it leaves the oven.

jocon.d: Chicken stewed in a green sauce of tomatillos, coriander and toasted pumpkin seeds. The green is not decoration: it is the colour of one of the four Mayan recados, base sauces classed by hue that Guatemalan cooking has distinguished since pre-Columbian times.
s: Poach the jointed chicken in salted water with the onion and garlic for forty minutes, and keep the broth.
Dry-toast the pumpkin and sesame seeds until they pop, then grind them while still warm.
Dry-char the tomatillos and spring onions on a griddle until the skin blackens in places: that charring gives the depth, and raw tomatillos give a sharp, flat sauce.
Blend tomatillos, coriander, ground seeds and two soaked tortillas — the tortilla is the only thickener, there is no flour and no cream.
Pour over the chicken, add broth to coat and simmer twenty minutes uncovered. Serve with white rice.

tamales-colorados.d: Large tamales with corn dough tinted by red recado, cooked in banana leaf. In Guatemala the Saturday night tamal is a family institution: fifty are made at once, and the whole day goes into it.
s: Toast the guajillo chillies dry for a few seconds a side, then soak them twenty minutes in hot water.
Char tomatoes, seeds and peppers on a griddle, blend everything with the chillies and strain: the recado must be perfectly smooth.
Slake the masa in hot broth and cook it over low heat, stirring without pause, for forty minutes, until it pulls from the base.
This pre-cooking of the dough is what sets the Guatemalan tamal apart from the Mexican: it gives a smooth, melting texture rather than a grainy one.
Pass the leaves through a flame, spread the dough, fill with chicken, recado, olive and raisin, fold into parcels and steam three hours.

fiambre.d: A cold salad of fifty ingredients or more, made once a year, for All Saints. Each family keeps its own list and passes it down; it is eaten in the cemetery, on the graves, and it is understood that it is never made on any other day.
s: Make the caldillo the day before: vinegar, oil, onion, capers, oregano and spices, left to stand twelve hours.
Cook each vegetable separately and to its own exact point, then cool them and marinate them apart in the caldillo.
Separately is the word: cooked together, the colours bleed and the beetroot reddens the whole dish.
Next day, lay a bed of lettuce and arrange the marinated vegetables in a crown, by colour.
Cover with cured meats, cheese, hard-boiled eggs and sardines. Eaten cold, never reheated.

hilachas.d: Shredded beef stewed in a tomato and chilli recado, with potatoes and carrots. Hilacha means loose thread: the meat is torn by hand along the grain, never cut, and that is what lets it drink up the sauce.
s: Boil the flank two hours with bay, onion and garlic, until it tears without resistance.
Let it cool in its broth before shredding: taken out scalding, it dries on the surface and becomes impossible to pull apart cleanly.
Char tomatoes, tomatillos and chillies on a griddle until they blacken, then blend them with a soaked tortilla.
Strain the recado — chilli skins stay as threads and spoil the texture.
Bring meat, sauce and diced vegetables together and simmer thirty minutes. Serve with rice and tortillas.

subanik.d: Three meats steamed in a mashán leaf with a three-chilli recado. It is a Kaqchikel ceremonial dish reserved for weddings and births; the name comes from a Mayan verb meaning to cook smothered.
s: Toast the three chillies dry, very briefly: a few seconds too long and they turn bitter, with no way back.
Soak them twenty minutes, then blend them with the charred tomatoes and tomatillos and the ground seeds.
Cut the three meats into pieces of the same size so they cook at the same rate.
Line a large dish with banana leaves, pour in meats and recado, and close the leaves into a sealed parcel.
Steam two hours without ever opening it. The parcel holds all the steam from the meats: that is the whole technique.

chiles-rellenos-guatemaltecos.d: Peppers stuffed with meat and vegetables, coated in beaten egg and fried. The Guatemalan version differs from the Mexican in the filling: no cheese and no dried fruit here, but a hash of meat and vegetables marinated in vinegar.
s: Char the whole peppers over a flame until the skin blisters, then seal them ten minutes in a closed bag.
The trapped steam lifts the skin by itself; without this step, peeling them means tearing them.
Slit them down one side, remove the seeds keeping the stalk, and marinate them an hour in vinegar.
Fry the meats and finely diced vegetables, drain the filling and cool it before stuffing.
Whip the whites, fold in the yolks, flour the peppers, dip them and fry at 175°C, spooning oil over them.

rellenitos.d: Plantain croquettes filled with sweetened black bean purée, fried and rolled in sugar. Pairing beans with sugar puzzles visitors; in Guatemala it is as ordinary as chocolate and hazelnut elsewhere.
s: Boil very ripe plantains in their skins for twenty minutes, then peel them hot and mash to a firm purée.
Choose plantains with black skins: yellow ones lack sugar and the dough will not hold.
Fry the cooked beans in lard with the sugar, cinnamon and chocolate, to a paste that can be rolled.
Cool both preparations completely — warm, they stick to the hands and the croquette will not close.
Form plantain balls around the filling, flatten into ovals and fry at 175°C for three minutes. Roll in sugar.

tapado-garifuna.d: A fish and seafood soup in coconut milk with green banana and cassava. The Garífuna descend from African castaways and Arawaks of Saint Vincent, deported to Honduras in 1797; theirs is the only Central American cooking to ignore chilli and corn.
s: Grate fresh coconut and press it twice: the first pressing gives thick milk, the second thin.
Cook the roots and green bananas in the thin milk first — thick milk would split over so long a cooking.
Add the thick milk only at the end, and never let it boil.
Lay the fish steaks and seafood on top and poach ten minutes at a tremble without stirring.
Lime and coriander off the heat. There is no chilli in this dish, and adding it would distort it.

chuchitos.d: Small tight tamales, cooked in corn husk rather than banana leaf. They are sold on the street in the evening, singly, husk included: you unroll it standing up and throw it away, which makes them Guatemala's only truly portable tamal.
s: Soak the dried corn husks an hour in hot water to soften them without tearing.
Beat the lard until it whitens, then work in the masa and broth little by little.
Chuchito dough stays firmer than tamal dough: that is what lets it stand up unsupported once unwrapped.
Char tomatoes and chillies, blend them with the seeds and reduce this recado for ten minutes.
Spread the dough on the husk, add pork and a spoonful of recado, roll tightly and steam an hour, standing upright.

caldo-de-pata.d: A long, gelatinous broth of ox feet, served in the morning at highland markets. The collagen in the feet dissolves into gelatine after four hours: the broth sets to a jelly as it cools, which is the sign it has been made properly.
s: Blanch the feet ten minutes and discard that water: it carries off the grey scum and the strong smell.
Start again in cold water with the onion, garlic and soaked chickpeas, and simmer four hours.
Skim regularly during the first hour; after that the broth clears by itself.
Salt only after three hours: early salt firms the collagen and slows its turning into gelatine.
Add the vegetables for the last half hour. Serve with lime, fresh mint and hot tortillas.

revolcado.d: A red stew of pork offal — head, liver, heart, kidneys — in a tomato and chilli recado. The name comes from revolcar, to tumble about: every piece is mixed into the same thick sauce, and nothing of the pig's head is set aside.
s: Soak all the offal two hours in acidulated water, changing it once.
Poach the head two hours with the bay, bone it hot and dice everything to one centimetre.
Poach the liver and kidneys separately, fifteen minutes only: cooked with the head they would turn mealy.
Char tomatoes, tomatillos and chillies, blend with the toasted seeds and tortillas, and strain.
Bring everything together, moisten with the head broth and simmer thirty minutes. The sauce should be thick and glossy.

atol-de-elote.d: A thick hot drink of ground fresh corn, sweetened with cinnamon. Atol descends from Nahuatl atolli, a corn drink older than the conquest; it is drunk in the street at dawn, from cups handed back to the vendor.
s: Choose ears with milky kernels: pierced with a nail, the kernel should give white liquid and not clear water.
Strip them and blend the kernels with the cold milk, then strain, pressing hard to hold back the skins.
Those skins are indigestible and give a sandy texture; letting them through is the commonest mistake.
Cook over low heat with the cinnamon and sugar, stirring without pause for twenty minutes — the starch catches instantly.
The atol is ready when it coats the spoon. Add the butter off the heat and serve scalding.

fry-jacks.d: Triangles of dough fried until they puff, served at breakfast with beans and eggs. They are slit with a knife to slip in a filling: the trapped air makes a natural pocket, which is why they are scored before frying.
s: Rub the flour, baking powder and fat together, then bind with milk without kneading more than a minute.
Long kneading develops the gluten and the fry jack turns elastic instead of puffing.
Rest thirty minutes, roll to 4 mm and cut ten-centimetre triangles.
Score each triangle with two short cuts at the centre: that is where the steam gathers and lifts the dough.
Fry at 190°C, forty seconds a side. They should puff at once; if they stay flat, the oil is not hot enough.

hudut.d: Fish in coconut milk served with plantain pounded in a mortar. The Garífuna hana is a metre-tall wooden mortar: the mash is worked standing, by two people, and its elastic texture cannot be got any other way.
s: Boil the green bananas and ripe plantains separately, twenty minutes, until they crush easily.
Pound them together while hot, striking steadily: it is the repeated pounding that makes the mash elastic, and a blender makes it gluey.
The ratio of green to ripe makes the flavour: two-thirds green to one-third ripe is the usual balance.
Fry onion, garlic and pepper, pour in the coconut milk and simmer ten minutes without boiling.
Poach the fish steaks eight minutes in that milk. Serve the mash separately, as a ball, in the broth.

stew-chicken-belize.d: Chicken caramelised in burnt sugar then stewed with red recado, Belize's national dish. Recado rojo is an annatto and spice paste inherited from the Yucatán Maya: it gives the chicken its brick colour and peppery scent.
s: Marinate the chicken four hours in recado slaked with vinegar, garlic, cumin and oregano.
Heat oil and brown sugar in a heavy pot, without stirring, until the caramel smokes and blackens.
This is the decisive moment: too pale and the chicken stays light; too far and the whole dish turns bitter. Seconds separate the two.
Drop the drained chicken into the caramel and stir to coat — it should take on a mahogany colour.
Moisten with water, simmer forty minutes, and serve with rice and red beans cooked in coconut milk.

johnny-cakes-belize.d: Small round rolls made with coconut milk, baked and split for filling. The name is said to come from journey cake, the bread that travelled: with no egg and no baker's yeast, it keeps two days without hardening thanks to the coconut fat.
s: Rub the flour, baking powder, salt and shortening together to a coarse meal.
Bind with the coconut milk all at once and gather the dough without kneading more than thirty seconds.
Roll egg-sized balls, flatten them slightly and prick them with a fork.
Those holes let the steam out; without them the bread domes and collapses hollow.
Bake 20 minutes at 200°C. Serve warm, split, with cheese, beans or fish.

chimole.d: A black turkey and dumpling soup, coloured by deliberately burnt chillies. Recado negro is made by charring chillies to charcoal then rinsing them: the soot gives the colour, the rinsing removes the bitterness.
s: If you make the recado yourself, burn the whole dried chillies until black and brittle, in the open air: the smoke is an irritant.
Rinse them at length in cold water before grinding — unrinsed, the soup is inedibly bitter.
Boil the jointed turkey an hour with the aromatics, then slake the recado in a little hot broth.
Shape pork dumplings around a whole hard-boiled egg, and bind them with masa.
Poach them twenty minutes in the black broth, at a tremble. Serve with hot tortillas.

curtido.d: Cabbage pickled with vinegar and oregano, obligatory beside pupusas. It is never served alone: its job is to cut the richness of the pupusa, and a pupusería that failed to put the jar on the table would be judged at once.
s: Shred the cabbage very finely and grate the carrots into long threads, not short pieces.
Scald them thirty seconds then drain at once: this softens them without taking away the crunch.
Raw, the cabbage stays hard and will not take the marinade; cooked longer, it goes limp overnight.
Mix with the vinegar cut with water, the oregano crushed between the fingers and the sliced chilli.
Macerate twenty-four hours in the cold before serving. Keeps two weeks and improves over the first days.

yuca-frita-salvadorena.d: Cassava boiled then fried, served with curtido and pork crackling. It is sold in the evening in the parks, on a banana leaf, and the cassava is always boiled before frying — never fried raw, unlike potato.
s: Peel the cassava and remove the woody central thread, which stays hard however long it cooks.
Boil it in lengths for thirty minutes, until it splits by itself, then drain and let it dry.
This step is not optional: raw cassava holds cyanogenic compounds that boiling destroys, and frying alone will not do it.
Cool completely — hot, it spits violently in the oil.
Fry at 180°C until the edges colour, and serve with curtido, tomato sauce and chicharrón.

panes-con-pavo.d: A sandwich of turkey braised in a spiced sauce, soaked in its own juices. It is the Salvadoran year-end feast dish: the turkey marinates for two days in a recado of toasted seeds, and the bread is dipped in the sauce before closing.
s: Marinate the turkey two days in the refrigerator with mustard, thyme, bay and crushed garlic.
Dry-toast the sesame and pumpkin seeds until they brown, then grind them finely.
Char tomatoes and chillies, blend with the seeds, and strain: the sauce must be velvety.
Braise the turkey three hours covered in that sauce at 160°C, basting every half hour.
Shred the meat, fill the rolls with salad and turkey, and spoon over sauce generously before closing.

pasteles-salvadorenos.d: Turnovers of corn masa filled with meat and vegetables, fried in half-moons. Not to be confused with Puerto Rican pasteles, cooked in leaves: here the dough is nixtamalised corn and the turnover is fried, never boiled.
s: Fry the meat with very finely diced vegetables until the filling is dry.
A wet filling soaks through the masa in the fryer and bursts the turnover in the oil.
Knead the masa with warm water and annatto until it no longer cracks when folded.
Press discs between two sheets of plastic, fill and fold into half-moons, sealing the edge.
Fry at 175°C for four minutes, turning. Serve with curtido, always.

empanadas-de-platano.d: Turnovers of plantain purée filled with pastry cream or beans, fried and sugared. They are eaten at breakfast or after dark, and the black bean version surprises visitors as much as Guatemalan rellenitos do.
s: Boil very ripe plantains in their skins, then peel them hot and mash with a ricer.
Work the mash by hand until it turns smooth and pliable, without adding flour.
Make a thick cornflour pastry cream and cool it completely, covered on the surface.
Shape discs of mash in your palm, fill with a spoonful of cream and close, sealing well.
Fry at 175°C, two minutes a side, then roll in cinnamon sugar while still hot.

riguas.d: Cakes of ground fresh corn, cooked between two corn husks on a griddle. The husk is not a wrapper but a tool: it keeps the very wet batter from sticking to the plate and gives it a green scent.
s: Strip the ears and grind the kernels in a mill or blender without adding a drop of water.
Fresh corn holds enough moisture; adding any gives a batter that runs and never sets.
Season with salt and a little sugar, and rest a quarter of an hour.
Spread two spoonfuls on a green corn husk, cover with a second husk and set on the griddle.
