Cook ten minutes a side over low heat. Serve with cream and fresh cheese.

tamales-de-elote.d: Tamales of fresh corn, lightly sweetened, with no filling. They are made only during the three-month harvest: dried corn will not do, lacking the sugar and moisture that make them what they are.
s: Peel off whole husks without tearing them and keep the widest for wrapping.
Strip and grind the kernels without water, then mix with beaten butter, sugar and cream.
Beat the batter five minutes: the air worked in is the only thing that lightens the tamal, there is no yeast.
Fill the husks only two-thirds full — the batter swells and would overflow.
Steam an hour, standing upright and packed close. Cool slightly before opening: hot, they fall apart.

carneada.d: A large Honduran barbecue where beef marinated in sour orange is grilled over charcoal. It is not a dish but an occasion: a carneada gathers the family for a whole Sunday, and the word means the party as much as the meal.'
s: Flatten the meat with a mallet to a centimetre: flank is fibrous and a thick piece stays tough on the grill.
Marinate it three hours in sour orange, crushed garlic, cumin and oregano.
Do not go beyond four hours: the citrus acid eventually cooks the surface and the meat turns mealy.
Grill over hot coals, three minutes a side, and rest five minutes before slicing across the grain.
Serve with tortillas, refried beans, fresh cheese, plantains and chimol — the raw tomato salad that accompanies everything in Honduras.

anafre.d: A fondue of black beans and cheese served scalding in a clay brazier. Anafre is first the name of the vessel: a small charcoal burner set on the table, and the dish ended up taking the name of its holder.
s: Fry the crumbled chorizo and onion in lard until the red fat runs.
Add the refried beans and loosen them with hot water: they should fall slowly from the spoon.
Too thick, the anafre sets into a crust over the fire; too thin, it will not sit on the tortilla.
Pour into the clay vessel, cover with cheese and let it melt over coals or in the oven.
Serve at once, the cheese still stretching, with fried tortillas for dipping.

yuca-con-chicharron.d: Boiled cassava served with crisp pork crackling and a cabbage salad. It is served on a banana leaf and eaten with the hands: the leaf is the plate, and nothing needs washing afterwards.
s: Cut the belly into batons with the rind and cook it covered in its own fat, over very low heat, for forty minutes.
Then uncover and raise the heat: the rendered fat becomes the frying bath, and no other is needed.
The chicharrón is ready when it stops crackling — the noise stops because all the water has gone.
Boil the cassava thirty minutes, drain it and remove the central thread.
Plate on the leaf: cassava, chicharrón, vinegared cabbage and tomato. Douse with sour orange.

pollo-chuco.d: Fried chicken on a bed of fried plantain and black beans, topped with cabbage and cream. Chuco means dirty in Honduran slang: the dish is named for its look, all jumbled and spilling off the plate.
s: Marinate the chicken an hour in garlic, cumin and salt, then flour it lightly.
Cut green plantains into thin lengthways slices with a peeler, to get crisps rather than coins.
Fry the plantains first at 160°C, drain them, then raise to 190°C and fry again to make them brittle.
Fry the chicken at 170°C for twelve minutes, until the juices run clear.
Build the plate in order: plantains, beans, chicken, vinegared cabbage, cream, cheese. It is not mixed before serving.

vigoron.d: Boiled cassava, chicharrón and a vinegared cabbage salad, served on a banana leaf. It was invented in 1914 by a vendor in Granada market, who named it after a tonic then in fashion.
s: Make the cabbage salad at least two hours ahead: it must be frankly sour, that is what balances the fat.
Shred the cabbage finely, salt it ten minutes then press it before adding the vinegar — otherwise it weeps and dilutes everything.
Cook the pork belly in its own fat, covered then uncovered, until the rind blisters.
Boil the cassava in large lengths without letting it collapse: it must stay in pieces you can pick up.
Plate on the leaf: cassava, chicharrón broken into pieces, salad over the top. Eaten without cutlery.

baho.d: Beef, plantain and cassava smothered for five hours in banana leaves. Bahó comes from vaho, steam: nothing is added to the bottom of the pot, and all the cooking is done in the water the ingredients release.
s: Marinate the brisket twelve hours in sour orange, garlic and onion — the acid tenderises a very fibrous cut.
Line a large pot with banana leaves passed through a flame, letting them overhang generously.
Stack in layers: beef at the bottom, then green plantains, then ripe, then cassava, salting each tier.
Fold the leaves over and seal tightly with a weighted lid. Do not add a drop of water.
Five hours over very low heat, never opening it. Serve with a vinegared cabbage salad.

quesillo-nicaraguayen.d: A tortilla rolled around a stretchy cheese, pickled onions and sour cream. It is served in a plastic bag, never on a plate: you bite the corner of the bag and squeeze, which is how it has always been eaten on the road to León.
s: Pickle the very finely sliced onions in salted vinegar at least two hours: they should turn translucent and lose their bite.
Use a fresh pasta filata cheese, unripened: elasticity is what matters, not flavour.
Warm the tortilla on the griddle until it turns supple, without letting it dry or harden.
Lay the cheese in the centre, add the drained onions then the cream, and roll tightly.
Serve at once. Cooled, the cheese contracts and the quesillo loses all its point.

indio-viejo.d: A shredded beef stew thickened with corn masa, scented with sour orange and mint. It is one of the best-preserved pre-Columbian dishes in Central America: beef replaced game, but the masa-thickening technique has not changed.
s: Boil the brisket an hour and a half, cool it in its broth then shred it by hand.
Slake the masa in cold broth, never hot: poured into hot liquid it lumps in a way nothing can undo.
Fry onion, garlic, pepper and tomato in lard coloured with annatto.
Add the meat, broth and slaked masa, and stir without pause for twenty minutes over low heat.
Finish with sour orange and mint off the heat. The right consistency runs slowly like a thick purée.

rondon-nicaraguayen.d: A Caribbean Creole stew of fish, root vegetables and coconut milk, slowly cooked in one pot. The name comes from English run down: the cook runs to fetch whatever is at hand, and the contents change every time.
s: Press the coconut twice and keep the two milks apart — the thin for the long cooking, the thick for the end.
Cook the root vegetables in the thin milk for forty minutes, with the thyme and garlic.
Add hand-rolled dumplings, simple balls of flour and water, and poach them twenty minutes.
Set the whole chilli in unpierced: it scents without burning, and is removed before serving.
Add fish, crab and shrimp then the thick milk, and simmer ten minutes without ever boiling.

chancho-con-yuca.d: Pork salted overnight then stewed, served with cassava and pickled cabbage. It differs from vigorón in the meat: here the pork is brined and cooked wet, whereas vigorón demands a dry, crisp chicharrón.
s: Rub the pork with coarse salt and crushed garlic and leave it twenty-four hours in the cold, uncovered.
Rinse it and taste a cooked fragment before going further: salt penetrates very unevenly depending on thickness.
Simmer it an hour and a half with the sour orange and onion, until it falls apart under a fork.
Boil the cassava separately in barely salted water, and remove the woody thread.
Plate on banana leaf with the vinegared cabbage, and spoon over the pork cooking juices.

rosquillas-somotenas.d: Crisp rings of corn masa and dry cheese, baked in wood-fired ovens. Somoto lives on them: the town has dozens of family ovens, and rosquillas are sold along the Pan-American highway at all hours.
s: Use white nixtamalised corn ground dry, coarser than tortilla masa: that grain gives the crunch.
Grate the dry cheese very finely — a fresh cheese would release water and the rosquilla would stay soft.
Work the butter and cheese to a cream, then work in the masa, eggs and sugar.
Shape seven-centimetre rings a finger thick, and let them dry half an hour in the air.
Bake 25 minutes at 190°C. They should sound hollow and harden as they cool.

casado.d: The complete Costa Rican plate: rice, beans, plantain, salad, a vegetable and a meat. The name means married: the elements are joined on one plate, and it is also said to be the lunch a wife packed for a working husband.
s: Cook the rice on a base of softened onion, garlic and pepper: plain rice is not served in Costa Rica.
Simmer the black beans an hour and a half with whole coriander, stems included.
Keep the bean cooking water: it is what makes tomorrow's gallo pinto, and throwing it away would be waste.
Fry very ripe plantains on the bias, until they caramelise at the edges.
Set each element side by side without mixing, and add a cabbage salad with lime.

chifrijo.d: A bowl layering beans, rice, chicharrón and pico de gallo. The name contracts chicharrón and frijoles; it was invented in the 1990s in a San José bar, and remains the subject of an unresolved trademark dispute.
s: Cook the red beans until tender but whole, and keep them in a little of their liquid.
Cook the diced pork belly in its own fat, covered for forty minutes then uncovered until it crisps.
Make the pico de gallo at the last minute and salt it only as you serve — salted ahead, it weeps.
Build the bowl in this order: rice at the bottom, beans with a little liquid, scalding chicharrón, pico de gallo, avocado.
The order matters: chicharrón laid under the beans goes soft in two minutes. Serve with fried tortillas.

tamal-tico.d: The Costa Rican Christmas tamal, of corn and potato masa, filled with pork and vegetables. They are cooked in pairs tied together, called piñas: they are never counted singly, always by twos.
s: Cook the pork in broth with aromatics, bone it and keep the broth for the masa.
Mash the boiled potatoes and mix them into the masa: that is what gives the tamal tico its softer texture than its neighbours'.
Loosen with melted lard and hot broth, beating, until the dough falls from the spoon in a ribbon.
Cut the leaves into rectangles, pass them through a flame and spread the dough thinly — a tamal tico is flat, not plump.
Fill, fold, tie the parcels in pairs and boil three hours.

patacones.d: Slices of green plantain fried twice and flattened between the two baths. The flattening midway is not cosmetic: it increases the exposed surface, and that is what makes a patacón crisp rather than floury.
s: Use frankly green plantains: as soon as they yellow, the sugar caramelises and they brown before they cook.
Peel them by scoring the skin lengthways, never like a banana — green skin will not come away.
Cut two-centimetre slices and fry at 160°C for five minutes, until tender but pale.
Drain, flatten each to half a centimetre, then dip them briefly in salted garlic water.
That salt-water dip makes the oil spit but gives the crispness. Second fry at 190°C for two minutes.

chorreadas.d: Thick pancakes of ground fresh corn, served with sour cream. The name comes from chorrear, to pour: the batter is so loose it spreads by itself on the griddle, and is never helped along with a spatula.
s: Grind the fresh kernels without water, or with a spoonful of milk at most if the corn is already mature and dry.
Sieve coarsely to hold back the largest skins, but keep some grain: a smooth batter gives a rubbery pancake.
Salt, sweeten lightly and rest ten minutes for the starch to hydrate.
Pour a ladleful onto a buttered griddle over medium heat and let the batter spread by itself, untouched.
Five minutes a side, until the edges brown. Serve with sour cream and fresh cheese.

arroz-con-leche-tico.d: A rice pudding with cinnamon and lemon zest, served warm. It came from Spain, and to Spain from the Moors; the Costa Rican version is marked by condensed milk, which replaces part of the fresh milk and gives a denser texture.
s: Cook the rice first in water with the cinnamon and zest, fifteen minutes, until all the water is absorbed.
Cooking straight in milk lengthens it by half: milk slows the starch's hydration.
Then add hot milk and simmer forty minutes, stirring regularly.
Add the condensed milk and sugar in the last ten minutes only — sugar too early hardens the grain.
Take it off the heat while it still looks too loose: it thickens a great deal as it cools.

hojaldres-panamenas.d: Fried dough cakes, puffed and flaky, served at breakfast. Despite the name there is no butter lamination: the flakiness comes from stretching the dough by hand until it is transparent.
s: Knead a soft dough and rest it an hour under a cloth, so the gluten relaxes.
Divide into balls, oil them generously and rest another thirty minutes: the oil keeps the dough from drying and helps the stretching.
Stretch each ball by hand, turning it, until it becomes translucent at the centre.
That stretching is what creates the layers, and a rolling pin will not replace it.
Fry at 180°C, one minute a side. The cake blisters and tears into leaves under the fingers.

tamal-de-olla.d: A tamal baked in a dish rather than in parcels, layered like a gratin. It is the hurried version of the Panamanian tamal: same dough, same filling, but two hours saved on folding leaves.
s: Poach the chicken, shred it and simmer it in a sofrito of tomato, pepper and annatto.
Cook the masa in the broth with the lard, stirring without pause for thirty minutes, until it pulls from the base.
This pre-cooking is essential: raw masa spread in a dish bakes unevenly and stays raw at the centre.
Line the dish with banana leaves, spread half the masa, the chicken, then the rest of the masa.
Bake 45 minutes at 180°C. Rest twenty minutes before cutting, or the layers slide.

carimanolas.d: Spindle-shaped cassava croquettes filled with minced meat, fried. The elongated shape with two pointed ends is not decorative: it lets you eat the croquette standing without it breaking, and it is identical from Panama to Cartagena.
s: Boil the cassava until it falls apart, remove the woody thread and mash it while still scalding.
Mashed cold it turns grainy and the dough cracks when shaped — the mistake that ruins the most carimañolas.
Work the mash by hand until it turns smooth and slightly tacky, with no flour.
Fry the meat until dry, and cool it before filling.
Form spindles around the filling, tapering both ends, and fry at 180°C for four minutes.

saus-panameno.d: Pig's trotters poached then marinated in lime, cucumber and chilli, served cold. The dish came with the English-speaking West Indians who dug the canal; its name is a corruption of souse, the same preparation in Jamaica.
s: Scrape and singe the trotters to remove remaining bristles, then rinse them at length.
Poach them three hours with garlic and oregano, until the flesh leaves the bone without effort.
Bone them warm, keeping the rind, and cut everything into bite-sized pieces.
Mix immediately with lime, vinegar and raw vegetables, while the meat is still warm.
It is by cooling in the marinade that the gelatine sets and coats everything. Chill six hours before serving.

pesada-de-nance.d: A thick cream of nance, a small yellow Panamanian fruit, bound with cornflour. Nance has a strong, cheesy smell that disconcerts at first; cooked and sweetened, it becomes a dessert the Azuero peninsula counts as its own.
s: Boil the whole nances twenty minutes with the cinnamon and cloves, until they split.
Push them through a sieve, pressing, and discard the stones and skins — they are bitter and spoil the texture.
Slake the cornflour in a little cold water before adding it, never straight into the hot.
Thicken over low heat, stirring without pause, ten minutes, until the cream coats the spoon.
Pour into bowls and set in the cold. Eaten cold, with a dry biscuit.

hangi.d: Meat and vegetables cooked in an earth oven on white-hot volcanic stones, under wet sacking. In Rotorua some families use geothermal steam directly: there the ground cooks the meal by itself.
s: Dig a pit a metre square and sixty centimetres deep, and stack volcanic stones on a hardwood fire in it.
Let them heat for three hours: the stones must be grey with heat and no longer black.
Rake out the wood, level the stones, and cover them with green leaves or wet cloths to prevent scorching.
Stack the baskets: meat at the bottom, roots in the middle, greens on top. Throw on a bucket of water to raise the steam.
Cover with wet sacking then earth, letting no steam escape, and leave for 3 hours. The hāngī is unearthed in silence.

boil-up.d: A broth of smoked pork bones, wild pūhā and kūmara, with dumplings called doughboys. It is the everyday Māori dish, made when the pot must feed everyone without warning.
s: Blanch the smoked bones for 10 minutes and throw away that first, very salty water.
Return them to three litres of clean water with the onion and simmer for 1 hour.
Wash the pūhā several times and rub it between your hands until the milky sap runs: this is what removes the bitterness.
Add the roots in large pieces and cook for 25 minutes.
Make the doughboys from flour, baking powder, butter and milk, drop them on the broth, cover and let them swell for 15 minutes. Add the pūhā last.

damper-au-feu.d: An unleavened bread baked under ash, invented by bush drovers who had neither oven nor yeast. It is broken by hand and eaten with golden syrup, never cut with a knife.
s: Build a hardwood fire and let it fall to thick embers: you need hot ash, not flame.
Mix the flour, baking powder and salt, then rub in the cold butter with your fingertips.
Pour in the milk all at once and bring the dough together in a few movements only: overworked, it bakes hard as a stone.
Shape a flattened round, cut a cross in the top and flour it generously.
Bury it under hot ash for 40 minutes, or bake for 35 minutes at 200°C. The loaf sounds hollow when it is done.

vakalolo.d: A cake of grated cassava cooked in leaves, coated with a caramel of coconut milk and cane sugar. It is shared at the lovo, the Fijian earth oven, and the first portion goes to the village elders.
s: Grate the peeled cassava finely and squeeze out some of the juice: too wet, the cake will not set.
Mix it with half the coconut cream, a third of the sugar and a pinch of salt.
Spread the paste 3 cm thick on banana leaves softened over a flame, and fold into a flat parcel.
Cook for 50 minutes by steaming or in the lovo, until the paste turns translucent.
Make a caramel with the remaining sugar, pour in the rest of the coconut cream off the heat and coat the warm cake with it.

panipopo.d: Yeasted buns baked in a coconut milk sauce that caramelises around them. Pani comes from English 'bun', popo means coconut: the name alone tells the history of the Pacific.
s: Dissolve the yeast and a spoonful of sugar in the warm milk, and let it froth for ten minutes.
Knead with the flour, melted butter, egg, 50 g of sugar and the salt for 10 minutes, then prove for 1 hour.
Shape 60 g balls and set them close together in a buttered dish, without quite touching.
Let them rise for 40 minutes, then pour round the coconut milk whisked with the remaining sugar and the cornstarch.
Bake for 30 minutes at 190°C: the buns swell as they drink the sauce, which caramelises underneath.

ota-ika.d: The Tongan cousin of kokoda, drier and more peppery, where the fish steeps only a few minutes. In Tonga it is made on Sunday after church, on the beach, with fish caught the day before.
s: Cut very fresh tuna into even cubes and keep it on ice until the last moment.
Salt it and pour over the lime juice: leave only ten minutes, the flesh must stay red at the centre.
Drain without pressing and discard the juice.
Add the coconut cream, thinly sliced red onion, tomato, cucumber and chilli.
Season generously with pepper and serve at once, before the salt draws water from the vegetables.

saksak.p: Rabaul, New Britain, Papua New Guinea
saksak.d: A pudding of sago starch and banana cooked in coconut cream, translucent and elastic. Sago comes from the heart of a felled palm: one tree feeds a family for months.
s: Slake the sago starch in cold water and let it settle, then pour off the clear water on top.
Mash the very ripe bananas with a fork and combine them with the sago paste.
Heat the coconut cream with the sugar and a pinch of salt, without letting it boil.
Pour in the mixture, stirring constantly: the paste turns translucent and starts to stretch within minutes.
Turn it out onto banana leaves, roll into a log, tie it and let it firm for an hour before slicing.

simboro.d: Rolls of grated cassava wrapped in island cabbage leaves and poached in coconut milk. It is the everyday laplap: quicker, without an earth oven, but still grated on stone.
s: Grate the peeled cassava very finely and squeeze out some of its juice, without drying it out.
Salt the paste and shape finger-sized rolls between wet palms.
Wrap each in two or three island cabbage leaves, pulled tight, and tie with a strip of leaf.
Pack them closely in a pot and cover with coconut milk let down with a little water.
Poach for 50 minutes over low heat without boiling, then finish with coconut cream and spring onion.

ika-mata-rarotonga.d: Raw tuna with coconut milk and lime, and very little else: spring onion, cucumber and salt. Restraint is the rule in the Cooks — you are meant to taste the fish, not the garnish.
s: Cut the tuna into 1.5 cm dice, discarding sinewy parts.
Toss it with salt and lime juice and leave 15 minutes, no longer.
Drain thoroughly: the fish should stay pink at the centre.
Add the fresh coconut milk, sliced spring onion, diced cucumber and tomato.
Serve immediately, in very cold bowls or half coconut shells.

poe-banane.d: A dense pudding of mashed banana and cassava starch, baked and drowned in fresh coconut milk. It was once cooked underground in the ahimaʻa; the modern oven shortened it without betraying it.
s: Choose very ripe, almost black bananas: all the sweetness of the dish comes from them.
Mash them with a fork, never in a blender, to keep some texture.
Mix them with the cassava starch, sugar, scraped vanilla and lime zest.
Pour into a buttered dish 4 cm deep and bake for 50 minutes at 180°C: the top should brown and the centre stay wobbly.
Let it cool, cut into squares and serve drowned in fresh coconut milk, never heated.

sausage-roll.d: A log of sausage meat rolled in puff pastry and baked. It is the mainstay of Australian bakeries and school canteens; more are eaten per head here than in the United Kingdom it came from.
s: Sweat the very finely chopped onion and cool it before adding it to the meat.
Raw onion releases water as it cooks and soaks the pastry from below — the commonest fault.
Mix the meat, breadcrumbs and seasonings, and fry a spoonful to taste for seasoning.
Shape an even log along the edge of the pastry, roll and seal under the roll, seam down.
Glaze with egg, cut three vents and bake 35 minutes at 200°C. Serve with tomato sauce, never anything else.

barramundi-grille.d: A barramundi fillet grilled with crisp skin, with lemon and herbs. The name comes from a Queensland Aboriginal language and means large-scaled fish; the species changes sex with age, every individual being born male.
s: Dry the skin thoroughly with paper and salt it twenty minutes ahead, uncovered.
That salting draws moisture to the surface where it evaporates: without it the skin sticks and never crisps.
Score the skin three times without reaching the flesh, to stop the fillet curling.
Lay it skin down in a hot pan and press ten seconds with a spatula, then leave it alone for four minutes.
Turn for one minute only, add the butter, garlic and lemon, and baste off the heat.

chicken-parmigiana.d: A crumbed escalope covered with tomato sauce, ham and melted cheese. The parma is the Australian pub dish par excellence, despite the Italian name: it descends from aubergine parmigiana, with chicken replacing the vegetable by way of America.
s: Butterfly the breasts and flatten them with a mallet to an even centimetre.
Crumb them in the standard way, pressing firmly, then rest twenty minutes in the cold so the coating adheres.
Fry the escalope in a pan first, until golden and cooked, before topping it.
Topped raw then baked, the crumb goes soft under the sauce and the dish loses all its crunch.
Add sauce, ham and cheese and grill for five minutes only. Serve with chips and a salad.

sausage-sizzle.d: A grilled sausage laid diagonally on a slice of white bread, with onion and tomato sauce. It is sold outside hardware stores and polling places; on federal election day it is the democracy sausage, and a national map tracks the stalls.
s: Cook the sliced onions first, at length over low heat, until frankly brown and sweet.
Push them to the edge of the plate: they go on confiting in the sausage fat throughout.
Grill the sausages twenty minutes over medium heat, turning often — over high heat the skin bursts and the juice is lost.
Never prick them: it is the mistake everyone makes and it gives a dry sausage.
Lay the sausage diagonally on the buttered bread, add onion and sauce, and fold the corners in. Eaten standing.

burger-with-the-lot.d: An Australian hamburger stacking beef, bacon, egg, beetroot and pineapple. The slice of pickled beetroot is the national signature: it exists nowhere else, and its absence alone disqualifies a burger in Australian eyes.
s: Shape wide, flat patties, wider than the bun: they shrink a good centimetre as they cook.
Press a dimple in the centre with your thumb, which stops the patty doming.
Drain the beetroot and pineapple thoroughly on paper before laying them on.
Beetroot juice goes through the bun in two minutes; that is where it is won or lost.
Stack in order: bun, lettuce, patty, cheese, bacon, egg, beetroot, pineapple, sauce. The lettuce underneath protects the bread.

salt-pepper-squid.d: Squid fried in starch, seasoned with Sichuan pepper and chilli. It came with the Cantonese of the nineteenth-century goldfields and settled so thoroughly that every pub serves it, without anyone thinking of it as Chinese.
s: Split the squid tubes, open them out and score the inner face in a lattice without cutting through.
Cut into squares: the scoring makes the pieces curl as they cook, and the flesh stays tender.
Dry-toast the Sichuan and black peppercorns, then grind them with the coarse salt — never the reverse, damp salt clogs the mill.
Coat the dry squid in starch alone, shaking off the excess, and fry at 190°C.
Ninety seconds, no more. Beyond two minutes squid turns rubbery and nothing recovers it.

caramel-slice.d: Three layers: a coconut shortbread, a condensed milk caramel, a chocolate top. No Australian school fête, café or bakery is without it; elsewhere it goes by millionaire's shortbread.
s: Mix flour, coconut, brown sugar and melted butter, press firmly into the tin and bake 20 minutes at 180°C.
Cook the caramel over low heat, stirring without pause for fifteen minutes: it should thicken and colour slightly.
Stir without stopping: condensed milk catches instantly and a burnt base carries through the whole slice.
Pour it over the still-warm base and return to the oven ten minutes, which sets the caramel and stops it running.
Cool completely before the chocolate, with a spoonful of oil added so it cuts without shattering.

dim-sim.d: A large parcel of pork and cabbage, steamed or fried, peculiar to Australia. It is not dim sum: it was created in Melbourne in the 1940s by a Cantonese cook for an Australian public, and it is three times the size of its model.
s: Chop the cabbage very finely, salt it twenty minutes and press it out thoroughly between your hands.
Without that purging, the cabbage water soaks the filling and the dim sim collapses as it cooks.
Work the pork in one direction until it turns tacky, then fold in the cabbage and starch.
Form large balls, twice the size of a dim sum, and wrap without pleating — the wrapper simply gathers into a purse.
Steam twelve minutes, then fry one minute at 190°C if you want them crisp.

chiko-roll.d: A large fried roll in thick pastry, filled with mutton, cabbage and barley. It was designed in 1951 to be eaten one-handed in football stands: the pastry is deliberately thick and tough, precisely so it will not tear.
s: Cook the barley thirty minutes, chop the mutton and vegetables very finely, and simmer everything until the filling is dry.
Cool it completely: a warm filling softens the pastry and the roll opens in the oil.
Make a firm flour and cornflour dough and roll it to two millimetres — far thicker than a spring roll wrapper.
Roll tightly, folding both ends in, and seal with slaked flour.
Fry at 180°C for six minutes. The pastry should blister and take an even amber colour.

flat-white.d: An espresso lengthened with finely textured microfoam, with no dry foam layer. Australia and New Zealand have disputed its invention since the 1980s; what sets it apart from a latte is not the quantity of milk but the texture of the foam, denser and glossier.
s: Pull a 40 ml double ristretto in twenty-five seconds, on a fine grind and an even tamp.
Use cold whole milk: the cold gives time to build the foam before the milk reaches 65°C.
Set the wand just under the surface to introduce air for three seconds only, then submerge it to spin the milk.
That vortex breaks large bubbles into microbubbles: this is where the whole flat white is made, and it cannot be fixed afterwards.
Stop at 60-65°C, tap the jug on the bench and pour from high then close, with no spoon.

halal-snack-pack.d: A tray of chips covered with kebab meat and three sauces. Born in the Lebanese and Turkish kebab shops of the suburbs, it took its name on social media in 2016; the three sauces — garlic, chilli, barbecue — are canonical.
s: Marinate the thinly sliced lamb in yoghurt, cumin and paprika, at least four hours.
Yoghurt tenderises through its enzymes and mild acidity, without cooking the surface as lemon would.
Fry the potatoes twice: at 150°C to cook them, then at 190°C to crisp them.
Grill the meat on a very hot plate in a thin layer, until the edges caramelise.
Build in the tray: chips, grated cheese that melts on contact, meat, then the three sauces in crossed lines.

vegemite-toast.d: Buttered toast under a very thin layer of salty yeast extract. Vegemite was born in 1922 from the yeast residue of Melbourne breweries; the universal foreign mistake is to spread it like jam, when barely a trace is wanted.
s: Toast the bread until golden and still hot, never cold.
Butter it generously while scalding, so the butter melts and soaks in.
The butter is not optional: the fat tempers the salt, and Vegemite alone is inedible to most people.
Take a tiny amount on the point of a knife and spread it almost transparently thin.
You should see the bread through it. If the toast is brown and opaque, there is ten times too much.

fairy-bread.d: Buttered white bread covered with coloured sugar sprinkles, cut into triangles. It has been the birthday staple of every Australian childhood since the 1920s; there is no recipe as such, only absolute rules about cutting and thickness.
s: Use very soft white sliced bread, never wholemeal and never toasted.
The butter must be at room temperature and spread right to the edges: one bare patch and the sprinkles will not stick.
Shower the sprinkles on generously, then press gently with your palm so they adhere.
Cut off the crusts and cut along both diagonals, never into squares or rectangles.
Triangles are the only permitted shape. Serve at once, the bread stales quickly.

vanilla-slice.d: A thick custard set between two sheets of puff pastry, iced with passionfruit. Mildura has run a national best vanilla slice competition since 1998; it is nicknamed the snot block, which has never harmed its popularity.
s: Bake both pastry sheets between two weighted trays: without weights they puff and the custard will not sit.
Bring the milk to the boil with the split vanilla, then pour it over the yolks beaten with sugar and cornflour.
Return to the heat and boil for two full minutes, whisking: cornflour thickens only after a proper boil.
A custard taken off too soon looks set but will slump back to liquid as it cools, and the slice will collapse.
Pour onto the first sheet, cover with the second, chill six hours then ice with passionfruit.

macadamia-crusted-fish.d: A white fish fillet under a crust of crushed macadamias. The macadamia is one of very few Australian native foods grown commercially worldwide; it grows wild in the forests of Queensland.
s: Crush the macadamias with a knife, roughly: blended, they release their oil and form a paste rather than a crust.
Mix them with the breadcrumbs, melted butter, parsley and lemon zest.
Brush the fish with mustard: that is what holds the crust on, there is no egg and no flour.
Press the crust onto the fillet and bake at 200°C for twelve minutes only.
Macadamia is very oily and burns fast; cover with foil if it colours before the fish is cooked.

bowen-mango-cheesecake.d: A no-bake cheesecake with Kensington Pride mango, known as the Bowen mango. The variety arose from a chance seedling at Bowen in the 1880s and now accounts for most of Australia's crop, with nobody knowing its parentage.
s: Crush the biscuits with a rolling pin rather than a blender, to keep an uneven texture, and bind with melted butter.
Press firmly and chill thirty minutes before filling: a soft base crumbles when cut.
Choose very ripe mangoes, red-blushed and soft to the touch, and purée two of them.
Bloom the gelatine in cold water then dissolve it in a little warm purée, never boiling — heat destroys it.
Whip the cream separately and fold it in with a spatula. Chill six hours and decorate with sliced fresh mango.

pineapple-fritters.d: Pineapple rings coated in batter and fried, sold in Queensland fish shops. They come from the same counter as fish and chips, in the same paper, and tropical Queensland pineapple is sharp enough to stand up to the sweet batter.
s: Cut the pineapple into one-centimetre rings and remove the woody core with a cutter.
Blot each ring very thoroughly between two cloths: pineapple is full of juice and batter slides off a wet surface.
Make a batter thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, and rest it twenty minutes.
Dip and fry at 180°C, two minutes a side, without crowding the oil.
Dust with cinnamon icing sugar and serve at once — pineapple weeps as it cools and softens the crust.

pie-floater.d: A meat pie upended in a pea soup and doused with tomato sauce. It was sold from Adelaide's night pie carts from the 1890s; South Australia declared it a State Heritage Icon in 2003.
s: Soak the split peas overnight and cook them two hours with the bay, until completely collapsed.
The soup must be thick enough for the pie to float without sinking — that is the name, and a thin soup fails the dish.
Simmer the minced beef with onion and stock for an hour, then dust with flour to thicken and cool it.
Line the tins with shortcrust, fill cold and cover with puff: shortcrust below to hold, puff above to rise.
Bake 30 minutes at 200°C. Serve the pie inverted, crust down, in the soup, and pour the tomato sauce over.

frog-cake.d: A small cake shaped like an open-mouthed frog, filled with cream and iced with fondant. Created in Adelaide in 1922, it was listed as a South Australian heritage icon in 2001; the open mouth is made by splitting the top of the cake in two.
s: Bake a firm sponge in a deep tin the day before and let it stale: fresh sponge cannot be carved.
Cut cylinders with a ring cutter, then round the top with a knife into a dome.
Slice the dome on the bias two-thirds up without detaching it completely: the upper part becomes the jaw.
Fill with jam then firm whipped cream, lifting the jaw to open the mouth.
Dip in warm coloured fondant, holding by the base, and let it set. Add the eyes in melted chocolate.

kitchener-bun.d: A doughnut split at the side, filled with jam and whipped cream. It was called a Berliner until 1915; South Australia, heavily German-settled, renamed it after Lord Kitchener during the First World War, and the name stuck.
s: Knead a soft enriched dough and let it double, an hour and a half somewhere warm.
Shape balls, flatten them slightly and prove a second time on floured paper.
Handle them by the paper when frying: picked up by hand they deflate and lose their pale ring.
Fry at 170°C, two minutes a side. The pale band around the middle proves the doughnut floated properly.
Split at the side without cutting through, fill with jam then whipped cream, and dust with icing sugar.

ab-yiros-pack.d: Chips covered with yiros meat, sauces and chicken salt, an Adelaide speciality. The initials stand for atomic bomb, coined at the Blue and White Café in the 1960s; it is the direct ancestor of Melbourne's halal snack pack, by twenty years.
s: Marinate the lamb in yoghurt, oregano and cumin for four hours, then grill it in a thin layer on a hot plate.
Cut the potatoes into thick chips and soak them an hour in cold water to remove surface starch.
That soaking stops the chips sticking together, which matters when they are drowned in sauce.
Fry twice, at 150°C then 190°C, and season with chicken salt straight out of the oil.
Build chips, meat, then the three sauces. Eaten with a plastic fork, straight from the tray.

lamb-chops-bbq.d: Lamb chops grilled on the barbecue, marinated with rosemary and garlic. Australian lamb is grass-fed year round: its fat is yellower and its flavour stronger than that of European shed-raised lamb.
s: Take the chops out an hour ahead: meat cold at the centre chars outside and stays raw within.
Marinate them in oil, rosemary and garlic, but salt only as they go on the grill.
Salt in the marinade draws out moisture and the meat boils in its own juices instead of searing.
Grill over high heat three minutes a side, standing the chops on their fat edge for thirty seconds to render it.
Rest five minutes under paper before serving, with lemon and coleslaw.

tasmanian-scallop-pie.d: An individual pie of scallops in a yellow curry sauce. The bright colour comes from curry powder, added by British settlers in the nineteenth century; the Tasmanian scallop has denser flesh than warm-water kinds and stands up to baking in pastry.
s: Remove the side muscle from the scallops, that small firmer rectangle that stays rubbery however it is cooked.
Do not cook them in advance: they weep and go dry, whereas they cook in eight minutes inside the pie.
Make a thick curried béchamel, toasting the powder thirty seconds in the butter before adding the flour.
Cool the sauce completely before folding in the raw scallops and filling the tins.
Line with shortcrust, cover with puff, glaze and bake 30 minutes at 200°C.

tasmanian-apple-pie.d: A double-crust pie of Huon valley apples with cinnamon. Tasmania was nicknamed the Apple Isle: it shipped some five million cases a year to Europe until Britain's entry into the Common Market in 1973 closed the trade.
s: Mix two varieties: a sharp one that collapses and a firm one that holds, or the filling is uniform and dull.
Macerate the sliced apples with the sugar for thirty minutes, then draw off the released juice and reduce it separately.
That reduced juice put back into the pie concentrates the flavour; left as it was, it would soak the base.
Thicken with cornflour and cool before filling the shortcrust-lined tin.
Cover, seal, cut three vents and bake 55 minutes at 190°C. Cool two hours before cutting.

leatherwood-honey-ice-cream.d: An ice cream made with leatherwood honey, from a tree endemic to Tasmania's rainforests. This intensely perfumed honey, almost floral and faintly peppery, is produced nowhere else on earth; the tree takes a century to flower abundantly.
s: Heat the milk and cream with the vanilla without boiling, then pour onto the yolks beaten with sugar.
Cook to the nappe at exactly 82°C: beyond 85°C the yolks coagulate and the custard turns grainy.
Off the heat, whisk in the honey — heated, it loses the volatile aromas that are its whole point.
Strain, cool rapidly over iced water and mature twelve hours in the refrigerator.
Churn. Honey lowers the freezing point: this ice cream stays soft and can be served straight from the freezer.

pepperberry-wallaby.d: Seared wallaby fillet crusted with Tasmanian mountain pepper. The berry of Tasmannia lanceolata bites gently at first then numbs the tongue thirty seconds later: it needs a light hand, unlike black pepper.
s: Wallaby is extremely lean meat: it takes no cooking beyond rare, and toughens abruptly at medium.
Crush the berries roughly and use half what you would of black pepper.
Sear the fillet two minutes a side in a scalding pan, then take it off the heat.
Rest it as long as it cooked, under paper, somewhere warm.
Deglaze with red wine, reduce with the stock and mount with cold butter off the heat. Serve with sweet potato mash.

kangaroo-steak.d: Kangaroo fillet seared rare, served with a Kakadu plum sauce. The meat is under 2% fat and rich in iron: it is never cooked beyond rare, and Australia is the only country in the world to regulate its commercial harvest.
s: Take the meat out an hour ahead and let it come to room temperature, with no acid marinade.
Kangaroo has almost no fat: a lemon or vinegar marinade toughens it rather than tenderising, unlike beef.
Oil the meat rather than the pan, and sear over maximum heat two minutes a side, no longer.
The centre must stay frankly red. At medium the meat goes dry and takes on a pronounced liver taste.
Rest ten minutes, slice across the grain and coat with a red wine and Kakadu plum sauce.

crocodile-curry.d: A coconut curry made with saltwater crocodile tail, farmed in the Top End. Tail meat is white, firm and close to chicken; the rest of the animal is darker and far tougher, and has no place in this dish.
s: Use tail meat only, cut into three-centimetre cubes, with all cartilage removed.
Sear it very briefly, a minute a side: it is lean and toughens exactly like chicken breast.
Fry the curry paste in hot oil until it splits and the oil takes colour.
Add the coconut milk in small additions, stirring, so it emulsifies rather than splitting.
Return the meat for the last fifteen minutes only, at a tremble. Lime off the heat.

witchetty-grubs.d: Large beetle larvae grilled on the coals, an Aboriginal food of the central desert. They are dug from the roots of the witchetty bush and are extremely dense in protein and fat: a few grubs make a meal.
s: Do not wash them in water: they puncture and lose their contents, which are the substance of them.
Simply wipe them by hand and pinch off the dark head.
Set them directly on hot ashes rather than live coals, which would burst them.
Three or four minutes is enough: the skin firms and turns golden, the inside stays creamy.
Eaten whole, unseasoned. They are also eaten raw, and taste of almond.

quandong-pie.d: A pie of quandong, the bright red and frankly sour desert peach. The tree is a hemiparasite: it draws part of its sap from neighbouring plants' roots, which makes cultivation difficult and long kept the fruit wild.
s: Use dried rehydrated quandongs or fresh stoned ones; the stone is very large and takes up half the fruit.
Stew them with the sugar for twenty minutes: the fruit is far sharper than apple and needs almost twice the sugar.
Taste before adding more sugar — the acidity varies greatly from tree to tree.
Thicken with cornflour and cool completely before filling the pie.
Cover, glaze with egg and bake 45 minutes at 190°C. Serve warm with cream.

green-ant-barramundi.d: Barramundi cooked in paperbark, seasoned with crushed green ants. The weaver ant's abdomen holds formic acid with a sharp lime flavour: it replaces citrus in a region where none grows.
s: Soak the paperbark an hour in water: dry, it burns immediately on the coals.
Crush the green ants in a mortar just before use; their acidity fades within hours.
Add no lemon: the two acidities fight each other, and the ants alone are more than enough.
Wrap the whole fish in two layers of bark, tie and set on moderate coals.
Twelve minutes a side. The bark blackens outside while the fish steams in its own moisture.

lemon-myrtle-chicken.d: Chicken marinated in lemon myrtle, a Queensland native. Its leaf holds up to 95% citral, the molecule that gives lemon its scent: the highest concentration known in the plant kingdom, far above lemongrass.
s: Use lemon myrtle sparingly: at that citral concentration, a spoonful is enough for a whole chicken.
Overdone, it turns frankly medicinal and dominates everything — the mistake of cooks meeting it for the first time.
Marinate the chicken two hours in yoghurt, garlic, honey and ground myrtle.
Roast at 190°C for forty minutes, basting twice with the released juices.
Scatter freshly ground myrtle over as it leaves the oven, off the heat: that is when the scent is sharpest.

canberra-truffle-pie.d: A braised beef pie scented with black truffle from the Canberra district. Australia harvests its Périgord truffle in June and July, opposite to the northern hemisphere: it supplies Europe in high summer, when none of its own exists.
s: Braise the beef cheeks three hours in red wine, until they fall apart under a spoon.
Cool the filling overnight before adding the truffle.
Truffle is not cooked: its aromas are volatile and an hour in the oven erases them entirely.
Grate it into the cold filling, mix and infuse two hours in the refrigerator, covered.
Fill the pies, cover with puff pastry and bake 30 minutes at 200°C. Grate a little more truffle as they are opened.

ali-nazik.d: A purée of smoked aubergine with yogurt and garlic, crowned with knife-chopped lamb. Legend says Sultan Selim, served in Gaziantep, asked whose gentle hand had made it: 'eli nazik'.
s: Char the whole aubergines directly over a flame until the skin is black and the flesh collapses.
Let them steam in a bag, peel them and drain them for 20 minutes: the bitter water must go.
Mash the flesh with a fork with the yogurt and pounded garlic, and keep it warm over a bain-marie — never direct heat.
Chop the lamb and fat by knife, sear them over high heat without stirring, add the tomato paste and tomato.
Spread the purée in the dish, hollow a well, spoon in the meat and pour over butter melted with Aleppo pepper.

perde-pilav.d: A pilaf of chicken, almonds and currants sealed in a golden dome of pastry. It was served to newlyweds: the curtain of dough stands for the home, the almonds for children to come.
s: Poach the chicken for 40 minutes; bone it, dice it and keep the stock.
Fry the blanched almonds and pistachios in butter, add the rinsed rice, then the stock, currants and spices. Cook for 15 minutes and let it cool.
Knead the flour, butter, eggs, yogurt and baking powder into a supple dough; rest it for 30 minutes.
Butter a deep mould and line it with dough rolled to 5 mm, leaving the edges hanging.
Fill with the pilaf, well packed, fold the dough over, glaze with egg and bake for 45 minutes at 180°C. Turn it out hot, in one movement.

manti-kayseri.d: Minuscule lamb dumplings served under garlic yogurt and chilli butter. In Kayseri they say a good daughter-in-law fits forty on one spoon: the size is an examination.
s: Knead the flour, eggs, water and salt for 15 minutes into a very firm dough, and rest it for an hour.
Chop the lamb with the onion and parsley, and season generously.
Roll the dough until you can see the grain of the table through it, then cut 2 cm squares.
Place a speck of filling the size of a rice grain on each, and pinch the four corners together at the centre.
Poach for 8 minutes in salted water, plate under garlic yogurt and pour over butter melted with chilli and dried mint.

tepsi-baytinijan.d: A gratin of fried aubergine, meatballs and tomato, layered in a tray. Tepsi means the tray itself: in Baghdad it was sent to the neighbourhood oven, since homes had none.
s: Cut the aubergines into thick rounds, salt them and let them drain for 30 minutes; pat them thoroughly dry.
Fry them until golden, then the potatoes and peppers in the same oil.
Mix the minced meat, grated onion, parsley and baharat, and shape small flat patties, which you sear.
Layer in a tray: aubergine, patties, potato, pepper, sliced tomato.
Pour over the tomato paste slaked in a glass of water and bake for 45 minutes at 190°C. Serve with white rice.

kibbeh-bil-sanieh.d: Two layers of pounded bulgur and lamb, hiding a filling of meat, onion and pine nuts. Diamonds are scored before baking: decorative, but above all it lets you cut portions without breaking the crust.
s: Rinse the fine bulgur and squeeze it; it should be damp, never sodden.
Pound the trimmed leg with a third of the onion and the spices, then work in the bulgur, adding iced water little by little until the paste is smooth.
Make the filling: softened onion, minced lamb, toasted pine nuts, pomegranate molasses, cinnamon.
Spread half the paste 1 cm thick in a buttered tray, cover with the filling, then the second half, smoothing with a wet hand.
Score diamonds with a blade, pour over melted butter and bake for 40 minutes at 200°C. Serve with minted yogurt.

maftoul.d: A Palestinian couscous hand-rolled into pearls far larger than in the Maghreb, served with chicken and chickpeas. Rolling maftoul is village knowledge: it is done by several people, on a large tray.
s: Moisten the fine bulgur with salted water and roll it on a tray, dusting with flour, in circular movements.
Continue until the pearls are the size of a peppercorn, then sift to remove loose flour.
Poach the chicken for 50 minutes with the whole spices and onion; keep the broth.
Steam the maftoul for 25 minutes above the broth, fluffing it twice with a fork.
Soften the sliced onions in olive oil, fold them into the maftoul with the chickpeas, and set the chicken on top.

galayet-bandora.d: Tomatoes seared in olive oil with garlic and green chilli, reduced until jammy. It is the September harvest dish: when tomatoes are abundant, they are scorched rather than stewed.
s: Choose very ripe tomatoes and cut them into large wedges, without peeling or seeding them.
Heat the olive oil until it shimmers, and drop in the crushed whole garlic and split green chillies.
Add the tomatoes all at once and let them sear untouched for 5 minutes: they should blacken in places.
Crush them roughly with a spoon and reduce uncovered for 20 minutes.
Season, add the Aleppo pepper and mint off the heat. It is eaten from the pan, dipping bread.

sayadieh.d: Brown rice cooked in a broth of fish and caramelised onions, topped with fried steaks and a tahini sauce. The colour comes from no spice: only from onions taken to a deep brown.
s: Salt the fish steaks and let them stand for 30 minutes, then pat dry and fry them; set aside.
Fry the sliced onions in the same oil for 30 minutes, to a deep brown: this step, and nothing else, gives the colour.
Take out a third for serving, and blend the rest with a litre of hot water; strain this brown broth.
Cook the rice in it with the cumin, cinnamon and bay, 18 minutes covered.
Whisk the tahini with lemon, garlic and a little water until it whitens. Plate rice, fish, fried onions, almonds and pine nuts, sauce alongside.

zurbian.d: A lamb rice with yogurt, saffron and potato, cooked in layers and scented with agarwood. It is smoked at the end: a coal set in a small dish in the heart of the rice, under the lid.
s: Marinate the lamb for 4 hours in the yogurt, garlic, ginger and hawaij.
Fry the sliced onions to a deep brown and set half aside.
Cook the lamb and its marinade for 1 hour with the whole spices, then add the potatoes.
Par-boil the rice for 6 minutes in plenty of salted water and drain it half cooked.
Layer meat, rice, fried onion, saffron and ghee; cover for 30 minutes over low heat, then smoke with a coal for 5 minutes.

qoozi-bahreini.d: A whole lamb set on a mountain of rice with dried fruit, cooked four hours at low temperature. It is served at the centre of the table for weddings, and taken apart by hand, without a knife.
s: Rub the lamb with baharat, salt and melted ghee, and leave it 6 hours in the cold.
Seal it in a covered dish with a little water and cook for 3½ hours at 150°C: the steam does all the work.
Strain the released juices and use them to cook the soaked rice, with the pierced dried limes and whole spices.
Fry the almonds, pine nuts and raisins separately in ghee, and candy the carrots cut into fine julienne.
Uncover the lamb and give it 25 minutes at 220°C to colour. Set it on the rice, covered with the nuts and saffron in rose water.

mashuai.d: A whole kingfish grilled over coals, served on black-lime rice. The fish is rubbed only with salt and turmeric: in Muscat a good fish is held to need nothing else.
s: Gut and scale the fish, and score it three times on each side down to the bone.
Rub it with turmeric, coarse salt and pounded garlic, working into the cuts, and leave it 1 hour.
Grill it over moderate coals for 20 minutes a side, basting with lemon ghee.
Cook the rice with the pierced dried limes, cardamom and fried onion, in barely salted water.
Serve the whole fish on the rice, with lemon and coriander. It is opened at the table, by hand.

balaleet.d: Sweet vermicelli with saffron and cardamom, covered with a thin savoury omelette. The simultaneous sweet and salty disconcerts visitors; in the Emirates it has always been the Eid breakfast.
s: Break the vermicelli by hand into 4 cm lengths and colour them in the ghee, stirring constantly.
They should turn hazelnut, not brown: ten seconds too long and they turn bitter.
Pour in boiling water to cover, barely salt it, and cook for 6 minutes.
Add the sugar, infused saffron, cardamom and rose water, and let it evaporate completely, uncovered.
Make a very thin, barely set omelette, seasoned, and lay it whole over the vermicelli. Pistachios on top.

khoresh-fesenjan.d: A dark brown stew of ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses, sweet-sour and very old. It appears on Assyrian tablets; in Sari it is served with duck rather than chicken.
s: Grind the walnuts very finely, almost to a paste, then dry-toast them for 10 minutes over low heat, stirring constantly.
Fry the onions golden, add the turmeric, then the chicken, and let it colour.
Add the walnuts and a litre of hot water, and simmer uncovered for 1½ hours, stirring often.
The walnut oil must rise and the stew darken to almost black-brown: it is the only test of doneness.
Add the pomegranate molasses, sugar and saffron, and give it another 30 minutes. Serve over saffron rice with pomegranate seeds.

dolma-azerbaidjan.d: Three stuffed vegetables served together — tomato, pepper and aubergine — called the three sisters. Azerbaijani dolma is UNESCO-listed; the mint and fennel in the filling set it apart from its neighbours.
s: Cut the tops off the three vegetables and hollow them carefully, keeping the lids: the walls must stay thick enough to hold.
Salt the inside of the aubergines and let them drain for 20 minutes, then rinse them.
Mix the minced lamb, raw rice, very finely chopped onion, chopped herbs and ground fennel.
Fill without packing — the rice swells — and replace each vegetable's lid.
Pack them tightly in a pot, add a glass of water and the butter, cover and cook for 50 minutes over low heat. Serve with garlic yogurt.

harissa-armenienne.d: A porridge of hulled wheat and chicken beaten until silky, unsalted until the very end. Tradition links it to the siege of Musa Dagh: villagers are said to have pooled the last of their wheat and poultry.
s: Soak the hulled wheat overnight in cold water.
Poach the chicken for 1 hour in four litres of water, bone it and return the meat to the broth.
Add the drained wheat and cook for 4 hours over very low heat, stirring every half hour so nothing catches.
Beat with a whisk or pestle for the last hour, until wheat and meat become a single cream.
Salt only at the very end — salted too early, harissa never binds. Serve under a pool of cumin-browned butter.

khinkali.d: Large meat dumplings whose broth is drunk first, biting into the side. You hold the khinkali by its dough tail, which is never eaten: guests count the tails left on the plate.
s: Knead the flour, water and salt for 15 minutes into a very firm dough, and rest it for an hour under a cloth.
Mix the minced meats, grated onion, garlic, coriander and spices with 200 ml of iced water: the filling must be frankly liquid, as it becomes the broth.
Roll 12 cm discs, thicker at the centre than at the edges.
Place a large spoonful of filling and pleat the edge round, counting at least nineteen folds, then pinch the tail.
Poach for 12 minutes in barely simmering salted water. Pepper generously, bite the side, drink the juice, then eat — leaving the tail.

chakapuli.d: Milk-fed lamb stewed in white wine with sour green plums and a mountain of tarragon. A strictly seasonal spring dish: without green tkemali and fresh tarragon, it is not made.
s: Cut the lamb into large pieces on the bone and lay it in a pot, with no fat and no prior browning.
Cover with a thick layer of sliced spring onions and the whole green plums.
Pour in the white wine — it should not cover the meat — put on the lid and cook for 40 minutes over low heat.
Only then add the picked tarragon in very large quantity, with coriander, parsley, garlic and chilli.
Continue for 20 minutes covered: the herbs should wilt without blackening. Serve in the pot, with bread.

beshbarmak-kazakh.d: Boiled horse and lamb served on wide squares of pasta and moistened with onions in broth. The name means 'five fingers': it is eaten by hand, and the eldest distributes the pieces by rank.
s: Simmer the meats for 2½ hours in a large pot, skimming relentlessly.
Knead the flour, eggs, a little broth and salt into a firm dough; rest it for 40 minutes.
Roll it very thin and cut 8 cm diamonds.
Poach them for 5 minutes in the skimmed broth — never in plain water, they would lose all their flavour.
Wilt the onion rings in a ladle of scalding broth. Plate the pasta, sliced meat and onions, and serve the broth separately, in bowls.

oshi-palav-tadjik.d: Tajik palov, with yellow and red carrots mixed, cooked in a kazan and served on a single platter. UNESCO-listed in 2016: it accompanies every birth and every wedding in the country.
s: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it in warm salted water.
Render the mutton fat in the kazan, remove the scratchings, and sear the meat over high heat.
Add the onion, then the yellow and red carrots in thick batons, never grated.
Cover with water, add chickpeas, quince, garlic heads and cumin, and let the zirvak simmer for 40 minutes.
Spread the rice on top without stirring, add boiling water to two fingers, let it evaporate then cover for 25 minutes. Invert onto the platter to serve.

dograma.d: Flatbread, meat and onion crumbled by hand into a scalding lamb broth. Everything must be torn by finger, never cut: the knife is banned, and the blade is said to spoil the taste.
s: Cook the lamb and fat for 2 hours in three litres of water with the bay, skimming.
Lift out the meat, let it cool, then shred it entirely by hand.
Crumble the churek bread between your fingers, into irregular pieces the size of a fingernail.
Slice the onion very finely, salt it and crush it by hand to soften it.
Combine bread, meat, onion and tomato in a large bowl, pour the scalding broth over and serve at once, before the bread collapses.

ashak.d: Dumplings of wild garlic chives under garlic yogurt and a meat sauce with split peas. The gandana chive grows only in Afghanistan; exiles substitute leek, and always apologise for it.
s: Knead the flour, water and salt for 12 minutes into a firm dough and rest it for an hour.
Slice the leek and spring onions very finely, salt them and let them drain for 20 minutes, then squeeze them hard: every drop must go.
Roll the dough very thin, cut 8 cm discs, fill them and seal into half-moons, pleating the edge.
Make a sauce with the onion, minced beef, soaked split peas, tomato paste and ground coriander, 40 minutes.
Poach the ashak for 6 minutes, set them on the garlic yogurt, spoon over the sauce and dust with dried mint.

sajji-baloutche.d: A whole chicken staked on a wooden skewer around an open fire, salted only, without spices. The Baloch judge doneness by sound: the skin must crack when struck with the back of a knife.
s: Score the chicken deeply and rub it with coarse salt, lemon and green papaya paste, which tenderises the fibres.
Leave it 4 hours: any longer and the papaya breaks the flesh down.
Stuff it with half-cooked rice, sew the opening shut and stake it on a green wooden skewer.
Plant the skewer at an angle forty centimetres from a wood fire and turn it every ten minutes, for 1½ hours.
Strike the skin: if it sounds hollow and splits, it is ready. Dust with chaat masala and serve with bread and raw onion.

buuz-mongol-oulan.d: Flat mutton pasties fried in fat, eaten by the dozen during Naadam. They are counted: a man who eats fewer than ten over the three days of festivities is thought unserious.
s: Knead the flour, water and salt into a firm dough and rest it for 40 minutes.
Chop the mutton and its fat by knife, mix with very finely chopped onion, garlic, caraway and a little water: the filling must stay moist.
Roll 12 cm discs, place a spoonful of filling, fold over and seal the edge with a flat pleat.
Flatten each pasty with the palm: this is what distinguishes them from steamed buuz.
Fry them 4 minutes a side in mutton fat at 170°C, until they blister and turn golden.

mirza-ghasemi.d: Smoked aubergines crushed with tomato, garlic and egg. The dish takes its name from a nineteenth-century governor of Gilan; it is the smoke, got by charring the aubergine skin over a naked flame, that makes it what it is.
s: Prick the aubergines a few times and char them whole over a fierce flame, turning until the skin is black all over.
An oven will not replace the flame: without charred skin there is no smoke, and mirza ghasemi becomes plain aubergine purée.
Let them cool in a sealed bag, peel them and crush the flesh with a fork, never in a blender.
Soften the sliced garlic in oil with the turmeric, then add the crushed tomato and reduce for a quarter of an hour.
Add the aubergine, fold over low heat, then break in the eggs and barely scramble them through. Serve with flatbread.

baghali-ghatogh.d: Broad beans stewed with dill and garlic, bound with egg. Gilan, on the Caspian shore, is Iran's wettest province: its cooking is green and herbaceous, the opposite of the saffron dishes of the central plateau.
s: Use dried beans soaked overnight, or fresh beans double-podded.
Slip the skin off every bean: it takes time, but left on it stays tough and the dish never reaches its melting texture.
Fry the garlic whole, cloves crushed but not chopped, in butter with the turmeric.
Add the beans and water to cover, and simmer forty minutes covered.
Add generous quantities of chopped dill, then break the whole eggs on top and cover five minutes without stirring.

tahchin.d: A saffron and yoghurt rice cake, golden and crisp, turned out in one piece. It turns tahdig — the rice crust every Iranian fights over — into a whole dish: here the bottom of the pot is not a bonus, it is the entire point.
s: Soak the rice two hours in salted water, then parboil it seven minutes only: it must stay hard at the centre.
Rice cooked through at this stage will be porridge after ninety minutes in the oven.
Infuse the ground saffron in two spoonfuls of hot water for twenty minutes, then mix into the yoghurt and yolks.
Fold half the rice into that cream, press it into the buttered dish, add the chicken, then the rest of the rice unpacked.
Cover tightly with foil and bake 90 minutes at 180°C. Turn out in one movement, crust upwards.

ash-e-doogh.d: A yoghurt soup with herbs and meatballs, served hot or cold. Heated yoghurt splits if you are careless: Azerbaijani cooks stabilise it first with egg and flour, and always stir in the same direction.
s: Beat the yoghurt with the egg and slaked flour to a perfectly smooth mixture, before any heat.
Heat very gently, stirring without pause and always in the same direction, a quarter of an hour, until the first tremble.
Only after that first tremble does the yoghurt stop being at risk of splitting, and you may stop stirring.
Add the cooked chickpeas, the rice and hazelnut-sized beef meatballs.
Finish with generous herbs and dried mint fried in butter, poured over as you serve.

gheymeh.d: A lamb stew with yellow split peas and dried lime, topped with chips. It is the dish given away free during Muharram, cooked in pots of several hundred litres and served to whole neighbourhoods.
s: Fry the onion at length, until it browns frankly: it gives the stew its colour and its base.
Add the turmeric and let it toast in the oil before the meat, or it keeps a raw powdery taste.
Pierce the dried limes twice and add them whole: cut further, they release their bitterness and make the dish inedible.
Cook the split peas separately for twenty minutes before adding them: in from the start, they collapse into purée.
Serve covered with matchstick chips, made separately and set on at the last moment.

sholeh-zard.d: A rice pudding with saffron, rosewater and cardamom, served cold and decorated. It is made as nazri, a votive offering distributed to neighbours in thanks for an answered prayer, and its cinnamon decoration often carries a pattern or a name.
s: Soak the rice two hours, then cook it in plenty of water until the grains break down completely.
Add the sugar only once the rice has fully burst: added earlier, it hardens the grain and the cooking never finishes.
Allow another hour after the sugar, over very low heat, stirring regularly.
Infuse the ground saffron in a little hot water for twenty minutes and add it, then the butter, cardamom and rosewater at the end.
Pour into shallow bowls and cool. Decorate with ground cinnamon and crushed pistachios.

bastani-sonnati.d: A saffron and rosewater ice cream studded with pistachios and shards of frozen cream. Its stretchy texture comes from salep, wild orchid flour: it pulls on the spoon and melts far more slowly than an ordinary ice cream.
s: Slake the salep in cold milk before any heat: poured into hot liquid it lumps in a way nothing later dissolves.
Heat gently, whisking, until the mixture visibly thickens, a good fifteen minutes.
Infuse the saffron separately and add it off the heat with the rosewater — heat carries off their aromas.
Spread thick cream on a tray and freeze it separately, then break it into shards.
Churn the ice cream and fold in the shards and pistachios at the end. Salep makes the texture deliberately stretchy, which is not a fault.

gaz.d: A white nougat with pistachios, scented with rosewater. Genuine gaz is made from tamarisk manna, a sweet sap an insect makes weep from the branches in the Zagros mountains; it is gathered by hand, and sugar replaces it only imperfectly.
s: Bring the sugar, glucose and water to 140°C on a thermometer, never stirring once it boils.
Whip the whites to firm peaks while the syrup cooks: they must be ready at the exact moment it reaches temperature.
Pour the syrup in a thin stream onto the whites, whisking without pause, down the side of the bowl and not onto the whisk.
Keep whisking ten minutes, until the mass turns very firm and loses its gloss.
Fold in the pistachios and rosewater, spread between two starch-dusted sheets and dry twelve hours.

nan-e-berenji.d: Rice flour shortbreads with cardamom, so short they dissolve in the mouth. They contain no wheat flour at all: with no gluten the dough holds only through fat, and the slightest overhandling crumbles it before baking.
s: Beat the clarified butter and icing sugar for twenty minutes, until the mixture pales and triples in volume.
That long beating is what replaces the gluten: it works in the air that will give the shortness.
Beat in the yolks, rosewater and ground cardamom, then the rice flour all at once, with a spatula.
Rest the dough two hours in the cold before shaping the discs, never kneading it.
Mark a pattern with a fork, scatter poppy seeds and bake 15 minutes at 160°C. They must stay white, without colouring.

shir-berenj.d: An unsweetened rice pudding served with jam or syrup on the side. Unlike sholeh zard it holds neither saffron nor sugar: it is a winter breakfast, and each person sweetens their own bowl.
s: Cook the rice in water first, fifteen minutes, until it has absorbed all the water and begins to split.
Then add hot milk in three additions, waiting each time for it to be absorbed before the next.
Poured in at once, the milk stops the starch releasing and the rice stays in separate grains instead of turning creamy.
Allow forty-five minutes over very low heat, stirring every five minutes.
Scent with rosewater and cardamom off the heat. Serve warm, with black cherry jam alongside.

dizi.d: A lamb and chickpea stew cooked in a stone pot, eaten in two courses. First the broth is drunk with torn bread, then the solids are pounded to a paste: one dish provides both a soup and a main course.
s: Soak the chickpeas and white beans twelve hours, changing the water twice.
Put everything in a clay or stone pot and cover with cold water, without salting.
Cook four hours over very low heat, or three hours in a 150°C oven: the pot should barely tremble.
Salt only in the third hour — early salt stops the pulses softening.
Strain the broth into a bowl, pound the solids to a smooth paste, and serve the two together.

mahi-shekam-por.d: A whole fish stuffed with herbs, walnuts and pomegranate molasses, roasted. It is the Nowruz dish of the Caspian coast: fish replaces the lamb of the plateau, and the sweet-sour stuffing is the same as fesenjan's.
s: Gut the fish through the gills rather than the belly if you can: the stuffing holds far better in a closed cavity.
Otherwise slit the belly and plan to sew it up with kitchen thread.
Chop the walnuts roughly and dry-toast them: raw, they make the stuffing pasty and faintly bitter.
Fry the onion, garlic and herbs, add the walnuts, barberries and pomegranate molasses, and cool before stuffing.
Roast 45 minutes at 190°C, basting with saffron oil every fifteen minutes.

ash-e-shalgham.d: A thick soup of turnip, pulses and herbs, held to be good against colds. In Iran turnip is classed as a warm food under the humoral system inherited from Greco-Arabic medicine, and it is eaten in winter for exactly that reason.
s: Soak the pulses overnight and cook them separately: they do not share a cooking time, and together some collapse while others stay hard.
Brown the sliced onions at length in oil, until frankly coloured.
Add the turmeric, then the turnips in large dice, and let them take colour before moistening.
Bring pulses, rice and turnips together and simmer forty minutes, until the soup thickens by itself.
Add the herbs at the end and serve with kashk and dried mint fried in oil.

kotlet.d: Flat patties of minced meat and grated potato, fried. They arrived from Europe in the early twentieth century along with the word itself; in Iran they are eaten cold, tucked into bread, and are the travelling meal par excellence.
s: Grate the raw potato and onion, then wring them in a cloth until all the water is out.
That water causes every failure: a wet mixture disintegrates in the oil and the patty falls apart.
Work the meat and grated vegetables by hand for ten minutes, until the mass turns even and tacky.
Rest an hour in the cold, then shape very flat oval patties, a centimetre at most.
Fry over medium heat in two centimetres of oil, four minutes a side. Eaten hot or cold, with bread and pickles.

noon-e-sangak.d: A large sourdough flatbread baked directly on a bed of scalding pebbles. Sangak means little pebble: the dough is thrown onto the stones, which leave hollow prints in the crumb, and the loaf must be shaken on leaving the oven to make them fall out.
s: Use wholemeal flour and very high hydration, around 75%: the dough must be frankly sticky.
Ferment twelve hours with sourdough at room temperature, until it triples and smells sour.
Heat a bed of clean pebbles in a 280°C oven for at least an hour — the stones must be scalding through.
Spread the dough by hand directly onto the pebbles, in a long oval, and scatter with seeds.
Ten minutes is enough. Shake the loaf on removal to knock out the stones, and never forget to check before biting.

doogh.d: A salted yoghurt drink with mint, often lightly sparkling. Traditional doogh ferments a few days and fizzes by itself; the industrial version adds gas, which Iranians tell apart at once by taste.
s: Use a full-fat plain yoghurt with a good sourness: a mild yoghurt gives a flat drink that salt will not rescue.
Whisk it alone first until perfectly smooth, before adding any water.
Add iced water little by little, whisking: poured in at once it leaves lumps of yoghurt suspended.
Salt frankly — doogh is a salted drink, and a timid hand makes it insipid.
Add dried mint crushed between the fingers and rose petals, and rest an hour in the cold.

chai-irani.d: Black tea brewed on a samovar, served in a narrow glass and drunk through a lump of sugar. The sugar does not go in the glass: it is held between the teeth and the tea passes through it, letting each sip be sweetened to taste.
s: Boil the water in the samovar body and scald the teapot standing on it before adding the tea.
Put the tea in the pot with the cardamom and only a little boiling water, to make a very strong concentrate.
Let that concentrate steep twenty minutes on the samovar, in the steam's heat and never over a direct flame.
Serve by pouring a little concentrate into the glass and lengthening it with boiling water, to the strength wanted.
The tea should be mahogany red and perfectly translucent. Cloudy, it has boiled and turns bitter.

shawarma.d: Spice-marinated meat roasted on a spit and served in flatbread with tahini. The word comes from Turkish çevirme, turning; the Levantine version is marked by its acidic vinegar and seven-spice marinade, more fragrant than döner.
s: Marinate the sliced meat twenty-four hours in vinegar, seven-spice and ground cardamom.
Cardamom is what distinguishes Levantine shawarma: it must be clearly noticeable without dominating.
Stack on the spit inserting fat every five centimetres, and crown it with a whole piece of fat.
That fat cap melts throughout and bastes the stack: without it, the top of the spit dries out.
Shave thinly and serve in pita with lemony tahini, pickles and sumac.

bourekas.d: Savoury pastries filled with cheese, spinach or potato. The shape indicates the filling: triangle for cheese, rectangle for potato, square for spinach — a code every Israeli bakery follows, for reasons of kashrut.
s: Respect the code of shapes: it is a practical necessity, kashrut forbids mixing meat and milk, and the customer must know what they are buying.
Squeeze the blanched spinach out thoroughly by hand: its water would soak the pastry from below.
Drain the ricotta an hour and mix it with crushed feta, adding no salt — the feta brings enough.
Glaze with egg and seed according to the filling: sesame on cheese, nigella on potato.
Bake 30 minutes at 200°C. Serve with a crushed hard-boiled egg and a spiced tomato relish.

rugelach.d: Small rolled crescents filled with chocolate and dipped in syrup. The Jerusalem version differs from the American: the dough is yeasted rather than a cream-cheese shortcrust, and the rugelach leave the oven to be plunged in sugar syrup.
s: Make an enriched yeasted dough and rest it overnight in the refrigerator: cold, it rolls without tearing.
Roll into a large circle, spread the chocolate paste and cut into triangles like a tart.
Roll each triangle from base to point, without tightening: rolled too tight, the rugelach unfurls as it bakes.
Prove an hour, glaze and bake 22 minutes at 190°C.
Plunge them scalding into cold syrup for ten seconds, drain on a rack. That bath gives the characteristic shine.

halva-tahini.d: A confection of sesame paste and sugar syrup, fibrous and crumbly. The fibres come from a brief kneading right after mixing: overworked, halva turns smooth and pasty, losing what makes it interesting.
s: Use a good tahini, entirely fluid, and stir it thoroughly: a separated tahini gives a greasy, unstable halva.
Bring the sugar, water and honey to 118°C, then let the syrup fall back to 105°C.
Pour it onto the warmed tahini and fold with a spatula in figures of eight, for thirty seconds only.
The mixture first turns liquid, then thickens abruptly and streaks: stop at that precise moment.
Pour into a mould without pressing and rest twelve hours at room temperature before slicing.

mandi.d: Lamb cooked in a pit oven above the rice that receives its juices. The taboon is a shaft heated with wood then emptied of coals: the meat hangs inside and the rice sits below, and the pit is sealed until the next day.
s: Rub the lamb with the hawaij spice blend and rest it two hours at room temperature.
Boil the meat for an hour first, and keep that broth: it will cook the rice, not plain water.
Pierce the dried limes twice and add them whole to the broth.
Lay the soaked rice in a dish, pour over the strained broth, and hang the meat above it without touching.
Seal tightly and cook three hours at 160°C. The meat juices fall into the rice throughout.

saleeg.d: A creamy rice cooked in chicken broth and milk, served with the whole bird. It is a dish of the Hejaz, in the west of the kingdom, and differs from every other rice of the peninsula in its texture: here creaminess is sought, elsewhere separate grains.
s: Poach the chicken an hour with the whole spices, then remove it and strain the broth.
Use a short-grain rice, never basmati: the short grain's starch gives the creaminess wanted.
Do not rinse the rice — unlike every other Gulf rice dish, here the surface starch is useful.
Cook it in the broth, stirring regularly like a risotto, for forty minutes.
Add hot milk little by little towards the end, and the pounded mastic. Serve the grilled chicken whole on the rice.

haneeth.d: Lamb cooked five hours in a pit oven, with no rice beneath the meat. It differs from mandi precisely there: mandi cooks the rice under the meat, haneeth cooks the meat alone, and the rice is made separately.
s: Score the leg deeply to the bone every three centimetres, and rub the marinade into every cut.
Marinate twelve hours in yoghurt, spices, garlic and lemon.
Wrap the meat in paper or leaves before it goes in: haneeth cooks smothered, not dry.
Cook five hours at 140°C, or in a pit oven if you have one.
The meat is ready when it leaves the bone with a light pull. Give it two minutes under the grill to colour the surface.

matazeez.d: Discs of dough poached in a lamb and vegetable stew. The dough is rolled very thin and laid on the stew at the end: it cooks in the broth's steam rather than in it, staying supple instead of disintegrating.
s: Knead a soft dough with water and salt and rest it an hour under a damp cloth.
Simmer the lamb an hour with the spices and pierced dried limes, then add the vegetables.
Roll the dough very thin and cut ten-centimetre discs, flouring them to stack.
Lay them in layers on the simmering stew, separated by a little broth, without pushing them under.
