Cover and cook twenty minutes in the steam. Submerged, the discs dissolve and thicken everything to glue.

maamoul.d: Semolina shortbreads filled with dates or pistachios, pressed in a carved wooden mould. The mould patterns are not decorative: each shape denotes a filling, so date maamoul can be told from nut maamoul without opening them.
s: Mix the semolina with melted clarified butter and rest twelve hours: the semolina must drink up all the fat.
That rest is obligatory; worked at once, the dough stays sandy and the maamoul crumbles on unmoulding.
Add the warm milk with the yeast and mahlab, and knead just enough to bring it together.
Form a cup in your palm, fill, close and press into the floured wooden mould.
Bake 20 minutes at 170°C: they must stay white. Browned, they are overcooked and turn dry.

luqaimat.d: Small fried dough balls, crisp outside and hollow within, drenched in date syrup. They are made throughout Ramadan and eaten at the breaking of the fast: their fast sugar was the first food of the evening before the meal.
s: Make a very loose batter, almost pourable, and prove it two hours until covered in bubbles.
The cornflour mixed into the flour is what gives the hollow: without it the ball is dense and solid.
Squeeze the batter between thumb and forefinger by closing your fist, and drop the ball into oil at 175°C.
Fry, stirring constantly with a skimmer so they turn and colour evenly, four minutes.
Douse with hot date syrup straight out of the oil, while they are still scalding.

qahwa-arabe.d: A very lightly roasted coffee with saffron and cardamom, served unsweetened in small cups. Its colour is straw yellow rather than black: the roast stops well short of the Western one, and the taste owes more to a spice infusion than to coffee.
s: Roast the green beans in a pan very lightly, to a straw colour: no brown and no smell of scorching.
Grind them coarsely with the cardamom, just before brewing.
Bring the water to a tremble, add the coffee and infuse ten minutes without ever boiling.
Add the saffron and cloves at the end of the infusion, and rest five minutes for the grounds to settle.
Serve in small handleless cups filled only a third, with dates alongside. It is never sweetened.

madrouba.d: A beaten chicken rice cooked to a smooth porridge. Madrouba means beaten: the rice is crushed with a whisk at the end until it loses all shape, and it is a Ramadan dish served to the elderly and the sick.
s: Poach the chicken an hour with the spices and dried limes, then bone it and keep the broth.
Cook the rice in that broth well past the normal point, forty minutes, until it collapses completely.
Return the shredded chicken and beat with a whisk for ten minutes, crushing the rice against the sides.
The texture must become perfectly smooth, with no identifiable grain: that is the whole principle.
Add hot milk to loosen it and top with scalding ghee and fried onion before serving.

tharid.d: A lamb and vegetable stew poured over thin bread. It is one of the oldest dishes of the peninsula, mentioned in the hadith; the bread, raqaq, is laid in the bottom of the dish and absorbs all the broth.
s: Brown the lamb then the onions, add the tomato paste and let it toast before moistening.
Pierce the dried limes and add them whole: split, they release a bitterness that dominates everything.
Simmer an hour and a half, then add the vegetables in order of firmness over the last half hour.
Line the serving dish with thin bread in layers, and pour the scalding broth over.
Wait five minutes for the bread to soak before arranging meat and vegetables on top. The bread should be melting, never crisp.

kunafa-golfe.d: Melting cheese under an orange-tinted semolina, drenched in syrup. It differs from Turkish künefe in the top layer: fine coloured semolina rather than shredded pastry, giving a sandy rather than stringy crust.
s: Desalt the akkawi cheese six hours in cold water, changing it four times, then grate it.
Insufficiently desalted cheese makes the dessert inedible, and there is no way to correct it afterwards.
Colour the semolina with annatto slaked in the clarified butter: industrial red colouring gives a garish tint and an aftertaste.
Press half the buttered semolina into the base, add the cheese without touching the edges, then the rest.
Bake 30 minutes at 200°C and pour cold syrup over the scalding kunafa, straight from the oven.

gersh.d: A saffron and cardamom cake, baked in a ring mould and covered with sesame. It bears the name of a Kuwaiti dhow captain who took it to sea: it keeps two weeks without drying out, which few cakes manage.
s: Infuse the ground saffron in warm rosewater at least two hours ahead: it needs time to give up its colour.
Whisk whole eggs and sugar for twenty minutes, until the mixture triples and forms a thick ribbon.
That whisking is what lightens the cake: there is no creamed butter, everything rests on air worked into the eggs.
Beat in the oil in a thin stream, very slowly, as for a mayonnaise, then fold in the sifted flour.
Butter the tin and line it with sesame before pouring in the batter. Bake 40 minutes at 175°C without opening the oven.

qursan.d: Dried wheat discs broken up and soaked in a lamb stew. The discs are made in advance and keep for months; it is nomad food, where the bread serves as both starch and thickener.
s: Knead a firm dough with salted water and roll it into very thin twenty-centimetre discs.
Cook them dry on a scalding plate, one minute a side, then air-dry them for two days.
They must become brittle as cardboard: badly dried, they mould in storage.
Make the lamb stew and simmer it an hour and a half, to a strong broth.
Break the discs into the dish, pour over the scalding broth and let them swell ten minutes before serving.

muqaddam.d: A spiced fish rice, half of it hidden under a layer of caramelised onions. The name means the one placed in front: the dish is turned out inverted, and the blackened onion layer that appears on top is the part served first.
s: Marinate the fish steaks in turmeric, garlic and tamarind for an hour.
Fry the sliced onions until frankly brown, almost black, a good half hour.
That hard caramelisation gives muqaddam its colour and gentle bitterness; pale gold onions will not do.
Brown the fish, then build in layers: parboiled rice, onions, fish, rice.
Cook thirty minutes covered over very low heat, then invert the whole dish onto a large tray.

welsh-rarebit-nordiste.d: Cheddar melted in brown ale, poured over toast lined with ham and crowned with an egg. Brought by Welsh miners to the north, it became the dish of the Opal Coast taverns.
s: Dice the cheddar and melt it very gently in the ale, never boiling: too hot and it strings and splits.
Add the mustard and Worcestershire sauce, and season well with pepper.
Toast the bread, line it with ham and set everything in individual dishes.
Cover with the melted cheese and give it 8 minutes under the grill, until the surface blisters and browns.
Set a fried egg on each welsh and serve with chips, as they do in the north.

ficelle-picarde.d: A pancake rolled around ham and mushrooms, gratinated under a cheese cream. Created in 1950 for a food fair in Amiens, it became the Sunday starter of the whole of Picardy.
s: Make a smooth pancake batter and rest it for an hour: without resting, the pancakes tear when rolled.
Sweat the sliced mushrooms with the shallot until all their water has gone.
Bind them with a third of the cream and let it cool.
Fill each pancake with a slice of ham and a little duxelles, then roll it tightly.
Pack them in a buttered dish, coat with the remaining cream, scatter gruyère and gratinate for 20 minutes at 200°C.

flamiche-aux-poireaux.d: A closed pie of leeks softened in cream, without a trace of bacon. The northern leek is cooked here almost to a jam: that long melting is what matters, not the pastry.
s: Rub the flour and 175 g of butter together, bind with a yolk and iced water, and rest for an hour in the cold.
Slice the leek whites very finely and melt them for 40 minutes, covered, in the remaining butter, without colouring.
They should lose three quarters of their volume and turn translucent: only then salt them.
Add the cream and two beaten eggs off the heat, and grate over the nutmeg.
Line a tin with pastry, fill it, cover with a second disc, seal the edges and bake for 45 minutes at 190°C.

caudiere-berckoise.d: The bouillabaisse of the north: Channel fish, potatoes and cream, without saffron or tomato. The name comes from the cauldron, the caudière, that Berck fishermen set on the sand when the tide returned.
s: Open the mussels in white wine, shell them and strain their liquor carefully through a cloth.
Soften the onion and leek in butter without colouring, then add the potatoes in thick slices.
Moisten with the mussel liquor let down with water, add the thyme and bay, and cook for 20 minutes.
Cut the heat and slide in the fish in large pieces: they poach in the residual warmth, 8 minutes.
Add the cream and the mussels, warm through without boiling, and cover with parsley. Serve with toast.

salade-au-lard-vosgienne.d: Dandelion or lamb's lettuce dressed with hot bacon and its deglazing vinegar, with warm potatoes and a soft-boiled egg. The scorching pan is poured over the leaves: they should hiss.
s: Wash the dandelion in several changes of water and dry it thoroughly: wet leaves refuse a hot dressing.
Boil the potatoes in their skins and peel them while warm.
Fry the bacon dry until crisp, and add the shallot off the heat.
Deglaze with vinegar — the pan should smoke — and pour it over the leaves at once, tossing.
Add the sliced potatoes, croutons, diced Munster and one soft-boiled egg per plate.

pate-lorrain.d: A puff pastry case filled with pork and veal marinated in vin gris from Toul. The marinade takes twenty-four hours: without it the filling stays flat, and Lorraine will not recognise it.
s: Cut the meats into 1 cm dice by knife: minced, they would make a dense filling.
Marinate them for 24 hours in the cold with the white wine, shallot, garlic, herbs, salt and plenty of pepper.
Drain them thoroughly and discard the marinade: kept, it would sog the pastry.
Roll the pastry into two rectangles, fill the first leaving a two-centimetre border, and cover with the second.
Seal, crimp the edges, glaze with egg, cut a steam hole and bake for 45 minutes at 200°C.

poulet-au-vinaigre.d: Chicken deglazed with wine vinegar, finished with cream and tomato. Paul Bocuse made it a bouchon dish: the sharpness should stay frank, and is not meant to be softened.
s: Joint the chicken into eight and colour it in butter on all sides, without hurrying.
Add the unpeeled garlic and the shallot, cover and sweat for 10 minutes.
Pour in the vinegar and reduce it by half uncovered: this is where the harshness goes and the flavour stays.
Add the wine, tomato, tomato paste and stock, and simmer covered for 30 minutes.
Lift out the chicken, finish the sauce with cream and cold butter, and add the tarragon off the heat.

gratin-de-cardons.d: Cardoon ribs long-blanched and gratinated under a beef marrow sauce. It is the Christmas vegetable in Lyon: found only in December, and it takes three hours to tame.
s: String the cardoon ribs like celery, removing every fibre, and drop them straight into acidulated water: in the air they blacken within a minute.
Cook them for 1½ hours in a blanc — water, slaked flour and lemon — which keeps them pale.
Soak the marrow for 2 hours in iced water, then poach it for 10 minutes and cut it into rounds.
Make a roux, moisten with beef stock, cook for 15 minutes and add cream.
Lay the drained cardoons in a dish, arrange the marrow, coat with sauce, scatter gruyère and gratinate for 30 minutes at 200°C.

poulet-gaston-gerard.d: Chicken with cream, mustard and comté, gratinated with breadcrumbs. Born of an accident in 1930: the Dijon mayor's wife spilt paprika into the pan and rescued it with cheese in front of Curnonsky.
s: Joint the chicken and colour it in butter, skin down first, in an ovenproof pot.
Dust with paprika, cover and cook for 30 minutes over low heat.
Lift out the chicken, deglaze with white wine and reduce by half.
Add the cream and mustard off the heat — boiled, mustard turns bitter — then half the comté.
Return the chicken, coat it, scatter the remaining cheese and the breadcrumbs, and gratinate for 15 minutes at 220°C.

gougeres-au-jambon-persille.d: A pudding of stale brioche, milk and walnuts, baked in the bread oven after the batch. It is made savoury with bacon or sweet depending on the village: Burgundy never agreed on it.
s: Cut the stale brioche into large cubes and pack them into a buttered dish.
Bring the milk to a bare simmer with the split vanilla and cinnamon, and infuse off the heat for 15 minutes.
Beat the eggs and sugar, pour in the hot milk in a thin stream while whisking, without scrambling them.
Pour over the brioche and let it drink for 30 minutes: it must be thoroughly soaked before it goes in the oven.
Scatter crushed walnuts and bake for 50 minutes at 170°C in a water bath. Serve warm with redcurrant jelly.

saupiquet-morvandiau.d: Slices of Morvan ham under a sauce of cream, juniper and vinegar. Saupiquet comes from 'salt that stings': the medieval sauce was sharp, and it has stayed so.
s: Sweat the chopped shallots in butter without colouring, with the crushed juniper berries.
Add the vinegar and reduce it almost to nothing: the smell should stop catching the nose.
Add the wine, reduce by half, then dust in a spoonful of flour and moisten with the stock.
Cook gently for 15 minutes, strain through a fine sieve pressing well, and finish with cream.
Warm the ham slices through in the sauce without letting them boil, and serve with steamed potatoes.

pounti-auvergnat.d: A meat loaf with chard and prunes, halfway between savoury and sweet. Auvergne serves it warm as a starter or cold in slices: the harvest dish, always.
s: Soak the prunes in warm tea while you prepare everything else.
Roughly chop the chard, onion, parsley, bacon and pork — by knife, to keep some texture.
Make a smooth batter with the flour, eggs and milk, then fold in the chopped mixture.
Pour half into a buttered tin, arrange the stoned prunes, and cover with the rest.
Bake for 55 minutes at 180°C. The pounti turns out warm and slices more cleanly cold.

chou-farci-auvergnat.d: A whole cabbage rebuilt leaf by leaf around a stuffing, tied and braised for three hours. It is not chopped: it is reassembled, leaf after leaf, until the original cabbage takes shape again.
s: Blanch the whole cabbage for 10 minutes, refresh it and peel the leaves off one by one, keeping them in order.
Pare away the thickest ribs with a knife, without piercing the leaf.
Mix the pork, bacon, squeezed soaked bread, softened onion, garlic, eggs and parsley.
In a cloth, rebuild the cabbage: the largest leaves at the bottom, then a layer of stuffing, leaves, stuffing, up to the heart.
Tie the cloth, set the cabbage on a bed of carrots, add wine and stock, and braise for 2½ hours at 160°C.

sanciau-bourbonnais.d: A thick pancake of wheat and buckwheat flour, cooked in lard, served savoury or dusted with sugar. It was supper in poor Bourbonnais: flour, an egg, and whatever milk was left.
s: Mix the two flours and the salt, make a well, break in the eggs and slacken with milk, lump-free.
Rest for an hour: the batter should stay thick, closer to blini batter than to crêpe batter.
Melt a good spoonful of lard in a cast-iron pan, until it just smokes.
Pour in a thick ladleful and let it set for 6 minutes untouched: the sanciau is flipped in one movement.
Serve it savoury with fried bacon, or sweet with pan-fried apples.

clafoutis-limousin.d: A baked black cherry custard whose fruit is emphatically not stoned. The stone perfumes the custard with almond as it bakes: removing it, in Limousin, is making something else.
s: Wash and stem the cherries without stoning them, and macerate them for 30 minutes in sugar and brandy.
Butter an earthenware dish generously and sugar it: the caramelised rim depends on it.
Whisk the eggs and sugar, add the flour, then the milk and cream in a thin stream, and the scraped vanilla.
Pack the cherries tightly over the base and pour the batter over them.
Bake for 40 minutes at 180°C. Serve warm, never cold, and warn your guests about the stones.

poulet-basquaise.d: Chicken stewed in a piperade of sweet peppers, tomatoes and Espelette chilli. The peppers must melt for an hour before the bird goes in: they are the dish, the meat is merely invited.
s: Colour the jointed chicken in olive oil, then set it aside.
Soften the onion, peppers in strips and garlic in the same oil, covered, for 40 minutes.
Add the peeled crushed tomatoes and reduce for another 20 minutes: the piperade should thicken, not swim.
Deglaze with white wine, add the Espelette chilli and the diced Bayonne ham.
Return the chicken, cover and simmer for 35 minutes. Serve with white rice.

chipirons-a-l-encre.d: Small squid stewed in a black sauce made from their own ink. They are stuffed with their chopped tentacles: nothing is wasted, and the ink colour frightens as much as it draws.
s: Clean the squid keeping the ink sacs intact in a bowl: burst too early, they are lost.
Chop the tentacles with a little garlic and parsley, and stuff the bodies with them, closed with a cocktail stick.
Soften the onion, pepper and garlic at length in the oil — 40 minutes covered — until jammy.
Add the tomato, wine, breadcrumb and the ink slaked in a little water, then blend and pass through a sieve.
Poach the squid for 25 minutes in this black sauce, over the gentlest heat: boiled, they turn to rubber.

aligot-saucisse-de-toulouse.d: The coiled sausage, pricked and grilled slowly, on a bed of beans in goose fat. It is never cut before cooking: it is seared whole, coiled on itself, and shared at the table.
s: Soak the beans overnight, then cook them for 1 hour with the carrot, clove-studded onion and bay.
Prick the sausage with a needle in a dozen places: without this it bursts and loses all its juice.
Cook it in goose fat for 25 minutes over very low heat, turning it halfway with two spatulas.
Fry the garlic and tomato in the rendered fat, add the drained beans and stew for 15 minutes.
Serve the whole coil set on the beans, with parsley, and cut it in front of your guests.

brouillade-aux-truffes.d: Eggs scrambled over a water bath, perfumed by a black truffle shut in with them the day before. The shell is porous: the egg takes the scent without being cracked, and that is the real secret.
s: The day before, shut the brushed truffle and the whole eggs in an airtight box in the cold.
On the day, beat the eggs barely, without aerating them: a brouillade is made with a fork, not a whisk.
Cook them over a simmering water bath, stirring constantly with a spatula, for a full 15 minutes.
Take them off the heat while still too runny: residual warmth finishes the job.
Fold in the cold butter, cream and grated truffle off the heat, and serve at once on toast.

grand-aioli.d: Poached salt cod and every vegetable from the garden around a mortar of aïoli. It is the Provençal Friday meal, and the whole dish takes its name from the sauce: without it, it is just a vegetable platter.
s: Soak the salt cod for 24 hours in cold water, changing the water five times.
Pound the degermed garlic with a pinch of coarse salt into a perfectly smooth cream: the mortar is not negotiable.
Add the yolks, then the olive oil drop by drop at first, always turning the same way.
If the sauce splits, start again with a fresh yolk and beat the failed sauce into it a spoonful at a time.
Poach the cod for 10 minutes without boiling, cook each vegetable separately, and arrange everything around the mortar.

boles-de-picolat.d: Pork and beef meatballs stewed with green olives and ceps, Catalan style. The Sunday dish of Roussillon; reheated on Monday, and everyone agrees it is better then.
s: Soak the breadcrumb in milk, squeeze it, and mix it with the meats, eggs, garlic and parsley. Rest for an hour in the cold.
Roll walnut-sized balls, flour them and brown them in lard, without stirring too soon.
Soften the onions in the same fat, add the tomato and the white wine.
Add the soaked ceps and their strained liquor, then return the meatballs.
Simmer for 45 minutes, adding the desalted olives for the last 15.

anchoiade-collioure.d: A paste of salted anchovies, garlic and olive oil, served warm with raw vegetables. Collioure has salted anchovies since the Middle Ages; they are rinsed but never fully desalted.
s: Rinse the salted anchovies in clean water and pat them dry, but do not soak them: they would lose their character.
Pound them in a mortar with the degermed garlic and blanched almonds, into a coarse paste.
Work in the olive oil in a thin stream, as for a mayonnaise, then the vinegar and picked thyme.
Warm the sauce over a water bath without ever letting it tremble: heated, it splits.
Serve in the mortar, with raw celery, radishes, fennel and thick slices of country bread.

tourte-aux-herbes-nicoise.d: A tart of long Nice squash, rice and parmesan, glazed with olive oil. It is eaten cold, cut into squares, and travels well: it was the dockworkers' lunch.
s: Knead the flour, olive oil, warm water and salt into a supple dough; rest it for an hour.
Coarsely grate the squash, salt it and let it drain for 30 minutes, then squeeze it hard between your hands.
Soften the onion in oil, cook the rice halfway, and let both cool.
Mix the squeezed squash, rice, onion, parmesan, eggs, chopped basil and nutmeg.
Line a tin with thin pastry, fill it, cover with a second disc, oil the top and bake for 45 minutes at 190°C.

sardines-farcies-provencales.d: Sardines opened flat, filled with spinach and parmesan, packed tightly in a dish. They are opened with the thumb, not a knife: the fish parts along the bone by itself if you do it right.
s: Scale the sardines, open them from the belly with your thumb and pull the backbone out towards the tail.
Wilt the spinach, squeeze it very dry and chop it.
Mix it with the squeezed soaked bread, parmesan, eggs, garlic and parsley.
Fill half the sardines, cover each with a second one flesh to flesh, and pack them tightly.
Drizzle with olive oil, scatter breadcrumbs and bake for 18 minutes at 200°C. Serve warm with lemon.

omelette-de-la-mere-poulard.d: An omelette beaten for twenty minutes and cooked over a wood fire in a long-handled pan. Annette Poulard fed pilgrims this way from 1888; she always refused to give the recipe, saying there wasn't one.
s: Separate the whites from the yolks. Beat the yolks with the cream, salt and pepper.
Whisk the whites to very stiff peaks, at length — that is the secret, and there is no other.
Fold the yolks gently into the whites, lifting the mass, never stirring.
Foam a large knob of butter in a scorching pan and pour in the mixture all at once.
Let it puff for 5 minutes untouched, fold it in two and serve immediately: it collapses within a minute.

douillons-normands.d: Whole pears sealed in shortcrust and baked, the stalk left poking out. In Normandy they are made with apple, as bourdelots; with pear they keep an elegance the apple lacks.
s: Rub the flour and cold butter together, bind with a yolk and iced water, and rest for an hour in the cold.
Peel the pears keeping the stalks, and core them from below with a corer.
Fill the hollow with a mixture of butter, sugar, cinnamon and a drop of calvados.
Roll out the pastry, cut discs, and wrap each pear by drawing the pastry up, leaving the stalk out.
Glaze with egg and bake for 40 minutes at 190°C. Serve warm with cream and redcurrant jelly.

lentilles-au-petit-sale.d: Green Puy lentils and salted pork ribs, simmered together and never boiled. Puy lentils are not soaked: the skin is so fine it would burst, and they must stay whole.
s: Soak the salt pork for 4 hours in cold water, then blanch it for 10 minutes and discard that water.
Rinse the lentils without soaking and put them in cold unsalted water: salted in advance, they stay hard.
Add the clove-studded onion, carrot, garlic, thyme and bay, and bring to a bare simmer.
Add the meat and cook for 45 minutes without ever boiling: a rolling boil would split the skins.
Add the sausage for the last 20 minutes. Salt at the end, add butter and serve with mustard.

kouign-amann-malouin.d: The individual version of the Douarnenez cake, baked in a mould rather than as one large round. Saint-Malo adopted it late, in the 20th century, and cut it to fit the hand: the edges caramelise more, which is the whole point.
s: Knead the flour, yeast slaked in warm water and salt, with no butter at all, and prove for 1½ hours.
Roll the dough into a rectangle, lay the very cold salted butter as a slab in the centre, and enclose it like a letter.
Give three single turns, sugaring generously between each, with 20 minutes' rest in the cold: the sugar must stay in layers, never dissolve into the dough.
Cut 10 cm squares, fold the four corners to the centre and set them in buttered, sugared muffin moulds.
Prove for 45 minutes, scatter pearl sugar, and bake for 35 minutes at 200°C. Turn out while scalding, or the caramel sets and the cake stays in the tin.

moules-a-la-malouine.d: Bouchot mussels opened in dry cider and finished with cream, with a hint of curry. The curry came from Saint-Malo shipowners, who brought back from the Indies what Brittany lacked: it barely registers, and is missed the moment it is left out.
s: Scrub the mussels and pull the beard towards the hinge; discard any that stay open after a sharp tap.
Soften the chopped shallots in salted butter, without colouring, with the thyme and bay.
Add the curry off the heat — thirty seconds too long and it turns powdery — then pour in the cider and bring to the boil.
Tip in the mussels all at once, cover, and shake the pot twice: they open within 4 minutes, no longer.
Lift them out, reduce the liquor by half, add the cream off the heat, and pour it back over. Never salt: the sea has seen to that.

madeleines-au-beurre-bordier.d: Madeleines made with churned Saint-Malo butter, whose hump depends on a shock of temperature. Jean-Yves Bordier has churned by the old method since 1985 in rue de l'Orme: his butter, worked with a wooden roller, stands comparison with any.
s: Melt the butter until it foams and smells of hazelnut, then let it cool: that is where the flavour comes from.
Whisk the eggs, sugar and honey to the ribbon, then fold in the flour sifted with the baking powder.
Add the warm browned butter and the zest, cover with cling film touching the surface and rest 12 hours in the fridge.
That rest is not a precaution: it creates the hump, by holding the rise back until the oven.
Fill very cold buttered moulds three-quarters full and bake 4 minutes at 240°C, then 8 minutes at 180°C.

craquelins-malouins.d: A ball of dough poached in boiling water before baking, which dries out hollow. Saint-Malo sailors took it to sea: with no yeast and no fat, it keeps for months and does not mould.
s: Knead the flour, eggs, milk, sugar and salt for 15 minutes: the dough should be very firm, almost hard to work.
Rest it for an hour under a cloth, then divide it into smooth 40 g balls.
Poach them in small batches in barely simmering water: they sink, then rise after about 3 minutes.
Drain them and let them dry for 30 minutes on a cloth, without stacking: that drying is what makes them hollow.
Bake for 25 minutes at 180°C, until pale gold and hollow-sounding. They keep for weeks in a tin.

huitres-de-cancale-gratinees.d: Cancale flat oysters given a few minutes under the grill, under a cider and shallot butter. The Cancale beds supplied Louis XIV's table, the oysters carried to Versailles by relays of horses.
s: Open the oysters with a flat knife and discard the first liquor: they make a second, finer one within minutes.
Free the oyster from its muscle so nobody has to do it at the table.
Reduce the chopped shallot in the cider until almost no liquid remains, then let it cool.
Work this into the softened salted butter with the parsley, and set a hazelnut of it on each oyster.
Steady the shells in a bed of coarse salt, scatter breadcrumbs, and give them 3 minutes under a fierce grill: the edge should barely curl. Longer and the oyster shrivels to rubber.

ravioles-au-saint-marcellin.d: Tiny squares of pasta, sixteen to a sheet, filled with the town's own cheese rather than Comté alone. The word raviole appears in Dauphiné as early as 1228; the cheese gave the town its name — or the reverse, the argument is unsettled.
s: Knead the flour, eggs, water and salt for 10 minutes, then rest the dough for an hour in the cold under a cloth.
Choose Saint-Marcellin at their peak, creamy under the rind: too young they stay chalky, too ripe they run and soak the filling.
Mash them with a fork together with the grated Comté, well-drained fromage blanc, crushed garlic, herbs and nutmeg.
Roll the dough to 0.6 mm — you should be able to read through it — set hazelnuts of filling every 3 cm, cover with a second sheet and seal with your fingertips before cutting with a wheel.
Poach for 1 minute in barely trembling water, never at a boil: they rise and it is done. Serve them coated in cream reduced with butter, or given 2 minutes under the grill.

galette-saucisse.d: A grilled pork sausage rolled in a cold buckwheat pancake, eaten standing at the Lices market and in the stands of the Roazhon Park. No butter, no mustard, no ketchup: in Rennes the question was settled long ago and is reopened every Saturday.
s: Mix the buckwheat flour, coarse salt and a third of the water, and work the batter by hand until it ribbons and bubbles.
Loosen it with the rest of the water and the egg, then rest it at least 3 hours — overnight is better: the buckwheat must hydrate fully.
Cook the pancakes on a very hot, barely greased griddle, 90 seconds on one side, 30 on the other, and stack them.
Grill the sausages slowly, without pricking them, until the skin is brown and crackling.
Set the sausage on a cold pancake and roll it tight. Hot on cold: the contrast is the whole point, and a reheated pancake cracks.

andouille-de-guemene.d: Pork chitterlings drawn one inside another then smoked over beech, which show perfect concentric rings when sliced. That Russian-doll assembly, not any mincing, is what draws the pattern: a badly threaded andouille shows at the first cut.
s: Clean and scrape the chitterlings in vinegared water, then dry-salt them for 24 hours with the thyme and bay.
Thread them smallest inside largest, like Russian dolls, pulling but never forcing: a torn casing ruins the pattern.
Truss the roll with string in a tight spiral and let it dry overnight in the cold.
Cold-smoke it over beech, 6 hours a day for several weeks for a keeping andouille — 12 hours is enough for one to be eaten soon.
Poach it for 3 hours in a cider and onion broth, never boiling. Serve warm, in thick slices, with buttered potatoes.

moules-a-la-normande.d: Marinière enriched with dry cider and Isigny cream, born on the Côte Fleurie when restaurateurs were trying to keep holidaying Parisians. Cider replaces white wine and leaves an edge of acidity that the cream rounds without erasing.
s: Scrub and beard the mussels in cold water and discard without hesitation any that stay open under finger pressure.
Sweat the chopped shallot in butter without colour, pour in the cider and let it bubble for 2 minutes to drive off the harshness.
Tip in the mussels, cover and shake the pot twice: they are done the moment they open, 3 to 4 minutes, no more.
Lift them out and keep them warm; strain the liquor, thicken it with beurre manié and add the cream off the heat.
Salt only at the end, and often not at all: the mussel liquor has already given everything. Coat and serve with chips.

tarte-au-maroilles.d: A risen-dough tart covered with melted Maroilles, served warm with a bière de garde. The cheese was born at Maroilles abbey in the 10th century; its formidable smell vanishes in the oven and leaves only hazelnut and cooked milk.
s: Knead the flour, the yeast dissolved in warm milk, one egg, the softened butter and salt for 10 minutes.
Prove for 1½ hours covered, then spread the dough in a deep tin and let it rise another 30 minutes.
Cut away the orange rind of the Maroilles and slice it thickly: it is the rind, not the paste, that carries the smell.
Beat the remaining eggs with the cream, pepper generously, and do not salt — the cheese sees to that.
Lay the slices on the dough, pour over the custard and bake for 35 minutes at 200°C. Let it settle for 15 minutes before cutting, or the tart runs.

croque-monsieur.d: It appeared around 1910 in a café on the rue des Capucines, and Proust mentions it as early as Within a Budding Grove. The name comes from the crunch; crowned with a fried egg it becomes a madame — the hat comparison is the explanation most often offered.
s: Make a tight béchamel: pale roux, hot milk in three additions, 8 minutes at a gentle boil, nutmeg and pepper.
It must coat the spoon and hold: too thin and it soaks the bread, and the croque collapses.
Butter the outside of the slices — never the inside, the béchamel handles that — and spread sauce on the inside.
Fill with ham and half the gruyère, close, then cover the top with the remaining béchamel and cheese.
Bake for 12 minutes at 200°C, high in the oven, until the top blisters and browns in patches.

jambon-beurre.d: The Parisian sandwich: half a baguette, butter, cooked ham, nothing else. There is nothing to hide behind — quality rests entirely on the three products, and the butter must be at room temperature, never straight from the fridge.
s: Choose a traditional baguette baked the same day, still ringing under the finger: a soft baguette makes a soft sandwich.
Take the butter out an hour ahead: cold, it tears instead of spreading, and tears the crumb with it.
Split the baguette without cutting through, and butter both faces generously, right to the ends.
Fold the ham in accordion pleats rather than laying it flat: you want thickness and air, not a flattened sheet.
Add a few gherkins, a touch of fleur de sel on the butter, and eat within the hour.

kouglof-alsacien.d: A raisin brioche baked in a glazed earthenware mould with twisted flutes, served on Sunday mornings with a glass of white wine. The mould is not decorative: its porous clay draws off moisture and makes the thin crust a metal tin never gives.
s: Plump the raisins in warm kirsch for at least 2 hours, and drain them thoroughly.
Knead the flour, the yeast dissolved in milk, the eggs, sugar and salt for 15 minutes, then work in the soft butter piece by piece.
The dough must leave the bowl and slap: it takes a while, and it is what makes the stringy crumb.
Prove for 1½ hours, fold in the raisins by hand, and butter the mould generously before laying a whole almond in the base of each flute.
Fill the mould two-thirds full, prove for an hour, and bake for 45 minutes at 180°C. Turn out hot and dust with icing sugar once cold.

andouillette-de-troyes.d: An andouillette of chitterlings cut into lengthwise strips, which gives it a fibrous grain rather than a smooth charcuterie paste. Legend has it that in 1560 royal troops broke off sacking Troyes to eat them, which gave the townspeople time to flee.
s: Prick the skin just three times with a needle: too many cuts and the andouillette empties as it cooks.
Brown it in a pan in butter over medium heat for 12 minutes, turning often — fierce heat would burst the skin before the centre is hot.
Set it aside in the warm and sweat the shallot in the same pan, without burning it.
Deglaze with white wine, reduce by half, add the cream then the mustard off the heat: boiled, mustard turns bitter.
Coat and serve with steamed potatoes. A cold Chablis, and nothing else.

escargots-de-bourgogne.d: Snails returned to their shells under a butter of garlic, parsley and shallot, given a blast of hot oven. The butter is the dish: the snail itself is nearly neutral, and one mops the shell with bread long after emptying it.
s: If starting from live snails, fast them for a week, purge them in coarse salt, then poach them for 2 hours in court-bouillon.
Chop the garlic, shallot and parsley very finely, then work them into softened butter with salt and plenty of pepper.
The butter must be green and even: chop by hand rather than in a blender, which turns the parsley bitter and the garlic acrid.
Slip a hazelnut of butter into each shell, the snail on top, and plug it with a generous amount more.
Wedge the shells opening upward, pour a splash of white wine into the dish, and bake for 10 minutes at 220°C: the butter should sizzle without darkening.

praluline.d: A brioche studded with crushed pink pralines, created in Roanne in 1955 and trademarked since. The pralines partly melt in the oven and stain the crumb with raspberry streaks; crushed too fine they vanish, too coarse they pierce the dough.
s: Knead the flour, yeast, eggs, sugar, milk and salt for 15 minutes, until the dough slaps against the bowl.
Add the cold butter in pieces, one at a time, and knead 10 minutes more: the dough must come back smooth and glossy.
Prove for 2 hours, knock back, then chill overnight — warm brioche dough is impossible to handle.
Crush the pralines with a rolling pin to pea-sized pieces, and fold them in by hand, in only a few turns.
Shape a crown, prove for 2 hours, and bake for 35 minutes at 165°C. Any hotter and the praline sugar would burn before the brioche was done.

fondue-savoyarde.d: Three Savoy cheeses — Beaufort, Comté and Savoy Emmental — melted in white Apremont wine. Unlike the Fribourg version, it mixes cooked pressed cheeses, which need more wine and more patience if they are not to string.
s: Rub the pot with a cut garlic clove, then discard it — raw garlic in cheese dominates everything.
Grate the three cheeses rather than dicing them: they melt evenly and do not form lumps.
Pour in the wine, heat it without boiling, and add the cheese by handfuls, stirring in figures of eight.
Add the next handful only when the previous one has disappeared: it is the only way to stop the fondue splitting.
Bind with a spoonful of cornstarch slaked in kirsch, add pepper and nutmeg, and keep it over a very low burner. The bread must be a day old, or it falls off the fork.

pate-de-pommes-de-terre.d: A puff-pastry pie filled with raw sliced potatoes, into which cream is poured through a chimney as it leaves the oven. The dish of Creuse farms, where potato stood in for the meat there was none of.
s: Slice the potatoes 2 mm thick and on no account rinse them: their starch is what will bind the filling.
Mix them with the sliced onion, garlic, parsley, salt and plenty of pepper, with a few knobs of butter.
Line a base with pastry, cover with a second disc, seal with a fork and glaze with egg yolk.
Cut a chimney in the centre, a finger wide, held open with a paper cone: without it the steam lifts the lid.
Bake for 1 hour at 180°C. On coming out, pour the scalding cream through the chimney and rest for 10 minutes before cutting.

pissaladiere.d: A bread dough covered with a kilo of melted onions, anchovies and Nice olives. The name comes from pissalat, a paste of salted fry once brushed over the dough; anchovies replaced it, but the word stayed.
s: Slice the onions very finely and melt them in olive oil with thyme and bay, covered, for an hour over very low heat.
They must become a pale, dry compote, never golden: the moment they colour they turn sweet and the dish loses its balance.
Meanwhile knead a soft olive-oil bread dough and let it rise for 1½ hours.
Roll it into a rectangle half a centimetre thick, spread with the cooled onions, and lay a lattice of anchovies.
Set an olive in each diamond and bake for 20 minutes at 220°C. Eaten warm, never scalding.

salade-nicoise.d: Tomatoes, broad beans or small artichokes, anchovies and hard-boiled egg, dressed with olive oil and nothing else. The Niçois are firm about it: no potatoes, no green beans, no vinegar, no cooked vegetable at all — it is a raw vegetable salad.
s: Quarter the tomatoes, salt them and let them drain for 20 minutes in a colander: their water would wash out the salad.
Pod the broad beans and slip off the inner skin if they are no longer young; slice the pepper and cucumber thinly.
Rub the bowl with garlic, then arrange the raw vegetables without tossing them.
Add the quartered hard-boiled eggs, anchovies, tuna and olives, and tear the basil by hand — a knife blackens it.
Dress with olive oil only, salt, and serve at once. Vinegar is the one prohibition all Nice agrees on.

tapenade.d: A paste of black olives, capers and anchovies pounded in a mortar. The name comes from tapeno, Provençal for caper, not from the olive: the caper, a minority by weight, gives the dish its name and the whole its acidity.
s: Stone the olives one by one with a knife rather than by machine, which crushes the pit and leaves bitterness.
Rinse the capers if they are salted, pat them dry, and soak the anchovies a few minutes in cold water.
Pound the garlic, then the capers, then the anchovies in a mortar, before adding the olives by handfuls.
Trickle in the oil as for mayonnaise, until you have a lumpy paste — never smooth: a blender gives a purée without character.
Sharpen with lemon juice, picked thyme, a spoonful of brandy and pepper. Do not salt: capers and anchovies see to that. Rest overnight.

calissons-d-aix.d: Diamonds of almond and candied melon paste set on rice paper and iced with egg white. Tradition ties them to King René's wedding in 1454, where the queen, said to smile rarely, tasted the sweet: di calin soun, they are little hugs.
s: Blot the candied melon and orange peel thoroughly: too wet a paste will never dry and the icing will craze.
Blend them with the ground almonds and sugar to a supple paste, then scent with orange blossom water.
Dry it out for 10 minutes in a pan, stirring constantly, until it comes away from the sides.
Spread it on the rice paper 1 cm thick, leave to dry for 12 hours in the open air, then cut out the diamonds.
Whisk the egg white with icing sugar and lemon juice, ice the tops, and give them 8 minutes at 100°C with the door ajar: the icing must set without colouring.

magret-de-canard.d: The breast of the fattened duck, seared skin-side until the fat renders, served pink. The word magret is a Gascon invention of the 1960s: until then fattened duck was eaten only as confit, and treating it like a piece of beef was thought a provocation.
s: Score the skin in a lattice without cutting the flesh: the cuts let the fat escape rather than swelling the skin.
Lay the breasts skin down in a cold pan, then bring it to medium heat: starting cold is what renders the fat instead of burning it.
Give them 8 minutes on the skin, pouring off the fat three times, then 3 minutes on the flesh side only.
Rest for 8 minutes under foil, flesh upward — without that rest all the juice ends up on the board.
Deglaze the pan with vinegar and honey, add the shallot and wine, reduce. Serve sliced on the bias, with sarladaise potatoes in duck fat.

foie-gras-du-perigord.d: A goose or duck liver deveined, seasoned, packed into a terrine and cooked at low temperature. The whole difficulty is in the deveining: a liver brought to room temperature opens without breaking, a cold one shatters.
s: Take the liver out an hour ahead and let it reach 18°C: it is the only temperature at which it deveins cleanly.
Open each lobe flat and draw out the main veins with tweezers, following their branching, without chasing the finest ones.
Season both faces — 12 g of salt and 3 g of pepper per kilo, never by eye — then moisten with port and brandy, and marinate 12 hours in the cold.
Pack into the terrine, expelling air at each layer, and cook in a bain-marie at 90°C until the centre reaches 55°C, about 25 minutes.
Press under a weight, set for 48 hours in the fridge, and slice with a knife dipped in hot water. Serve cool but not chilled, on warm toast.

farci-poitevin.d: A loaf of greens — sorrel, spinach, cabbage, leek — bound with egg and wrapped in green cabbage leaves, poached for three hours. The Easter dish of the Marais Poitevin, eaten cold, in slices, in the punts.
s: Blanch the large cabbage leaves for 3 minutes and refresh them: they must fold without cracking to wrap the farci.
Chop all the greens raw, very finely, and salt them for half an hour so they give up their water; press them hard.
Poorly drained greens make a farci that falls apart as it cooks: that is the only real difficulty in the dish.
Mix them with the beaten eggs, the crumb soaked in milk, the chopped bacon, the garlic and parsley.
Line a cloth with cabbage leaves, fill it, tie it tight like a bundle and poach for 3 hours in barely simmering water. Cool under a weight before slicing.

pate-de-chartres.d: A raised game pie of feathered game, traditionally red-legged partridge, presented to the bishops of Chartres since the 16th century. The jelly is not decoration: poured in cold through the chimney, it drives out the air and keeps the pie for weeks.
s: Bone the partridges, keep the breasts whole and mince the rest with the pork, shallot and juniper.
Marinate breasts and forcemeat for 12 hours in brandy: without it the game stays dry and scentless.
Line a pie mould with pastry, alternate forcemeat, breasts, foie gras and pistachios, pressing at each layer.
Cover, seal, glaze with yolk and cut two chimneys; bake 15 minutes at 210°C then an hour at 160°C.
Cool completely, then pour the jelly, warm but not set, through the chimneys. Wait 48 hours before slicing: the pie must firm up.

gaufre-lilloise.d: A flat oval waffle, split while hot and filled with a cream of brown beet sugar and Madagascar vanilla. It keeps for days and travels: which is what has made it, since 1849, the thing you bring back from Lille.
s: Knead a rich yeasted dough with the flour, yeast, warm milk, eggs, 80 g of butter and the sugar, and prove for 1½ hours.
Divide into 50 g balls, prove for 30 minutes, then bake 90 seconds in a hot flat waffle iron.
Split each waffle horizontally while it is scalding: once cool it crumbles under the knife.
Cream the remaining butter with the vergeoise, scraped vanilla and rum, until the sugar no longer grates under the spatula.
Fill with a thin layer, close and press lightly. Rest overnight: the cream must soak into the dough.

figatellu.d: A Corsican sausage of pork liver and meat, smoked over chestnut wood, grilled on coals and eaten on bread that catches the fat. It is made only in winter, from November to March, when the free-ranging pigs have finished the chestnuts.
s: Cut the liver and meats by knife into small dice: a mincer crushes the liver and gives a bitter paste.
Salt at 25 g per kilo, pepper heavily, add the crushed garlic and red wine, and rest for 24 hours in the cold.
Fill the casings loosely and dry for three days somewhere cool and airy.
Cold-smoke over chestnut wood for a week, an hour or two a day: the smoke should scent, not cook.
Grill the figatellu on the coals, split lengthwise, and serve it on a slice of bread placed beneath it while it cooks, with fresh brocciu.

fougasse-aux-olives.d: A flat bread slashed into an ear of wheat, thrown into the oven to test its heat before the real batches went in. From that use — the Roman focacia, the hearth bread — the fougasse takes its name and its open-worked shape.
s: Knead the flour, yeast, warm water, salt and half the oil for 12 minutes, to a supple, slightly tacky dough.
Prove for 1½ hours, then fold in the stoned olives and rosemary, without kneading again.
Stretch by hand into a one-centimetre oval on a tray, and let it relax for 20 minutes.
Cut boldly right through with a scraper, then pull the cuts open by hand: if they do not go through, they close again in the oven.
Oil, scatter coarse salt and bake for 18 minutes at 240°C with a little steam.

pompe-a-huile.d: A brioche-like flatbread with olive oil and orange blossom, one of the thirteen desserts of the Provençal Christmas supper. It is broken by hand and never cut: cutting the pompe, they say, would ruin the coming year.
s: Make a starter with the yeast, a little warm water and 100 g of flour, and let it double for an hour.
Add the rest of the flour, the sugar, olive oil, orange blossom water and zest, and knead for 10 minutes.
The dough must stay soft and oily: add water rather than flour if it resists.
Prove for 2 hours, flatten to a 2 cm disc and cut six well-spaced slashes in a star.
Bake for 25 minutes at 180°C and brush with olive oil and orange blossom water as it leaves the oven.

bugnes-lyonnaises.d: Diamonds of dough fried for carnival, thin and crisp in Lyon, thick and soft in Savoy. The quarrel is old and unrefereed: it hangs on how thin the dough is rolled and how long it rests, not on the recipe.
s: Knead everything except the oil and icing sugar for 10 minutes, to a smooth, non-sticky dough.
Rest it in the cold for at least 4 hours: that rest is what makes a bugne snap rather than chew.
Roll very thin — 2 mm for the Lyon version — and cut slit diamonds, passing one tip through the slit.
Heat the oil to 170°C: hotter, and the bugne browns without puffing; cooler, and it drinks the oil.
Fry 40 seconds a side, drain on paper, dust with icing sugar once warm. They are eaten the same day.

barboton-ardechois.d: A gratin of chard and potatoes with ewe's tome, the garden dish for when the chard all bolts at once. To barboter, in Ardèche dialect, is to soak: the stems soak in the cream while the leaves stay on top.
s: Separate the stems from the leaves: the stems need 15 minutes' cooking, the leaves three.
Cut the stems into lengths and blanch them in salted water, then drain them well.
Wilt the leaves in a pan with the onion and garlic, and press them to drive out all the water.
Combine both with thinly sliced raw potato, the cream beaten with the eggs, nutmeg and half the tome.
Turn into a buttered dish, cover with the remaining cheese and bake for an hour at 180°C. Rest 10 minutes before serving.

roquefort-poires-noix.d: France's first protected cheese — a Toulouse parliament ruling in 1666, an appellation in 1925 — ripened in the fleurines of the Combalou, the fissures that naturally ventilate the caves. Served plainly, with pears and walnuts, it needs nothing else.
s: Take the Roquefort out an hour ahead: chilled, its paste is dry and its bite crushes everything else.
Cut it with a wire rather than a knife, in wedges taken from the centre out to the rind, so each portion carries as much blue.
Choose pears just ripe, firm under the thumb, and cut them at the last moment.
Toast the walnut halves dry for 3 minutes, until they smell — that short roasting is enough to wake the oil.
Serve on a board with buttered country bread and a trickle of honey. A sweet wine, never a tannic red.

pogne-de-romans.d: A brioche crown scented with orange blossom, golden and light, born as an Easter cake in the Dauphiné. The name comes from poignée, a handful: the dough was shaped with full hands, and the crown formed around the fist.
s: Dissolve the yeast in warm milk with a spoonful of sugar and let it foam for 15 minutes.
Knead the flour, eggs, sugar, salt and orange blossom water for 15 minutes, then add the softened butter in three goes.
Prove for 2 hours, knock back, and chill the dough for 4 hours — a pogne is shaped cold, otherwise it sticks to the hands.
Form a ball, punch a hole through the centre with your fist and widen it generously: it will close by half as it rises.
Prove for 2 hours, glaze, scatter pearl sugar and bake for 35 minutes at 170°C. The crumb must stay stringy and yellow.

pain-d-epices-de-dijon.d: A honey and spice loaf made with wheat flour, softer than the Reims version made with rye. The dukes of Burgundy brought it back from Flanders in the 14th century; the Dijon guild of spice-bread makers was recognised in 1711.
s: Warm the honey with the milk and butter, without going above 50°C: any hotter and the honey loses its scent.
Combine the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt and all the finely ground spices.
Pour in the warm honey in a stream, mixing with a spatula, then add the egg and zest.
Rest the batter for 24 hours, covered, at room temperature: that rest alone gives the softness and marries the spices.
Pour into a lined loaf tin and bake for 1 hour at 150°C. Wrap it warm in a cloth and wait two days before slicing.

crepes-de-froment.d: The sweet wheat crêpe, distinct from the savoury buckwheat galette with which it is often confused. In Lower Brittany both carry the same Breton name, krampouezh; it is the flour, not the filling, that separates them.
s: Mix the flour, sugar and salt, make a well and break in the eggs, then work outward from the centre.
Add the milk little by little: poured in at once it makes lumps no whisk really rescues.
Add the melted butter and rum, and rest the batter for an hour — the gluten must relax, or the crêpes shrink in the pan.
Heat the griddle until a drop of water dances, grease it with a buttered cloth, and spread a ladleful with the rozell in one circular sweep.
A minute on one side, thirty seconds on the other. Salted butter and sugar, and nothing more for the first one.

pate-de-paques-berrichon.d: A pork and veal pie in which whole hard-boiled eggs are lined up, so that every slice shows a perfect round. It is eaten cold on Easter Monday: the eggs mark the end of Lent, and the cut must reveal them whole.
s: Hard-boil six eggs for 9 minutes, refresh them in iced water and peel them carefully: a torn white shows in the slice.
Chop the meats and bacon coarsely, mix them with the shallot, parsley, wine, four-spice, salt and the remaining egg.
Line a mould with pastry, spread half the forcemeat, line the whole eggs end to end down the centre, and cover with the rest.
The eggs must be buried and well centred: set too high, they break through the lid as it bakes.
Close, seal, glaze, cut a chimney and bake 15 minutes at 210°C then 45 minutes at 170°C. Eaten cold, the next day.

rillettes-de-tours.d: Brown, dry rillettes, cooked long and uncovered until the meat caramelises — the opposite of those of Le Mans, pale and fatty. Balzac, a Touraine man, called them 'that brown pork confit' and held them to be his province's glory.
s: Cut the meats into finger-sized strips along the grain: they must shred, not turn to purée.
Salt them and rest for 12 hours in the cold with the thyme and bay.
Melt them in lard uncovered over very low heat for 4 hours, never putting a lid on: evaporation is what gives the brown colour.
Raise the heat for the last half hour until the meat catches lightly on the base and turns mahogany — that is the whole difference from Le Mans.
Deglaze with white wine, shred with a fork, pepper, and pot them, pressing down. Cover with fat and wait three days.

canistrelli.d: Corsican shortbread biscuits made with oil and white wine, scented with anise, lemon or almonds. They hold neither egg nor butter: the wine binds the dough, which is why they keep for weeks in a tin.
s: Combine the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt and lightly crushed anise seeds dry.
Pour in the oil then the white wine and bring the dough together with your fingertips, without kneading: overworked, it turns hard instead of short.
Roll it 1.5 cm thick and cut diamonds with a knife, not a cutter.
Roll each diamond in caster sugar before it goes in the oven: that is what gives the crackling crust.
Bake for 25 minutes at 180°C until pale gold and cracked. Cool completely on a rack: warm, they seem soft.

aziminu.d: The Corsican rockfish soup, cousin to bouillabaisse but scented with the maquis — myrtle, immortelle, wild fennel — and without saffron or orange. It is made from whatever the boat brought back: scorpionfish, conger, hogfish, never a noble fish.
s: Scale and gut the fish, and keep the heads: they are where the body of the broth comes from.
Soften the onion, garlic and fennel in olive oil, add the tomato and paste, and let it melt down for 15 minutes.
Moisten with boiling water — never cold, which would seize the flesh — and cook the heads and bones for 25 minutes.
Pass through a food mill, pressing hard, return to the heat and cook thick potato rounds in it for 15 minutes.
Lay the whole fish on top for the last 8 minutes, without stirring. Serve the broth first, on garlic-rubbed bread, and the fish after.

pulenda.d: A Corsican polenta of chestnut flour, turned out onto a cloth and cut with a thread, served with figatellu and brocciu. The Castagniccia takes its name from its chestnut trees: until the 20th century they fed the mountains in place of the wheat they could not grow.
s: Bring the salted water to the boil and rain in the chestnut flour very finely with one hand, whisking with the other.
Chestnut flour lumps far faster than maize: never stop stirring, and pour slowly.
Then work with a wooden spoon, lifting the mass and folding it back, for 30 minutes over low heat.
It is ready when it comes away from the sides of the pot in one block and a crust forms on the base.
Turn it out onto a floured cloth, shape a ball and cut it with a butter wire — never a knife, which tears it. Serve with fresh brocciu.

cacavellu.d: An Easter brioche crown enclosing a whole egg, shell and all, held down by two crossed strips of dough. The egg bakes with the bread; godparents gave them to their godchildren, and the size said how much they were loved.
s: Knead the flour, the yeast dissolved in warm milk, three eggs, the sugar, zest, anise and salt for 15 minutes, then work in the butter.
Prove for 2 hours: the dough must double and smell of anise before it is handled.
Shape a thick crown and set the two whole raw eggs on it, unwashed, pressing them halfway into the dough.
Cross two strips of dough over each egg and seal them firmly: as it bakes the dough swells and ejects a badly anchored egg.
Prove for an hour, glaze the bread only — never the eggs — and bake for 35 minutes at 175°C.

presskopf-alsacien.d: A pressed pork head set in its own jelly, sliced thin and served as a salad with onion vinaigrette. Nothing is wasted: the whole head, the tongue, the rinds, and it is the rind alone that sets the jelly, without a gram of added gelatine.
s: Soak the head for 12 hours in cold water, changing it three times, to draw out the blood.
Poach it for 3 hours with the rinds, vegetables, white wine, bay and cloves, never boiling: a cloudy broth gives a cloudy jelly.
Bone it while hot and cut the meat, tongue and rind into one-centimetre dice, discarding the cartilage.
Mix them with chopped parsley and a little reduced broth, pack into a terrine and press under a weight for 24 hours in the cold.
Slice very thinly and serve with a vinaigrette of raw onion and gherkin, and rye bread.

berawecka.d: An Alsatian Christmas loaf made almost entirely of dried fruit — pears, figs, prunes, nuts — held together by a few spoonfuls of dough. Berawecka means pear bread: the dried pear is its base, and its steeping in kirsch lasts a week.
s: Soak the dried pears overnight in water, then poach them for 20 minutes; keep the cooking water.
Dice all the fruit, mix with the chopped nuts, spices and orange peel, douse with kirsch and steep for a week in the cold, stirring every other day.
Make a small yeasted dough with the flour, yeast, sugar and warm pear water, and let it double.
Fold it into the fruit: there must be no more than is strictly needed to bind, a berawecka is a fruit loaf and not a cake.
Shape short, dense loaves, rest for an hour and bake for an hour at 160°C. Wrap them and wait three weeks before slicing, very thinly.

andouille-de-cambrai.d: A Cambrésis andouille of chitterlings rolled in a spiral and gently smoked, served cold in slices with a mustard vinaigrette. Unlike the Vire version it is not smoked for weeks: a few days suffice, and the flesh stays pale.
s: Scrape and turn the chitterlings, wash them in vinegared water then dry-salt them for 24 hours with thyme and bay.
Cut them into wide bands and roll them in a spiral one over another, tightening as you go.
Truss with string into an even roll: it is the evenness of the rolling that gives the marbled slice.
Cold-smoke over beech for three days, then poach for 2½ hours in a white wine and onion broth at 80°C, never boiling.
Cool in the broth, slice thinly and serve with a mustard vinaigrette of onion and gherkin.

boeuf-miroton.d: The leftovers of a pot-au-feu sliced and gratinated under an onion and vinegar sauce. It was the Tuesday dish of 19th-century bourgeois kitchens; it only works with yesterday's meat, fresh meat falls apart in it.
s: Slice the onions finely and let them turn golden in butter for 25 minutes: they must colour, not merely soften — that is where the dish's flavour is born.
Dust with flour, cook it for two minutes, then moisten with the pot-au-feu broth and let it thicken for 10 minutes.
Add the vinegar and mustard off the heat: a miroton sauce must be frankly sharp, or the boiled beef stays dull.
Slice the cold beef 5 mm thick — hot, it shreds — and lay the slices overlapping in a buttered dish.
Coat with the sauce, scatter breadcrumbs and gratinate for 15 minutes at 200°C. Gherkins and parsley on serving.

macarons-de-nancy.d: An old-style macaron, cracked, with no smooth shell and no filling, made of three ingredients only. Two nuns turned out of their convent by the Revolution sold them to live in Nancy in 1793: they were called the macaron sisters, and the recipe has not moved since.
s: Mix the ground almonds and sugar, and add the whites unbeaten, merely loosened with a fork.
On no account whip the whites: that is what separates the Nancy macaron from the Parisian one, and a meringue would give a smooth shell.
Work with a spatula to a thick, sticky paste, and rest it for 30 minutes.
Drop spoonfuls onto baking paper, well spaced, without smoothing them: the crack must come by itself.
Bake for 18 minutes at 160°C. They must stay soft in the middle — take them out when the top is golden but the centre still yielding.

souffle-au-fromage.d: A béchamel lightened with whipped whites, which triples in the oven and falls within three minutes. The word appears in Beauvilliers in 1814: the first French dish whose success is measured to the second, and one waits for the soufflé, never the reverse.
s: Butter the dish from bottom to top in vertical strokes, and line it with grated cheese: the soufflé grips the sides to climb.
Make a thick béchamel, let it cool a little, then beat in the yolks one at a time, the cheese, nutmeg and pepper.
Whip the whites with a pinch of salt to the bird's beak, firm but not grainy — overbeaten, they will no longer fold in.
Loosen the base with a third of the whites using the whisk, then fold in the rest with a spatula, lifting, in some twenty movements only.
Fill three-quarters full, run your thumb round the rim to free the mixture, and bake 30 minutes at 190°C without once opening the door. Serve within the minute.

tarte-normande.d: An apple tart flooded with a cream custard and scented with calvados. The choice of apple is everything: a reinette or a boskoop holds its shape, a golden collapses into purée and the custard turns watery.
s: Line the tin, prick the base and blind-bake it for 12 minutes at 190°C under baking beans.
Dust the pre-baked base with ground almonds: they will drink the apple juices and stop the pastry going soggy.
Cut the apples into thick wedges and cook them 5 minutes in butter with a little sugar, then flame with calvados.
Arrange them in a tight rosette and pour over the custard of eggs, remaining sugar, cream and cinnamon.
Bake for 45 minutes at 180°C. The custard should still tremble at the centre as it comes out: it finishes setting as it cools.

gateau-a-la-broche.d: A spiked cone of cake built layer upon layer on a spit turning before a wood fire. Each ladleful poured on the scalding cone hardens before the next; the spikes are not decoration, they are the drips of batter set hard.
s: Beat whole eggs with the sugar at length, at least 10 minutes, until the mixture triples and ribbons thickly.
Fold in the warm melted butter, then the sifted flour, rum, orange blossom water and zest: the batter must run off the whisk in an unbroken ribbon.
Line the cone with buttered paper and turn it before the coals until it is scalding.
Pour a ladleful of batter onto the turning cone and wait for it to brown completely before the next: fifteen to twenty layers, two hours of patience.
Cool on the spit before unmoulding. The cake keeps a month and is cut crosswise, with a saw or a long knife.

fouace-nantaise.p: Nantes, Pays de la Loire, France
fouace-nantaise.d: An orange-blossom brioche flatbread, shaped as a six-pointed star and baked flat. Rabelais made it famous: the Picrocholine war in Gargantua breaks out over a few fouaces refused to some shepherds.
s: Knead the flour, the yeast dissolved in warm milk, the eggs, sugar, salt and orange blossom water for 12 minutes.
Work in the softened butter and knead 8 minutes more, until the dough clearly leaves the bowl.
Prove for 1½ hours, knock back, then roll the dough into a 3 cm thick disc on a tray.
Cut six even points with a knife, from the edge toward the centre without reaching the middle: that star shape is what makes a fouace.
Prove for an hour, glaze with yolk and bake for 30 minutes at 180°C. Eaten warm, with salted butter.

briau-sarthois.d: A savoury custard of spinach, bacon and cream on shortcrust, baked in a deep dish. The briau is the Sarthe garden dish for when the spinach bolts: as much is made as grows, and it is eaten warm or cold.
s: Wilt the spinach in a pan in three batches, without water, then press it hard between your hands.
A kilo of raw spinach gives barely three hundred grams once pressed: that is normal, and it is the remaining water that would ruin the custard.
Fry the bacon and onion in butter, and mix them with the knife-chopped spinach.
Beat the eggs with the cream, nutmeg and pepper, and salt barely — the bacon salts it already.
Fill the pastry case, pour in the custard and bake for 45 minutes at 180°C. A knife point must come out dry.

prefou-vendeen.d: A flat bread split and filled with garlic butter, warmed through and torn by hand. Its name comes from pré-four, before the oven: Vendée bakers threw in a piece of dough to test the heat, and ate it with whatever came to hand.
s: Knead a soft bread dough and prove it for an hour.
Roll it into two oval flatbreads 1.5 cm thick and bake them 10 minutes at 220°C: they must stay very pale, barely set.
That short pre-bake is what matters — a browned bread will not open again without breaking.
Cream the salted butter with finely crushed garlic and parsley, adding nothing else.
Split each warm flatbread horizontally, spread generously, close and return for 8 minutes at 200°C, until the butter bubbles at the edges.

tourton-des-alpes.d: Small fried pillows of thin dough, savoury with potato or sweet with apple, known as the infant Jesus's pillows. They were made at evening gatherings in the Champsaur, several pairs of hands at once: one rolls, one fills, a third fries.
s: Knead the flour, egg, melted butter, water and salt to a smooth dough, and rest it for an hour under a cloth.
Prepare the two fillings: mashed potato with cheese and parsley for the savoury, apples softened with sugar and cinnamon for the sweet.
Roll the dough as thinly as possible — you should half see your hand through it — and cut 8 cm squares.
Set a spoonful of filling on each, damp the edges, fold into a rectangle and seal with a fork: a badly sealed tourton opens in the fryer.
Fry at 175°C, 2 minutes a side, until they blister and brown. Drain and serve scalding.

tarte-tropezienne.d: A pearl-sugar brioche split and filled with a cream half pastry cream, half butter. Created in 1955 by a Polish pastry cook settled in Saint-Tropez, it was named by Brigitte Bardot during the filming of And God Created Woman.
s: Knead the brioche for 15 minutes, work in the butter, prove for 2 hours then rest overnight in the cold.
Make a pastry cream with the milk, yolks, sugar, cornstarch and vanilla, and cool it completely, covered in contact.
Loosen it with a whisk, then fold in the stiffly whipped cream and the orange blossom water: that marriage of two creams is what gives the lightness.
Roll the brioche into a 2 cm disc, prove for 1½ hours, scatter pearl sugar and bake 25 minutes at 175°C.
Split it horizontally once cold, pipe in the filling generously and chill for 2 hours before serving.

bacalhau-a-gomes-de-sa.d: Flaked salt cod, potatoes and onion, gratinated in olive oil with black olives and hard-boiled egg. José Luís Gomes de Sá traded cod in Porto; he bequeathed the recipe with the note 'change nothing'.
s: Soak the cod for 36 hours in cold water, changing it six times.
Poach it for 10 minutes then let it stand in hot milk for an hour: this is what makes it tender and creamy.
Flake it by hand into large petals, removing skin and bones.
Boil the potatoes in their skins, peel them warm and cut into thick rounds.
Soften the sliced onion in olive oil with the garlic, combine everything in an earthenware dish and bake for 25 minutes at 200°C. Garnish with hard-boiled egg, olives and parsley.

bacalhau-a-lagareiro.d: A loin of salt cod roasted under a rain of olive oil, with potatoes crushed by fist. Lagareiro means the man at the oil mill: the dish exists to taste the oil, and the cod is its pretext.
s: Soak the cod loins for 36 hours, then pat them thoroughly dry.
Boil the potatoes whole and unpeeled in heavily salted water for 25 minutes.
Crush them with your fist or the flat of your hand, without breaking them up: the skin should split and the flesh stay in pieces.
Lay the cod and potatoes in an earthenware dish, cover with sliced garlic and onion.
Drown it in olive oil — half the dish, and that is not an exaggeration — and bake for 35 minutes at 200°C.

feijoada-de-buzios.d: Whelks stewed with white beans, chouriço and coriander. The Algarve makes its feijoada from the sea: shellfish replace the pork, and coriander goes in by the handful.
s: Purge the whelks for 2 hours in salted water, then boil them for 25 minutes and pull them from their shells.
Remove the operculum and the black tip: it is the only bitter part of the shellfish.
Soak the beans overnight and cook them for 50 minutes with the bay.
Make a refogado of onion, garlic, pepper and tomato in olive oil, 20 minutes.
Bring together the beans, whelks and chouriço, add white wine and give it 20 minutes. Cover with coriander off the heat.

frango-a-cafreal.d: A spatchcocked chicken marinated in coriander and piri-piri, grilled until charred at the edges. Brought back from Mozambique and Goa, it became the Sunday-night dish of Lisbon's churrasqueiras.
s: Spatchcock the chicken by cutting along the backbone, and flatten it with the heel of your hand on the breastbone.
Blend coriander, garlic, piri-piri, lemon, white wine and olive oil into a fragrant green marinade.
Score the flesh where it is thick and work the marinade in; leave 12 hours in the cold.
Grill the chicken skin side first, away from the coals, for 25 minutes, then turn it for 15 more.
Baste with reserved marinade at the end. Serve with roast potatoes and lemon.

bifes-de-cebolada.d: Slices of beef drowned under onions melted in white wine and bay. The cebolada is not a garnish but the sauce itself: three onions per person, and nobody finds that excessive.
s: Flatten the beef slices with a mallet and salt them only at the last moment.
Sear them 90 seconds a side in scorching oil and lift them out: they will finish in the sauce.
Melt the sliced onions in the same oil, covered, for 30 minutes, until golden.
Add the garlic, bay, paprika, tomato and white wine, and reduce for 10 minutes.
Return the meat and its juices for 5 minutes. Serve with chips and a fried egg on each plate.

acorda-de-savel.d: An açorda thickened with bread and egg, with shad from the Sado and a great deal of coriander. Shad is full of fine bones: you poach it, flake it patiently, and the soup repays the work.
s: Poach the shad for 12 minutes in salted water with the onion and bay; strain and keep the broth.
Flake the fish by hand with patience, removing every bone: the only long job in the dish.
Pound the degermed garlic and coriander in a mortar with coarse salt and olive oil.
Crumble the bread into a deep dish, spoon the green paste over it, then the scalding broth, and stir with a fork.
Break the eggs into the soup and stir for 2 minutes off the heat: they should thread, not set. Add the fish.

perdiz-a-alcantara.d: Partridges stuffed with foie gras and truffles, stewed in port. The recipe was seized from a convent at Alcántara by one of Napoleon's generals in 1807; his widow published it, and Portugal has never forgiven it.
s: Draw the partridges and keep the livers. Mix them with the foie gras and chopped truffle, and season.
Stuff the birds with this and truss them tightly, so the filling cannot escape.
Marinate them for 24 hours in the port with the bay and thyme, turning twice.
Colour them in duck fat, add the onion and carrot, then the marinade and stock.
Cover and simmer for 1½ hours over very low heat. Strain the sauce, reduce it and coat the birds.

moelas-guisadas.d: Chicken gizzards stewed in white wine, tomato and piri-piri, served as petiscos in the tascas. They need an hour to stop being tough: that is the only secret.
s: Trim the silvery membrane from the gizzards: left on, it stays tough whatever you do.
Blanch them for 10 minutes and discard that water.
Make a refogado of onion, garlic and bay in olive oil for 15 minutes, then add the paprika off the heat.
Add the gizzards, tomato, white wine and piri-piri, and cover with water.
Simmer covered for 1 hour, then 15 minutes uncovered so the sauce coats. Serve with bread.

arroz-de-forno-minhoto.d: An oven-baked rice with smoked meats and chouriço, crisp on top and yielding below. The Minho bakes what other regions leave on the hob: the crust is half the pleasure.
s: Cook the pork for 40 minutes with the bay; keep the broth and dice the meat.
Make a refogado of onion and garlic in oil, add the paprika off the heat, then the white wine.
Add the rice and let it turn pearly, then add two parts broth to one of rice.
Add the diced meats, chouriço and presunto, and cook for 12 minutes on the hob: the rice must stay very wet.
Turn into an earthenware dish, break three eggs on top and bake for 20 minutes at 210°C to form the crust.

bola-de-berlim.d: A doughnut filled with egg cream, split rather than injected, sold by hawkers on Algarve beaches. Brought by German Jewish refugees in the 1930s, it acquired a yellow cream Berlin never knew.
s: Dissolve the yeast in warm milk, add 60 g of sugar, the flour, two eggs, the butter and the zest. Knead for 12 minutes.
Prove for 1½ hours, then shape 60 g balls and let them rise another 45 minutes on a floured cloth.
For the cream: bring the remaining milk to a simmer, pour it over the yolks beaten with sugar and cornstarch, and thicken for 3 minutes.
Fry the balls at 165°C, 3 minutes a side: hotter, and they brown before the centre is cooked.
Roll them in sugar while warm, split them halfway without cutting through, and pipe in the cream generously.

tigelada-beira.d: An egg and cinnamon custard baked in an earthenware bowl in the wood oven. No caramel, no pastry: eggs, milk and a great deal of cinnamon, and the brown crust that forms on top.
s: Bring the milk to a simmer with the lemon zest and a cinnamon stick, then infuse off the heat for 20 minutes.
Beat the whole eggs with the sugar without aerating them: a tigelada should not rise.
Add the sifted flour, then the cooled milk in a thin stream, and strain the mixture.
Butter earthenware bowls and fill them three-quarters full.
Bake for 30 minutes at 200°C: the top should brown frankly and the centre stay wobbly. Dust with cinnamon.

polvo-guisado-acoreano.d: Octopus stewed in Pico wine with local chilli and sweet potato. In the Azores a cork goes into the pot with it: the custom is stubborn, the explanation less so.
s: Freeze the octopus then thaw it: the fibres break and the flesh turns tender without effort.
Stiffen it dry in the pot until it gives up its water, and discard that first water.
Add the oil, sliced onion, garlic and bay, and soften for 20 minutes covered.
Pour in the white wine, tomato and piri-piri, and simmer for 40 minutes without adding water.
Add the sweet potato in large cubes for the last 25 minutes, and cover with parsley.

molho-de-figado.p: Ponta Delgada, São Miguel, Azores, Portugal
molho-de-figado.d: Pig's liver marinated in wine and garlic, stewed with local chilli, served at Christmas. In the Azores the molho is made on the evening of the 24th and eaten for breakfast on the 25th, with maize bread.
s: Cut the liver and belly into cubes and marinate them for 24 hours in the wine, pounded garlic, chilli and spices.
Drain the meat keeping the marinade, and pat it dry: wet, it would boil instead of searing.
Colour it in small batches in the lard, over high heat.
Pour in the strained marinade, add the orange zest, and simmer covered for 1 hour.
Uncover for the last 20 minutes: the sauce should coat. Serve with maize bread.

sopa-de-castanhas.d: A soup of chestnuts and white beans, thickened without cream or flour. Before the potato, chestnuts fed Trás-os-Montes all winter: they were called the bread of the poor.
s: Soak the beans overnight, then cook them for 50 minutes with the bay.
Score the chestnuts with a cross and boil them for 20 minutes: both skins then come away together, while hot.
The second, thin skin must come off completely: left on, it makes the soup bitter.
Soften the onion, leek and garlic in olive oil, add the chestnuts and carrot, and moisten with the bean broth.
Cook for 30 minutes, blend only half of it, and serve with crisped presunto dice and mint.

bolas-de-berlim-natario.d: Manuel Natário's shop, opened around 1935 near the costume museum, sells more than a thousand a day and the queue spills onto the pavement. Unlike the Algarve beach version, which is split open, this one is piped through the side after being rolled in cinnamon sugar — and it is eaten warm, straight from the fryer.
s: Dissolve the yeast in 150 ml of warm milk with a spoonful of sugar, and wait for it to foam.
Knead it for 15 minutes with the flour, whole eggs, two yolks, 80 g of sugar, the butter, zest and salt: the dough should leave the bowl and stay supple.
Prove for 1½ hours, shape 55 g balls, flatten them barely and let them rise for an hour on a floured cloth — that second rise is what gives the pale belt around the middle.
Meanwhile make a custard with the remaining milk, six yolks, 100 g of sugar, the cornstarch and the vanilla; cover it in contact and let it cool completely before whisking it smooth.
Fry at 165°C, 3 minutes a side, roll them straight away in the cinnamon sugar, then pipe in the cream through a hole made in the side. They do not keep: that is the price of the queue.

poulet-de-mamie.d: A chicken stewed in white wine and colorau, the sweet paprika the Minho measures by the tablespoon rather than the pinch. A family recipe from Areosa, where the skin comes off and the olive oil is never stinted: it is the oil that carries the colour of the pepper.
s: Joint the chicken and take off the skin: without it the sauce stays clean and takes the colour of the pepper rather than of fat.
Sweat the sliced onions and the lardons in olive oil, generously — a good glassful at least.
