Add the chicken pieces and turn them for 5 minutes, without trying to brown them hard.
Pour in two glasses of white wine, the sweet paprika, the cayenne and salt, then water to cover. Simmer covered for 1 hour over low heat.
Add the peas a quarter of an hour before the end. Serve with plain rice, or oven-baked rice if the meal is a Sunday one.

pataniscas-de-bacalhau.d: Flat fritters of shredded salt cod, served with a bean rice black with coriander. This is the lunch of Lisbon tascas: a patanisca must be irregular and ragged at the edges, a perfectly round one betrays too much flour.
s: Desalt the cod for 24 hours, changing the water four times, then poach it for 8 minutes and shred it by hand into coarse strands.
On no account chop it: a patanisca must keep fibres you can recognise between the teeth.
Beat the eggs with the flour and milk, add grated onion, garlic and plenty of parsley, and rest for 30 minutes.
Fold in the cod: the batter should hold on the spoon but stay loose, otherwise add milk.
Drop spoonfuls into oil at 175°C without spreading them and turn halfway. Serve with a coriander bean rice.

prego-no-pao.d: A garlic steak in a soft roll, eaten standing at the counter or at the end of a meal, after the fish. Prego means nail: garlic cloves were once nailed into the meat to tenderise it, and the name outlived the practice.
s: Flatten the steaks with the palm, not a mallet: the aim is to widen them, not to break the fibres.
Pound the garlic with salt and crumbled bay, and rub it into both sides; rest for 20 minutes.
Heat the pan white hot, barely oil it, and sear 90 seconds a side: any longer and a thin steak turns to shoe leather.
Deglaze with white wine and a knob of butter and scrape up the sediment — that spoonful of sauce is all that separates a good prego from a bad one.
Split the roll, pour the juices inside so the bread drinks them, add the steak, a little mustard and piri-piri. Eaten at once.

bife-a-marrare.d: The cream-and-pepper steak of the Marrare café, where literary Lisbon gathered in the 19th century. A single pan served the whole evening unwashed: the sediment built up, and the last customer's sauce was better than the first's.
s: Take the meat out an hour ahead and pat it dry: a wet steak boils instead of searing.
Crack the pepper in a mortar rather than grinding it, and press it onto both faces.
Sear in foaming butter with crushed unpeeled garlic and bay, 2 minutes a side for a centimetre and a half.
Set the meat aside, deglaze with wine, reduce almost dry, then pour in the cream and let it thicken without boiling.
Return the steaks for a minute so the sauce coats them. Serve with thin chips and nothing else.

ovos-moles-de-aveiro.d: A cream of egg yolks and sugar enclosed in wafer shells moulded as seashells and salt barrels. The convents of Aveiro made them from the 16th century with the yolks left over from starching sails and linen.
s: Bring the sugar and water to 108°C — soft ball — and let it cool to 40°C with the zest.
Push the yolks through a fine sieve to remove the chalazae: they are what form the white specks nothing can undo.
Pour the warm syrup onto the yolks in a stream, whisking, then return to very low heat.
Stir constantly with a spatula, scraping the base, until the cream pulls away in one mass — about 12 minutes. A second's inattention and the eggs scramble.
Cool for 12 hours, then fill the wafer shells, seal them with water and trim with scissors.

sopa-de-cacao.d: A dogfish soup thickened with flour, green with coriander and sharpened with vinegar, poured over stale bread. The Alentejo is a land without a coast: dogfish, cheap and free of small bones, came up salted from Setúbal.
s: Soak the fish for an hour if salted, then poach it for 10 minutes with the onion and bay; keep the broth.
Flake the flesh in large pieces and remove the central cartilage, which comes away in one piece.
Pound the garlic, coriander and salt in a mortar: this is the base of the dish, and a mortar releases coriander oil as no knife does.
Turn the flour golden in olive oil, moisten with the cooking broth and let it thicken for 10 minutes.
Add the pounded paste, the vinegar and the fish, heat without boiling, and pour over slices of stale bread in the plates.

dom-rodrigo.d: Egg threads and a cinnamon almond cream, twisted in coloured foil like a sweet. The name is said to come from Dom Rodrigo Lobo da Silveira, governor of Lagos; the wrapper came much later, when the sweet took to the markets.
s: Make a syrup at 105°C with 300 g of the sugar, the water and the zest, and keep it at a tremble.
For the fios de ovos, sieve eight yolks and pour them in a fine stream into the syrup through a funnel, moving in circles: they set into golden threads in 20 seconds.
Lift them out with a skimmer the moment they float — a second too long and the threads turn brittle.
Make an almond cream with the remaining sugar, the ground almonds, six yolks and the cinnamon, cooked gently until it pulls away.
Set a spoonful of cream on a square of foil, crown it with egg threads and twist the ends. Keeps for two weeks.

conquilhas-a-algarvia.d: Wedge clams gathered at low tide from the sand of the Ria Formosa, opened in two minutes with garlic and coriander. Nothing is ruined faster: thirty seconds too long and a wedge clam shrinks to rubber, past saving.
s: Purge the clams for 2 hours in water salted to 35 g per litre, changing it twice: they must give up all their sand.
Discard any that stay open, then rinse them under plenty of cold water and drain.
Turn the sliced garlic pale gold in olive oil without burning it — burnt, it makes the sauce bitter and nothing saves it.
Tip in the clams over high heat with the white wine, cover and shake the pan: they open in 90 seconds.
Kill the heat the moment the last one opens, add chopped coriander and lemon juice. Serve in the pan, with bread for the juices.

espada-com-banana.d: Breaded fillets of black scabbardfish, served with pan-fried Madeiran banana and passion fruit. The espada is caught a thousand metres down, at night, on longlines: its huge eyes and silver skin do not survive the ascent.
s: Marinate the fillets for 20 minutes in lemon juice, crushed garlic and salt: the flesh is mild and short of acidity.
Pat them thoroughly dry, flour them then dip in beaten egg — in that order, or the flour slides off.
Fry in oil 2 minutes a side: the fillet is thin, and cooks before you have finished turning it.
Halve the bananas lengthwise and caramelise them in butter, without stirring, until golden.
Plate the fish, banana on top, and spoon over passion fruit pulp. The acidity is what links the sweetness to the fish.

picado-madeirense.d: Cubes of beef with garlic and Madeira wine, tipped over a bed of chips, set in the middle of the table with as many forks as there are people. There are no plates: you pick — picar — straight from the dish, and that is where the name comes from.
s: Cut the beef into 2 cm dice and marinate for an hour with crushed garlic, bay, salt and piri-piri.
Cut the potatoes into thick chips and fry them twice: blanched at 150°C, browned at 180°C.
Pat the meat dry and sear it in butter over fierce heat, in small batches: crowded, it would weep and boil.
Deglaze with Madeira, reduce by half and return the meat for a minute.
Tip the meat and its juices over the scalding chips, scatter parsley and pepper, and set the dish in the middle of the table.

milho-frito.d: Cubes of cornmeal with cabbage and wild fennel, chilled overnight then fried until they crack. The obligatory partner to Madeiran espetada: the centre must stay creamy under a crust that resists, which only a full chilling allows.
s: Boil the salted water with the finely shredded cabbage, garlic and chopped wild fennel for 15 minutes.
Rain in the cornmeal, whisking constantly, to avoid the smallest lump.
Stir for 25 minutes with a wooden spoon over low heat: it is long, and it is what stops the porridge tasting raw.
Add the lard, pour into a dish 3 cm deep, smooth the top and chill overnight.
Cut 4 cm cubes and fry at 180°C until golden on every side. A warm cube falls apart in the oil.

lapas-grelhadas.d: Limpets prised off the black rocks, grilled in their shells under garlic butter and doused with lemon. They are lifted with a knife in a single movement: hesitate a second and the limpet clamps to the stone with a force nothing overcomes.
s: Scrub the shells under cold water and let the limpets purge for 30 minutes in seawater or heavily salted water.
Cream the butter with the crushed garlic, parsley and piri-piri.
Set the limpets flesh upward on a scalding plate or straight on the coals.
Drop a hazelnut of butter on each as soon as they start to sizzle, and give them 4 minutes in all — cooked longer they toughen and cling.
Squeeze lemon over as they come off and serve with corn bread for the butter left in the shells.

cracas-cozidas.p: Praia da Vitória, Terceira, Azores, Portugal
cracas-cozidas.d: Giant barnacles chiselled off the volcanic rock, boiled in seawater and eaten with a pin. They grow only on lava beaten by the Atlantic swell and are sold as whole plates, like a piece of reef.
s: Rinse the plates under plenty of cold water, scrubbing the rock to remove sand and weed.
Bring heavily salted water to the boil — 40 g per litre, or seawater if you have it — with the bay.
Drop in the barnacles and count 6 minutes from the return to the boil, no longer: overcooked, they retract to the bottom of their cone and become impossible to extract.
Drain and serve scalding, with a pin or a snail fork per person.
Melted butter with piri-piri and a wedge of lemon are enough. The flesh is already salty: do not salt again.

pastel-de-chaves.d: A puff-pastry half-moon filled with raw minced veal and pork, protected by a geographical indication since 2011. The original recipe, appearing around 1862, is passed on by word of mouth: the filling goes in raw and cooks in its own juices, sealed by the pastry.
s: Chop the meats with a knife rather than a processor: the filling must stay in distinct grains, not a paste.
Mix them with grated onion, garlic, parsley, white wine, nutmeg, salt and plenty of pepper, and rest for 4 hours in the cold.
Roll the pastry to 2 mm and cut ovals: it must be thin, because it puffs a great deal.
Set the raw filling on one half, damp the edge, fold and seal by pinching firmly — the least leak empties the pastel of its juices.
Glaze with yolk and bake for 25 minutes at 200°C. Eaten warm, within the hour: cold, they lose the crispness that is the whole point.

bola-de-lamego.d: A flat bread filled with presunto, chouriço and bacon, baked as a golden slab and cut into squares. This is the Douro harvest snack: it travels, it is eaten cold, and it keeps a man going until evening.
s: Knead the flour, the yeast dissolved in warm milk, two eggs, the softened butter and salt for 12 minutes, and prove for 1½ hours.
Slice the charcuterie very thinly: diced, it would pierce the dough and let the fat escape.
Divide the dough in two and roll each half very thin — 3 mm — on an oiled tray.
Cover the first with a single layer of charcuterie, without overlapping, lay the second sheet on and seal all round by folding.
Prick the surface with a fork, glaze with egg and bake for 45 minutes at 190°C. Let it cool before cutting into squares.

morcela-de-arganil.d: A Beira blood sausage with cumin and wine, dried then slowly smoked over oak. Unlike northern black puddings it holds neither rice nor onion: only blood, fat and spice, which makes it tight and almost dry when cut.
s: Collect the blood, whisking it at once with a little salt to stop it setting, then pass it through a sieve.
Dice the fat small and render it only halfway: fully rendered, it would give nothing to chew on.
Pound the garlic with the cumin, paprika, cloves and salt, and slake it all in the red wine.
Combine blood, fat and spices, fill the casings loosely and tie them into horseshoes — the mixture swells as it cooks and an overfull sausage bursts.
Poach for 40 minutes at 80°C, never boiling, then dry for three days and smoke over oak for a week. Grill for a few minutes on the coals to serve.

bucho-de-arganil.d: A pig's stomach stuffed with meats and bread, sewn shut and boiled for three hours, the dish of slaughter day at Christmas. It is served in thick slices with the cozido vegetables, and a share of the filling always goes to the neighbours who came to help.
s: Turn the stomach inside out and scrape it in vinegared water, then soak it for 12 hours, changing the water three times.
Cut the meats into one-centimetre dice and marinate them overnight with garlic, paprika, cumin and white wine.
Add the crumbled stale bread and beaten eggs: the bread soaks up the juices which, without it, would burst the stomach.
Fill the stomach only two-thirds full and sew it up with kitchen thread in close stitches.
Poach for 3 hours in barely simmering water, pricking the stomach with a needle after 20 minutes to release the air. Add the greens and potatoes to the broth for the last half hour.

queijada-da-graciosa.p: Santa Cruz da Graciosa, Azores, Portugal
queijada-da-graciosa.d: Small cakes of egg yolk and milk, with no cheese despite the name, baked in pleated paper cases. Graciosa has no fresh cheese to spare: its queijadas are made with butter and starch, and rise into a split dome.
s: Warm the milk with the butter, zest and a pinch of salt, without letting it boil.
Whisk the yolks with the sugar until pale and ribboning.
Add the sifted cornstarch and flour, then the warm milk in a stream, whisking constantly.
Rest the batter for 30 minutes: the bubbles must rise, otherwise the queijadas sink as they cool.
Fill the cases three-quarters full and bake for 25 minutes at 190°C. The tops must split: that is the Graciosa mark.

alcatra-terceirense.p: Angra do Heroísmo, Terceira, Azores, Portugal
alcatra-terceirense.d: Beef stewed four hours in a Vila Franca clay pot, with vinho de cheiro and allspice. The pot is not a detail: its unglazed interior lets moisture escape slowly and concentrates the sauce without ever catching.
s: Rub the inside of the clay pot with bacon, then line the base with thickly sliced onions.
Lay in the meat in large pieces, the garlic, the whole allspice and the bay, and cover with a second layer of onions.
Pour in red wine to cover, add the butter, salt, and on no account add water: the onions will give enough.
Bake covered for 4 hours at 150°C, never stirring or lifting the lid before the third hour.
Uncover for the last half hour to let the sauce reduce and the surface colour. Serve with the island's sweet bread.

torresmos-transmontanos.d: Pieces of pork belly confited in their own fat then finished over high heat until the rind blisters. They are the by-product of slaughter day: the lard was rendered for the year, and what stayed in the cauldron was that evening's meal.
s: Cut the belly into 4 cm cubes with the rind on, and marinate them 12 hours with crushed garlic, paprika, white wine and salt.
Drain and pat them dry: marinade left on the meat would make the fat spit dangerously.
Confit them for 1½ hours in lard at 90°C, uncovered, never simmering — this is gentle cooking, not frying.
They are ready when a skewer passes through the rind without resistance. Lift them out and let them cool for 20 minutes.
Bring the fat to 190°C and return them for 4 minutes to blister the rind. Serve with cornmeal porridge and orange quarters, whose acidity cuts the fat.

arroz-de-lingueirao.d: A wet rice with razor clams, gathered from the sand of the Ria Formosa by pouring salt into their hole. The salt mimics the rising tide and the clam comes up by itself: the only way to take it whole.
s: Purge the razor clams for 2 hours in salted water, then steam them open in 90 seconds and keep every drop of liquor.
Take out the flesh, remove the dark sac and cut the foot into lengths; keep a few shells for serving.
Make a long refogado of onion, garlic and pepper in olive oil, then add grated tomato and let it melt down.
Pearl the rice, moisten with white wine then the strained clam liquor made up with water — three parts to one of rice: this rice must stay soupy.
Cook for 14 minutes, add the clams and coriander off the heat, and serve at once in the pan.

bacalhau-a-minhota.d: A thick cod loin floured and fried, laid on rounds of fried potato and onion, all flooded with olive oil and finished in the oven. The Minho never sets its cod on boiled potatoes: they must have been fried, to hold up under the oil.
s: Desalt the cod for 36 hours in the fridge, skin up, changing the water four times — thick loins need longer than flakes.
Pat them dry, flour them and fry 4 minutes a side in hot oil, to a pale gold crust.
Fried separately in thick rounds, the potatoes must stay firm and the onion turn translucent without browning.
Arrange potatoes and onions in the base of an earthenware dish, set the cod on top and cover with sliced garlic and bay.
Douse generously with olive oil and give it 15 minutes at 200°C. The oil is not thrown away: it is mopped up with bread.

stargazy-pie.d: A pilchard pie with the heads breaking through the crust to face the sky. Mousehole makes it on 23 December, for Tom Bawcock who braved the storm and saved the village from famine.
s: Gut and bone the sardines keeping head and tail attached: the whole staging of the dish depends on it.
Fry the bacon and onion, and hard-boil three eggs.
Line a round dish with pastry and fill with bacon, onion and quartered eggs.
Arrange the sardines like the spokes of a wheel, heads outward, and pour over the cream beaten with the remaining eggs and the wine.
Cover with pastry, pushing each head through it, glaze and bake for 40 minutes at 190°C.

laverbread-gallois.d: Laver seaweed boiled at length, rolled in oatmeal and fried in bacon fat. Richard Burton called it Welsh caviar; it takes eight hours of boiling to become edible.
s: Wash the seaweed in several changes of water to remove every grain of sand: some always remains, and you taste it.
Boil it for 6 to 8 hours in unsalted water, until it becomes a smooth black purée.
Drain and press it: it should have the consistency of a thick jam.
Grill the bacon and keep the rendered fat in the pan.
Shape patties of the laver rolled in oatmeal and fry them 3 minutes a side. Serve with bacon, cockles and lemon.

hachee-amsterdam.d: A beef and onion stew with vinegar and cloves, simmered so long it falls apart at the spoon. Served with red cabbage and apple: the Dutch cannot conceive of one without the other.
s: Cut the beef into cubes and sear it in butter in batches, without crowding the pot.
Lift it out and melt the sliced onions for 25 minutes: you need as much onion as meat.
Dust with flour, add the vinegar and reduce it, then moisten with the stock.
Add cloves, bay, juniper and sugar, return the meat and simmer covered for 2 hours.
Serve with braised red cabbage and apple, and boiled potatoes.

waterzooi-de-poisson.d: River fish poached in a vegetable broth thickened with egg yolks. Ghent waterzooi was fish long before it was chicken: pollution in the Scheldt tipped the recipe over in the 20th century.
s: Cut all the vegetables into julienne of the same thickness: in a waterzooi they must cook together.
Sweat them in butter without colouring, then moisten with the stock and cook for 15 minutes.
Cut the heat and slide in the fish in large lengths: they poach in the residual warmth, 8 minutes.
Beat the yolks and cream, temper with a ladle of broth, then stir into the soup off the heat.
Never let it boil again: the liaison would split. Lemon and parsley as you serve.

malakoff-vaudois.d: A fritter of grated gruyère on a slice of bread, deep-fried and served scalding with white wine. Vaud mercenaries are said to have brought it back from the siege of Malakoff in 1855; the village of Vinzel still lives on it.
s: Coarsely grate the gruyère and let it come to room temperature: cold, it will not bind.
Mix it with the eggs, flour, white wine, kirsch, pounded garlic and nutmeg, into a dense paste.
Rest it for 2 hours in the cold: the paste should hold its shape without slumping.
Cut 7 cm rounds of bread and set a flattened ball of paste on each, barely overhanging.
Lower them bread side up into oil at 175°C for 4 minutes, until the cheese puffs and colours. Serve immediately.

arroz-caldoso-de-marisco.d: A shellfish rice deliberately left soupy, eaten with a spoon. Unlike paella, arroz caldoso never dries: it must run when the plate is tilted, and is eaten within twenty minutes.
s: Peel the prawns and make a strong stock with the heads and shells, 25 minutes; strain it.
Make a sofrito of onion, garlic, pepper and tomato in olive oil, 20 minutes, until it darkens.
Add the paprika off the heat, then the rice, and let it turn pearly for a minute.
Pour in four parts scalding stock to one of rice — twice a paella — with the infused saffron.
Cook uncovered for 16 minutes, add the shellfish and fish for the last 6, and serve at once.

kalops.d: A beef stew with allspice, served with pickled beetroot. The name comes from English 'collops', slices of meat: Swedish sailors brought it back from Scotland in the 18th century.
s: Cut the beef into large cubes, flour them lightly and sear them in butter in batches.
Lift out the meat and soften the thickly sliced onions in the same fat until golden.
Return the beef, add the whole allspice and the bay, and moisten with the stock.
Simmer covered for 2 hours over the gentlest heat: the stew should never come to a rolling boil.
Add the carrot for the last 30 minutes. Serve with steamed potatoes and pickled beetroot.

fiskesuppe-bergen.d: A white fish soup, thickened with cream and sharpened with vinegar and sugar. That sweet-sour edge, inherited from the Hanseatic League, surprises at first and is sorely missed when removed.
s: Cut all the vegetables into fine julienne and sweat them in butter without colouring.
Moisten with the stock and cook for 12 minutes: the vegetables should stay crisp.
Beat the yolks and cream, temper with a ladle of hot broth, then thicken the soup off the heat.
Sharpen with vinegar and sweeten: taste and adjust, the balance should be felt without being named.
Slide in the cubed fish and poach for 4 minutes off the heat. Add the prawns and chives at the last moment.

ploughmans-lunch.d: Bread, cheddar, pickle and a pickled onion, laid on a board with not a single hot dish. The name smells of ploughed fields but dates from the 1950s: the Cheese Bureau invented it to revive pub cheese sales after rationing.
s: Take the cheddar out two hours ahead: cold, it is brittle and tasteless, and it is the centrepiece.
Choose a farmhouse cheddar aged at least twelve months, with a paste that crumbles rather than cuts.
Break it into large uneven pieces, as much by hand as by knife — tidy slicing has no place here.
Set out on a board the bread, butter, cheese, ham, pickled onions, gherkins and quartered apple.
Assemble nothing in advance: the bread dries and the salad wilts. A brown pickle and a pint of ale finish the plate.

steak-and-kidney-pie.d: A stew of chuck and beef kidney sealed under a crust, moistened with stout. The kidney is not there to bulk it out: it gives the gravy an iron depth the beef alone never reaches, and it needs to be a quarter of the total weight.
s: Soak the kidney for 30 minutes in milk or vinegared water, then trim the white core fat, which would give a urinous taste.
Flour and sear the diced beef in small batches in a scalding pot: crowded, it would weep instead of browning.
Soften the onion, return the meats, deglaze with stout and moisten with broth, Worcestershire and herbs.
Simmer covered for 2½ hours, then cool completely: a hot filling would melt the puff pastry before it could bake.
Fill the dish, cover with pastry, seal, glaze, cut a vent and bake 35 minutes at 200°C.

beef-wellington.d: A seared beef fillet lined with mushroom duxelles and cured ham, then sealed in puff pastry. The whole problem is moisture: the duxelles must be dried until it releases nothing more, or the pastry underneath stays raw.
s: Sear the tied fillet on all sides over fierce heat, 4 minutes in all, brush it with mustard and let it cool.
Chop the mushrooms very finely by knife and dry them out in a dry pan for 25 minutes, stirring: they must lose three-quarters of their volume and stop sizzling.
Lay the cured ham in a rectangle on cling film, cover with duxelles, set the fillet on it and roll very tightly. Chill for an hour.
Wrap this roll in puff pastry, seam underneath, glaze twice twenty minutes apart and chill again for 30 minutes.
Bake 35 minutes at 200°C to 52°C at the centre, then rest 15 minutes before carving. Without that rest, all the juice escapes and soaks the pastry.

melton-mowbray-pork-pie.d: A pie of coarsely chopped pork, raised by hand without a tin, its jelly poured through the top hole after baking. The meat is not cured with nitrate: which is why it stays grey rather than pink, unlike every other English pie.
s: Boil the water with the lard and pour it onto the salted flour: this is hot water crust, and it only works while warm.
Keep a quarter of the dough warm for the lid and raise the rest by hand around a floured jar, pinching the walls upward.
Chop the pork by knife into pea-sized pieces — a mincer would give a paste, and the slice would lose its grain.
Season heavily with salt, white pepper, sage and nutmeg, pack it into the crust, set the lid on and pierce a hole in the centre.
Bake 30 minutes at 200°C then 1½ hours at 160°C. Pour the warm bone jelly through the hole, and set for 24 hours in the cold.

toad-in-the-hole.d: Sausages baked in Yorkshire pudding batter that puffs up around them. The name comes from the sausages breaking the surface like toads in a pond; the original 18th-century version used up leftover meat.
s: Beat the flour, eggs, milk and salt, and rest the batter at least an hour — cold and rested, it rises far more.
Heat the beef dripping in the dish at 220°C until it smokes: this is the decisive point of the recipe.
Brown the sausages separately, then set them in the smoking fat and pour in the batter all at once.
Bake 30 minutes without once opening the door: the least draught of cold air collapses the batter for good.
Meanwhile make a gravy of softened onions, broth and mustard. Serve straight from the oven.

bangers-and-mash.d: Grilled sausages on mashed potato, flooded with onion gravy. The word banger dates from the Great War: sausages were then so padded out with water that they burst in the pan with a bang.
s: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins in salted water: cut up, they take on water and the mash turns gluey.
Peel them scalding, pass them through a ricer — never a blender, which breaks the starch into glue — and beat in the butter then the hot milk.
Cook the sliced onions gently for 25 minutes until brown and sweet.
Dust with flour, moisten with broth, add the Worcestershire and mustard, and reduce for 10 minutes.
Cook the sausages slowly for 20 minutes, turning often, without pricking them. Set them on the mash and flood with gravy.

eton-mess.d: Strawberries, whipped cream and broken meringue, tumbled together without order. Served at Eton College during the cricket match against Harrow; a persistent legend says a labrador sat on the pudding, which would explain both the mess and the name.
s: Whisk the whites to peaks and firm them with the sugar rained in, until the meringue is smooth and glossy.
Bake it 90 minutes at 100°C, then let it dry in the switched-off oven with the door ajar: it must be brittle right through.
Crush a third of the strawberries to a purée with a little icing sugar and the lemon juice, and cut the rest into pieces.
Whip the cream without tightening it: it must stay soft, a stiff cream would make the pudding heavy.
Break the meringue by hand into uneven pieces and fold everything once, barely. Serve within ten minutes, or the meringue dissolves.

eccles-cake.d: A small puff-pastry parcel packed with currants, so tightly that the fruit shows through. They are nicknamed dead fly pies; the Puritans banned them in the 17th century as too tied to religious feasts, which only made them more popular.
s: Melt the butter with the brown sugar, add the currants, orange peel and spices, and cool completely.
A warm filling would melt the pastry as you assemble: that is the one absolute rule of the recipe.
Cut 10 cm discs, set a good spoonful in the centre and gather the edges to the middle like a purse.
Turn the parcel seam down and flatten it gently by hand until the currants show through.
Cut three slashes on top, brush with egg white, dust with sugar and bake 20 minutes at 200°C.

trifle.d: A pudding built in layers in a glass bowl: sponge soaked in sherry, fruit, custard and whipped cream. The first recipe with sponge dates from 1751; before that a trifle was merely a flavoured cream, and it was the sherry that changed everything.
s: Make a custard thickened with cornstarch, and cover it in contact so it does not skin as it cools.
Line the base of the bowl with sponge and douse it with sherry: it must be soaked but not sodden, or the layer collapses.
Cover with roughly crushed fruit and a little sugar, without reducing it to a coulis.
Pour on the completely cold custard: warm, it would bleed into the layers and the trifle would lose its clean bands.
Finish with whipped cream and toasted almonds, and set for 6 hours in the cold before serving with a spoon, digging right to the bottom.

spotted-dick.d: A suet pudding studded with currants, steamed in a cloth and served drowned in custard. The spots are the fruit; as for dick, the word is said to come from dough said in a northern accent — the etymology is unsettled and has raised laughs for two centuries.
s: Combine the flour, grated suet, sugar, baking powder, salt and zest, then add the currants.
Pour in the milk and bring the dough together without working it: an overworked pudding turns rubbery and heavy.
Roll it into a cylinder in buttered greaseproof paper then in a cloth, leaving a pleat down the middle — the pudding swells by a good third.
Tie both ends and the centre, and steam for 2 hours, topping up with boiling water and never cold.
Turn out, cut thick slices and serve under a hot, pourable custard.

scotch-pie.d: A small mutton pie in hot water crust, with straight walls standing proud of a sunken lid. That rim is no ornament: hollow, it holds the mash, beans or gravy, which is what makes it edible standing up in a football ground.
s: Boil the water and lard and pour them at once onto the salted flour; work with a spoon then by hand as soon as you can.
Raise the warm dough around a floured glass, with straight walls standing 1.5 cm proud: once cold it cracks instead of shaping.
Mix the minced mutton with breadcrumbs, grated onion, broth, nutmeg, mace and plenty of white pepper.
White pepper and mace are what separate a Scotch pie from an English one: do not swap them for black pepper.
Fill, set a lid sunk 1 cm below the rim, pierce it in the centre and bake 45 minutes at 190°C.

shortbread-ecossais.d: Three ingredients in the proportion one-two-three: one part sugar, two butter, three flour. Mary Stuart is said to have loved it; the petals of the round mould recall the Twelve Apostles' skirts, and the biscuit descends from yesterday's bread dried in the oven.
s: Rub the cold butter and sugar together with your fingertips, without creaming: aerated butter would make the biscuit rise, which is not wanted.
Add the flours and salt and bring the dough together in only a few movements — the more it is worked, the harder it sets.
The rice flour is not optional: it is what gives the sandy grain that snaps under the tooth.
Press the dough 1.5 cm thick into a tin, prick it with a fork and chill for 30 minutes.
Bake 45 minutes at 150°C: shortbread must stay pale, barely golden at the edges. Sugar and cut it as it comes out, while still soft.

stornoway-black-pudding.d: A Hebridean pudding with coarse oatmeal and beef suet, protected by a geographical indication since 2013. It stands apart for its higher proportion of oatmeal, which gives it a crumbly rather than a yielding texture.
s: Whisk the blood as soon as it is collected with a little salt to stop it setting, then pass it through a fine sieve.
Chop the onion very finely and dice the suet small — large pieces would melt away and leave holes.
Mix everything with the coarse oatmeal, salt, add white pepper and let it swell for 30 minutes: the oatmeal drinks part of the blood.
Fill the casings loosely, only half full, because the oatmeal swells further in cooking and would burst the skin.
Poach 1½ hours at 80°C, never boiling, pricking with a needle after 10 minutes. Cut thick and fry in butter.

stovies.d: Potatoes stewed slowly in the fat and juices of yesterday's roast, until half of them collapse. The word comes from the French étuver: it is the Monday dish, and every Scottish family maintains that theirs is the only true one.
s: Melt the dripping and soften the thickly sliced onion in it for 15 minutes.
Cut the potatoes into uneven pieces: the small ones will collapse into purée, the large ones hold, and that mixture is what you want.
Add them with yesterday's meat, diced, season, and pour in only a shallow layer of broth.
Cover and stew for an hour over very low heat, stirring no more than twice: stovies steam, they do not boil.
They are ready when a golden crust forms on the base. Serve with oatcakes and pickled beetroot.

arbroath-smokie.d: Haddock salted, tied in pairs by the tail and hot-smoked in a buried barrel covered with hessian. The name is protected across Europe: only smoking within eight kilometres of Arbroath may carry it.
s: Gut and behead the haddock but keep them whole, leaving the tails joined.
Dry-salt them for only 2 hours: long salting would give a hard fish, and a smokie must stay tender.
Rinse and dry overnight in the cold until the skin is dry to the touch — without that pellicle the smoke will not take.
Tie them in pairs by the tail, hang them over a beech fire in a covered barrel, and hot-smoke for 45 minutes: the flesh must cook as it smokes.
Serve warm, opened with a thumb along the backbone, with butter, lemon and bread. There is nothing else to do.

scottish-tablet.d: A milk sugar that snaps then melts, more crumbly than fudge and softer than hard toffee. The whole difference lies in the beating: the mass is stirred off the heat until it grains, producing minute crystals instead of a smooth paste.
s: Melt the butter in the milk, add the sugar and stir until fully dissolved before it boils — one undissolved grain crystallises the lot.
Bring to the boil and cook 20 minutes to 118°C, washing the sides down with a wet brush.
Add the condensed milk and continue 5 minutes, stirring constantly: the base catches very quickly.
Off the heat, beat hard with a wooden spoon for 8 minutes, until the mass thickens, loses its shine and sounds like sand.
Pour at once into a buttered tin and score the squares with a blade after 10 minutes, before it sets hard.

clootie-dumpling.d: A dried-fruit pudding boiled for four hours in a cloth — the cloot — which gives it its characteristic brown skin. A coin and a thimble were once hidden in it to tell the children's fortunes; it is eaten hot at Christmas, and cold, sliced and fried, for breakfast.
s: Scald the cloth, wring it out and flour it generously: that flour is what will form the pudding's skin as it cooks.
Mix all the dry ingredients, add the grated suet, the fruit, treacle, egg and buttermilk for a soft batter.
Set it in the centre of the cloth, gather it into a purse leaving slack, and tie: the pudding swells by a quarter.
Boil for 4 hours in a large pot, on an upturned saucer so the cloth does not touch the base, topping up with boiling water.
Turn out and dry for 20 minutes in a 150°C oven to firm the skin. Serve with custard.

rumbledethumps.d: A gratin of mashed potato, cabbage and onion under cheddar. The name says the action: rumble, to stir, and thump, to bash — the Borders have their version of what Ireland calls colcannon and England bubble and squeak.
s: Boil the potatoes in their skins, peel them hot and crush them roughly with a fork.
Fry the finely shredded cabbage and onion in butter for 12 minutes: they must stay crisp, boiled cabbage would weep into the gratin.
Combine everything with the remaining butter, the milk, chives, salt and plenty of pepper, without aiming for smoothness.
Turn into a buttered dish and rough up the surface with a fork, leaving peaks — they are what will brown.
Cover with grated cheddar and bake 30 minutes at 190°C, until the top is brown and blistered.

aberdeen-rowie.d: A flat, salty, greasy lard-laminated roll, the croissant's brutal cousin. It was devised for North Sea fishermen: its fat and salt content keeps it for weeks at sea without going rancid or stale.
s: Knead a plain bread dough with the flour, yeast, water, sugar and salt, and prove it for an hour.
Cream the lard and butter together and divide into three parts.
Roll out the dough, dot it with a third of the fat in small nuggets, fold in three and rest 40 minutes in the cold.
Repeat twice: a rowie is not laminated with a sheet of butter like a croissant, but with fat dabbed on, which gives its irregular flaking.
Cut squares, flatten them by hand without rolling, prove 45 minutes and bake 20 minutes at 200°C. They should be swimming in their own fat halfway through.

glamorgan-sausage.d: A meatless sausage of Caerphilly cheese, leek and breadcrumbs, crumbed and fried. It is recorded from 1850, long before vegetarianism was an idea: it was simply the sausage for days when there was no pig.
s: Slice the leek very finely and sweat it for 8 minutes without colour, then cool it completely.
Mix it with the grated cheese, 150 g of the breadcrumbs, the herbs, mustard, two egg yolks and the milk.
Salt lightly: Caerphilly already is, and an oversalted sausage cannot be rescued.
Shape finger-sized rolls and chill them for an hour — warm, they collapse in the pan.
Dip them in beaten egg white then in the remaining crumbs, and fry 8 minutes in oil, turning on every side.

welsh-cakes.d: Currant cakes cooked on a cast-iron bakestone, neither baked nor fried. Miners' wives slipped them into lunch tins: they are eaten cold, survive a day in a pocket, and need no oven — which mattered in the terraces.
s: Rub the cold butter into the flour, baking powder, salt and nutmeg, to coarse crumbs.
Add the sugar and currants, then the egg and just enough milk to bring the dough together.
Roll to 8 mm and cut 6 cm rounds: thicker, the centre stays raw; thinner, the cake dries out.
Heat a cast-iron bakestone with no fat and cook 3 minutes a side over medium-low heat.
They should be light brown and still soft in the middle. Sugar them warm and cool on a rack.

faggots-gallois.d: Balls of pork liver and belly wrapped in caul fat, baked in their own gravy. The dish of the Welsh mining valleys: the caul melts away entirely and is there only to hold the ball together for the first half hour.
s: Soak the caul for 20 minutes in warm vinegared water to relax it: dry, it tears at the slightest handling.
Chop the liver and belly together, neither too fine nor too coarse, and mix with the sweated onion, breadcrumbs, sage and mace.
Shape balls the size of a tennis ball and wrap each in a square of caul, tucking it underneath.
Pack them tightly in a dish — they hold each other up — and bake 20 minutes at 200°C to colour them.
Pour over the flour-thickened broth, drop to 170°C and give them 40 minutes more. Serve with mushy peas.

teisen-lap.d: A flat, moist, dense currant cake baked on a plate rather than in a tin. Teisen lap means hand cake: flat, it fitted in a miner's hand and his tin, and its shallowness kept it from being crushed.
s: Rub the butter into the flour, baking powder, salt and nutmeg, then add the sugar and currants.
Beat the eggs with the milk and pour them in at once: the batter must be far looser than a cake batter, almost pourable.
That wetness is what makes a teisen lap: too firm and it becomes an ordinary fruit cake and dries out in a day.
Pour into a buttered pie plate, only 3 cm deep, and smooth the top.
Bake 35 minutes at 180°C until the top is golden and the centre still yielding. Eaten warm or cold, with nothing.

ulster-fry.d: The Ulster fried breakfast, set apart from the English one by its two griddle breads: the soda farl and the potato bread. No beans, no mushrooms — the breads take their place, and that is what makes it Northern Irish.
s: For the potato bread, mash hot potatoes with 60 g of the flour and melted butter, roll to 1 cm and cut triangles.
For the soda farl, mix the remaining flour, buttermilk, bicarbonate and salt without kneading, flatten into a round and quarter it.
Cook both breads on a dry griddle, 5 minutes a side: they are griddled and never baked, and that is the whole difference.
Fry the bacon, sausages and black pudding, and keep the rendered fat in the pan.
Fry the breads in that fat until they crisp, then fry the eggs and serve everything together, without delay.

champ.d: Mashed potato with spring onion and milk, hollowed into a well where a knob of butter melts. You eat from the outside in, dipping each spoonful in the butter at the centre; unlike colcannon, no cabbage or kale goes in.
s: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins, in generously salted water.
Slice the spring onions, whites and greens apart, and infuse them 10 minutes in hot milk without boiling.
That infusion is the whole dish: thrown in raw, the onions stay sharp and sit apart instead of scenting it.
Peel the potatoes scalding, rice them and beat in the infused milk with its onions, then half the butter.
Mound it up, hollow a well in the centre with a spoon and drop in the remaining butter. Serve before it melts away.

fifteens.d: A no-bake roll whose recipe is its name: fifteen digestive biscuits, fifteen marshmallows, fifteen glacé cherries. Condensed milk binds it, coconut coats it, and the oven is never lit.
s: Crush the biscuits in a bag with a rolling pin, to coarse crumbs with a few larger shards.
Quarter the marshmallows and cherries; dust the knife with coconut so the marshmallows do not stick.
Mix everything with the condensed milk: the mass should be sticky but hold together in a ball.
Roll it into a log in cling film, tightly, then roll the log in coconut until entirely coated.
Chill at least 4 hours, then cut one-centimetre slices, wiping the knife between cuts.

yellowman.d: A brittle, honeycombed toffee sold at Ballycastle's Ould Lammas Fair since 1606, eaten there with dried dulse. Bicarbonate thrown into the boiling sugar makes it foam at once: that surge is what makes the honeycomb.
s: Butter a deep tray very generously and keep it within reach: what follows leaves you no more than three seconds.
Melt the butter, syrup, sugar, water and vinegar over low heat, without stirring once the sugar has dissolved.
Take it to 149°C, hard crack: lower and the yellowman stays tacky; higher and it turns bitter.
Off the heat, throw in the bicarbonate all at once and whisk for two seconds only — the mass triples instantly and overflows a small pan.
Pour without spreading and let it cool untouched: smoothing it would collapse the bubbles. Break it with a hammer when cold.

dublin-bay-prawns.d: Langoustines grilled under garlic and parsley butter, dredged from the mud of the Irish Sea. The name comes from the trawlers that landed them at Dublin; elsewhere they are scampi, but it is the same Nephrops norvegicus.
s: Buy them alive and cook them the same day: a dead langoustine degrades within hours and turns woolly.
Split them lengthwise along the back, and lift out the dark gut with a knife point.
Cream the butter with the crushed garlic, parsley, lemon zest, a pinch of cayenne and the white wine.
Set a hazelnut of it in each half and give them 5 minutes under a fierce grill, flesh upward.
They are done the moment the flesh turns opaque: a minute more and it shrinks. Serve with bread and the butter from the dish.

barmbrack.d: A yeasted fruit loaf whose fruit is steeped in tea, served at Halloween with objects hidden in the crumb. A ring meant marriage within the year, a pea poverty, a rag a bad match: the custom survives, with the ring alone.
s: Brew a very strong black tea and pour it scalding over the dried fruit; let it swell overnight.
Drain them the next day keeping the liquid, warm it and dissolve the yeast in it.
Knead the flour, sugar, spices, salt, butter and egg with that yeasted tea for 12 minutes.
Fold in the fruit at the end: added too early, its sugar would hinder the rise.
Prove 1½ hours, shape a round loaf, prove 45 minutes and bake 50 minutes at 180°C. Sliced thin and buttered.

drisheen.d: A Cork pudding of sheep's blood and milk, with no cereal, whose texture is nearer a custard than a sausage. It was sold by the cup at the English Market; it is eaten with tripe, and the flesh stays almost pale under a grey skin.
s: Whisk the blood as it comes with salt and pass it twice through a fine sieve: the least fibre would spoil the smooth set.
Mix it with warm milk at a ratio of one to two, season, and scent with tansy.
Fill the casings very loosely, or simply pour into ramekins: drisheen needs no skin, it sets by itself.
Poach 45 minutes at 75°C — any hotter and the blood splits irrecoverably and weeps.
Cool, cut thick slices and fry in butter. In Cork it is served with tripe stewed in milk and onion.

waterford-blaa.d: A very floury white roll with a soft, pale crust, protected by a geographical indication since 2013. It is said to come from French Huguenots settled in Waterford in the 17th century; the name from blanc, and it is eaten within four hours.
s: Knead a soft, fairly wet dough for 12 minutes, and prove it for 1½ hours.
Divide into 80 g pieces and shape them loosely: a blaa must stay slack to keep its cottony crumb.
Set them on the tray almost touching: that contact is what stops a crust forming on the sides.
Dust them generously through a sieve, twice, before and after the second 45-minute prove.
Bake 18 minutes at 220°C. They must stay white: a browned blaa is no longer a blaa, and it is eaten the same day.

irish-apple-cake.d: A dense cake of sharp apples under a crumble top, served hot with custard. It was once made in a cast-iron pot hung over the turf fire, with embers set on the lid to cook the top.
s: Take 80 g of the flour, 60 g of the butter and 60 g of the sugar and rub them to crumbs for the topping; chill.
Cream the remaining butter and sugar, add the eggs one at a time, then the flour, baking powder, cinnamon and milk.
Peel the apples and cut them into large wedges, never slices: big pieces keep their sharpness at the heart of the cake.
Fold them into the batter, turn into a tin, cover with the crumble and scatter sugar.
Bake 50 minutes at 180°C. Serve hot, under a custard made with the milk, yolks and vanilla.

irish-coffee.d: Coffee, whiskey, sugar and a cream that floats without mixing. Joe Sheridan invented it in 1943 to warm flying-boat passengers stranded at Foynes; asked whether it was Brazilian coffee, he answered that it was Irish coffee.
s: Whip the cream very lightly, just until it coats the spoon: whipped stiff, it collapses in lumps instead of floating.
Scald the stemmed glasses and empty them: a cold glass cracks and drops the cream.
Pour the whiskey and sugar into the base and stir until fully dissolved — it is the sugar that, by making the coffee denser, lets the cream hold.
Add the scalding coffee and stir once more.
Pour the cream gently over the back of a spoon held at the surface. Do not stir again: the hot coffee is drunk through the cold cream.

hakarl.d: Greenland shark fermented for three months then dried for four, served in cubes with a glass of brennivín. The fresh flesh is toxic — the shark has no kidneys and excretes urea through its skin — and fermentation alone makes it edible.
s: Cut the flesh into large blocks and bury it in a pit of gravel and sand, covered with stones.
The weight of the stones presses the fluids out of the flesh: it is the expulsion of urea and trimethylamine oxide, not cold or salt, that detoxifies the shark.
Ferment for six to twelve weeks depending on the season, then dig out the blocks and rinse them.
Hang them for four months in a shed open to the wind, until a brown crust forms.
Trim the crust, cut the pale flesh into one-centimetre cubes and serve on cocktail sticks, with rye bread. It is not cooked: it is prepared over seven months and eaten as it is.

rugbraud.d: A black, sweet rye bread baked for twenty-four hours buried in the hot sand of a geothermal spring. It is called hverabrauð, spring bread; with no oven to watch, you mark the spot with a stake and come back the next day.
s: Mix the flours, raising agents and salt, then add the milk, syrup and brown sugar: the batter should pour, almost like a cake mix.
Pour into a greased loaf tin or metal can, filling only two-thirds.
Seal it airtight: it is steaming in a closed vessel, with no evaporation, that gives the moist crumb and the black colour.
Bury the container 30 cm down in geothermal sand at 90°C — or failing that, bake covered in a bain-marie for 12 hours at 100°C.
Turn out the next day and let it cool. Sliced very thin, with salted butter and herring or smoked trout.

hardfiskur.d: Haddock dried in the wind, without salt or smoke, torn by hand and buttered. It was medieval Iceland's currency: rents and tithes were paid in dried fish, and a man lived on it all winter.
s: Gut and behead the fish, then split them along the backbone leaving the two fillets joined at the tail.
Do not salt: harðfiskur is one of the few dried fish in the world that is not, and salt would stop the wind doing its work.
Hang the pairs astride poles in a shed open to every wind, between 0 and 5°C.
Dry for four to six weeks, sheltered from rain and sun: above 8°C the fish spoils before it dries.
It is ready when it snaps cleanly and tears into strips. Eaten as it is, spread with butter — never rehydrated.

svid.d: Half a sheep's head singed, boiled and served whole, eye and cheek included. A dish of the þorrablót, the midwinter feast: on an island without timber or grain, no one could afford to throw away an animal's head.
s: Singe the heads with a blowtorch to burn off the wool, then scrape them with a knife and rinse in cold water.
Split them lengthwise, remove the brain, and soak them 4 hours in cold salted water.
Poach them 1½ hours at a bare tremble with the salt and bay, skimming for the first few minutes.
A boiling broth would split the skin and loosen the cheek, which is the best part.
Serve hot with mashed swede and potatoes. What is left is pressed into a terrine and eaten cold, as sviðasulta.

slatur.d: Two puddings sewn into sheep's stomach: blóðmör with blood and lifrarpylsa with liver. Families make them together in autumn at slaughter time; what is not eaten at once goes into sour whey, where it keeps a year.
s: Cut the stomach into squares, fold them into pouches and sew two sides with linen thread.
For blóðmör, mix the sieved blood, diced suet, rye, oats and salt; for lifrarpylsa, replace the blood with liver blended with milk.
Fill the pouches only two-thirds — the cereals swell a great deal and would burst the seam.
Sew the last side and poach 2½ hours at 85°C, without boiling, pricking each pudding after 20 minutes.
Serve hot with potatoes and swede. The rest keeps in sour whey, where it becomes súrsað.

sursadir-hrutspungar.d: Ram's testicles boiled, pressed into a terrine then kept in sour whey. One of the pieces on the þorramatur platter; the whey, the only preservative on an island without salt or spice, acidifies without ever salting.
s: Remove the outer membrane and soak the pieces 6 hours in cold water, changing it three times.
Poach them 2 hours at a simmer with the bay, until a needle passes through without resistance.
Pack them tightly into a terrine and press under a weight for 24 hours: pressing is what welds them into a sliceable block.
Submerge the block completely in sour whey and let it acidify two to three months in the cold.
The whey must always cover it: a piece that breaks the surface moulds. Serve in thin slices on buttered rye bread.

laufabraud.d: Discs of dough as thin as a leaf, cut with geometric patterns and fried, served at Christmas in northern Iceland. Flour was so scarce that it was stretched to the limit: the thinness was not a feat, it was a necessity.
s: Bring the milk to a tremble with the butter and pour it scalding onto the flour, sugar, baking powder, cardamom and salt.
Knead hard for 10 minutes: the dough must be very firm, almost hard — a soft dough will not roll thin enough.
Divide into balls and roll each until you can see the worktop grain through it, then cut a 20 cm disc.
Cut the patterns with a knife or a laufabrauðsjárn, lifting each tab to one side: that lifting is what makes the raised design.
Fry 20 seconds a side in mutton fat at 190°C, then press flat under a board as they cool.

vinarterta.d: A cake of five to seven layers of dry biscuit separated by cardamom prune compote. It has nearly vanished from Iceland but survives untouched in Manitoba, where emigrants took it around 1875: Canadian Icelanders still make it as they did in the 19th century.
s: Simmer the stoned prunes in water for 30 minutes, crush them with 100 g of the sugar, the cardamom and cinnamon, and cool: the compote must be thick, almost a paste.
Cream the butter and remaining sugar, add the eggs, milk, then the flour and baking powder for a firm dough.
Divide into five equal parts, roll each into a 22 cm disc and bake 10 minutes at 180°C. They must stay pale and dry.
Stack the discs, spreading compote between them and pressing lightly at each layer.
Wrap the cake and let it rest a week before slicing: the dry layers must drink the moisture from the compote, or the cake shatters under the knife.

kleinur.d: Cardamom dough diamonds, twisted by passing one tip through a slit, and fried in mutton fat. They exist across Scandinavia, but Iceland makes them with soured milk and fries them in tallow, which gives a flavour butter does not replace.
s: Rub the butter into the flour, sugar, raising agents, cardamom and salt, then bind with the eggs and buttermilk.
Rest the dough an hour in the cold: that rest is what stops kleinur puffing into round doughnuts.
Roll to 5 mm, cut 8 cm diamonds and slit each in the centre for two centimetres.
Pass one tip of the diamond through the slit and pull gently: the twist must hold by itself, without being tight.
Fry 90 seconds a side at 180°C in mutton fat. They should be dark brown — pale, they are raw inside.

pylsur.d: The Icelandic hot dog, made with lamb sausage, served with fried onion under the sausage and raw onion on top. You order it eina með öllu, one with everything; the order of the toppings is not negotiable, and the crisp onion goes at the bottom of the bun.
s: Slice one onion thinly, flour it and fry at 170°C until brown; drain on paper.
Chop the other two onions raw into very small dice and keep them cold.
Poach the sausages 7 minutes in barely simmering water — never boiling, which would burst the skin — and steam the buns above them.
Spread the crisp onion in the base of the bun first, then lay the sausage on it: that way it stays crisp instead of going soggy.
Finish with sweet ketchup, sweet brown mustard, gherkin remoulade and raw onion. Eaten standing, within the minute.

escudella-andorrana.d: The pot-au-feu of the Catalan Pyrenees, served in two acts: first the broth with its pasta, then the meats and vegetables on a platter. At the centre sits the pilota, a large meatball each family seasons its own way and which is only divided at the last moment.
s: Soak the chickpeas overnight in warm salted water, and cook them in a separate net: otherwise they would be lost in the pot.
Start the meats in cold water and bring them up slowly, skimming without pause for the first fifteen minutes — that is when, and only when, the broth turns clear.
Let it tremble for 2 hours with the carrot and celery, never boiling: an agitated broth clouds and cannot be recovered.
Shape the pilota from the minced pork, eggs, breadcrumbs, garlic, parsley and a pinch of cinnamon; roll it into a large oval, flour it and lower it gently into the broth for the last hour.
Add the cabbage and potatoes at the end. Serve the soup first, with the pasta cooked in it, then the carn d'olla on a platter, the pilota sliced at the centre.

trinxat-de-la-cerdanya.p: Pas de la Casa, Encamp, Andorra
trinxat-de-la-cerdanya.d: A crush of winter cabbage and potato, fried in bacon fat until it takes a crust. Trinxar means to chop: only curly kale picked after the first frosts is used, which loses its bitterness and turns sweet.
s: Boil the roughly cut cabbage and the potatoes in large pieces together in salted water for 25 minutes.
Drain them at length and press them against the colander: trinxat always fails for the same reason, too much water.
Crush them with a fork along with the pounded garlic — roughly, recognisable pieces must remain, never a smooth purée.
Fry the diced bacon in the lard until crisp, lift it out and tip the crush into the hot fat.
Press it into a cake and let it set for 8 minutes untouched, then flip it in one movement using a plate. Crown it with the crisp bacon.

conill-amb-tomaquet.d: Hutch rabbit stewed in a long-cooked tomato sofregit, with an almond and liver picada to bind the sauce. The picada is the Catalan gesture par excellence: it thickens not by flour but by pounding, and always goes in during the last ten minutes.
s: Joint the rabbit, keep the liver aside, and brown it all over in olive oil before lifting it out.
Make the sofregit in the same oil: grated onion for 20 minutes, then grated tomato for 25 more, until no water is left and the mass is brick-red and glossy.
A hurried sofregit stays acidic: it is the one step that cannot be shortened.
Return the rabbit, deglaze with white wine, add the herbs and moisten to cover; simmer covered for an hour.
Pound the garlic, almonds, hazelnuts, fried bread, sautéed liver and chocolate in a mortar, slake with a little sauce and stir it in for the last ten minutes.

xai-rostat-de-muntanya.d: A quarter of valley lamb roasted slowly on a bed of potatoes, with white wine and thyme from the Coma Pedrosa. Andorran lamb summers at fifteen hundred metres on aromatic plants: its fat keeps the taste, which is why so little seasoning goes on it.
s: Rub the lamb with lard, salt and crushed garlic twelve hours ahead, and take it out of the cold an hour before it goes in the oven.
Line an earthenware dish with onion and thickly sliced potato, moisten with oil and set the meat on top.
Roast 20 minutes at 230°C to seize the crust, then drop to 160°C.
Baste every twenty minutes with the juices and the white wine poured down the side of the dish, never over the meat — direct basting softens the crust you have just made.
Allow 2 hours in all and rest it 15 minutes out of the oven before carving. The potatoes will have drunk every drop.

truites-a-l-andorrana.d: Valira trout stuffed with bacon and pan-fried, browned in nut butter and garlic. The river comes down from the Ordino cirques in freezing water: trout grow slowly there, and the firm flesh needs neither marinade nor sauce.
s: Gut the trout without scaling them — river trout barely have scales — and wipe the cavity without rinsing it.
Salt the inside, slip in two slices of bacon and a sprig of parsley, and close with a wooden pick.
Flour them lightly, tapping off the excess: thick flour makes a shell instead of a crisp skin.
Fry 4 minutes a side in hot oil, then lift them out and discard the oil.
Foam the butter with sliced garlic and flaked almonds until it smells of hazelnuts, pour over the trout and squeeze lemon over.

canelons-a-l-andorrana.p: Santa Coloma, Andorra la Vella, Andorra
canelons-a-l-andorrana.d: Cannelloni filled with the leftovers of the Christmas roast, covered in béchamel and gratinated. They are eaten on 26 December, Sant Esteve: the filling is not made for them, it is what is left from the day before, and that is the whole logic of the dish.
s: Mince yesterday's cooked meats with the sautéed livers, twice through the mincer: the filling must be fine and even.
Sweat the onion, add the filling, flame with brandy and moisten with a ladle of béchamel to bind it.
Cook the sheets or tubes in salted water keeping them very firm, and spread them on a damp cloth without overlapping.
Fill and roll tightly, then lay the canelons side by side, seam down, in a buttered dish.
Coat with béchamel until they are entirely covered — a cannelloni that breaks the surface dries and hardens — scatter cheese and gratinate 25 minutes at 200°C.

coca-massegada.d: A flat coca with lard and anise, kneaded at length then stretched by hand and covered with sugar and pine nuts. Massegar means to knead without end: it is the working of the dough, not a leaven, that gives it its tight crumb and long keeping.
s: Dissolve the yeast in warm water and let it foam, then knead it with the flour, two eggs, 80 g of the sugar, the zest, anisette and salt.
Add the soft lard in small pieces and knead a good twenty minutes, until the dough turns smooth and elastic under the hand.
That long kneading is what makes a coca: skimp it and you get a crumbly cake instead of a dough that tears into strands.
Prove for an hour, then stretch by hand into a rectangle barely a centimetre thick, with no rolling pin, pulling from the centre.
Glaze with egg, cover with sugar and pine nuts, prove 30 minutes and bake 25 minutes at 190°C.

bringuera-andorrana.d: An Andorran sausage of pork liver and lung, dried a few weeks then poached or grilled. It is born of the matança, the December killing: offal does not keep, so it is cased at once, and the bringuera is eaten before the noble charcuterie.
s: Poach the liver and lung 20 minutes in salted water to firm them: raw, they clog the mincer and give a mush.
Mince them with the belly on the medium plate, and mix with crushed garlic, paprika, pepper, salt and white wine.
Rest the mixture 12 hours in the cold so the salt penetrates, and taste a fried patty before casing.
Fill the casings loosely, tie into horseshoes and prick out the air bubbles with a needle.
Dry for three weeks at 12°C, then poach 40 minutes at 80°C or grill over coals. Serve with cabbage and potatoes.

donja-llonganissa-dolca.d: A sweet Andorran longaniza made with mountain honey, dried two months and eaten in thin slices. The sugar is no whim: in a valley without sea salt, honey helped preserve as much as it flavoured, and donja is served at dessert as readily as before a meal.
s: Cut the meat and fat by knife into half-centimetre dice, never by mincer: a donja is known by the visible grain of its slice.
Mix them with salt, cracked pepper, cinnamon, crushed garlic, white wine and lightly warmed honey.
Macerate 24 hours in the cold, stirring twice: the honey must be entirely absorbed, or it weeps during drying.
Fill thin casings firmly, tie every twenty centimetres and prick out every air pocket carefully.
Dry two months at 12°C and 75% humidity, until it has lost a third of its weight. White bloom on the surface is normal; green mould is brushed off with vinegar.

bull-negre-andorra.d: A fat blood pudding cased in the large intestine, cut in wide slices and fried. Bull comes from boiled: unlike dry puddings it does not keep, and is eaten within the week of the matança, with mountain beans.
s: Poach the pig's head 2 hours, bone it while hot and dice the meat and rinds small.
Melt the onion in the rendered fat for 40 minutes over very low heat, until pale and dry.
Combine the sieved blood, the meat, the onion and the spices; the mass should be loose enough to fall slowly from the ladle.
Case it in the large intestine, filling only two-thirds, and tie both ends firmly.
Poach 1½ hours at 80°C, pricking with a needle after 15 minutes; a prick that runs clear means it is done. Cut thick and fry.

bisbe-blanc.d: The great white pudding of the Andorran matança, filled with tongue, rinds and lean meat, without a drop of blood. It is called a bishop for its size and whiteness; it was kept for the meal that closed the killing, and is cut in centimetre slices.
s: Poach the tongues for an hour, peel them hot — the skin comes away in one piece while they are scalding — and cut them into large dice.
Cook the rinds an hour until tender, and chop them coarsely with the shoulder and fat.
Mix everything with the salt, cracked pepper, nutmeg, garlic and white wine, and rest overnight.
Fill the stomach three-quarters full and sew it with close stitches, expelling the air as you go.
Poach 3 hours at 80°C, then press under a board for 24 hours in the cold: pressing is what makes the slice compact and even.

formatge-de-tupi.d: Leftover ewe's cheeses crushed, doused with brandy and left to ferment for months in an earthenware pot. The tupí is the pot itself: it is never emptied, more cheese goes on top, and some family pots have been running for generations.
s: Take dry, hard ewe's cheeses, the ones nobody wants any more: tupí is made precisely for them.
Cut off the rind, grate them coarsely and pound them with the garlic and pepper to a lumpy paste.
Pack into a stoneware pot, expelling air at each layer, and cover with a finger of brandy.
The brandy must always sit on top: it is what keeps mould off while fermentation works underneath.
Cover with a cloth and a loose lid, and leave in the cellar two to four months. Stir weekly. Spread on toast, in very small quantities.

borra-andorrana.d: A thick soup of toasted flour and milk, with an egg broken into it at the last moment. It was the shepherds' breakfast before going up to the summer pastures: it costs nothing, takes a quarter of an hour and holds a body until evening.
s: Melt the lard and throw in the flour; stir constantly over low heat until it turns hazelnut brown and smells of toast.
That toasting takes a good ten minutes: it is where all the flavour of borra comes from, white flour gives only a bland paste.
Pour in the hot milk in a stream, whisking hard, so that not a single lump forms.
Let it thicken for 20 minutes over very low heat, stirring often — the base catches in an instant.
Break the eggs into the simmering soup and let them set for 3 minutes without stirring. Sugar and cinnamon, or salt, depending on the hour.

cargols-a-la-llauna.p: Aixirivall, Sant Julià de Lòria, Andorra
cargols-a-la-llauna.d: Snails grilled dry on a sheet of tin, mouth upward, and dipped in aioli. The llauna is the tin itself: set over coals, it heats fiercely enough for the snail to cook in its own juice without a drop of fat.
s: Fast the snails a week in an airy box, then purge them 2 hours in coarse salt and rinse until the water runs clear.
Set them on the tin mouth upward, packed tight, and give each a pinch of coarse salt.
Put the tin over the coals: they froth for a few minutes, then the froth dries and the snail retracts — the sign they are half done.
Allow 20 minutes in all and baste with nothing: any fat would drown the flavour and make the tin smoke.
Meanwhile make an aioli with pounded garlic and oil trickled in. Serve the snails scalding, on picks, with the aioli and bread.

torro-d-andorra.d: A nougat of mountain honey and hazelnuts, darker and rougher than the Alicante kind. Andorran pedlars sold it across Catalonia at Christmas; the heather honey of the high valleys gives it a bitterness sugar alone never reaches.
s: Roast the hazelnuts 12 minutes at 160°C and rub them in a cloth to remove the skins: one skin left makes the nougat bitter in patches.
Cook the honey alone for 20 minutes over low heat to drive off its water, then add the sugar and take it to 140°C.
Whisk the whites to firm peaks and pour in the scalding honey in a thin stream, whisking without pause: poured at once it would scramble them.
Keep beating 15 minutes over a bain-marie, until a drop thrown into cold water hardens immediately.
Fold in the warm nuts, pour between two sheets of rice paper and press under a weight for 24 hours before cutting.

mato-amb-mel.d: A fresh unsalted curd cheese, served drowned in mountain honey and walnuts. Mató is never salted and never aged: it is eaten within two days, and its complete lack of salt is what leaves all the room to the honey.
s: Heat the raw milk to exactly 35°C: any hotter and the rennet works too fast and the curd turns rubbery.
Add the rennet, stir for ten seconds then leave it absolutely still for 45 minutes, never touching the vessel — the least jolt breaks the forming curd.
Cut the curd in a 2 cm grid and let it firm up for 15 minutes.
Lift it out with a skimmer into moulds; drain for 2 hours, without pressing.
Turn out, pour honey over generously and scatter walnut halves. Do not salt under any circumstances.

coques-d-oli-i-anis.d: Thin sweet biscuits of olive oil and anise, baked without leaven and crisp as glass. They were made for the village patron saints' days: they travel unbroken in a cloth and keep for a whole month.
s: Warm the olive oil with the anise seeds and zest, and infuse for an hour before straining.
Mix it with the flour, 80 g of the sugar, the anisette, white wine and salt, and bring the dough together without kneading.
Rest it for 30 minutes: relaxed, it rolls twice as thin.
Roll to 2 mm and cut ovals by hand rather than with a cutter, to keep uneven edges.
Sprinkle with the remaining sugar and bake 12 minutes at 190°C. Take them out as soon as the edges go gold: a browned coca is bitter.

civet-d-isard.d: Pyrenean chamois marinated three days in red wine then long stewed, the sauce bound with blood. The animal lives above two thousand metres and its flesh is lean and sinewy: without the marinade and the bacon that feeds it, it would stay dry.
s: Marinate the meat in large pieces for three days in the cold, in the wine, vegetables, juniper and herbs, turning it daily.
Drain and pat the meat thoroughly dry: wet meat boils instead of searing, and the civet loses its dark colour.
Sear it in small batches, dust with flour, return the strained marinade and the vegetables, and simmer covered for 3 hours.
Collect the blood mixed with vinegar — the vinegar stops it setting — and add it only at the very last moment, off the heat.
The blood must never boil, or the sauce grains irrecoverably. Add the chocolate, stir and serve at once.

truita-de-riu-amb-pernil.d: A trout wrapped in a slice of dry-cured ham and pan-fried, with no other seasoning. The ham does the work of fat, salt and crust all at once: the dish of valleys where fish and pig were the only two reliable resources of the year.
s: Gut the trout and wipe them; on no account salt them, the ham does that and a double salting would be inedible.
Slip a crushed garlic clove and a sprig of parsley into each belly.
Wind two slices of ham in a spiral around each fish, overlapping slightly.
Fry in hot oil 5 minutes a side, starting on the seam of the ham so that it seals as it cooks.
The ham should be crisp and the flesh just opaque at the bone. Pepper, squeeze lemon and serve at once.

bunyols-de-quaresma.d: Small yeasted fritters with anise and zest, fried and rolled in sugar, eaten through Lent. They are lean in the religious sense: no butter, no lard, only oil — and that is precisely why they were permitted.
s: Dissolve the yeast in warm milk and let it foam for a quarter of an hour before adding anything else.
Knead with the flour, eggs, 60 g of the sugar, the zests, anisette, olive oil and salt for 12 minutes.
Prove for 1½ hours: the dough should be soft and sticky, worked with oiled hands and never floured ones.
Form rings by piercing each ball with an oiled finger and let them rise 30 minutes on a cloth.
Fry 2 minutes a side at 170°C — no hotter, or they brown before the centre cooks. Roll them warm in the remaining sugar.

vi-calent-de-muntanya.d: Red wine warmed with honey, cinnamon and orange peel, served in the refuges after the descent. The whole difficulty is temperature: above 78°C the alcohol evaporates and nothing is left but a warm, characterless syrup.
s: Pare the orange and lemon zest with a peeler, avoiding the white pith which would bring bitterness.
Stud a whole orange with cloves and put it in the cold wine with the zests, cinnamon and star anise.
Bring slowly to 70°C and hold it there for 20 minutes without ever letting it tremble: this is an infusion, not cooking.
Add the honey and sugar off the heat and stir until dissolved, then the brandy last.
Strain and serve scalding in thick glasses scalded beforehand, otherwise they crack.

pescaito-frito.d: A fry of small fish coated in durum flour and dropped into scalding olive oil. Andalusian frying uses neither egg nor breadcrumb: flour alone makes a film so thin the fish's skin shows through it.
s: Salt the whole fish half an hour ahead, then blot them: salt draws out the surface water, and it is that water that makes oil spit.
Flour them in a sieve of semolina flour and shake them hard — excess flour falls off into the oil and burns it.
Bring the olive oil to 190°C: cooler, the fish drinks it; hotter, the flour blackens before the flesh cooks.
Fry in small handfuls, 90 seconds only, never filling more than a third of the pan.
Drain upright in a colander rather than flat on paper, so steam does not soften the underside. Salt and lemon at the table.

tortillitas-de-camarones.d: Lace-edged fritters of minute shrimps, made from a batter of chickpea flour and seawater. The camarones are eaten whole, shell and all; the batter must be so thin that it spreads by itself in the oil.
s: Mix the two flours, the very finely chopped spring onion and parsley, and the paprika.
Whisk in cold water to the consistency of pouring cream — far thinner than pancake batter.
Add the raw whole shrimps and rest for an hour in the cold: the batter must relax, and the shrimps give up a little of their salty water.
Salt lightly, or not at all, if you have used seawater as they do in San Fernando.
Pour a ladleful into oil at 190°C without spreading it: it should run out by itself into a lacy disc. 90 seconds a side, and serve at once.

ajo-blanco.d: A cold soup of almonds, garlic and bread, served with muscat grapes. It predates gazpacho by centuries: it is the soup of al-Andalus, made before the tomato arrived from America, and garlic stands in for the pepper.
s: Blanch the almonds for a minute and pinch off the skins: one skin left specks the soup brown and bitter.
Soak the stale crumb in a little water, then barely press it — it must stay wet.
Blend the almonds, bread, garlic and salt at length with a third of the water, at least 4 minutes, until perfectly smooth.
Trickle in the olive oil with the motor running, as for mayonnaise: that emulsion is what gives the whiteness and the body.
Loosen with the rest of the iced water, sharpen with sherry vinegar and chill for 3 hours. Serve with peeled muscat grapes.

flamenquin-cordobes.d: A roll of pork escalope wrapped around serrano ham, crumbed and fried. The name is said to come from the golden colour, recalling the fair hair of the Flemings at Charles V's court; it is eaten cold as a tapa as readily as hot on a plate.
s: Cut the loin into escalopes and beat them between two films to 3 mm, striking with the flat and not the edge of the mallet.
Pepper but do not salt: the serrano ham brings all the salt needed.
Lay a slice of ham on each escalope and roll very tightly, expelling the air; chill 30 minutes so the roll holds.
Flour, dip in beaten egg then breadcrumbs, and repeat egg and crumb a second time — that double coating is what stops the roll opening.
Fry 5 minutes at 170°C, rolling them in the oil, and drain upright. Cut on the bias.

espetos-de-sardinas.d: Six sardines threaded on a cane and planted at an angle before a wood fire, in an old boat filled with sand. They are made only in the months without an R, May to August, when sardines are fat: lean, they dry out before they are done.
s: Neither gut nor scale the sardines: the viscera scent the flesh as it cooks and the scales protect the skin from the fire.
Thread them through the flank, under the backbone, six to a cane, all heads facing the same way.
Salt generously with coarse salt half an hour ahead, working it into the skin, and leave them in the open air.
Plant the cane at an angle in the sand, thirty centimetres from the coals, belly side to the fire first.
Give them 4 minutes on that side then turn the whole cane: a sardine is done when the eye whitens and the skin splits. Never turn it twice.

cazon-en-adobo.d: Cubes of dogfish marinated in vinegar, garlic and cumin, then floured and fried. The adobo is not a seasoning but a preservation: vinegar kept the fish two days before refrigeration, and the cumin is a direct inheritance from al-Andalus.
s: Cut the cazón into 3 cm cubes, removing the central cartilage, which comes away in one piece.
Pound the garlic with the cumin, oregano, paprika and salt, then slake with the vinegar and water.
Marinate the fish at least 4 hours, ideally 12: less and the adobo does not penetrate; longer and the vinegar cooks the flesh and turns it mealy.
Drain without rinsing, blot, and flour with fine semolina just before frying.
Fry 3 minutes at 180°C, in small batches. Serve scalding, without lemon: the acidity is already in the fish.

polea-andaluza.d: A porridge of flour, milk and anise, covered with fried croutons and cinnamon. It is the pudding of the hungry years, when there were neither eggs nor sugar to spare; Sevillians still eat it out of nostalgia and serve it at All Saints.
s: Infuse the milk with the anise seeds, zest and a cinnamon stick for 15 minutes without boiling, then strain.
Slake the flour in a glass of cold milk before anything hot goes in: the only sure way to avoid lumps.
Pour the hot infused milk onto the slaked flour, whisking, then return to low heat with the sugar.
Stir without pause for 20 minutes, scraping the corners of the pan: poleá catches the instant you stop.
Fry bread dice in olive oil, drain them, and set them on the warm porridge with cinnamon. They must stay crisp.

pringa.d: The meats from a cocido crushed with a fork and packed into a small round roll. Pringar means to dip: a leftovers dish that has become Seville's most-ordered tapa, and it is never crushed in a machine.
s: Take the meats from an already-cooked cocido, still warm: cold, the fat sets and crushing becomes impossible.
Skin the chorizo and the black pudding, and remove any bone and gristle from the belly.
Crush everything with a fork on a board, working each meat separately before combining: they do not yield alike.
The texture must stay stringy and lumpy — that is the difference between a pringá and a potted meat.
Pepper, add a touch of crushed garlic, and pack it generously into a barely warm roll. Eaten with no cutlery.

pa-amb-tomaquet.d: Toasted bread rubbed with ripe tomato, dressed with olive oil and salted. The tomato is never laid on in slices: it is halved and rubbed until only the skin is left in your hand, so the pulp goes into the crumb.
s: Choose a country loaf with a tight crumb and a thick crust: too airy a bread tears under the rubbing.
Toast the slices on both sides until golden but still soft in the middle.
Rub very lightly with a cut garlic clove — the garlic is optional, and many in Barcelona go without.
Halve the tomato and rub the cut flesh onto the hot crumb, pressing, until the slice is red and damp.
