Trickle over olive oil and salt with coarse salt. Eaten within five minutes, or the bread goes soggy.

botifarra-amb-mongetes.d: A Catalan sausage grilled with white beans sautéed in its own fat. Mongetes del ganxet, whose skin is so fine it vanishes under the tooth, grow only within fifty kilometres of Vic and Barcelona.
s: Soak the beans overnight and cook them 1½ hours at a bare simmer with the bay, unsalted — salt hardens the skin.
Salt only at the end, and let them cool in their liquid: that is how they keep their shape.
Prick the botifarres just twice with a needle and cook them 15 minutes in a pan over low heat, turning often.
Lift them out, keep every drop of rendered fat and turn the sliced garlic pale gold in it without burning.
Tip the drained beans into that fat and sauté 5 minutes, moving them by shaking the pan, never with a spoon which would break them. Add parsley.

canelons-de-sant-esteve.d: The cannelloni of 26 December, filled with the remains of the previous day's escudella and gratinated under béchamel. Italian cooks who came to work in Barcelona in the 19th century brought the pasta; Catalans filled it with what they had, and the tradition was born of a household need.
s: Make a sofregit of onion and grated tomato, 40 minutes over low heat, until only a brick-red paste remains.
Mince yesterday's cooked meats and the sautéed livers twice, add them to the sofregit and flame with brandy.
Bind the filling with a ladle of béchamel and cool it completely: warm, it tears the pasta as you roll.
Cook the sheets al dente, spread them on a damp cloth, fill and roll tightly, seam down.
Coat with nutmegged béchamel until covered, scatter cheese and pine nuts, and gratinate 25 minutes at 200°C.

gilda.d: An olive, a pickled green chilli and an anchovy on a cocktail stick, dressed with oil. Created at Casa Vallés in 1946, it is named after the Rita Hayworth film: verde, salada y un poco picante — green, salty and a little spicy, like the heroine.
s: Choose pickled Ibarra guindilla peppers, long and pale: they are barely hot, only sour.
Drain and blot them, and the anchovies too, or vinegar runs down your fingers at the first bite.
Pull off the pepper stalks and fold each in two or three depending on its length.
Thread onto the stick in this order: olive, folded pepper, coiled anchovy, folded pepper, olive. The order matters: the anchovy must sit in the centre, shielded by the vinegar.
Trickle over olive oil and serve at once, at room temperature. A cold gilda has no flavour at all.

talo-con-chistorra.d: A maize flatbread cooked on a griddle, rolled around a grilled chistorra. Talo was the daily bread of the Basque Country before wheat became common there; it survives only at village festivals, made in front of the crowd.
s: Mix the maize flour, salt and very hot water, working with a spoon then by hand as soon as you can: the water must be boiling, warm water will not take the flour.
Knead 5 minutes into a supple ball and rest it 15 minutes under a damp cloth.
Flatten balls between two films into 2 mm discs: without gluten the dough tears, and you patch it with your fingertips.
Cook on a very hot dry griddle, 2 minutes a side — the flatbread puffs a little and blisters brown.
Grill the chistorra, lay it on the scalding talo with a shaving of ewe's cheese, roll it and eat with your hands at once.

bocadillo-de-calamares.d: Fried squid rings piled into a roll, with no sauce and no garnish. Madrid is three hundred kilometres from the sea: the bocadillo was born at the freight station where fish arrived overnight, and the city made it its most improbable emblem.
s: Clean the squid and cut it into rings exactly a centimetre wide: thinner they dry out, thicker they stay raw in the middle.
Soak them 2 hours in milk — the only tenderising Madrid practises, and it transforms frozen squid.
Drain, blot, then flour them in a shaken bag, and sieve off the excess.
Fry at 190°C for 90 seconds, in small handfuls: beyond two minutes the flesh shrinks and turns elastic.
Split the roll without buttering it and pile in the scalding rings. A wedge of lemon on the side, never a sauce.

callos-a-la-madrilena.d: Beef tripe stewed with chorizo, black pudding and snout, in a red paprika sauce. The gelatine from the calf's foot binds the sauce without flour: that is how good callos are known, they stick to the lips.
s: Scrub the tripe with coarse salt and vinegar, rinsing seven or eight times, until the water runs perfectly clear — it takes a while and it is essential.
Blanch 15 minutes, throw the water away, then cook 3 hours with the calf's foot, snout, bay and cloves.
The calf's foot is not there for flavour: it brings the gelatine that will bind the sauce, and without it callos stay thin.
Make a sofrito of onion and garlic, add the ham, and the sweet and hot paprika off the heat — burnt, paprika turns bitter in three seconds.
Combine tripe, sofrito, chorizo and black pudding, and simmer an hour more. Rest overnight and reheat: they are better the next day.

huevos-estrellados.d: Fried eggs broken over a bed of chips, crushed with a fork at the table so the yolk runs everywhere. Estrellar means to smash: the gesture is part of the dish, and it belongs to the customer, never the cook.
s: Cut the potatoes into thick batons and first confit them 12 minutes at 140°C in olive oil, without letting them colour.
Lift them out, let them cool for twenty minutes, then return them at 190°C to brown — the two baths are not negotiable.
Fried once only, they would be soft inside and would collapse under the yolk.
Fry the eggs in the same very hot oil, spooning it over the white, until the edges are lacy and the yolk still liquid.
Set them on the chips, add the ham in strips, salt with coarse salt and smash everything with a fork in front of your guests.

torreznos-de-soria.d: Belly pork with rind blown into even bubbles, crisp as glass. The Soria torrezno is the only one in Spain with a guarantee mark; the secret is not in the frying but in the three days of drying that precede it.
s: Dry-salt the belly, rind included, and leave it 24 hours in the cold; rinse then dry it for three days in cool air.
That drying of the rind is the whole secret: damp, it will never bubble and stays leathery.
Cut 3 cm strips and lay them rind down in a cold pan with a finger of water.
Heat gently: the water evaporates, the fat renders and replaces the liquid without the rind burning. Allow 45 minutes over very low heat, rind always down.
Finally take the oil to 190°C: the rind bursts into bubbles in about thirty seconds. Lift them out at once and salt.

all-i-pebre.d: Lagoon eels stewed with garlic, paprika and almond in an earthenware pot. The dish of the Albufera fishermen: no tomato, no onion, only garlic — the name, garlic and pepper, states the whole recipe.
s: Have the eels cut into sections by the fishmonger and rinse them at length: all their mucus must go, or the sauce stays slimy.
In the earthenware pot, turn the whole unpeeled garlic, the almonds and the slice of bread golden, then lift them out.
Pound them in a mortar with the parsley and a little water to make the picada.
Off the heat, throw the paprika into the hot oil and stir for two seconds before adding the water immediately: this is the critical gesture, burnt paprika makes the dish bitter.
Cook sliced potatoes 15 minutes in that broth, add the eels and the picada, and simmer 12 minutes without ever stirring — you shake the pot instead.

esgarraet.d: Roasted red peppers torn by hand and mixed with raw desalted cod, garlic and oil. Esgarrar means to tear: the knife is banned, because a blade cuts the fibres instead of separating them and the pepper then weeps.
s: Roast the whole peppers 40 minutes at 200°C, turning them, until the skin blisters and blackens in patches.
Shut them in a sealed bag for 20 minutes: the steam lifts the skin, which then comes away in one movement.
Peel them without running them under water — water would carry off all the juice the roasting concentrated — and tear them into strips by hand.
Desalt the cod for 24 hours, changing the water four times, blot it and shred it raw into coarse strands.
Mix everything with finely sliced garlic and olive oil, and macerate 6 hours in the cold. Served cold, with bread.

arroz-al-horno.d: Rice baked in an earthenware cazuela, crowned with a whole head of garlic and slices of potato. It was made the day after the cocido with its broth: the head of garlic planted in the centre is no ornament, it is squeezed into the rice at the table.
s: Brown the pork ribs in the cazuela with the oil, then the potato slices and the halved tomatoes; set everything aside.
Tip the rice into the scented oil and stir 2 minutes to pearl it, then add the paprika off the heat.
Pour in boiling broth in the exact ratio of two and a quarter parts to one of rice: this rice is not stirred again and cannot be corrected.
Distribute the meats, potatoes, chickpeas and black pudding, and plant the whole head of garlic in the centre.
Bake 45 minutes at 200°C without once touching the dish. The rice must be dry, every grain separate, with a light crust formed on top.

horchata-de-chufa.d: A tiger nut milk, white and sweet, drunk iced with fartons dipped in it. The chufa is a tuber the Arabs brought to Valencia; in Europe it grows on barely four hundred hectares north of the city, and industrial horchata has nothing to do with the fresh kind.
s: Wash the tiger nuts under plenty of water, scrubbing, then soak them 12 hours: dry, they are hard as gravel and no blender touches them.
Rinse them again and blend with a third of the water, at length, to a gritty purée.
Add the rest of the water, the zest and cinnamon, and macerate 3 hours in the cold.
Strain through a fine cloth, twisting hard: it is that pressing, not the blending, that extracts the fat and gives the velvet.
Sweeten, stir until dissolved and serve very cold, almost frosted. It keeps two days at most and separates: shake before pouring.

agua-de-valencia.d: Orange juice, cava, vodka and gin, served by the jug. Created at the Café Madrid in 1959 for a group of Basques who wanted something other than the usual cava; the owner served them this saying it was water from Valencia, and the name stuck.
s: Squeeze the oranges the same day: yesterday's juice loses its scent and takes on a bitter peel taste.
Strain it through a wide sieve to hold back the pips but let the pulp through, which gives the body.
Dissolve the sugar in the cold juice, stirring at length, before any alcohol goes in.
Add the vodka and gin, stir, then chill for an hour: everything must be freezing before the next step.
Pour the cava in last, gently, down the side of the jug, and stir only once, slowly. Serve without ice, which would water it down.

tarta-de-santiago.d: An almond cake with neither flour nor leaven, marked with the cross of Saint James in icing sugar. Only three ingredients go in: it is the quantity of egg, and the air whisked into it, that gives all the lightness to an otherwise dense cake.
s: Whisk the whole eggs with the sugar for at least 10 minutes, until the mixture triples and ribbons for three seconds.
With no flour and no leaven, that aeration is the only thing keeping the cake from being a dense disc.
Fold in the ground almonds, zest and cinnamon with a spatula, lifting, in some twenty movements.
Pour into a buttered 24 cm tin and bake 40 minutes at 175°C: a skewer should come out just dry.
Cool, set a stencil of the cross of Santiago on top and dust with icing sugar before lifting it straight up.

caldo-gallego.d: A soup of turnip tops, white beans and potato, enriched with unto — aged rancid lard. Unto is what separates a real caldo from a vegetable soup: its slight rancidity, deliberately sought, gives a depth neither bacon nor oil replaces.
s: Soak the beans and the salt pork separately, overnight each, changing the pork's water twice.
Start the beans, bones and pork in cold water and simmer for an hour, skimming at the beginning.
Add the lard and the potatoes broken with a spoon rather than cut — breaking releases the starch and thickens the broth by itself.
Wash the turnip tops and blanch them 3 minutes separately if the season is late: after flowering they turn bitter and would spoil the whole pot.
Bring everything together and cook 40 minutes more. Salt only at the end, and rest an hour before serving.

pimientos-de-padron.d: Small green peppers fried whole in olive oil and salted with coarse salt. The local saying goes uns pican e outros non, some are hot and some are not — about one in ten, and nothing tells you before you bite.
s: Choose small peppers, four to five centimetres: larger ones are older, more fibrous and far more often hot.
Wash and dry them carefully: the least drop of water makes the scalding oil explode.
Do not remove the stalks — they are the handle for eating — but pierce each one with a knife point so it does not burst.
Toss them over high heat in hot oil for 5 minutes, shaking the pan constantly, until the skin blisters and browns in patches.
Drain on paper and salt with coarse salt while scalding: salt does not stick to a cooled pepper.

cachopo.d: Two veal escalopes sealed around ham and cheese, crumbed and fried, as wide as a plate. It is ordered for two and shared: a single-portion cachopo does not exist on Asturian menus.
s: Have the butcher beat the escalopes to 4 mm, in two pieces of identical size.
Pepper the inside but do not salt: ham and cheese already bring all the salt.
Lay the ham then the cheese leaving two centimetres clear all round, and set the second escalope on top.
Seal the edges pressing firmly with your fingertips, then pinching: a cachopo that opens empties its cheese into the oil.
Flour, egg and crumb twice, then fry 6 minutes at 170°C — low and long, so the centre melts before the crust burns.

sobao-pasiego.d: A small butter cake baked in a paper case, dense and moist, in which butter is a third of the weight. It grew out of leftover sweet bread that the Pas valley women reworked with butter; sobar means to knead long by hand.
s: Take the butter out three hours ahead: it must be perfectly soft, neither melted nor firm, or nothing emulsifies.
Beat it with the sugar for at least 8 minutes, until it pales and nearly doubles.
Add the eggs one at a time, waiting for each to be fully absorbed: poured in together they split the mixture.
Fold in the sifted flour and baking powder, the zest, honey, rum and salt, without working it.
Fill the paper cases three-quarters full and bake 22 minutes at 200°C. The top should be dark brown and the centre still moist.

quesada-pasiega.d: A custard of curdled milk, butter and cinnamon, baked shallow until the top browns. It was made from milk that had turned: a thrift pudding, and fresh milk never gives the same acidity in the background.
s: Drain the fresh cheese 2 hours in a colander: too wet, the quesada does not set and stays liquid in the middle.
Crush it with a fork with the sugar, then add the eggs one at a time and the warm melted butter.
Fold in the sifted flour, the milk, cinnamon, zest and salt; the batter should ribbon thickly off the whisk.
Pour into a buttered rectangular tin, 3 cm deep at most — this is a quesada, not a cake, and its shallowness makes its texture.
Bake 45 minutes at 180°C until the top is dark brown. Cool completely before cutting into squares.

morcilla-de-burgos.d: A blood pudding with rice and onion, in which rice is nearly a quarter of the whole. It is bound with neither crumb nor flour: the grains swell in the blood and show distinctly in the slice, which sets Burgos apart from every other Spanish pudding.
s: Confit the very finely sliced onion in the fat for an hour over low heat, until translucent and entirely dry.
Cook the rice only halfway, 8 minutes, and refresh it: fully cooked, it would burst inside the pudding.
Combine the warm onion, the rice, the spices and salt, then pour in the sieved blood, stirring.
Fill the casings only half full — the rice doubles again while poaching, and a full skin bursts without fail.
Poach 45 minutes at 80°C, never boiling, pricking with a needle after 10 minutes. Cut thick and fry or grill.

botillo-del-bierzo.d: A large casing stuffed with pork ribs, tail and bones, smoked then boiled for three hours. It is served whole in the middle of the table and opened with a single cut: the pieces keep their bones, and they are eaten with the fingers.
s: Cut the ribs and tail into sections with their bones: the bone gives a botillo its flavour and its gelatine, and a boned botillo is no longer one.
Rub every piece with crushed garlic, paprika, oregano and salt, and macerate 24 hours in the cold.
Pack the casing by hand, pressing firmly, tie it and hang it to dry for three days.
Cold-smoke over oak for a week, then prick it in five or six places before poaching — without those pricks it bursts in the pot.
Poach 3 hours at a bare simmer, changing the water once, and cook the cabbage, chorizo and potatoes in the second broth.

patatas-revolconas.d: A mash of potato crushed with paprika, bright orange, crowned with crisp torreznos. Revolcar means to wallow: the mash is not whipped, it is rolled in the paprika fat until it is soaked through.
s: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins with bay and salt, and keep a glass of the cooking water.
Fry the belly lardons until crisp, lift them out and keep every drop of fat.
Turn the garlic golden in that fat, then take the pan off the heat before adding the paprikas and cumin: over the flame they burn in two seconds and turn bitter.
Peel the potatoes hot and crush them straight into the pan with a fork, rolling them in the red fat.
Loosen with a little cooking water, salt and crown with the crisp lardons at the moment of serving.

migas-manchegas.d: Stale bread crumbled and dampened, fried at length with oil and garlic until every crumb separates. It was the breakfast of La Mancha shepherds: they set out with the week's bread, and the previous night's rain served to dampen it.
s: Crumble two-day-old bread with a knife into pieces the size of a maize grain — never in a processor, which gives powder.
Sprinkle it with salted water, mix by hand, wrap it in a damp cloth and leave it overnight.
The bread must be supple but not sodden: too much water and the migas clag into mush, too little and they stay hard.
Fry the unpeeled garlic, chorizo and belly in the oil, lift them out and add the paprika off the heat.
Tip in the crumbs and stir constantly for 30 minutes over medium heat, lifting with a spatula: they must end golden, dry and perfectly separate. Serve with grapes.

caldereta-extremena.d: A milk-lamb stew bound with a picada of liver, bread and almonds, cooked in a cauldron over the fire. Transhumance shepherds made it with whichever beast had injured itself on the road: nothing goes in that a mule cannot carry.
s: Sear the lamb in large bone-in pieces in scalding oil, in small batches, until well coloured.
Fry the onion, garlic and pepper in the same oil, add the paprika off the heat and return the meat.
Moisten with white wine and water to cover, add the bay and cloves, and simmer covered for 2 hours.
Sauté the lamb's liver and fry the bread, then pound them in a mortar with the almonds, raw garlic and a little sauce.
Add this picada 20 minutes before the end: it is what binds and what gives the flavour, and it must on no account boil long, or the liver turns grainy.

zorongollo.d: A warm salad of roasted red peppers, tomato and hard-boiled egg, with Extremaduran oil. The pepper is peeled without ever going under water: the juice collected during roasting is the dressing, and rinsing it would be throwing the dish away.
s: Roast the whole peppers and tomatoes 45 minutes at 200°C, turning them halfway, until the skin blisters and lifts.
Shut them under a cloth or in a sealed bag for 20 minutes, while the steam frees the skins.
Peel them over a bowl to catch every drop of juice, and tear the flesh into strips by hand.
Strain the juice and mix it with the oil, vinegar, crushed garlic, cumin and salt: that is the whole dressing.
Add the chopped hard-boiled eggs and macerate 2 hours at room temperature — never in the fridge, cold kills the flavour of the pepper.

migas-aragonesas.d: Bread crumbs fried with Teruel ham and grapes, fattier and coarser than the La Mancha kind. In Aragon they are cut into dice rather than crumbs, and served with hot chocolate at breakfast — the custom surprises, but it is old.
s: Cut the stale bread into half-centimetre dice rather than crumbling it: that is the Aragonese cut, and it gives a firmer mouthful.
Dampen with salted water sprinkled by hand, mix, and rest under a cloth for six to twelve hours.
Fry the unpeeled garlic, the belly and the diced ham in the oil, and lift them out.
Tip the bread dice into the fat and stir without pause for 25 minutes over medium heat — this is an arm exercise, there is no shortcut.
Add the paprika off the heat, return the meats and the fresh grapes, and serve scalding. The grapes bring the acidity that cuts the fat.

bacalao-ajoarriero.d: Shredded salt cod stewed with garlic, choricero pepper and tomato. The name comes from the arrieros, the muleteers who carried salt cod across Spain: they cooked it on the road, with the garlic they always carried.
s: Desalt the cod 36 hours in the fridge, changing the water five times, then shred it raw by hand into strands.
Soak the choricero peppers 2 hours in hot water and scrape the pulp with a spoon: it, not paprika, gives the colour and the flavour.
Confit the onion and green pepper 30 minutes over low heat, then add the sliced garlic without letting it brown.
Add the grated tomato and the choricero pulp, and reduce for 20 minutes to a thick paste.
Fold in the cod and move it by shaking the pan rather than with a spoon: the gelatine from the skin binds the sauce by itself. 10 minutes, and not one more.

tumbet-mallorqui.d: Layers of potato, aubergine and pepper fried separately, flooded with tomato sauce. Each vegetable is fried alone because none shares the same cooking time or the same way of drinking oil: it is slow, and it is the very definition of the dish.
s: Slice the aubergines, salt them and let them drain 45 minutes in a colander, then blot them thoroughly.
This step is not optional: an undrained aubergine drinks three times the oil and weeps into the dish.
Fry each vegetable separately in the same oil: potatoes first, then peppers, aubergines last — from the most neutral to the most scented.
Make a long tomato sauce, 40 minutes, with the garlic, bay and a pinch of sugar, and pass it through a sieve.
Build the layers in an earthenware dish, salting each, coat with sauce and bake 20 minutes at 180°C. Eaten warm or cold, never scalding.

gofio-escaldado.d: Toasted grain flour scalded with fish broth, beaten to a thick purée and eaten with a spoon. Gofio is the inheritance of the Guanches, the Canaries' people before the conquest: they toasted barley before grinding it, and the practice has never stopped.
s: Make a broth from fish heads and bones, strained and full-flavoured: gofio is made with water only in years of hardship.
Pound the garlic, mint, coriander and a little salt in a mortar to a green paste.
Pour the boiling broth onto the gofio all at once, whisking hard from the moment they meet: poured slowly it lumps beyond rescue.
Work it 5 minutes with a wooden spoon: the paste must come away from the sides and fall in a heavy ribbon.
Fold in the herb paste, mound it up and hollow the top with a spoon to hold a trickle of oil and some raw sliced onion.

mojo-picon.d: A red sauce of garlic, palmero chilli, cumin and paprika, mounted with oil and vinegar. There is a mojo for everything: red for meat and potatoes, green with coriander for fish, and they are not swapped.
s: Soak the dried chillies 30 minutes in hot water, open them and scrape the pulp with a spoon, discarding seeds and skins.
Pound the garlic with the coarse salt in a mortar: the salt acts as an abrasive, and the garlic turns to cream instead of leaping into the corners.
Add the cumin, paprika and chilli pulp, and keep pounding to an even paste.
Pour in the vinegar then the oil in a thin stream, turning the pestle always the same way — this is an emulsion, and it splits if you hurry.
Add a soaked crumb of bread if the mojo stays thin. Rest it 24 hours: it is poor on the first day and excellent on the second.

bienmesabe-canario.d: A thick cream of almonds, egg yolks and syrup, scented with lemon and cinnamon. The name means it tastes good to me: it came from al-Andalus by way of Antequera, and Canarian convents adopted it in the 17th century, making it denser.
s: Bring the water and sugar to 105°C with the zest and cinnamon, then take it off and let it fall to 50°C.
Stir the ground almonds into the warm syrup and return to very low heat for 10 minutes, stirring.
Beat the yolks separately, pour a ladle of the hot mixture onto them whisking, then return everything to the pan.
This tempering is no idle precaution: yolks poured straight into hot syrup scramble into lumps beyond recovery.
Cook 10 minutes below 80°C, never boiling, until the cream coats the spoon. Scent with rum and serve cold over sponge.

tajarin-al-tartufo.d: Very fine tagliolini made with thirty egg yolks to the kilo, served in butter and shaved with white Alba truffle. The dough is almost orange: it contains not a single white, and that richness is what lets it be cut so fine without breaking.
s: Knead the flour and yolks for 15 minutes: the dough is very dry at first and seems impossible, it smooths out with work.
Wrap it and rest it an hour — without rest it shrinks back as you roll and never goes thin enough.
Roll until you can see your hand through it, dust with semolina, roll the sheet on itself and cut one-millimetre ribbons with a knife.
Cook 90 seconds only in generously salted water: these noodles are done almost before they reach the bottom.
Melt the butter without colouring it, bind the tajarin with a spoonful of cooking water, and shave the truffle at the table, never before.

agnolotti-del-plin.d: Tiny ravioli closed with a pinch of thumb and forefinger — the plin — filled with three roasted meats. They are traditionally served on a napkin, with no sauce at all, so that no moisture masks the taste of the filling.
s: Roast the three meats together in butter and rosemary, deglaze with white wine and let them cool in their juices.
Mince them twice on the fine plate with blanched, pressed spinach, and bind with parmesan, yolks and nutmeg.
Roll the dough very thin and set hazelnuts of filling every two centimetres along a single strip.
Fold the dough over, expel the air, then pinch between each mound: that pinch is the plin, and it seals without dampening.
Cut with a wheel and cook for 2 minutes. Serve in sage butter, or on a napkin with a few drops of the roasting juices, as in the Langhe.

gianduiotto.d: An elongated chocolate ingot made with Piedmont hazelnuts, born of the continental blockade of 1806. With cocoa scarce and dear, Turin chocolatiers cut it with hazelnut paste: a shortage produced the most copied chocolate in the world.
s: Roast the hazelnuts 15 minutes at 160°C and rub them in a cloth: not one skin must remain, or the paste turns bitter and gritty.
Blend them at length, ten minutes at least, scraping the sides: they pass through powder, then paste, then oil — that last stage is the one to reach.
Melt the chocolate and cocoa butter to 45°C, then bring it down to 27°C stirring on marble before raising it to 31°C.
This tempering is not optional: without it the gianduiotto blooms within days and melts between the fingers.
Combine hazelnut paste, tempered chocolate and icing sugar, then mould into three-sided ingots or pipe them. Crystallise 12 hours at 16°C.

fonduta-valdostana.d: Fontina melted in milk and bound with egg yolks, served as a cream and not as a stringy mass. Unlike the Swiss and Savoyard fondues it holds neither wine nor starch: it is an egg custard, nearer to a sauce than to a pot.
s: Slice the fontina thinly and soak it in the milk for 12 hours in the fridge: without that soaking it never melts evenly.
The next day, melt the butter in a bain-marie and add the cheese with its milk.
Whisk without pause until the mixture is even; never go above 70°C, beyond which the cheese separates into strings and oil.
Add the yolks one at a time, off the heat, whisking briskly after each.
Return to the bain-marie for 3 minutes until the cream coats the spoon, pepper and serve over toast or polenta, with shaved white truffle.

focaccia-genovese.d: A low, oily focaccia dimpled with deep holes where oil and brine pool. In Genoa it is dipped in cappuccino at breakfast; the holes are not decorative, they hold the brine that keeps the dough from drying in the oven.
s: Knead the flour, warm water, yeast, malt, 40 ml of oil and salt for 12 minutes: the dough should be supple and slightly tacky.
Prove for an hour, then spread it by hand in an oiled tray to 1.5 cm and let it relax for 45 minutes.
Push your fingers straight down to the bottom of the tray, hand held vertical: the holes must go through the dough, not merely mark it.
Beat the remaining water, coarse salt and remaining oil into a salamoia, and pour it over the whole surface.
Prove 45 minutes more — the brine will be half absorbed — and bake 18 minutes at 230°C. It must stay soft and glossy.

cotoletta-alla-milanese.d: A veal cutlet on the bone, crumbed and fried in clarified butter, a finger thick. It is not flattened: the true milanese keeps the thickness of the chop, and it is the later Viennese version that is beaten with a mallet.
s: Ask for two-centimetre veal chops with the bone, and on no account flatten them.
Clarify the butter: melt it gently, skim the foam and pour it off leaving the whey behind. Whole butter would burn long before the cooking ends.
Beat the eggs without salting them — salt thins the egg and the crumb slides off — and dip the whole chop, bone included.
Press firmly into fine breadcrumbs on both sides, pushing with the flat of your hand so they grip.
Cook 6 minutes a side in the foaming clarified butter over medium heat, spooning it over. Salt on coming out, lemon at the table.

panettone.d: A Christmas bread raised on natural leaven, with raisins and candied peel, proved over thirty-six hours. It cools hanging upside down on two skewers: its crumb is so airy and so fragile that it would collapse under its own weight.
s: Refresh the starter three times in a day, four hours apart: it must triple in three hours and smell of milk, never of vinegar.
Make a first dough in the evening with half the flour, sugar, butter and yolks, and prove 12 hours at 26°C until tripled.
Next day add the remaining ingredients and knead 25 minutes; work in the butter last, little by little, then the fruit by hand.
Prove 6 hours in the paper mould, until the dough reaches the rim — never sooner, on pain of a tight crumb.
Cut a cross, set a knob of butter in the centre and bake 55 minutes at 160°C. Skewer it at the base and hang it upside down for 12 hours.

gorgonzola-e-polenta.d: Yellow polenta covered with sweet gorgonzola melting over it, the dish of the Po plain towns. Sweet gorgonzola is not cooked: laid on scalding polenta it runs by itself, and an oven would turn it to oil.
s: Bring the salted water to the boil and rain in the maize meal very finely with one hand, whisking hard with the other.
Then switch to a wooden spoon and stir for 45 minutes over low heat, always the same way, scraping the sides.
Polenta cooked for less than forty minutes keeps a raw taste that neither butter nor cheese hides.
It is ready when it comes away from the pot in one block and a crust forms on the base; then beat in the butter and parmesan.
Pour it scalding into the plates, set the gorgonzola on top in large pieces and scatter walnuts. Do not stir: the cheese must run by itself.

baccala-mantecato.d: Stockfish beaten with oil into a white foam, served on toast. Venetians use air-dried stockfish, not salt cod: the confusion of terms is five centuries old and dates from a shipwreck in the Lofoten islands in 1432.
s: Soak the stockfish for three full days under running water or changing the water four times a day: it is dry wood, and nothing shortens that.
Poach it 30 minutes in milk and water with the bay, without boiling, then let it cool in its liquid.
Remove skin and bones carefully, working by hand: a single bone ruins the texture of a mantecato.
Put the flesh in a bowl and beat with a wooden spoon while trickling in the oil, as for mayonnaise, for a full 20 minutes.
The flesh must whiten and triple in volume. Add a little of the poaching liquid if it tightens too much. Serve on grilled polenta croutons.

spritz-veneziano.d: White wine, a bitter and soda, served with an olive and a slice of orange. The name comes from German spritzen, to spray: 19th-century Austrian soldiers in the Veneto watered down the local wines, which they found too strong.
s: Chill the stemmed glasses in the freezer for ten minutes: a warm glass melts the ice and unbalances everything within two minutes.
Fill them with ice to the top — plenty of ice melts more slowly than a little, contrary to what people think.
Keep the Venetian proportion of three, two, one: three parts prosecco, two of bitter, one of soda.
Pour the prosecco first then the bitter, which is heavier and falls through the glass in an orange trail; stir just once.
Finish with the soda, half a slice of orange on the rim and a green olive on a stick. In Venice the olive is compulsory.

bigoli-in-salsa.d: Thick wholemeal spaghetti served with a sauce of melted onion and anchovy, without a scrap of cheese. It is a fast-day dish: no meat, no egg, no parmesan, and Venice still eats it on Good Friday and Christmas Eve.
s: Knead the wholemeal flour and warm water for 15 minutes into a very firm dough, and rest it an hour.
Extrude it through a bigolaro, or failing that the widest die of a pasta machine: bigoli must be rough, that is what holds the sauce.
Slice the onions very finely and melt them in the oil for 45 minutes over very low heat, adding a little water whenever they catch.
Desalt the anchovies, remove the bone, and crush them into the hot onions: they must dissolve entirely, not one piece should remain visible.
Deglaze with white wine, pepper, and bind the bigoli, cooked 8 minutes, with a little of their water. Never cheese, under any circumstances.

tagliatelle-al-ragu.d: The ragù registered in 1982 with the Bologna chamber of commerce, served on tagliatelle and never on spaghetti. The official recipe prescribes eight millimetres of width for the raw pasta and forbids garlic, herbs and any tomato beyond a little purée.
s: Render the chopped pancetta then the soffritto of very finely cut onion, carrot and celery, 25 minutes over low heat.
Add the coarsely minced beef and let it colour without stirring too much, until no water remains in the base.
Deglaze with white wine, add the purée and simmer 3 hours uncovered, moistening with broth as it goes.
Pour in the milk during the last hour: it is what tenderises the meat and rounds the acidity, and its absence is noticed at once.
For the pasta, knead flour and eggs 15 minutes, roll very thin, roll up the sheet and cut 8 mm ribbons. Cook 2 minutes and bind with butter and parmesan.

lasagne-alla-bolognese.d: Green spinach pasta sheets alternated with ragù and béchamel, in at least eight layers. Bologna's pasta is green, not yellow: the spinach adds almost no flavour, but it colours and makes the sheet more supple to roll.
s: Make the ragù the day before: it is better rested, and overnight lets the fat rise so it can be lifted off.
Blanch the spinach, press it thoroughly dry and chop it by knife before kneading it with the flour and eggs.
Roll very thin, cut rectangles and blanch them 45 seconds; refresh and lay them on cloths without overlapping.
Build eight layers beginning and ending with béchamel, with very little filling per layer: a lasagne is judged by its number of sheets, not the thickness of its ragù.
Bake 35 minutes at 190°C, then rest 10 minutes out of the oven before cutting: hot, a lasagne runs across the plate.

panzanella.d: A salad of soaked stale Tuscan bread, tomatoes and red onion, with oil and vinegar. Tuscan bread is made without salt: which is why it goes stale fast without moulding, and why so many dishes were invented to use it up.
s: Use unsalted bread at least two days old: fresh bread turns to glue and salted bread unbalances the seasoning.
Cut it into large pieces and soak them 10 minutes in the water with a little vinegar added.
Then press them hard between your hands and crumble them: they must be damp but not sodden, and on no account puréed.
Soak the sliced red onion 20 minutes in cold water to take off its bite, and salt the tomatoes separately to collect their juice.
Combine everything with the tomato juice, oil, vinegar and torn basil, and rest an hour at room temperature before serving.

cantucci-di-prato.d: Almond biscuits baked twice, so hard that they are dipped in vin santo. Biscotto means twice cooked: the second baking dries the crumb entirely, and that is what lets them keep for months in a tin.
s: Do not blanch or toast the almonds: Prato cantucci use them raw and whole, skins on.
Beat the eggs and sugar, add the flour, baking powder, zest and salt, and fold in the almonds last by hand.
The dough is very sticky: flour the worktop generously and shape flat logs 5 cm wide, without trying to smooth them.
Glaze with yolk and bake 25 minutes at 180°C, then take them out and let them cool for exactly ten minutes.
Slice on the bias at 1.5 cm while still warm — cold, they shatter — and bake the slices flat for another 12 minutes at 150°C.

lampredotto.d: Beef abomasum stewed then served in a roll dipped in its own broth, with two sauces, green and hot. Florence's lampredottai have kept their carts since the 15th century; the name comes from the lamprey, which the tripe resembles in shape.
s: Rinse the abomasum at length in cold water and blanch it 10 minutes, then throw that first water away.
Cook it again for 3 hours with onion, carrot, celery, tomato and bay, at a bare simmer — an agitated broth toughens tripe.
It is ready when a blade passes through without effort. Cool it in its broth, then slice it thinly.
Make the salsa verde by pounding parsley, garlic, capers, anchovies and oil, and a salsa piccante of chilli and oil.
Split the roll, dip the top in the scalding broth — dipped, never dry — fill with lampredotto and both sauces.

suppli.d: Croquettes of tomato risotto with a mozzarella centre, fried, broken in two to see the cheese pull into a thread. They are called supplì al telefono because of that thread, like a handset cord; without it the croquette has failed.
s: Make a tomato and meat risotto, but moisten it a little less than usual: it must be tight, almost dry.
Spread it on a tray and cool it completely, at least 4 hours — warm risotto cannot be shaped.
Cut the mozzarella into batons and drain them an hour on paper: it is the mozzarella's water that bursts supplì.
Shape ovals around each baton, making sure the cheese is entirely enclosed in rice.
Egg, then crumb, and fry 4 minutes at 175°C. Rest two minutes before breaking, or the cheese runs instead of pulling.

carciofi-alla-giudia.d: A whole artichoke fried twice until it opens like a flower, the outer leaves as crisp as crisps. It is the dish of the Roman Ghetto where Roman Jews were confined for three centuries; the romanesco artichoke, choke-free, is found only from February to April.
s: Turn the artichokes in a spiral with a knife, taking off the tough leaves down to the pale ones, and trim the stem leaving it long.
Drop them into lemon water as you go: a cut artichoke blackens within three minutes.
Press them head down on the worktop to open the leaves, and season between them.
First frying at 130°C, 10 minutes, head down: it cooks the heart without colouring. Lift them out and drain head down for 20 minutes.
Second frying at 180°C, 3 minutes, spooning oil over: the leaves open and brown. Flick a little cold water in at the end, and the steam makes them bloom at once.

pastiera-napoletana.d: An Easter tart of cooked wheat, ricotta and orange blossom, latticed with seven strips of pastry. It is made on Maundy Thursday and eaten on Sunday: it needs three days for the scents to marry, and it is frankly better on the third.
s: Cook the wheat with the milk, a little butter and the zest for 30 minutes over low heat, until creamy: it is that wheat cream, not whole grains, that makes a pastiera.
Make a rich shortcrust with lard or butter, without working it, and rest it 2 hours in the cold.
Sieve the ricotta and beat it at length with the sugar, then add the yolks one at a time, the candied fruit, orange blossom water and cinnamon.
Finally fold in the whites whisked to soft peaks: they lighten an otherwise dense filling.
Fill the tin, lay seven pastry strips in a lattice and bake 1 hour 20 at 170°C. Cool in the switched-off oven and wait two days.

baba-al-rum.d: A mushroom-shaped brioche soaked in rum syrup until it drips. It came to Naples with the French cooks of the Bourbons in the 18th century; Neapolitans adopted it so completely that sei nu babà, you are a babà, became a compliment.
s: Knead the flour, yeast and three eggs for 10 minutes, then add the other eggs one at a time, waiting for full absorption.
Work in the softened butter last and knead 15 minutes more: the dough must be so elastic it stretches to a veil without tearing.
Prove 2 hours, fill the moulds only a third full and let them rise to the rim, about an hour.
Bake 25 minutes at 180°C then let the babàs dry overnight in the open air: a fresh babà will not drink, a stale one drinks everything.
Boil the water, sugar and zests, let it fall to 60°C, add the rum and submerge the babàs. Turn them and press gently with a spatula.

ragu-napoletano.d: Large pieces of meat stewed six hours in tomato, the sauce dressing the pasta and the meat serving as a second course. Nothing to do with Bolognese ragù: the meat is not minced, and Neapolitans say the sauce must pippiare, barely burble, throughout.
s: Make braciole: flatten the chuck, fill with pancetta, garlic, parsley, pine nuts and raisins, roll and tie.
Brown them with the pork ribs in oil, then lift them out and melt thickly sliced onion for 40 minutes.
Return the meats, deglaze with red wine and let it evaporate entirely before adding the purée, then the tomato passata.
Let it pippiare for 6 hours over minimal heat, half covered, stirring with a wooden spoon every half hour so nothing catches.
The sauce must turn from bright red to dark brown: that is the only reliable indicator. Serve on hand-broken ziti, the meat afterwards.

frittura-di-paranza.d: A fry of the gulf's smallest fish, floured and thrown whole into the oil. The paranza is the trawler: you do not choose what you fry, you fry what came up, and the mix changes daily.
s: Gut only the fish over ten centimetres: the smallest are eaten whole, and gutting would make them fall apart.
Blot everything carefully then flour with fine semolina in a sieve, shaking hard.
Keep the species apart: squid needs two minutes, anchovy forty seconds, and frying them together ruins one or the other.
Take the oil to 190°C and fry in small handfuls, never more than one at a time, so the temperature does not fall.
Drain in a colander, never on paper laid flat, and salt as they come out. Eaten within five minutes, from a paper cone.

focaccia-barese.d: A potato focaccia covered with crushed cherry tomatoes and black olives. The mashed potato in the dough is no eccentricity: it holds water and keeps the focaccia soft for two days, which flour alone cannot do.
s: Boil the potato whole, peel it hot and rice it: cold, it would lump in the dough.
Knead it with both flours, the yeast, warm water, 40 ml of oil and salt for 12 minutes. The dough must stay very soft, almost pourable.
Prove 1½ hours, tip into a generously oiled round tin and spread with your fingertips without working it.
Press the halved cherry tomatoes into the dough cut side up, sinking them halfway, and scatter whole unstoned olives.
Salt with coarse salt, moisten with oil, prove 45 minutes and bake 25 minutes at 230°C. The base should be fried in oil, not merely baked.

tiella-barese.d: Layers of potato, rice and raw mussels baked together, with no broth made first. The rice cooks in the water released by the mussels and the potatoes: it is the only possible method, and it forbids opening the oven before the end.
s: Open the mussels raw with a knife, keeping each on its half shell and collecting every drop of their liquor: on no account cook them open.
Strain that liquor through fine cloth: it is the dish's main seasoning, and it already holds all the salt needed.
Oil the tiella, line the base with onion then a layer of 3 mm potato slices.
Arrange the mussels on their shells, scatter the dry raw rice over by hand, then the tomatoes, garlic, parsley and pecorino.
Finish with a second layer of potato, pour in the mussel liquor made up with clear water to just cover, and bake 55 minutes at 190°C without ever opening the door.

panzerotto-barese.d: A pizza-dough turnover filled with tomato and mozzarella, fried rather than baked. It is eaten standing and scalding, held point down: the first bite releases a jet of steam that has scalded generations of Bari children.
s: Knead a supple pizza dough and prove it slowly for 4 hours, or overnight in the cold: too young a dough drinks oil.
Drain the diced mozzarella at least 3 hours on paper, and reduce the tomato purée until thick.
Moisture is the only enemy: a wet filling bursts the panzerotto in the boiling oil.
Cut 15 cm discs, fill one half leaving a two-centimetre border, fold and seal with a fork, pressing hard.
Fry at 175°C for 3 minutes, turning once, until they puff and brown. Drain upright and eat at once.

peperoni-cruschi.d: Sweet peppers sun-dried then fried for three seconds, crisp as crisps and sweet. Crusco means crunchy in Lucanian dialect; the Senise pepper has skin so thin that it dries whole in a fortnight without ever moulding.
s: Wipe the dried peppers with a dry cloth — never water — and shake out the stalk and seeds.
Heat the oil to exactly 160°C, and test with a small piece: it should swell and change colour in two seconds.
Plunge the peppers for three seconds, no longer: at the fourth they blacken and turn bitter, beyond rescue.
Lift them out with a skimmer and stand them on paper: they harden as they cool, and it is in cooling that they crisp.
Salt and serve as they are, or crumble them over salt cod and garlic-fried bread, as they do in Basilicata.

fileja-alla-nduja.d: Pasta rolled by hand around an iron rod, served with nduja melted into tomato. Nduja dissolves entirely in the heat: it is not a piece of charcuterie added to the dish, it becomes the sauce itself.
s: Knead the semolina and warm water for 15 minutes into a very firm dough, and rest it 30 minutes under a bowl.
Roll pencil-thick ropes, cut 8 cm lengths and wind each around an iron rod or knitting needle.
Withdraw the rod by rolling the pasta on the table: what remains should be a hollow, irregular tube, never smooth.
Fry the onion in oil, add the nduja and crush it with a spoon until it melts entirely and turns the oil red.
Add the tomato and cook 20 minutes. Bind the fileja, cooked 8 minutes, with a little of their water and serve with pecorino.

cannoli-siciliani.d: Fried pastry tubes filled with sweetened sheep's ricotta, filled only to order. A shell filled in advance goes soft within twenty minutes: in Palermo a pastry cook who fills his cannoli ahead loses his name in a season.
s: Drain the ricotta 24 hours in a cloth under a weight: it is the one step that decides success, and it cannot be shortened.
Knead the flour, 40 g of the sugar, the lard, cocoa, marsala and salt into a very firm dough, and rest it 2 hours.
Roll it to 1 mm — you should be able to read through it — cut ovals and wrap them around metal tubes, sealing with beaten egg.
Fry 2 minutes at 180°C: the shell must blister into small bubbles, the sign the dough was thin enough. Cool before sliding off the tubes.
Sieve the ricotta with the remaining sugar, without whipping it, and pipe it in at the last moment, filling from both ends.

granita-al-limone.d: A scraped lemon ice, eaten at breakfast with a brioche col tuppo. Sicilians eat it in the morning, dipping the brioche in; the texture must be creamy and not gritty, despite the name, and regular scraping is what gives it.
s: Make a syrup with the water, sugar and zest pared without pith, bring to a tremble and cool completely with the zest in it.
Strain, add freshly squeezed lemon juice and a minute pinch of salt, which lifts the acidity without being tasted.
Keep the proportion: one part juice to four of syrup. More juice and the granita freezes into a hard block.
Pour 3 cm deep into a flat tray and freeze; scrape with a fork every twenty minutes, working the edges which set first.
Allow five or six scrapings over three hours. Serve at once with a warm brioche — a granita that waits becomes a block again.

cassata-siciliana.d: A ricotta cake lined with green marzipan and covered with candied fruit, iced with sugar. It comes from Palermo's convents; the green marzipan imitates the nuns' habit, and the candied fruit laid in a crown recalls Norman mosaics.
s: Drain the ricotta 24 hours under a weight, then pass it twice through a fine sieve without ever whipping it: whipped, it weeps and the cassata runs.
Mix it with the sugar, chocolate chips and a little diced candied fruit, and chill.
Make the marzipan with ground almonds, icing sugar, water and green colour from blended pistachios; roll it to 5 mm.
Line a sloping-sided mould alternating strips of marzipan and marsala-soaked sponge, pressed tight against each other.
Fill with the ricotta, close with a layer of sponge, press and chill 12 hours. Turn out, ice with icing sugar and water, and crown with whole candied fruit.

panelle.d: Fried chickpea-flour wafers, served in a sesame roll. They are a direct Arab inheritance: ground chickpea reached Sicily in the 9th century, and the panella remains Palermo's cheapest street food.
s: Whisk the chickpea flour into cold water, then pass it through a fine sieve: a single lump becomes a hard bump in the panella.
Set it over medium heat and stir without pause for 20 minutes with a wooden spoon, always the same way.
The batter is ready when it comes away from the sides in one block and a spoon stands up in it.
Pour it scalding onto an oiled marble and spread it with a spatula to 3 mm, as fast as you can: it sets within a minute.
Cut rectangles once cold and fry 3 minutes at 180°C, until they blister. Serve in a sesame roll, with lemon.

pasta-con-le-sarde.d: Bucatini with fresh sardines, wild fennel, raisins and pine nuts. The sweet-and-savoury is Arab, the wild fennel Sicilian: legend gives the dish to the cook of general Euphemios, landed in 827, who had only fish and herbs to hand.
s: Boil the wild fennel 15 minutes in plenty of salted water, drain it keeping the water, and chop it.
That cooking water will cook the pasta: it carries the fennel through the whole dish, and throwing it away would lose half the recipe.
Fillet the sardines, soften the onion, add the desalted anchovies and crush them until they dissolve entirely.
Add the sardines, plumped raisins, pine nuts and saffron, and cook 10 minutes without stirring much, to keep pieces whole.
Cook the bucatini in the fennel water, combine, and cover with dry-toasted breadcrumbs — never cheese, Sicily does not allow it on fish.

porceddu-sardo.d: A suckling pig spitted and roasted upright before a fire of myrtle and mastic, seasoned with nothing but salt. It is traditionally served buried in fresh myrtle branches for half an hour: the myrtle steam scents it better than any marinade.
s: Split the pig, spit it on a green wood pole and plant the spit at an angle in the ground, in front of the fire and never over it.
Cooking is by radiant heat, never direct flame: fat falling into the fire would set the skin alight.
Allow 3 hours, turning the spit a quarter turn every twenty minutes, and salt only halfway through.
Baste the skin with a rind of pork fat on the end of a stick, which feeds it and browns it evenly.
Carve it and bury the pieces under a bed of fresh myrtle in a closed box for half an hour, before serving warm.

pane-carasau.d: Sheets of semolina bread so thin they are called music paper, baked twice. The first baking blows them into a balloon; they are then split into two discs and baked again separately, and they keep for a year — the bread of shepherds gone six months.
s: Knead the fine semolina, warm water, yeast and salt for 20 minutes: the dough must be very firm and perfectly smooth.
Prove 2 hours, divide into 100 g balls and roll each into a 1 mm disc, dusting with semolina.
Bake at 300°C at least, on a scalding stone: the disc must balloon within two minutes. In a cooler oven it dries without separating.
Take it out at once and cut round the edge with a knife to get two discs, protecting yourself from the steam.
Stack the discs under a board to flatten them, then bake each again for 2 minutes until golden and brittle.

malloreddus-alla-campidanese.d: Small saffron semolina gnocchi, ridged on a wicker basket, with a sauce of fresh sausage and tomato. Malloreddus means little calves in Sardinian: women shaped them like beasts for feast days, on baskets called ciuliris.
s: Infuse the saffron in the warm water for 20 minutes: it must dye the water deep yellow before it goes into the dough.
Knead with the semolina and salt for 15 minutes into a firm dough, and rest it 30 minutes.
Roll thin ropes, cut one-centimetre pieces and press each against the wicker of the basket with your thumb, rolling it.
The ridges are not decorative: they hold the sauce, and a smooth malloreddu lets it slide into the plate.
Make the sauce by crumbling the raw sausage into the onion, without chopping it, and simmer 45 minutes with the tomato. Bind the pasta, cooked 12 minutes, and cover with pecorino.

gnocco-fritto.d: Diamonds of bread dough fried in lard, which puff into hollow cushions, served with charcuterie. Lard cannot be replaced by oil: it is what gives the flavour, and in Modena it goes into the dough as well.
s: Knead the flour, warm milk, yeast, 50 g of lard and salt for 12 minutes, and prove 1½ hours.
Roll the dough to exactly 3 mm: thicker it stays raw inside, thinner it does not puff.
Cut 8 cm diamonds with a wheel and rest them uncovered for 15 minutes, so the surface dries.
Melt the remaining lard and take it to 180°C; drop in two or three diamonds at a time, no more.
They puff within ten seconds: ladle fat over them so they fill with air, turn them and lift them out at 30 seconds. Serve scalding with the charcuterie.

torta-al-testo.d: An unleavened flatbread cooked on a stone or cast-iron disc, split and filled with charcuterie or sautéed greens. The testo is the stone itself: heated in the hearth, it cooks the bread by contact and mass, with no oven — a household bread needing no baker.
s: Mix the flour, bicarbonate and salt, add the water and oil and knead 8 minutes into a supple but non-sticky dough.
Rest it 30 minutes under a cloth: without rest it shrinks back as you roll and bakes into a hard disc.
Divide in two and roll one-centimetre discs, the exact diameter of your testo or cast-iron pan.
Heat the testo dry and very hot, and cook 8 minutes a side, pricking the blisters with a fork as they appear.
Split the scalding torta horizontally and fill with charcuterie, pecorino or chard sautéed with garlic. Eaten within the half hour.

gricia.d: Pasta with guanciale and pecorino, no tomato and no egg: the mother from which amatriciana and carbonara derive. It is sometimes called white amatriciana; in truth it is older, born before the tomato reached the Apennines.
s: Cut the guanciale into half-centimetre lardons, keeping the rind on to remove it afterwards.
Render it dry in a cold pan over low heat for 10 minutes: it must give up its fat slowly and crisp without burning.
Crack the pepper in a mortar and toast it 30 seconds in the rendered fat, off the heat: that is what wakes its scent.
Cook the pasta very al dente and transfer it to the pan with two ladles of its water.
Off the heat, add the grated pecorino in three goes, stirring briskly: tipped in at once onto a hot pan it strings and forms lumps beyond rescue.

spaghetti-alla-chitarra.d: Square-sectioned spaghetti cut by pressing the dough onto a wooden frame strung with wires, the chitarra. The square section is no detail: the sharp edges grip sauce as no round spaghetti does, and the instrument dates from the early 19th century.
s: Knead the flours and eggs for 15 minutes into a firm dough, and rest it an hour under a bowl.
Roll sheets to exactly the thickness of the wire spacing — two millimetres — because that thickness is what gives the square section.
Lay the sheet on the chitarra and run the pin over it, pressing: the wires cut, and the spaghetti fall into the frame.
Make pallottine, minute meatballs of the three minced meats, hazelnut-sized, and brown them before they go into the sauce.
Simmer the sauce for an hour, cook the pasta 3 minutes and combine. Serve with Abruzzo pecorino.

barbajuans.d: Fried ravioli filled with chard, ricotta and parmesan, the Principality's national dish. They are eaten on 27 January for Saint Dévote; the name is said to come from uncle John, barba Juan in Ligurian, credited by legend with the idea of frying leftover ravioli filling.
s: Knead the flour, one egg, the olive oil, a pinch of salt and a little warm water for 10 minutes, and rest the dough an hour under a cloth.
Separate the stems from the chard leaves: only the leaves go into the filling, the stems will serve elsewhere.
Wilt them in a pan with the sliced onion and leek, then press them thoroughly dry between your hands — a wet filling bursts the barbajuan in the oil.
Chop them by knife and bind with the drained ricotta, parmesan, remaining eggs and nutmeg.
Roll the dough to 1 mm, set hazelnuts of filling on it, close into squares cut with a fluted wheel and fry 3 minutes at 175°C. Eaten warm, with the fingers.

stocafi-monegasque.d: Stockfish stewed three hours in tomato, Nice olives and brandy, the dish of the harbour fishermen. Stockfish is not salt cod but wind-dried cod, hard as wood: it needs five days of soaking before it can be cut at all.
s: Soak the stockfish for five days under running water or changing the water morning and evening: it takes time, and no shortcut works.
Cut it into large pieces keeping the skin, which brings the gelatine that binds the sauce.
Make a sofrito of onion and garlic in olive oil, add the crushed tomato and reduce for 30 minutes to a thick paste.
Flame with marc, moisten with white wine, add the fish, herbs and olives, and simmer 2½ hours without ever stirring with a spoon.
Shake the pot instead of stirring: stockfish shreds at the first touch of a spoon. Add the potatoes for the last half hour.

fougasse-monegasque.d: A flat brioche with anise and orange blossom, strewn with walnuts, almonds and red and white aniseed comfits. It closes the thirteen desserts of the Monegasque Christmas Eve; the coloured comfits echo the flag, and it is not cut — it is broken.
s: Dissolve the yeast in warm milk with a spoonful of sugar and let it foam for a quarter of an hour.
Knead with the flour, two eggs, sugar, salt, anise, orange blossom water and rum for 15 minutes, then work in the softened butter.
Prove 1½ hours, then flatten the dough by hand into a 2 cm oval — never with a pin, which would drive out the air.
Cut three fan-shaped slashes on top, glaze with egg and cover with chopped walnuts and almonds.
Prove 45 minutes and bake 30 minutes at 180°C. Scatter the aniseed comfits as it comes out, while the surface is still tacky.

brandamincium.d: The Monegasque ancestor of brandade, cod pounded in a mortar with milk and oil into an ointment. The Latinate name is recorded on the Rock from the Middle Ages; unlike the Nîmes brandade it contains neither potato nor cream.
s: Desalt the cod 36 hours in the fridge, skin up, changing the water five times.
Poach it 10 minutes in the milk with the bay, never boiling, then drain it keeping the milk.
Remove the skin and every bone by hand, flaking the flesh: a single bone ruins the texture.
Pound in a mortar with the garlic, then mount it by pouring in the warm oil and hot milk alternately, in thin streams, as for a mayonnaise.
That alternation is the whole method: poured too fast, either one splits the ointment. Season with white pepper and serve warm, on toast.

bouillabaisse-monegasque.d: A rockfish soup from the Larvotto, lighter than the Marseille version and without potato. Monaco adds neither excess saffron nor orange: the broth stays clear, and the mussels added to it are a liberty Marseille would never permit.
s: Gut and scale the rockfish, keep the heads, and fry them 10 minutes in oil with the onion, fennel and garlic.
Moisten with boiling water — never cold, which would seize the flesh and cloud the broth — and cook 25 minutes at a bare simmer.
Pass through a food mill pressing the bones, then through a fine chinois: the broth must be velvety and free of a single splinter.
Make the rouille by pounding garlic, an egg yolk, a pinch of cayenne and bread crumb soaked in the broth, mounted with oil.
Poach the whole fish 8 minutes in the broth, add the mussels for the last minute, and serve the broth first, the fish after.

salade-monegasque.d: A cold rice salad with anchovies, green beans and hard-boiled egg, born in the kitchens of the Hôtel de Paris in the 1920s. The rice is what separates it from the niçoise: Monaco introduced it to make a buffet dish that holds a whole evening.
s: Cook the rice in plenty of salted water, drain it and refresh it at once under cold water to stop the cooking and rinse off the starch.
Spread it on a tray and trickle oil over while it is still warm: that is the only moment it absorbs any.
Blanch the green beans for 4 minutes then plunge them into iced water: they must stay bright green and snap.
Salt the quartered tomatoes and let them drain for twenty minutes in a colander, or their water washes out the salad.
Combine everything at the last moment with the lemon juice and oil, and tear the basil by hand. Serve cool but not chilled.

beignets-de-fleurs-de-courgettes.d: Courgette flowers filled with herbed ricotta, dipped in beer batter and fried. Only the male flowers are picked, those on a bare stalk: the female ones carry the forming courgette, and taking them would sacrifice the crop.
s: Pick or buy the flowers the same day: after a night they close and wilt beyond rescue.
Open each flower gently and remove the pistil, which is bitter, without tearing the petals.
Work the well-drained ricotta with the parmesan and chopped basil and mint, and pipe it in without filling more than two-thirds.
Make the batter at the last minute with the flour, egg and very cold beer, deliberately leaving it lumpy — a smooth, rested batter gives a heavy crust.
Dip the flowers holding them by the stalk and fry 2 minutes at 180°C, turning them once only. Salt and squeeze lemon as they come out.

omelette-plate-aux-herbes.d: An omelette cooked flat, never folded, scattered with fresh herbs and parmesan. It is the croupiers' omelette, served between night shifts: it is eaten warm or cold, cut in wedges, and stands waiting better than a runny one.
s: Chop the herbs just before beating the eggs: chopped in advance they blacken and lose their scent within a quarter of an hour.
Beat the eggs with a fork rather than a whisk, some thirty strokes only: overbeaten, they rise and then collapse.
Add the herbs, parmesan, salt and pepper, and rest five minutes while the bubbles rise.
Heat the butter and oil in a 24 cm pan until the butter foams without colouring, and pour in all at once.
Cook 5 minutes over low heat without stirring, then flip it in one movement using a plate and give it 2 minutes on the other side. Served warm, with salad.

poulpe-a-la-monegasque.d: Octopus stewed two hours in red wine, tomato and violet olives, the dish of the fishing families of the breakwater. Octopus contracts violently on meeting heat: it is dipped three times in boiling water before cooking, so the tentacles curl instead of toughening.
s: Freeze the octopus for 48 hours then thaw it: freezing breaks the fibres and stands in for the beating on the rocks the fishermen used to give it.
Bring a large pot to the boil and dip the octopus by the head three times, five seconds each, before leaving it in.
Blanch it 20 minutes, drain it and cut the tentacles into three-centimetre lengths.
Make a sofrito of onion, garlic and tomato, add the octopus, red wine, orange zest and herbs, and simmer 1½ hours covered.
Salt only at the end: octopus releases a great deal of seawater, and salted too early the dish becomes inedible. Add olives and potatoes for the last half hour.

rougets-a-la-monegasque.d: Red mullet flamed with pastis and cooked with wild fennel gathered on the Tête de Chien. Mullet is the one fish cooked ungutted: its liver, left inside, melts into the juices and scents them — which is why it is called the woodcock of the sea.
s: Scale the mullet without gutting them, working against the grain from tail to head under running water.
On no account remove the liver: it is what makes the dish, and a gutted mullet loses all its point.
Slice the fennel very finely and melt it in olive oil with the garlic for 15 minutes, without colour.
Flour the mullet barely and sear them 3 minutes a side over high heat, then flame with pastis, tilting the pan.
Add the fennel, cherry tomatoes and a splash of water, cover and give them 4 minutes. Crush the liver into the juices as you serve.

epaule-agneau-monegasque.d: A boned shoulder stuffed with chard and rice, roasted and served with white beans. It is the Rock's Easter dish, as served at the Palace; the rice stuffing is Monegasque rather than Provençal, and it swells as it cooks, so it must not be packed too tight.
s: Soak the beans the day before and cook them 1½ hours with the bay, unsalted, in water that never comes to a rolling boil.
Cook the rice only halfway, 7 minutes, and refresh it: fully cooked, it would burst inside the stuffing.
Wilt the chopped chard with the onion, press it thoroughly dry and bind it with the rice, eggs and parmesan.
Lay the boned shoulder out flat, fill without packing — the stuffing swells by a good quarter — roll and tie with string every three centimetres.
Sear 20 minutes at 220°C, then 2 hours at 160°C basting with the white wine and juices. Rest 15 minutes before carving, string still on.

oignons-farcis-monegasques.d: Large sweet onions hollowed out and filled with sausage meat and chard, gratinated. Cebe farcie are the Rock's thrift dish: the flesh scooped from the onion goes back into the filling, and nothing is wasted — not even yesterday's bread as crumbs.
s: Poach the whole unpeeled onions 20 minutes in salted water: cooked, they hollow out without tearing; raw, they break into layers.
Cut a lid, scoop them out with a melon baller leaving two layers of wall, and chop the flesh removed.
Fry that flesh with the garlic and chopped chard, press it dry, and mix with the sausage meat, egg, parmesan and breadcrumbs.
Fill the onions in a dome, pack them tightly in an oiled dish — tight, they hold each other up and do not collapse.
Pour broth to a third of their height and bake 55 minutes at 180°C, basting twice. Eaten warm.

escargots-a-la-monegasque.d: Small grey snails returned to their shells under a butter of walnut, parsley and white wine. The walnut is the Monegasque signature: it replaces part of the garlic and gives the butter a grain the smoother Burgundian version lacks.
s: If starting from live snails, fast them for eight days, purge them in coarse salt and poach them 2 hours in a thyme court-bouillon.
Crush the walnuts with a knife rather than a blender: you want shards that crunch, not powder.
Cream the butter with the walnuts, parsley, garlic, shallot and the white wine reduced to nothing.
Slip a hazelnut of butter into each shell, the snail on top, then plug generously and dust with breadcrumbs.
Bake 12 minutes at 220°C, openings up: the butter should sizzle and the crumbs go gold, without the butter running over.

girella-monegasque.d: A bread rolled in a spiral around anchovies, onions and green olives, cut into slices. Street sellers cried girella cauda! in the lanes of the Condamine; the spiral is not decorative, it spreads the salty filling through every mouthful.
s: Knead a soft olive-oil bread dough and prove it 1½ hours covered.
Confit the sliced onions 30 minutes over very low heat, until pale and dry, and cool them completely.
A warm filling melts the dough as you roll and the spiral unwinds: that is the only real difficulty.
Roll the dough into a 5 mm rectangle and spread the onions, chopped anchovies, olives and oregano, leaving a two-centimetre border.
Roll very tightly lengthwise, seal, prove 40 minutes and bake 25 minutes at 210°C. Cut into one-centimetre slices, warm.

tarte-citron-menton-monaco.d: A tart of Menton lemon cream under a torched meringue, served in the palaces of Monte-Carlo. The Menton lemon has almost no biting acidity and a thick, highly scented rind: it is the zest, more than the juice, that makes the difference.
s: Line the tin, prick the base, line with paper and beans and blind-bake 15 minutes at 180°C, then 5 minutes uncovered.
Dust the still-hot base with ground almonds: they will drink the cream's moisture and keep the pastry crisp.
Infuse the zest in the juice for an hour before cooking anything — that is where the scent is decided, not in the cooking.
Cook the zested juice, 150 g of the sugar, the eggs and cornstarch over a bain-marie to 82°C, then blend in the cold diced butter off the heat with a stick blender.
Whisk the whites with the remaining sugar to a firm meringue, pipe it onto the cold tart and torch it. Do not chill afterwards: the meringue would weep.

biscuit-chataigne-miel.d: A rustic biscuit of chestnut flour and acacia honey from the Jardin Exotique. It was made for the workers on the Fontvieille site, reclaimed from the sea in the seventies: dense and honey-sweet, it kept a man going to the end of the shift.
s: Sift the chestnut flour twice: it clumps into hard nuggets no beater will later break up.
Warm the honey with the butter without going above 50°C, beyond which acacia loses its floral scent.
Beat the eggs, add the warm mixture, then the flours, baking powder, cinnamon and salt, and finally the milk.
The batter is heavier than an ordinary biscuit dough: chestnut has no gluten and barely rises, which is normal.
Drop well-spaced spoonfuls on the tray, scatter chopped walnuts and bake 22 minutes at 170°C. They harden as they cool and keep a fortnight.

endives-au-jambon.d: Braised endives wrapped in ham and gratinated under béchamel. The chicon was discovered by accident around 1830: a Schaerbeek grower had abandoned chicory roots in his cellar, and they had produced white shoots.
s: Cut out the bitter cone at the base of each endive with a pointed knife: it, not the leaf, carries the bitterness.
Braise them covered in butter for 30 minutes with a pinch of sugar and a squeeze of lemon, adding no water.
Then press them firmly between your hands: a waterlogged endive thins the béchamel and the gratin swims.
Wrap each endive in a slice of ham and pack them tightly, seam down, in a buttered dish.
Coat with a nutmegged béchamel, scatter cheese and gratinate 25 minutes at 200°C, until the top blisters.

appeltaart.d: A very tall apple tart with a thick shortcrust and a lattice top, served with whipped cream. The Dutch recipe is recorded from 1514; unlike the French tart it is baked in a deep springform tin and eaten in upright wedges.
s: Rub the cold butter into the flour with half the sugar, bind with one egg and bring together without kneading; chill an hour.
Plump the raisins in warm rum and cut the apples into large wedges, never slices.
Line a 24 cm springform tin, taking the pastry 5 cm up the sides: an appeltaart is tall, that is its signature.
Scatter breadcrumbs over the base before filling — they will drink the apple juices and keep the pastry crisp.
Cover with a lattice, glaze and bake 1 hour 20 at 175°C. Cool completely in the tin, or the tart collapses when released.

kibbeling.d: Chunks of cod in beer batter, fried and sold in a cone with tartare sauce. The word once meant cod cheeks, an offcut fishmongers sold cheap; today it is diced fillet, but the name has stuck.
s: Cut the cod into 4 cm cubes, salt them and chill 20 minutes to firm the flesh.
Blot them thoroughly: wet flesh makes the batter slide, and it peels off in sheets in the oil.
Make the batter at the last minute with very cold beer, leaving it lumpy — a rested batter turns heavy and soft.
Flour the cubes, dip them and lower them into oil at 180°C, six at a time, for 3 minutes.
Drain upright in a colander, salt and serve with a tartare of mayonnaise, chopped gherkin and capers.

oliebollen.d: Balls of yeasted dough with raisins and apple, fried and buried in icing sugar, eaten on 31 December. The custom is said to go back to the Germanic tribes, who threw them into the fields on Yule nights so that if the goddess Perchta slit a belly, her blade would slide off the fat.
s: Plump the raisins for an hour in warm water, then drain and blot them — wet, they make the oil spit.
Beat a soft, almost pourable yeasted batter: an oliebol is spooned out and never shaped by hand.
Fold in the raisins and diced apple, and prove for an hour covered until the batter bubbles on the surface.
Scoop with two oiled spoons and drop into oil at 175°C: the balls turn themselves if they are round enough.
Allow 7 minutes in all, turning if needed — hotter, and they brown before the centre cooks. Dust with icing sugar while warm.

gromperekichelcher.d: Cakes of grated potato with parsley and onion, fried and sold at every fairground in the Grand Duchy. They are eaten with apple sauce; the word gromper comes from grumpire, a Lorraine corruption of pomme de terre.
s: Grate the potatoes coarsely and press them at once in a cloth: a large glassful of water should come out.
Let that water settle for five minutes, pour off the clear liquid and recover the white starch at the bottom, which goes back into the gratings.
That recovered starch is what binds the cake: without it you need three times the flour and the result turns pasty.
Mix with grated onion, sliced leek, eggs, parsley and salt, and work fast — the gratings darken within minutes.
Flatten spoonfuls into a centimetre of oil at 180°C and let them set 4 minutes a side, untouched. Serve with apple sauce.

bouneschlupp.d: A soup of green beans, potato and bacon bound with cream, the Luxembourgish national dish. It is made with the stringy late-summer beans, snapped by hand rather than cut: the break follows the fibre and takes the string with it.
s: Snap the beans by hand into three-centimetre lengths, pulling away the string that comes loose at each break.
Render the diced bacon, add the onion and let it turn golden without burning.
Moisten with water, add the potatoes in large pieces and the savory — it is the bean herb, and without it the soup lacks depth.
Cook 35 minutes, then crush a few potatoes roughly against the side of the pot to thicken it.
Bind with the cream mixed with a spoonful of flour, off the boil, and rest a quarter of an hour before serving.

quetschentaart.d: A tart of damsons stood upright in the pastry, made in September when the purple plum ripens. The plums are set vertically, skin down: they release their juice as they bake and it must stay in the fruit and not in the pastry.
s: Make a shortcrust with cold butter bound with an egg, and rest it an hour in the fridge.
Stone the damsons by opening them out without separating the halves, so that they will stand up.
Scatter ground almonds and semolina over the pastry base: the mixture absorbs the juice, which damsons give in quantity.
Stand the plums upright and tightly packed, skin down, overlapping slightly — they shrink by a third.
Sugar and cinnamon, and bake 45 minutes at 190°C. Sugar again as it comes out, when the juice rises.

frell-am-reisleck.d: Trout poached in a Riesling from the Luxembourg Moselle, the sauce bound with cream. The wine must tremble rather than boil: brought to the boil, a Riesling loses its fine acidity and leaves a bitterness cream cannot rescue.
s: Gut the trout, salt them inside and rest them twenty minutes before cooking.
Sweat the chopped shallot in butter without colour, then lay the trout on top, head to tail so they sit flat.
Pour in the Riesling and a little water to half their depth, cover and poach 12 minutes at a tremble — never at a rolling boil.
Lift out the fish, take off the fillets and keep them warm under buttered paper.
Reduce the liquor by half, add the cream and mushrooms, thicken 5 minutes and whisk in cold butter off the heat.

kachkeis.d: A cooked, melted cheese, runny and yellow, spread on black bread with mustard. It was born of the need to rescue a failed curd: it was left to ripen until translucent, then melted — a cheese never eaten in slices.
s: Drain fresh curd 12 hours in a cloth, then crumble it and let it ripen two days at room temperature under a tea towel.
It is ready when it begins to smell strongly and the grains turn translucent at the edges: that ripening is everything.
Dust with bicarbonate, mix and wait an hour: the curd begins to melt of its own accord under the alkalinity.
Melt it over very low heat with the butter and milk, stirring without pause to a smooth, stringy mass.
Bind with a beaten egg off the heat, salt and scent with caraway. Pour it hot into a pot and serve warm on black bread, with mustard.

mielzepudder.d: A semolina and milk pudding with raisins, baked and served warm. Mielz means semolina in Luxembourgish; it was the everyday pudding, made from what was always in the house — flour, milk and eggs.
s: Plump the raisins in warm rum for half an hour and drain them.
Bring the milk to a tremble with the zest, salt and half the sugar, then rain in the semolina, whisking without pause.
Cook 8 minutes over low heat, stirring: the semolina must thicken until a spoon stands up in it.
Let it cool to 50°C before adding the yolks — poured into scalding semolina they set into lumps.
Fold in the whites whisked to soft peaks and the raisins, turn into a buttered dish and bake 45 minutes at 180°C. Serve warm, never cold.

obatzda.d: An overripe camembert crushed with butter and paprika, served in beer gardens with a pretzel. Katharina Eisenreich is said to have put it on the menu in 1920 to use up her runny cheeses; obatzt means mashed in Bavarian, and the gesture is in the name.
s: Choose a frankly ripe camembert, runny under the rind: a young cheese will not mash and stays in rubbery lumps.
Crush it with a fork, rind and all — the rind carries the flavour, and removing it makes a bland spread.
Cream the butter separately, then work it into the cheese by crushing, never by whisking.
Add the paprika, caraway, grated onion and a splash of beer to loosen it: the beer is the Bavarian element, bringing the bitterness that cuts the fat.
