Rest it 2 hours in the cold, take it out half an hour ahead, and serve with a pretzel and radishes.

dampfnudeln.d: Balls of yeasted dough cooked covered in a shallow layer of buttered milk, soft on top and caramelised beneath. It all hangs on one rule: the lid is never lifted, or the steam escapes and the dumplings collapse for good.
s: Knead a soft yeasted dough with the flour, yeast, 150 ml of warm milk, one egg, 30 g of sugar and the softened butter, and prove for an hour.
Shape 70 g balls and prove them 30 minutes on a floured cloth, well spaced.
In a wide pot, melt the remaining butter with the milk and sugar: the liquid should come up barely a centimetre, no more.
Set the balls in without touching, cover with a heavy lid and give them 30 minutes over low heat — never lifting the lid.
You will hear the liquid evaporate then the base sizzle: the sign the crust is forming. Serve with a vanilla custard.

halve-hahn.d: A buttered rye roll with a thick slice of aged Gouda, mustard and onion. The name means half a cockerel and contains no chicken at all: legend has a Cologne joker order it that way to catch out a guest, and the name stuck.
s: Use a roggenbrötchen, a caraway rye roll: wheat bread cannot stand up to an aged Gouda.
Choose a Gouda of at least eighteen months, crystalline and brittle, and cut a slice a good centimetre thick.
The slice must be thicker than the butter and overhang the bread: in Cologne a thin halve Hahn is an offence.
Butter both faces generously, lay on the cheese, then the mustard on the side of the plate — never spread on it.
Add raw onion rings and a gherkin. Eaten by hand, with a Kölsch served in a narrow two-hundred-millilitre glass.

leipziger-allerlei.d: A stew of spring vegetables with crayfish and marrow dumplings, bound with crayfish butter. Legend has it that the people of Leipzig served this meatless dish to beggars and tax collectors to look poor, while feasting on what it concealed.
s: Cook each vegetable separately in boiling salted water and refresh it at once: none shares a cooking time or a colour to preserve.
The carrots are glazed in butter and sugar, the asparagus poached three minutes, the peas two, the cauliflower five.
Shell the crayfish and pound the shells in a mortar with butter, then melt that butter and strain it: this is crayfish butter, and it gives the taste and the colour.
Make a velouté with the crayfish butter, flour and the vegetable cooking liquid, then bind with cream.
Combine everything off the heat, warm through without boiling, and serve at once: the vegetables lose their colour within ten minutes.

quarkkeulchen.d: Small cakes of quark and yesterday's potato, pan-fried and dusted with cinnamon sugar. It is a leftovers dish: the potatoes must have been boiled the day before, cooled and grated, as fresh potato would make the batter sticky and grey.
s: Boil the potatoes in their skins the day before and cool them twelve hours: the starch retrogrades and firms up.
Peel and grate them coarsely, then drain the quark in a cloth for an hour.
Mix everything with your fingertips without working the batter: overworked, it turns elastic and the cakes shrink in the pan.
Shape cakes 8 cm across and a centimetre thick, lightly floured.
Fry in butter 4 minutes a side over medium heat, and dust with cinnamon sugar while scalding. Serve with apple sauce.

braunkohl-mit-kassler.d: Curly kale long stewed with smoked pork loin and caramelised potatoes. It is made only after the first frosts: cold turns the kale's starch to sugar, and a leaf picked before November stays tough and bitter.
s: Strip the kale from its central ribs, blanch it 5 minutes and chop it roughly by knife.
Render the bacon and onion in lard, add the kale and let it stew down 20 minutes before adding liquid.
Set the smoked loin on top and simmer 2 hours covered over low heat, never stirring the base.
Thicken with the oats in the last half hour: it is the northern thickener, and flour will not replace it.
Sauté the potatoes separately in lard with a spoonful of sugar, until they caramelise. Serve everything with strong mustard.

frankfurter-grune-sosse.d: A cold sauce of seven compulsory herbs, served over hard-boiled eggs and potatoes. The composition is protected: borage, chervil, cress, parsley, salad burnet, sorrel and chives, no more and no fewer — Goethe, born in Frankfurt, was said to love it.
s: Wash the seven herbs and dry them thoroughly: a single drop of water left thins the sauce and turns it within two hours.
Chop them very finely by knife, all together — a blender oxidises herbs and the sauce turns olive brown.
Crush four hard-boiled yolks with the mustard, vinegar and oil to make an emulsified base.
Fold in the smetana and yoghurt, then the herbs, and dice the remaining whites to add.
Rest 3 hours in the cold, no longer: beyond that the herbs blacken. Serve over hard-boiled eggs and hot potatoes.

ahle-worscht.d: A dry sausage from northern Hesse, cased with meat still warm from the slaughter. That is its whole peculiarity: the meat must be worked within two hours, before the pH falls, otherwise it no longer binds and the sausage crumbles.
s: Work the meat within two hours of slaughter, still warm: that is the imperative condition of Ahle Worscht.
Mince the shoulder and belly on the medium plate, keeping visible fat, and salt at 25 g per kilo.
Pepper very generously and knead for five minutes only: overworked, the mass warms and the fat melts.
Fill the casings firmly, expelling air, and tie into horseshoes or straight lengths according to the village's tradition.
Dry three weeks at 15°C, then age three to six months in a cellar. It must lose a third of its weight and just hold together when sliced.

birchermuesli.d: Oat flakes soaked overnight, mixed with grated apple, nuts and condensed milk. Maximilian Bircher-Brenner devised it around 1900 in his Zurich sanatorium: it was not a breakfast but a starter, served before every meal, and apple far outweighed oats.
s: Soak the oats in milk overnight in the fridge: soaked for an hour they stay dry and harsh at the centre.
The next day, grate the unpeeled apples at the last moment, straight over the bowl.
Douse them at once with lemon juice: without it grated apple browns within three minutes and the müesli turns grey.
The original recipe holds three times more apple than oats — the reverse of what modern packets sell.
Fold in the condensed milk, cream, honey and chopped nuts, and serve immediately, still cold.

luxemburgerli.d: Tiny macarons, smaller and lighter than the Parisian kind, filled with an aerated ganache. A Luxembourgish apprentice at Sprüngli brought them back around 1957; his Zurich colleagues named them after him, and the name has been trademarked since.
s: Sift the ground almonds and icing sugar together twice, then a third time through a fine sieve: a single grain makes a crater in the shell.
Whisk an Italian meringue by pouring syrup cooked to 118°C onto the whites, and beat until the bowl cools.
Macaronner by pressing the mass against the side until it ribbons and settles within thirty seconds — no more, no less.
Pipe shells only 2 cm across, rap the tray and let them skin for 30 minutes: you should be able to touch the surface without it sticking.
Bake 12 minutes at 150°C, fill with a whipped ganache and mature 24 hours in the cold before serving.

engadiner-nusstorte.d: A closed shortcrust tart filled with caramelised walnuts in cream. Engadine emigrants who worked as confectioners in Italy and France brought it back in the early 20th century; it keeps three weeks without loss, which made it the cake of mountain passes and long journeys.
s: Make a rich shortcrust with butter and one egg, and rest it 2 hours: it is fragile and worked cold.
Make a dry caramel with the sugar, with no water and no stirring — stirred, it crystallises and you must start again.
Stop the cooking with hot cream poured in three additions, standing back: it spits violently and seizes for a moment before smoothing.
Add the roughly chopped walnuts and the honey, and cool completely before filling.
Line, fill, cover with a disc, seal, glaze and prick the top. Bake 45 minutes at 180°C and wait two days before cutting.

capuns.d: Chard leaves wrapped around a spätzle batter and cured meats, poached then baked in cream. Every Grisons valley has its version and nobody agrees on the size: some make them thumb-sized, others like a cigar, and the argument passes for conversation.
s: Blanch the chard leaves 20 seconds and refresh them: any longer and they tear when folded.
Flatten the central rib with a knife laid flat, without cutting it — it must bend and not snap.
Beat a thick spätzle batter with the flour, eggs, milk and salt, and fold in the diced bacon and salami.
Set a spoonful on each leaf and roll it up, folding the sides in like a small parcel, seam underneath.
Poach 12 minutes in simmering broth, pack them tightly in a dish, coat with cream and cheese and bake 15 minutes at 200°C.

kiachln.d: Rounds of yeasted dough stretched by hand with a thick rim, fried in lard. The rim is left thick and the centre almost translucent: it is filled with lingonberry jam or, in the savoury version, sauerkraut — the hollow is deliberate.
s: Knead a soft yeasted dough with warm milk, eggs, sugar, rum and butter, and prove it 1½ hours.
Divide into 80 g balls and prove them 30 minutes under a cloth.
Stretch each ball by hand over the backs of your fists, turning: the centre must go almost transparent, the rim stay thick.
A rolling pin would flatten the rim and the Kiachl would have no hollow: the shaping is done by hand, without exception.
Lower them flat into lard at 175°C, 90 seconds a side. Fill the hollow with lingonberry jam or hot sauerkraut.

salzburger-rindfleisch.d: Beef braised with mushrooms in a cream and red wine sauce, served with Spätzle. This is the bourgeois cooking of alpine Austria: the sauce is thickened with neither flour nor starch but by reduction, which means never covering the pot at the end.
s: Sear the beef in large cubes in butter in small batches, until frankly coloured on every face.
Lift it out, soften the onion, deglaze with red wine and let it evaporate entirely before adding the broth.
Braise 1½ hours covered with the bay and juniper, then uncover for the last half hour.
Sauté the mushrooms separately over high heat in a very hot pan: added raw to the pot they would weep and thin the sauce.
Add them with the cream and reduce uncovered until the sauce coats. Serve with Spätzle.

aebleskiver.d: Small balls of batter cooked in a dimpled pan, served with icing sugar and jam through Advent. The name means apple slices: one was once slipped into the centre, a habit long abandoned, but the name has stayed and so has the hollow.
s: Separate the eggs: the yolks go into the batter, the whites whisked to peaks are folded in last.
The whites are what give the lightness: without them an æbleskiv is a dense, dull ball.
Heat the dimpled pan and butter every hollow generously before each batch, never once for all.
Fill the hollows three-quarters full and wait for the edge to set, then turn a quarter turn with a knitting needle.
Repeat the quarter turn four or five times: the still-raw batter runs downward at each rotation and closes the sphere. Dust with sugar and serve with jam.

rugbrod.d: A dense, almost black rye bread studded with seeds, the compulsory base of smørrebrød. It is baked in a rectangular tin rather than as a round: it must slice thin and even to carry a topping, and the average Dane eats several slices a day.
s: Soak the seeds overnight in the beer and a little water: dry, they would draw water out of the dough and the bread would be dry.
Mix the starter, warm water, flours, treacle and salt — rye dough is sticky and is not kneaded, it is stirred with a spoon.
Do not try to develop gluten: rye has almost none, and working the dough only makes it gummy.
Pour into a buttered loaf tin, smooth with a wet spatula and prove 4 to 6 hours, until cracks appear on the surface.
Bake 1 hour 40 at 180°C, turn out and cool 24 hours before slicing: cut warm it clings to the knife and seems raw.

remoulade-danoise.d: A pale yellow sauce with chopped vegetables and turmeric, served on hot dogs and breaded fish. Little remains of the French remoulade: the Danes added cauliflower, sugar and turmeric, and get through over two kilos a head each year.
s: Blanch the cauliflower in very small florets for 4 minutes and refresh it: raw, it stays hard and acrid in the sauce.
Chop the gherkins, cauliflower, capers and onion by knife into one- or two-millimetre dice — long work with no substitute.
Steep the onion ten minutes in the sweetened vinegar, then drain it keeping the vinegar.
Mix everything into the mayonnaise with the mustard, turmeric, sugar and the reserved vinegar.
Rest 24 hours in the cold: the sauce is bland on the first day and right on the second. The turmeric keeps colouring overnight.

koldskal.d: A cold buttermilk soup with vanilla and lemon, eaten with a spoon in summer with small biscuits. It appears in Danish kitchens when the thermometer passes twenty degrees and vanishes in September: supermarkets sell pallets of it for three months and none the rest of the year.
s: Whisk the yolks with the sugar and scraped vanilla until pale and ribboning.
Koldskål is never cooked: the yolks stay raw, which requires very fresh eggs and serving the same day.
Pour in the very cold buttermilk in a stream, whisking without pause, so the mixture does not split.
Add the yoghurt, cream and lemon zest, then the juice, drop by drop and last — poured too early it curdles the buttermilk.
Chill 2 hours and serve iced, with cut strawberries and crumbled kammerjunker on top.

braendende-kaerlighed.d: Mashed potato hollowed into a crater and filled with fried bacon and onion. The name means burning love: the crater of golden fat in the white suggested a volcano, and it was the end-of-the-month meal in Danish households.
s: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins and peel them scalding: cut before cooking they take on water.
Rice them and beat in the butter then the hot milk, never using a blender.
Fry the bacon gently so it renders before it crisps, then soften the onion in that fat for twenty minutes.
The fat is not discarded: it is the heart of the dish, and it is what fills the crater.
Mound the mash, hollow it with a spoon, fill it with the scalding mixture and serve with pickled beetroot.

golabki.d: Cabbage leaves stuffed with meat, rice and mushrooms, stewed in tomato sauce. The name means little pigeons: Poland shares the practice with Russia, but almost always adds dried mushrooms, giving the filling a woodland depth golubtsy lack.
s: Soak the dried mushrooms an hour in warm water and keep the strained liquid: it is worth a broth.
Freeze the whole cabbage for two days then thaw it: the leaves then come away by themselves, without blanching, and do not tear.
Cook the rice halfway, 7 minutes, and mix it with the meats, chopped mushrooms, onion and marjoram.
Roll tightly, folding the sides in, and line the base of the pot with damaged cabbage leaves so nothing catches.
Pack the rolls in, pour over the tomato and mushroom liquor, and simmer 1½ hours covered without ever stirring. Serve with smetana.

placki-ziemniaczane.d: Fried grated potato cakes, served with sour cream or sugar. In Silesia they come under a goulash, elsewhere with apple sauce: one of the few Polish dishes eaten equally savoury or sweet, and the argument is unresolved.
s: Grate the potatoes on the fine holes, not the coarse: the Polish placki is finer and smoother than a latke or a rösti.
Grate the onion at the same time straight into the gratings: its acidity slows oxidation and delays the darkening.
Press only lightly — unlike the Luxembourg cake, a placki keeps some of its water, which makes it soft in the middle.
Add the eggs, flour, salt and plenty of pepper, and cook without delay: the batter breaks down within a quarter of an hour.
Fry in half a centimetre of hot oil, 3 minutes a side. Serve with sour cream, or sweetened with apple sauce.

sernik.d: A cake of twaróg, the Polish fresh cheese passed three times through a sieve, denser and less sweet than a cheesecake. Twaróg is not cream cheese: it is lean and grainy, and it is the repeated sieving, not the fat, that gives the smooth texture.
s: Pass the twaróg three times through a fine sieve: twice is not enough, and a blender makes it elastic instead of smooth.
Cream the softened butter with the sugar for 8 minutes, then add the yolks one at a time, waiting for full absorption.
Fold in the cheese, the potato starch — never cornstarch, which leaves a taste — the zest and vanilla.
Whisk the whites to soft peaks and fold them in three times with a spatula: they are what stop a sernik being solid.
Bake 1 hour 20 at 160°C, then cool for an hour with the door ajar: taken out suddenly, it sinks in the centre and cracks.

kielbasa-grillee.d: A smoked pork and beef sausage, split and grilled, served in bread with mustard. Kiełbasa wiejska, the country sausage, is sold by weight in a coil; splitting it before grilling is no detail, it is what stops it bursting and losing its juices.
s: Choose a smoked but uncooked kiełbasa, yielding under the finger: pre-cooked sausages dry on the grill and turn mealy.
Split it lengthwise without cutting through the skin underneath, so it opens flat like a book.
Grill it cut side down first over grey, flameless coals for 6 minutes, then turn it onto the skin.
The skin should swell and brown without splitting: if it hisses and spurts, your fire is too fierce and the juice is going.
Grill the onion rings in the fat that has fallen on the plate, and serve the sausage in rye bread with strong mustard.

ciorba-de-perisoare.d: A sour soup of meatballs and rice, soured with borș. Romanian borș is not the Russian beetroot but a liquid of fermented wheat bran; it is made separately, keeps for weeks, and gives an acidity lemon does not reproduce.
s: Make the borș several days ahead: wheat bran, cornmeal and warm water, left to ferment three days covered.
It should smell frankly sour and bready; surface mould can be skimmed off, but a smell of rot means throwing it all away.
Make the meatballs with raw rice: it swells in the broth and lightens them, whereas cooked rice makes them dense.
Poach them in the trembling vegetable broth for twenty minutes, never letting it boil.
Add the separately boiled borș at the very end, and the lovage off the heat. That is what signs a Romanian ciorbă.

tochitura.d: A stew of diced pork served on polenta with an egg and salty cheese. It is the dish that follows the December pig killing: every cut that will not keep goes in, and it is eaten the same day in the farmyard.
s: Cut all the meats into two-centimetre dice and fry them separately, each at its own pace.
The liver goes in last and very briefly: cooked with the rest it turns mealy and passes on its bitterness.
Bring everything together, deglaze with white wine and simmer an hour covered.
Make the mămăligă by showering the cornmeal into boiling salted water, stirring without pause for thirty minutes.
Serve the stew on the polenta, with a fried egg and grated telemea cheese over the top.

cozonac.d: A twisted brioche filled with walnut paste, baked for Christmas and Easter. Tradition holds that one must not speak loudly or open windows while it rises; behind the superstition lies a sound observation, draughts make the dough collapse.
s: Make a sponge with warm milk, yeast and a little flour, and wait for it to triple, a good half hour.
Then knead at least thirty minutes, until the dough slaps against the bowl and stretches into a veil.
That long kneading is the key to cozonac: it gives the crumb that pulls into long threads.
Grind the walnuts and mix them with cocoa, sugar and a whipped egg white, for a filling that will not run.
Roll out, fill, roll up then twist two ropes together before putting them in the tin. Prove another two hours.

piftie.d: A jelly of pig's trotters with garlic, set with no added gelatine. It is made for Christmas and New Year; the set comes entirely from the collagen in the trotters and ears, and a piftie is judged by its firmness when the plate is tilted.
s: Singe and scrape the trotters and ears to remove every bristle, then soak them two hours in cold water.
Blanch ten minutes and discard that water: it is what gives a clear rather than cloudy jelly.
Cook five hours at a tremble, never boiling — boiling emulsifies the fat and the jelly turns milky.
Strain the broth through muslin, degrease it cold, then stir in the raw crushed garlic off the heat.
Cooked garlic loses all its bite: it goes into the warm broth, just before pouring into the dishes.

zacusca.d: A savoury preserve of grilled aubergine and peppers, jarred for winter. Making it is an October ritual: families char tens of kilos of peppers outdoors on sheet metal, and fill whole cellars with jars.
s: Char the whole aubergines and peppers over a flame or coals until the skin is black all over.
Seal them warm in a closed bag for half an hour: the steam lifts the skin, which then comes off effortlessly.
Let them drain overnight in a colander: the water they release would boil the zacuscă rather than confit it.
Chop by knife rather than in a blender — the texture must stay coarse and the pieces recognisable.
Cook three hours over low heat, stirring often. It is ready when the oil frankly rises to the surface.

doner-kebap.d: Meat stacked on a vertical spit and shaved as it roasts. The vertical spit was invented in Bursa in the nineteenth century by Iskender Efendi: lying down the meat sat in its own juices, upright it drains and grills.
s: Slice the lamb into wide thin escalopes and marinate them twenty-four hours in yoghurt, grated onion and spices.
Yoghurt and onion bring enzymes that tenderise the fibre without cooking it, unlike lemon.
Stack the escalopes on the spit alternating with slices of fat, in an even, tightly packed pile.
Roast slowly, turning: only the surface should cook, and it is shaved as it browns.
Shave thinly and vertically, from top to bottom, and serve at once — the shavings dry within two minutes.

pide.d: A boat-shaped flatbread, topped and baked in a wood oven. The edges are folded and pinched at both ends to form the hull: without that pinch the topping escapes and the bread flattens into a disc.
s: Knead a soft dough and prove it two hours: it should be wetter than a pizza dough.
Stretch it by hand into a long oval, leaving two centimetres bare all round.
Fill the centre, fold the edges over the filling and pinch both points firmly to close the boat.
Bake at 280°C on a scalding stone for eight minutes, until the edges puff and brown.
Crack the egg into the centre halfway through if you like, and brush the rim with melted butter as it comes out.

mercimek-corbasi.d: A velvety red lentil soup served with chilli butter and lemon. It is the soup every Turkish restaurant serves at any hour; the chilli butter poured over at the last moment is not a garnish but part of the recipe.
s: Rinse the red lentils until the water runs clear: their surface starch would make the soup gluey.
Fry the onion, carrot and potato at length before adding liquid — that gives the sweet base.
Add the tomato paste and let it toast a minute in the fat before the stock.
Cook thirty minutes then blend very finely: the soup must be perfectly smooth, without a single grain.
Melt the butter with the chilli and dried mint until it reddens, and pour it over each bowl.

kunefe.d: Fresh cheese between two layers of shredded pastry, cooked in butter and drenched in syrup. The cheese must stretch without turning salty: an unripened cheese is used, desalted in water for several hours beforehand.
s: Desalt the cheese three hours in cold water, changing it, then press and grate it.
Chop the kadayif finely with scissors and work it with clarified butter by hand, until every strand is coated.
Press half into a copper dish, add the cheese without touching the edges, then the rest of the kadayif.
Cook on the hob over low heat for ten minutes, then flip it in one piece and do the other side — never in the oven.
Pour cold syrup over the scalding künefe, never the reverse: the temperature contrast draws it in without sogging.

ayran.d: A drink of beaten salted yoghurt, topped with a white foam. The foam is not decorative: it proves the yoghurt was beaten long enough, and an ayran served without it is judged slapdash anywhere in Turkey.
s: Use a full-fat yoghurt with a good sourness: a mild one gives a flat drink that salt will not lift.
Whisk it alone until perfectly smooth, before adding any water at all.
Add iced water in a thin stream, whisking without pause, and keep going a good two minutes after the last addition.
That prolonged whisking is what raises the foam: added too fast, the water gives a flat, lumpy liquid.
Salt frankly and serve at once, in a tall glass or a copper bowl, the foam still intact.

tzatziki-grec.d: Strained yoghurt with grated cucumber, garlic and olive oil. It all turns on water: cucumber is 96% water, and tzatziki nearly always fails because it was not purged enough.
s: Strain the yoghurt two hours in muslin, even if already thick: a good glass of whey still comes out.
Grate the cucumber with its skin, salt it and let it purge thirty minutes in a sieve.
Then squeeze it with both hands, firmly, until it gives up not another drop.
Pound the garlic with a pinch of salt rather than chopping it: the salt acts as an abrasive and the paste disperses better.
Mix everything and rest two hours in the cold before serving. The oil goes on top at the last moment.

dolmades.d: Vine leaves stuffed with rice and herbs, served cold with olive oil. The meatless Greek version, yalantzi, means lying: it imitates the meat dolma without containing any, and is served cold rather than hot.
s: If the leaves are brined, soak them an hour and blanch two minutes; if fresh, blanch only.
Fry the onions twenty minutes, until they melt, then pearl the raw rice in them.
Cook the rice only halfway: it will finish inside the leaves, and already-cooked rice would burst the rolls.
Roll tightly but not too tightly: the rice needs room to swell by a third.
Pack them close in the pan, set a plate on top to weight them, and poach an hour covered in lemony water.

gyros.d: Pork roasted on a vertical spit, served in pita with chips and tzatziki. The chips inside the bread are a Greek particularity, absent from the Turkish döner from which gyros descends; they have been there since the 1950s and no one removes them.
s: Slice the shoulder into thin escalopes and marinate them overnight in yoghurt, vinegar, oregano and paprika.
Stack them on the spit alternating lean and fat, packing firmly so no air pocket remains.
A loosely packed stack dries between the layers and the slices come off in chunks rather than shavings.
Roast over moderate heat, turning, and shave only the browned surface, as it goes.
Warm the pita on the spit in the dripping fat, then fill with meat, chips, tomato, onion and tzatziki.

trahanas.d: A soup of cracked wheat fermented in soured milk, dried and kept a year. Trahanas is a preservation technique older than refrigeration: surplus summer milk was fixed in wheat and sun-dried, keeping it until the following winter.
s: Cook the cracked wheat in the soured milk until fully absorbed, a good hour, stirring often.
Ferment the mass three days covered, stirring daily: it should smell frankly sour.
Spread it thinly on sheets and sun-dry it for a week, crumbling it every day.
It must become as hard as gravel; badly dried, it moulds and the whole batch is lost.
For the soup, boil the trahanas twenty minutes in stock, stirring, and add diced halloumi at the end.

pourgouri.d: Bulgur cooked with toasted vermicelli and tomato, served with yoghurt. In Cyprus bulgur long replaced rice, which was dearer and imported; it remains the everyday side, while rice keeps the status of a feast dish.
s: First toast the broken vermicelli in oil, alone, until they take a frank hazelnut colour.
That toasting gives all the aroma: pale vermicelli leave the dish flat and without character.
Add the onion then the tomato, and reduce ten minutes before the bulgur.
Tip in the bulgur and moisten with one and a half times its volume in boiling stock, never cold.
Cook fifteen minutes covered, then cut the heat and rest ten minutes without lifting the lid.

daktyla.d: A village bread scored into segments and covered with sesame and nigella. Daktyla means fingers: the deep cuts divide the loaf into sections pulled apart by hand, with no knife, each with crust on every side.
s: Mix fine semolina into the flour: it gives the yellow, slightly grainy crumb of Cypriot bread.
Knead a soft dough and prove it two hours, until doubled.
Shape a long log, wet it and roll it in the sesame and nigella mix until entirely covered.
Score deeply, three-quarters through, every five centimetres.
Prove an hour and bake 30 minutes at 220°C. The cuts open and every finger browns on all sides.

loukoumi.d: Cubes set with starch and rosewater, rolled in icing sugar. Geroskipou loukoumi has held a European geographical indication since 2007; it has been made in the village since 1895, in copper cauldrons stirred with an oar.
s: Bring the sugar, water and lemon juice to exactly 118°C, never stirring once it boils.
Slake the cornflour in cold water separately and thicken it apart, to a translucent paste.
Pour the hot syrup into the starch in a stream, whisking without pause: the reverse gives irrecoverable lumps.
Then cook an hour and a half over very low heat, stirring regularly, until the mass turns amber and very elastic.
The duration makes the loukoumi: cut short, it stays soft and sticky; it must leave the spoon in one piece.

smorgastarta.d: A savoury cake layered with sliced bread, filled and iced with cream cheese. It is served at Swedish birthdays and christenings like a birthday cake, decorated and cut into slices: the resemblance to a pastry is entirely deliberate.
s: Cut off the crusts and lay the bread in tight layers, filling the gaps with offcuts.
Lightly moisten each layer with cream: dry bread absorbs the filling and the cake collapses.
Alternate the fillings — salmon and dill, shrimp and mayonnaise, hard-boiled egg — over three tiers.
Chill four hours under a light weight before icing: that settling is what allows a clean cut.
Ice with cream cheese loosened with cream, using a palette knife as for a cake, and decorate at the last moment.

pyttipanna.d: A hash of potato, onion and leftover meat, fried and served with an egg. The name means small pieces in the pan: it is an unashamed leftovers dish, and Swedes also buy frozen versions by the million portions.
s: Cut everything into exactly one-centimetre dice, potatoes included: matching sizes is the dish's only real principle.
Cook each element separately in the same pan, starting with the potatoes.
Cooked together, the ingredients weep and the whole thing boils instead of browning.
Bring it all together at the end and toss two minutes over high heat to marry the flavours.
Serve with a fried egg and pickled beetroot — both obligatory in Sweden.

blodpudding.d: A blood pudding baked in a dish rather than a casing, sliced and fried, served with lingonberry jam. The jam is no whim: its acidity cuts the iron of the blood, and the pairing is constant throughout Scandinavia.
s: Strain the blood through muslin to remove clots, without exception: a single clot shows as a lump in the slice.
Whisk it into the milk and rye flour, then strain again.
Add the syrup and spices: sugar is what distinguishes Swedish blood pudding from French, and it takes a frank hand.
Bake in a water bath an hour and a half at 150°C, until a blade comes out clean.
Cool twelve hours before slicing, then fry in butter with bacon. Serve with lingonberry jam.

saffransbullar.d: Saffron buns shaped like an S, studded with raisins, baked for Saint Lucy's day. The 13th of December was the longest night in the old calendar: the bright yellow of the saffron stands for light, and the coiled shape for the sun.
s: Grind the saffron with a spoonful of sugar in a mortar: the sugar acts as an abrasive and releases far more colour.
Infuse it in the hot milk for at least an hour, or the night before — it needs time.
Quark in the dough is not traditional everywhere, but it keeps the buns soft for three days rather than one.
Knead ten minutes, prove an hour, then roll ropes and coil them into an S at both ends.
Set a raisin in the centre of each spiral, prove an hour and bake 12 minutes at 220°C.

lefse.d: A supple potato flatbread cooked dry and spread with butter and sugar. The dough contains almost no flour: the potato makes the body, and flour must be kept minimal or the result is a rubbery pancake.
s: Boil the potatoes in their skins the day before and rice them while scalding hot.
Chill the mash twelve hours: cold, it absorbs far less flour, and that is the whole issue.
Work in the flour just before rolling, never earlier: the dough slackens as it waits and always demands more.
Roll very thin on a heavily floured surface, with a grooved pin if you have one.
Cook on a dry plate at 250°C, one minute a side, and stack the rounds under a damp cloth to keep them supple.

raspeball.d: Large dumplings of raw grated potato, poached and served with salt pork. They carry a dozen names across Norway's valleys — komle, klubb, kumpe — and Thursday is traditionally the day for making them.
s: Grate half the potatoes raw and press them out thoroughly in a cloth, keeping the liquid.
Let that liquid settle ten minutes: the starch sinks, and it goes back into the dough.
Mix with the rest of the potatoes, boiled and mashed, then work in the flours little by little.
Shape fist-sized dumplings with wetted hands and poach them in the pork broth, at a tremble.
An hour's poaching, never boiling: at a rolling boil the dumplings disintegrate into mash.

sursild.d: Salted herring marinated in sweetened vinegar with onions and spices. The herring arrives salted in barrels: the marinade does not preserve it but desalts and reseasons it, which is why the initial soaking determines everything.
s: Desalt the herring fillets twenty-four hours in cold water, changing it four times.
Taste a fragment before stopping: depending on the original cure, twelve more hours are sometimes needed.
Boil the vinegar, water and sugar with the spices, then cool completely.
Poured hot over the herring, the liquid would cook it and the flesh would turn white and mealy.
Pack the fillets in a jar with sliced onion and carrot, cover with cold marinade and wait three days.

krumkake.d: A very thin waffle rolled into a cone straight off the iron and filled with cream. It must be rolled within five seconds of cooking: cooled, it hardens instantly and shatters instead of curling.
s: Melt the butter and let it cool before adding: hot, it cooks the eggs and the batter goes grainy.
Whisk eggs and sugar to the ribbon, then fold in flour and butter without working it.
Rest the batter an hour: the bubbles subside and the waffle comes out without holes.
Set a spoonful in the centre of the hot iron and press: thirty seconds a side, no longer.
Roll immediately around the wooden cone, holding it with a cloth. You have five seconds, no more.

pinnekjott.d: Salted, dried lamb ribs steamed over birch sticks. The name means stick meat: the peeled birch branches lift the meat above the water and give it a light resinous scent.
s: Dry-salt the ribs for two days, then air-dry them three weeks somewhere cold and ventilated.
Soak them thirty hours in cold water before cooking, changing it three times.
That desalting is decisive: too little and the meat is inedible; too much and it loses all its flavour.
Lay the peeled birch sticks in the bottom of the pot and set the meat on them, clear of the water.
Steam three hours covered, topping up with boiling water. Serve with mashed swede.

mammi.d: A dessert of malted rye cooked slowly to near black, served cold with cream. It is eaten only at Easter and its appearance universally repels foreigners; Finns joke about it themselves while eating millions of kilos each spring.
s: Mix part of the malt and flour into water at 70°C and let it saccharify an hour, covered.
Repeat three times, adding flour, malt and hot water each time, with an hour's rest between.
That staged saccharification is what makes mämmi sweet: there is almost no added sugar.
Rest the mass overnight at room temperature, then salt it and scent it with orange zest.
Bake three hours at 150°C in a birch-bark dish, then chill three days before serving.

rosolli.d: A salad of diced beetroot, potato and carrot served with a pink cream. The cream is coloured only as it is served, with a little beetroot juice: mixed ahead, it turns a dull brown within hours.
s: Cook each vegetable separately and whole, in its skin: peeled, they take on water and the salad goes watery.
Cook the beetroot apart and far longer than the rest, up to an hour and a half.
Cut everything into one-centimetre dice and let the beetroot cool alone, away from the others.
Combine the vegetables only at the last moment: beetroot dyes everything pink within minutes.
Whip the cream with the vinegar and a spoonful of beetroot juice, and serve it separately.

pulla.d: A cardamom-scented braided bun baked to go with coffee. Finland drinks more coffee per head than any other country, and pulla is its obligatory companion: workplace coffee breaks are written into collective agreements there.
s: Use cardamom seeds you grind yourself: shop-bought powder has lost most of its scent.
Be generous — a properly dosed pulla should smell of cardamom across the room.
Knead the dough fifteen minutes, until it leaves the bowl and stretches into a veil.
Prove an hour, plait in three strands and prove a second time for forty minutes.
Glaze with egg, scatter pearl sugar and bake 18 minutes at 200°C, no longer — overbaked, it dries within a day.

karjalanpaisti.d: A stew of three meats baked four hours, with nothing seared. Nothing is browned beforehand: everything goes raw into the pot with water and salt, and the length of cooking does all the work.
s: Cut the three meats into large four-centimetre cubes, keeping the fat and sinew.
On no account brown them: that is the dish's particularity, and searing changes its flavour entirely.
Stack meats, onions and spices in a cast-iron pot, add the water and cover.
Use whole allspice berries, unground: it is Karelia's signature spice, and ground it dominates everything.
Bake four hours at 150°C without ever opening it. Serve with boiled potatoes and pickles.

suya.d: Strips of beef coated in yaji, a groundnut and spice powder, grilled over coals. Hausa mallams sell them at night from wooden racks; the yaji goes on again after grilling, never only before.
s: Dry-roast the peanuts, rub off the skins between your hands, then grind them.
Press the powder in a cloth to squeeze out the oil: too oily, it will not cling to the meat.
Mix it with the paprika, cayenne, ginger, garlic and onion powder and the crumbled stock cube: this is yaji.
Cut the beef into very thin strips, thread them concertina-style on skewers, oil and roll in the yaji.
Grill for 6 minutes, turning, then dust with yaji again as it comes off. Serve with raw onion, tomato and cabbage.

attieke-poisson.d: Fermented cassava semolina, served with grilled fish and a sharp onion relish. Attiéké is known by its sourness: that is the cassava fermenting, and it answers the oily fish.
s: Scale and gut the fish, score it three times each side and rub it with lemon and salt.
Pound the garlic, ginger, one onion, the chilli and the stock cube, and push the paste into the cuts and the belly.
Marinate for an hour, then grill over moderate coals 15 minutes a side, basting with oil.
Steam the attiéké for 15 minutes and fluff it with a fork to separate the grains.
Make the raw relish: sliced onion, tomato, chilli and lemon, uncooked. Serve everything together.

poulet-moambe.d: Chicken stewed in palm nut pulp, with cassava leaves alongside. It is the national dish of both Congos; eaten with the fingers and chikwangue, the cassava paste in its wrapper.
s: Marinate the chicken for 2 hours in pounded garlic and ginger with lemon.
Slake the palm nut pulp in a litre of hot water and pass it through a sieve to remove the fibres.
Colour the chicken in palm oil, add the onion and tomato, then pour in the palm juice.
Simmer uncovered for 50 minutes: the orange oil must rise clearly to the surface.
Separately cook the pounded cassava leaves for 1 hour with the groundnut. Serve the two side by side, with rice.

djenkoume.d: A maize flour cake cooked in tomato sauce, cut into squares and served with chicken. It turns out like a cake and is eaten by hand: Togo makes it the dish of Sundays and christenings.
s: Marinate the chicken in garlic, ginger and stock cube, then fry it until golden.
In the same oil, fry the onion and tomato paste, then add the blended tomato and chilli.
Reduce for 25 minutes: the sauce should be very concentrated, almost a paste.
Take out two thirds of the sauce, let it down with boiling water and rain in the maize flour.
Work for 20 minutes until the paste leaves the sides, turn into an oiled tin, let it set and cut into squares.

riz-gras-guineen.d: Rice cooked in a broth of smoked fish, tomato and sweet potato leaves. Guinea smokes its fish on wooden racks: it is that smoke, more than the tomato, that flavours the rice.
s: Soak the smoked fish for 20 minutes in hot water, then flake it, removing the bones.
Fry the tomato paste in the oil for 8 minutes, until the oil turns red.
Add the onion, garlic, fresh tomato and smoked fish, and reduce for 20 minutes.
Add two litres of water, the leaves, okra and whole chilli, and cook for 25 minutes.
Lift out the vegetables, pour the rice into the remaining broth and let it absorb for 25 minutes, covered.

cachupa-rica.d: A stew of cracked maize, beans and every available meat, simmered half a day. The next day it is fried with an egg: cachupa guisada, and many prefer it that way.
s: Soak the maize and beans separately overnight: cracked maize needs twelve hours.
Cook the maize for 1½ hours in a large pot, then add the beans for 45 minutes.
Add the meats in large pieces, the onion, garlic and bay, and simmer for 1 hour.
Add the roots and squash in order of firmness, then the cabbage for the last 20 minutes.
Crush a little squash against the side to thicken. Next day, fry it in a pan with a fried egg.

thiebou-yapp.d: The meat rice of the Senegal River, browned with tomato and long-cooked onion, without fish. It is served in a single dish set on the ground, each person eating from the quarter facing them.
s: Colour the lamb in large pieces in the oil, then lift it out.
Melt the sliced onions in the same oil for 40 minutes, until they brown: they give the colour.
Add the tomato paste and let it darken, then the fresh tomato, garlic and two litres of water.
Return the meat and simmer for 50 minutes, then add the vegetables in order of firmness and remove each when done.
Pour the washed rice into the remaining broth, cover and let it absorb for 25 minutes over very low heat.

riz-au-gras-burkinabe.d: Rice simmered in a tomato and meat broth, cooked in a single pot. It is the dish of the maquis bars and of ceremonies; the rice must stay firm and each grain keep its colour.
s: Marinate the chicken in garlic, ginger and crumbled stock cube for an hour.
Colour it in the oil, lift it out, and fry the tomato paste for 8 minutes in the same oil.
Add the onion, blended tomato and whole chilli, and reduce for 20 minutes.
Add three litres of water, return the chicken and cook for 30 minutes, then add the carrot and cabbage.
Lift out the meat and vegetables, pour in the washed rice and let it absorb the broth for 25 minutes, covered.

kilishi.d: Sheets of beef sun-dried, coated in spiced groundnut paste, then grilled. The meat is sliced so thin you can read through it: a kilo of beef yields under three hundred grams of kilishi.
s: Cut the beef into 2 mm sheets along the grain: the knife must be long and perfectly sharp.
Spread them on racks and sun-dry for 6 hours, turning, until they stiffen.
Grind the roasted peanuts and mix them with water, ginger, garlic, cayenne and stock cube into a thin paste.
Dip each sheet in the paste and return it to dry for 3 hours, until the coating sets.
Grill for 4 minutes over gentle coals, watching closely: groundnut burns in seconds.

kanyah-liberien.d: A bar of toasted rice, groundnut and sugar, pressed by hand and cut into squares. It is the Liberian travelling ration: no cooking, keeps a week, and sees a man through to evening.
s: Dry-toast the raw rice in a heavy pan, stirring constantly, until it browns and pops.
Roast the peanuts separately and rub off the skins between your hands.
Grind the toasted rice very finely, then the peanuts, into an oily powder.
Mix the two with the sugar, nutmeg and salt, and add the oil a spoonful at a time until the mass holds together.
Press firmly into a flat mould, let it firm for an hour and cut into squares.

gozo-sauce-koko.d: A cassava paste with a sauce of koko leaves, smoked meat and groundnut. The koko leaf is a forest vine that is never cultivated: it is gathered, and slicing it is an art.
s: Slice the koko leaves into hair-fine ribbons: it takes time, and it makes the texture of the sauce.
Soak the smoked fish, flake it and remove every bone.
Heat the palm oil, add the onion, garlic and chilli, then the leaves and half a litre of water.
Simmer for 40 minutes: the leaves should lose their bitterness without turning black.
Slake the groundnut and stir it in with the fish for 20 minutes. Serve with gozo, the cassava paste worked with boiling water.

haricots-bananes-vertes.d: Red beans stewed with green plantains and palm oil. It is the daily meal of the Burundian hills: the bean for strength, the banana to last until evening.
s: Soak the beans overnight, then cook them for 1 hour in unsalted water.
Peel the green plantains under water — their sap stains the hands lastingly — and cut them into lengths.
Fry the onion, garlic, leek and celery in palm oil, and add the tomato.
Pour this sofrito over the beans with their liquid, add the plantains and the whole chilli.
Simmer for 40 minutes: the plantains should turn meltingly soft and the broth thicken by itself.

matapa.d: Cassava leaves pounded with coconut milk, with crab and prawns, served over rice. Mozambique pounds the leaf and the groundnut in the same mortar: the two merge and the sauce turns green and rich.
s: Pound the cassava leaves and peanuts together, at length, into a coarse paste.
Blanch them for 20 minutes in plenty of water and squeeze them dry: the raw leaf is toxic, and long cooking is compulsory.
Fry the onion and garlic in oil, add the pressed paste and half a litre of water.
Simmer for 30 minutes, then pour in the coconut milk and continue for 15 minutes without boiling.
Add the crab and prawns for the last 8 minutes only. Serve with white rice.

potjie-de-gibier.d: An oryx or kudu stew cooked in layers in a three-legged pot over embers. Namibia eats game as others eat beef: the meat is lean, and the bacon added to it is not a luxury.
s: Marinate the game for 12 hours in red wine with juniper and bay: the marinade tenderises and softens the venison note.
Render the bacon in the pot set over moderate embers, then sear the drained meat.
Add the onion, strained marinade and stock, and simmer covered for 2 hours.
Arrange the vegetables in distinct layers, longest-cooking first, and never stir again.
Give it another hour. Serve by digging in from the edge, to keep the tiers visible.

papa-ea-poone.d: A paste of freshly grated maize, cooked slowly, served with moroho, the greens from the garden. Lesotho makes it with harvest maize, still milky: it is sweet without anything being added.
s: Grate the fresh maize kernels on a coarse grater, catching the milk that runs from them.
Cook them gently with the collected milk for 25 minutes, stirring: the mass thickens by itself.
Rain in the maize flour to firm it up, and work for another 15 minutes with a stick.
For the moroho, wilt the greens with the onion and tomato, covered, for 20 minutes.
Serve the paste as a dome, hollowed into a well of butter, with the greens alongside.

sishwala.d: A maize porridge thicker than pap, served with a stewed farmyard chicken. Sishwala can be cut with a knife once cool: that is what sets it apart from the region's other pastes.
s: Colour the jointed chicken in the oil, then add the onion and garlic.
Add the crushed tomato and crumbled stock cube, barely moisten and simmer covered for 50 minutes.
Bring a litre and a half of salted water to the boil and rain in the maize flour, whisking.
Work it for 30 minutes over low heat with a wooden stick: sishwala should be firmer than an ordinary pap.
Serve the paste moulded in a wetted bowl, with the chicken and pumpkin leaves in groundnut.

cari-poisson-seychellois.d: A reef fish curry with fresh coconut milk, turmeric and curry leaves. Seychelles grate the nut on a bladed stool, the grajeur: hand-pressed milk tastes nothing like the tin.
s: Cut the fish into thick steaks and rub them with turmeric, salt and lime; leave 20 minutes.
Fry the pounded onion, garlic and ginger in oil with the curry leaves and cinnamon.
Add the tomato and the remaining turmeric, and reduce for 10 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a bare simmer, never boiling: it would split.
Slide in the steaks and poach for 12 minutes uncovered, basting. Lime at the last moment.

vindaye-de-poisson.d: Fried fish marinated in turmeric, mustard and vinegar, eaten cold. Vindaye descends from Goan vindaloo; in Mauritius it keeps a week and improves daily.
s: Cut the tuna into thick slices, rub them with turmeric and salt, and fry them until coloured.
Crush the mustard seeds in a mortar with the garlic, ginger and a little vinegar.
Fry this paste in the oil for 8 minutes, without letting it burn: the mustard would turn bitter.
Add the sliced onion and split chillies, and barely wilt them: they should stay crunchy.
Pour in the rest of the vinegar, let it cool, then submerge the fish in it. Wait 24 hours and serve cold.

langouste-a-la-vanille.d: Lobster in coconut milk scented with Comoran vanilla. The islands grow ylang-ylang and vanilla; pairing the pod with shellfish is an island idea, and it works.
s: Split the live lobsters lengthways in one clean stroke, and remove the grit sac.
Sear them flesh down in foaming butter for 4 minutes, then lift them out.
Sweat the shallot, garlic and ginger, deglaze with white wine and reduce by half.
Add the coconut milk and the split, scraped vanilla pods, and infuse for 10 minutes at a simmer.
Return the lobsters shell down and cook for 8 minutes, basting. Lime and coriander at the end.

oladii.d: Small thick pancakes made with kefir, taller and softer than blini, served at breakfast with jam. The kefir must be frankly sour: its acidity reacts with the bicarbonate and lifts the batter, with no yeast and no waiting.
s: Take the kefir out an hour ahead: cold, it does not react with the bicarbonate and the oladii stay flat.
Beat the egg, sugar and salt into the kefir, then tip in the sifted flour all at once and mix in twenty turns only.
Add the bicarbonate last and stop stirring altogether: the bubbles form at once, and stirring drives them out.
Rest ten minutes untouched — the surface should crater — then spoon it out without disturbing the bottom.
Cook in a centimetre of hot oil, 2 minutes a side. Serve with apricot jam and smetana.

pirog-au-chou.d: A large brioche pie of melted cabbage and hard-boiled egg, cut into squares and served at feasts. In the north a coin was hidden inside to mark who would be lucky that year; the cabbage must be long melted, or it weeps and soaks the dough.
s: Knead a brioche dough with the flour, warm milk, yeast, one egg, the butter and salt, and prove for 1½ hours.
Slice the cabbage very finely and melt it in a pan for 40 minutes with the onion, covered at first then uncovered.
It must have lost three-quarters of its volume and stopped weeping altogether: that is the whole success of a pirog.
Cool it completely, then add three chopped hard-boiled eggs and the dill.
Line a tin, fill, cover with a second sheet, seal by pinching, glaze and bake 50 minutes at 180°C. Eaten warm, cut into squares.

koulibiak-royal.d: A layered pie: salmon, rice, mushrooms and egg, separated by thin pancakes. The pancakes are no ornament: they absorb the moisture of each layer and stop the base pastry staying raw, and Escoffier kept them when he took it to Paris.
s: Make three very thin pancakes with the flour, milk and one egg, and cool them flat on a cloth.
Dry out the chopped mushrooms in a pan for 20 minutes with the shallot, until they stop sizzling.
Cook the rice, hard-boil two eggs, cut the salmon into slabs and let everything cool completely.
Build on the pastry: pancake, rice, salmon, mushrooms, chopped egg, pancake, pressing each layer and salting at every stage.
Close, seal, glaze, cut two chimneys and bake 20 minutes at 210°C then 35 minutes at 170°C. Rest 15 minutes before slicing.

chebureki.d: Large lamb turnovers fried in boiling oil, their dough blistered with bubbles. The filling holds set broth that melts as it cooks: the first bite releases scalding juice, and a chebureki is always held tilted downward.
s: Knead the flour, iced water, salt and a spoonful of vodka into a firm dough: the vodka boils off in the fryer and is what makes the blisters.
Rest the dough for an hour, wrapped, so it stretches without shrinking back.
Chop the onion very finely — almost to a purée — and mix it with the lamb and the cold broth set to a jelly.
Roll 20 cm discs to 1 mm, spread a thin layer of filling on one half only, and seal with a fork, expelling all the air.
Fry 3 minutes at 190°C, ladling oil over the top: the dough must blister into large brown bubbles. Eat scalding, tilted over the plate.

belyashi.d: Small yeasted buns open at the centre, filled with meat and pan-fried, hole down first. The hole is not decorative: it lets steam escape instead of bursting the dough, and it half closes as it cooks.
s: Knead a soft yeasted dough with the flour, warm milk, yeast, egg, sugar and salt, and prove for 1½ hours.
Mix the minced meats with grated onion and two spoonfuls of iced water: that water becomes the juice, and without it the filling stays dry.
Do not pre-cook the filling: it goes in raw and cooks inside the bun, which is what separates a belyash from an ordinary filled fritter.
Flatten 60 g balls, fill them, gather the edges to the centre in pleats and leave a hole a finger wide.
Fry in two centimetres of oil at 165°C, hole down for 4 minutes, then turn for 4 more. Low heat: the raw meat must cook before the dough browns.

echpochmak.d: A triangle of yeasted dough filled with raw beef and potato, pierced at the top so broth can be poured in. The name means three corners in Tatar; meat and potato go in raw and cook together sealed, which needs a full hour of oven and no less.
s: Knead a yeasted dough with milk, butter and one egg, and prove it for 1½ hours.
Cut the beef and potato by knife into 5 mm dice — minced they would turn to mush; larger, they would not cook.
Mix them with very finely chopped onion, salt heavily and pepper: it is the only seasoning, and it must be forthright.
Cut 15 cm discs, fill the centre and raise three sides, sealing them into a triangle and leaving a one-centimetre hole at the top.
Bake 20 minutes at 200°C, then pour a spoonful of hot broth through the hole and continue 40 minutes at 170°C. Repeat once halfway through.

pryanik-de-toula.d: A flat spice bread filled with jam and stamped from a carved wooden mould. Tula was capital both of gunsmithing and of the pryanik; it was presented to tsars, and it keeps three months, growing softer rather than drying out.
s: Heat the honey and sugar to 110°C, then pour them scalding onto the flours mixed with the spices, and work with a spoon.
This scalded dough is the key: it gelatinises the starch and gives the pryanik its lasting suppleness.
Cool it completely, then work in the eggs, butter and bicarbonate, and rest it 12 hours in the cold.
Roll two 5 mm sheets, spread apple jam on one leaving a two-centimetre border, and cover with the second, sealing.
Stamp the pattern with a floured wooden mould, pressing once cleanly and never twice, and bake 22 minutes at 190°C. Glaze with sugar as it comes out.

ptichye-moloko.d: A cake of agar mousse under a dark chocolate shell, created at the Praga restaurant in 1968. It is the only Soviet cake to have been patented; its name comes from bird's milk, the unobtainable food of ancient myth, and people queued two hours to buy one.
s: Soak the agar for an hour in cold water, then bring it to the boil with the sugar and hold it 2 minutes at 110°C.
Agar is not gelatine: it must boil to activate, and it sets at 40°C, which leaves very little time to work.
Whisk the whites with the lemon juice, then pour in the boiling syrup in a stream, whisking without pause, and beat until it cools.
Fold in the softened butter creamed with the condensed milk, in three additions, with a spatula and without delay.
Pour onto a sponge base baked separately, smooth it and set 3 hours in the cold, then coat with melted chocolate cooled to 30°C.

smetannik.d: A Bashkir soured-cream cake, soft and tangy, built in thin layers. The smetana does everything: its fat replaces butter in the batter and its acidity activates the bicarbonate, so no leaven is needed.
s: Beat 400 g of the smetana with the eggs, 150 g of the sugar and the salt, then add the flour and bicarbonate.
The bicarbonate foams on meeting the smetana: pour into the tins at once, a batter that waits collapses.
Divide the batter in two and add cocoa to one half, then bake four thin 20 cm discs, 10 minutes each at 180°C.
Whisk the remaining smetana with the remaining sugar without ever whipping it like cream: overbeaten, it splits and weeps whey.
Build alternating pale and dark discs, coat the top and sides, scatter walnuts and let it soak 6 hours in the cold.

vatrushka.d: A yeasted bun hollowed into a well of sweetened tvorog, round as the sun. It was a pagan offering to the hearth god before becoming the pastry of every Soviet canteen; the tvorog must be well drained, or it swells and overflows the well.
s: Drain the tvorog 3 hours in a cloth: it is the only precaution that matters, and it decides everything else.
Knead a yeasted dough with the flour, warm milk, yeast, one egg, the butter and 40 g of the sugar, and prove 1½ hours.
Sieve the tvorog with a yolk, the remaining sugar, the vanilla and a spoonful of semolina, which will take up any residual moisture.
Shape 70 g balls, flatten them and press the well with the floured base of a glass, leaving a two-centimetre rim.
Fill, glaze the rim only, prove 30 minutes and bake 22 minutes at 190°C. The tvorog should barely colour.

koulitch.d: A tall narrow raisin brioche, iced white and sprinkled with coloured strands, blessed at church on Holy Saturday. It is taller than it is wide because it imitates the prosphoron, the liturgical bread; a dried piece is kept all year.
s: Make a starter with the yeast, warm milk and 150 g of the flour, and let it double for an hour.
Add the yolks beaten with the sugar, the saffron infused in a spoonful of hot milk, the vanilla and salt, then the remaining flour.
Knead 20 minutes before working in the softened butter little by little: this dough is very rich and takes a long time to come smooth.
Prove 3 hours, fold in the rum-soaked fruit, fill the tall tins only halfway and prove 2 hours more.
Bake 50 minutes at 170°C, covering with paper as soon as the top colours. Cool it lying on its side, turning regularly, then ice with egg white and sugar.

kasha-grechka.d: Toasted buckwheat cooked by absorption, served with butter, mushrooms and onion. The proverb says kasha is our mother: it has been the base of the Russian army's diet since Suvorov, and it is never stirred while it cooks.
s: Toast the buckwheat dry in the pan for 4 minutes, stirring, until it smells of hazelnuts — untoasted buckwheat gives a soft, bland kasha.
Pour in exactly two parts boiling salted water to one of grain, and do not measure by eye.
Bring to the boil, cover tightly and drop to the lowest heat: from that point the lid is not lifted and nothing is stirred.
Give it 20 minutes, then kill the heat and let it swell 10 minutes more, still covered.
Meanwhile fry the onion with the fresh mushrooms and the rehydrated dried ones. Add the butter and mushrooms with a fork, fluffing the grains.

golubtsy.d: Cabbage leaves stuffed with meat and rice, stewed in a tomato and smetana sauce. Golub means pigeon: the plump rolls reminded Russians of roast pigeon, a rich man's dish they imitated with cabbage.
s: Cut out the cabbage core and plunge the whole head into boiling water for 10 minutes, peeling off leaves as they soften.
Flatten the central rib of each leaf with a rolling pin or knife: without that it snaps as you fold and the filling escapes.
Cook the rice only halfway, 7 minutes, and mix it with the meat and the grated onion and carrot, salting heavily.
Roll them folding the sides inward like a parcel, and pack the rolls tightly seam down in the pot.
Coat with tomato and smetana let down with water, cover and simmer 1¼ hours over very low heat, never stirring.

vinegret.d: A bright pink winter salad of beetroot, gherkins and sauerkraut, without a trace of meat. It was the Lenten salad, the one permitted on fast days; the unrefined sunflower oil, which smells of toasted seed, cannot be swapped for a neutral one.
s: Boil the beetroot, potatoes and carrots whole in their skins, separately: cooked together, everything takes the colour of the beetroot.
Cool them completely then peel and cut them into even one-centimetre dice.
Coat the beetroot dice alone with a spoonful of oil before mixing them with the rest: the oil seals them and stops the salad turning uniformly red.
Add the gherkins, pressed sauerkraut, onion and beans, then the remaining oil, salt and pepper.
Rest 2 hours in the cold before serving, and toss only at the last moment. Never add mayonnaise: it is no longer a vinegret.

salade-mimosa.d: A layered salad of tinned salmon, egg and cheese, crowned with crumbled yolk. It is served on 8 March, women's day, when mimosa arrived from Georgia and Abkhazia: the grated yolk on top imitates the flower, and that is where the name comes from.
s: Hard-boil the eggs 9 minutes, refresh them and separate the whites from the yolks carefully: the salad depends on that separation.
Freeze the butter for an hour: grated frozen it forms threads that melt in the mouth, softened it would make a greasy layer.
Mash the salmon with a fork removing skin and bones, and soak the chopped onion ten minutes in cold water.
Build inside a ring: grated potato, salmon, onion, grated white, grated butter, cheese, carrot, with a thin layer of mayonnaise between each.
Finish with the yolks pushed through a fine sieve, rained on lightly and not pressed down. Set 4 hours in the cold before lifting the ring.

seledka-pod-shuboy.d: Salted herring buried under layers of grated vegetable and mayonnaise, topped with violet beetroot. A 1918 legend says the colours spell out the revolution — red for the Bolsheviks, white for bourgeois mayonnaise; historians disbelieve it, and the dish is served every New Year regardless.
s: Fillet the herring, pull every bone with tweezers and cut it into one-centimetre dice.
Soak the chopped onion for twenty minutes in vinegared water: raw, it dominates every layer above it.
Boil the beetroot, potatoes and carrots whole and cool them completely — grated warm, they soak the mayonnaise.
Build in a dish: herring, onion, potato, carrot, egg, beetroot, with a thin layer of mayonnaise between each, without pressing.
Rest 12 hours in the cold: that rest is what carries the herring's salt into the vegetables and pulls the dish together.

khychin-balkar.d: A very thin flatbread filled with cheese and potato, cooked dry then buttered. The Balkars, a people of the high Caucasus valleys, stack ten of them and cut them in wedges like a cake; the kefir dough must be so thin the filling shows through.
s: Mix the kefir and bicarbonate and wait for them to foam before adding the flour and salt: that reaction stands in for yeast.
Knead briefly, without force, and rest the dough 30 minutes under a bowl — overworked, it shrinks back and will not roll.
Mash the hot potato with the fresh cheese and spring onion, or replace the potato with blanched nettles in spring.
Enclose a ball of filling in a ball of dough, seal it, then roll very gently out to 25 cm across.
Cook on a dry griddle 3 minutes a side, prick the blisters, and butter generously on both sides as it comes off.

shurpa-daguestan.d: A lamb soup with vegetables left whole, cooked in a kazan over the fire. The vegetables are not cut: they cook keeping their shape and are served apart from the meat, and the broth is drunk on its own from a bowl, before the rest.
s: Soak the chickpeas overnight, then start the meat and bones in cold water and bring them up slowly.
Skim without pause for the first fifteen minutes: in Dagestan a shurpa is judged by the clarity of its broth.
Add the chickpeas and simmer 1½ hours without ever boiling, uncovered, topping up the evaporated water.
Then add the whole vegetables — onions, carrots, potatoes — and give them 40 minutes more.
Serve in three acts: the broth first, in a bowl, then the vegetables, then the meat on a platter, with coriander and ground cumin.

veau-orloff.d: A roasted veal loin, sliced then reassembled with duxelles and soubise between each slice, coated in Mornay and gratinated. Created in Paris by the French chef of Prince Orlov, the tsar's ambassador: a Russian dish never cooked in Russia before it came back there.
s: Roast the loin 40 minutes at 180°C to 58°C at the centre, and let it cool: veal is never sliced hot, it crumbles.
Make the soubise by cooking the sliced onion and rice in the milk for 30 minutes, then blend and dry it out to a thick purée.
Make the duxelles by drying the chopped mushrooms in a pan for 20 minutes, until they release nothing more.
Slice the veal 1 cm thick, spread each slice with soubise and duxelles, and rebuild the loin, tying it lightly.
Coat with a gruyère Mornay, scatter cheese and gratinate 25 minutes at 200°C. Remove the string before serving.

kournik.d: A tall domed pie of seven layers — chicken, rice, mushrooms, egg — separated by thin pancakes. It is the Cossack wedding pie: it was cut before the couple, and the number of layers said how many children were wished on them.
s: Poach the chicken 45 minutes, bone it hot and shred the meat; keep the broth to cook the rice.
Make four thin pancakes and cool them flat: they divide the layers and absorb the moisture of each.
Prepare the fillings separately — rice in broth with dill, mushrooms dried out with onion, chopped hard-boiled egg, chicken bound with a little broth — and cool everything.
Line with shortcrust and stack into a dome: chicken, pancake, rice, pancake, mushrooms, pancake, egg, narrowing toward the top.
Cover with puff pastry, seal, glaze, cut a chimney and bake 20 minutes at 200°C then 50 minutes at 170°C.

kalatch-de-mourom.d: A wheat bread shaped like a padlock, with a handle to hold it by without soiling it. The handle was not eaten: it was given to the poor or to dogs, and from that comes the Russian phrase to have reached the handle, to have hit rock bottom.
s: Refresh the starter twice during the day: kalach is made on leaven alone, and a weak starter gives a flat bread.
Knead a very firm dough, then work it at length on the table, slapping and folding it, for a good half hour.
That prolonged beating drives out the large bubbles and gives the tight, satiny crumb that separates a kalach from ordinary bread.
Prove overnight in the cold, then shape a thick ring, drawing one end out into a slim handle.
Bake 30 minutes at 240°C with steam for the first ten. The belly should be golden and the handle almost white.

kharcho.d: A Georgian beef soup with rice, walnuts and sour tkemali plum, heavily spiced. The acidity comes from neither lemon nor vinegar but from fermented green plum: it is what makes a kharcho, and without it you have an ordinary beef soup.
s: Start the beef in cold water and bring it up slowly, skimming, then simmer 1½ hours with the bay.
Pound the walnuts in a mortar until they release their oil: it is that oil, not the fragments, that binds the soup.
Melt the very finely chopped onion for 20 minutes, add the tomato purée and let it darken slightly.
Bring everything together with the rice and cook 20 minutes, then add the tkemali and khmeli-suneli off the heat.
The spice mix must never boil: cooked, it loses its fenugreek and dill scent. Add the pounded garlic and coriander at the last moment.

pyshki-petersbourg.d: Rings of yeasted dough fried and buried in icing sugar, an institution on Bolshaya Konyushennaya street since 1958. In Petersburg they are never called doughnuts: a pyshka has no filling, is eaten standing and comes with milky coffee served in a glass.
s: Dissolve the yeast in warm milk with a spoonful of sugar and wait until it foams properly.
Knead with the flour, eggs, sugar, salt and melted butter for 12 minutes: the dough must stay soft and slightly tacky.
Prove for an hour, then roll to 1.5 cm and cut rings with a cutter, re-rolling the trimmings once only.
Prove them 25 minutes on a floured cloth, uncovered: a light skin forms and keeps the pyshka from drinking oil.
Fry 90 seconds a side at 180°C, drain and roll them in icing sugar while they are still scalding.

plombir-sovietique.d: An ice cream of very rich cream, with no stabiliser and no flavouring, as the GOST standard defined it. Mikoyan, commissar for food, brought the machines back from the United States in 1936 and imposed fifteen per cent fat; it was sold outdoors, even at minus twenty.
s: Infuse the split vanilla pod in the hot milk for half an hour off the heat, then lift it out, scraping the seeds in.
Whiten the yolks with the sugar, pour the warm milk over and cook to the nappe at 83°C, never above.
At 85°C the yolks coagulate and the custard grains: that is the only real difficulty, and a thermometer beats an eye.
Strain, cool fast in an iced water bath, add the cold cream and mature 4 hours in the fridge.
Churn, then harden 3 hours in the freezer. With no stabiliser it crystallises within two days: it is eaten the same day.

sbiten.d: A hot honey and spice drink, sold in Russian streets before tea arrived from China in 1638. Street sellers carried it in copper samovars on their backs crying sbiten!; the name comes from sbivat, to beat together.
s: Bring the water and sugar to the boil with sliced fresh ginger, cinnamon, cloves, star anise and a few peppercorns.
Infuse 20 minutes covered over very low heat, never at a rolling boil.
Take it off and let it fall to 60°C before stirring in the honey: above that it loses its aromas and leaves only its sugar.
Add the mint and lemon zest and infuse ten minutes more, off the heat and covered.
Strain and serve scalding in thick glasses scalded beforehand. Wine was once added, which remains optional.

kvass-blanc.d: A fermented drink of toasted rye bread, barely alcoholic, drunk iced in summer. It appears in the chronicle of 996, when Vladimir baptised the Rus' and had kvass distributed to the people; it was sold from street tankers into the 1990s.
s: Cut the rye bread into slices and brown them in the oven 20 minutes at 180°C, until the edges are nearly black.
That deep toasting gives the colour and the flavour: merely dried bread makes a pale, bland kvass.
Pour boiling water over the bread and infuse 8 hours, then strain through a cloth without pressing.
Add the sugar and the slaked yeast, cover with a cloth — never an airtight lid — and ferment 24 hours at room temperature.
Bottle with three raisins per bottle, close and leave 24 hours more in the cold. Open over the sink: the pressure is real.

tchakhokhbili.d: A poultry stew with tomatoes and herbs, cooked without a drop of water. The name comes from khokhobi, Georgian for pheasant, replaced by chicken in Soviet times; the meat is seared dry in the pot first, and its own juices make the sauce.
s: Joint the chicken and colour the pieces in a dry pot, with no fat: the skin releases enough for what follows.
Lift them out and melt thickly sliced onion in that fat for 25 minutes, until pale and yielding.
Peel the tomatoes after thirty seconds in boiling water, and crush them roughly by hand.
Return the chicken with the tomato, cover and simmer 40 minutes without adding water: the tomato and onion give enough.
Add the pounded garlic, khmeli-suneli and chopped herbs only in the last five minutes, off the boil.

balyk-de-saumon.d: The back of a sockeye salmon salted then air-dried in the cold, sliced as thin as possible. Balyk uses only the dorsal part, the fattest and densest; the belly, too thin, is set aside and smoked separately under the name teysha.
s: Take the back of the salmon off in one piece, without the belly, and pull every bone with tweezers.
Mix the salt, sugar, cracked pepper and crumbled bay, and bury the fish in it, flesh to flesh if there are two pieces.
Cure 48 hours in the cold, turning morning and evening, and pouring off the brine each time.
Rinse, blot, then hang in cold moving air — between 2 and 6°C — for five to seven days, wrapped in muslin against flies.
It is ready when it has lost a third of its weight and the flesh is translucent and firm. Slice with a long knife, almost flat, and serve on buttered rye bread.

pelmeni-au-renne.d: Reindeer dumplings shaped by the hundred and frozen outdoors, in the Yakutian cold. Reindeer meat is so lean it would stay dry: marrow or pork fat is added, and the pelmeni keep all winter in a sack hung under the eaves.
s: Knead the flour, egg, iced water and salt for 15 minutes into a very firm dough, and rest it an hour wrapped.
Chop the meat and fat by knife, not in a processor, and add grated onion with its juice and two spoonfuls of iced water.
That water is the pelmen's juice: without it the reindeer cooks dry and the dumpling has no point.
Roll to 1 mm, cut 6 cm rounds, fill, fold into half-moons then join the two points into a ring.
Freeze them flat for an hour before cooking: they hold better. Poach 6 minutes in simmering broth until they rise, and serve with smetana.

omoul-fume-du-baikal.d: A whitefish found only in Lake Baikal, salted then hot-smoked over alder on the shore. Omul lives nowhere else and its fishing has been restricted since 2017; its flesh is so fatty that it needs no added fat to stay moist.
s: Gut the fish without scaling them and remove the gills, which would bring bitterness to the smoking.
Dry-salt them, rubbing inside and out, and leave them 12 hours in the cold under a light weight.
Rinse, then hang them to dry for 3 hours in the air: the skin must be dry to the touch, otherwise the smoke slides off without taking.
Lay dampened alder chips in the smoker and hold 80°C: this is hot smoking, the fish cooks as it takes the smoke.
Allow 2½ hours until the skin is golden brown and the flesh lifts from the bone. Eaten warm, with the fingers, and black bread.

chou-a-la-sakhaline.d: Chinese cabbage fermented with chilli, garlic and kelp, a Russian cousin of kimchi. The island was Japanese until 1945 and holds a deported Korean community: this cabbage was born of that meeting, and the kombu in it is the local addition.
s: Quarter the cabbages lengthwise, salt between every leaf and let them drain 4 hours, turning twice.
Rinse three times in clear water and press: just enough salt must remain for the leaf to fold without snapping.
Soak the kombu 30 minutes, then blend it with the garlic, ginger, sugar and fish sauce into a paste.
Mix that paste with the Korean chilli to a bright red purée, and coat every leaf, one by one, with a gloved hand.
Pack into a jar expelling the air, ferment 2 days at room temperature then move to the cold. It is eaten from a week on and keeps all winter.

pelmeni-de-sakhaline.d: Dumplings of crab, scallop and prawn, born in the canteens of the island's oil platforms. The filling is not minced: the flesh stays in recognisable pieces, and the dumpling poaches for less time than its meat cousin.
s: Knead the pelmeni dough as usual and rest it an hour: it must be firm and thin, the sea does not forgive thick pastry.
Cut the scallop and prawn by knife into half-centimetre pieces, and shred the crab by hand.
Blend nothing: a seafood filling reduced to a paste loses its texture and takes on a tinned taste.
Add the spring onion, grated ginger, a pinch of salt and nothing more — certainly no egg, which would mask everything.
Shape them and poach 4 minutes only in simmering salted water. Serve with melted butter and soy, and a few drops of sesame oil.

manty-siberiens.d: Large steamed dumplings of a hundred grams, filled with beef, onion and pumpkin. The pumpkin is no cheap filler: it melts and releases its sweet water as it cooks, feeding a lean meat that nothing else would moisten.
s: Knead a firm dough with warm water and rest it an hour: manty are folded a great deal and a brittle dough tears.
Cut the meat, fat and pumpkin by knife into 5 mm dice, and chop the onion very finely.
The proportion matters: as much onion as half the weight of meat, otherwise the filling stays dry.
Cut 12 cm squares, fill them and bring the four corners to the centre, then seal the four openings in pairs.
Oil the steamer trays — manty stick and tear otherwise — and steam 40 minutes. Serve with melted butter and smetana.

langue-de-renne-dolgane.d: Reindeer tongues poached with juniper berries, pressed and served cold in thin slices. The Dolgans, nomadic herders of Taymyr, keep them for honoured guests; the skin comes off in one piece while the tongue is scalding, and never afterwards.
s: Soak the tongues 6 hours in cold water, changing it twice, to draw out the blood.
Poach them 2½ hours with the onion, carrot, juniper, bay and pepper, at a bare tremble and never boiling.
They are ready when a needle passes through the base without resistance: the tip is always done first, the base decides.
Lift them out and peel them immediately, under cold running water — once cool the skin clings and must be cut away.
Press them 12 hours in the cold under a weighted board, then slice very thinly on the bias. Serve with horseradish smetana and black bread.

shangi.d: Open rye cakes topped with mashed potato and brushed with smetana. They are the ancestors of the vatrushka, baked in the Russian ovens of the far north: the topping is not set in a well but spread over the whole surface, right to the edge.
s: Knead both flours, the warm milk, yeast and salt: rye dough is sticky and heavy, and there is no point trying to make it elastic.
Prove it 1½ hours; it will not double — rye rises little, which is normal.
Make a firm mash, beaten with butter and an egg yolk but no milk: it must sit on the cake without running.
Flatten 12 cm discs, leave a one-centimetre rim and spread the mash over the whole surface.
Brush generously with smetana and bake 22 minutes at 220°C. Butter them as they come out, and stack them under a cloth to stay soft.
