tchoudou-daghestanais.d: A very thin flatbread filled with meat, nettles or pumpkin, cooked dry then buttered. Dagestan has fourteen official languages and as many chudu: every people has its own, and a family is known by the thickness it gives its dough.
s: Mix the kefir, bicarbonate and salt, wait for the foam, then add the flour and knead briefly.
Rest it 30 minutes: it is that rest, not the kneading, that makes the dough supple enough to stretch without tearing.
For the meat filling, mix the raw lamb with grated onion and two spoonfuls of water; for the green one, blanch the nettles thirty seconds and press them thoroughly dry.
Enclose the filling in a ball of dough, seal it, then roll very gently out to 28 cm — the filling should show faintly through.
Cook on a scalding dry griddle, 3 minutes a side, pricking the blisters. Butter generously on both sides and stack under a cloth.

pian-se.d: A large steamed Korean bun filled with spiced cabbage and pork, sold on the streets of Vladivostok. Primorye Koreans brought it in the 1920s; it is eaten standing in the cold, three hundred grams apiece, held in both hands for the warmth.
s: Knead a soft yeasted dough with the flour, warm water, yeast and sugar, and prove 1½ hours.
Salt the shredded cabbage and let it drain 40 minutes, then press it hard: its water is what would sog the bun.
Mix it with the raw pork, onion, garlic, Korean chilli, soy and sesame oil, and taste a fried patty before filling.
Flatten 100 g balls, fill generously and close by gathering the edges to the centre, seam firmly pinched underneath.
Prove 30 minutes on paper squares, then steam 25 minutes without once lifting the lid — a draught of cold air collapses the dough.

kovrizhka-de-siberie.d: A Siberian spice loaf of rye and taiga honey, rougher and denser than the pryanik. It kept six months in an unheated izba; taiga honey, gathered from the flowers of the vast boreal forest, is nearly black and faintly bitter.
s: Warm the honey with the water without going above 50°C, then let it cool: heated further, taiga honey loses what sets it apart.
Crush the juniper berries in a mortar with the cinnamon and cloves — the juniper is what gives a kovrizhka its resinous, Siberian taste.
Mix the flours, spices, salt and bicarbonate, then pour in the honey, oil and beaten eggs.
The batter is thick and sluggish: do not beat it to lighten it, a kovrizhka must stay dense.
Pour into a lined tin 4 cm deep, scatter walnuts and bake 45 minutes at 165°C. Wrap it warm and wait three days.

pastilla-de-fes.d: A pie of warqa leaves filled with pigeon, almonds and cinnamon, dusted with icing sugar. The sweet-savoury comes from al-Andalus, whose exiles peopled Fes in the 15th century: pastilla is the Andalusian dish that survived in Morocco after vanishing from Spain.
s: Braise the pigeons 1 hour with grated onion, saffron, ginger and herbs, then bone them and shred the meat.
Reduce the cooking juices until almost no liquid remains, then pour in the beaten eggs, stirring without pause.
The eggs must set into fine, dry curds: that layer absorbs the moisture and stops the warqa going soggy.
Fry the almonds, chop them roughly and mix them with the icing sugar and cinnamon.
Build three layers — eggs, meat, almonds — between buttered sheets, bake 30 minutes at 200°C and dust in a lattice as it comes out.

harira.d: A soup of tomato, lentils and chickpeas thickened with tadouira, a fermented flour-and-water starter. It is the fast-breaking soup of Ramadan; the tadouira is made the day before and must sour slightly, or the harira stays without depth.
s: Make the tadouira the day before: slake the flour in two glasses of water and ferment it covered at room temperature for 24 hours.
Fry the diced lamb with the onion, smen and spices, add the soaked chickpeas and cover with water; allow 1 hour.
Blend the tomato with the coriander and parsley and pour it in: never crushed, it must be liquid and smooth to bind with the tadouira.
Add the lentils and give them 30 minutes, then pour in the tadouira in a thin stream, whisking without pause.
Poured in at once it lumps beyond rescue. Thicken 20 minutes, add the vermicelli and serve with dates and lemon.

briouates.d: Small warqa triangles filled with minced meat or seafood, fried. They are folded like a flag, the strip turned over itself in successive triangles; the last flap is sealed with flour paste, never egg, which would blister in the oil.
s: Cook the filling until it releases nothing more, and cool it completely: a warm filling softens the warqa as you fold.
Cut the sheets into 8 cm strips and keep them under a damp cloth — warqa dries and cracks within three minutes in the air.
Set a spoonful at one end and fold into a triangle, then keep turning the triangle over itself to the end of the strip.
Seal the last flap with a paste of flour and water, not with egg.
Fry at 170°C, 2 minutes a side, six at a time. Drain upright: laid flat they go soft underneath.

zaalouk.d: A cooked salad of aubergine and tomato crushed with garlic, cumin and olive oil, served cold. It is one of the Moroccan salads set out in small bowls before the main dish; the aubergines are crushed with a fork and never blended, which makes them foamy.
s: Char the whole aubergines over a flame until the skin blackens and the flesh slumps.
That direct charring is what gives the smoky taste: boiled or oven-baked, aubergines have no character at all.
Peel them and let them drain half an hour in a colander — their bitter water would wash out the whole dish.
Cook the grated tomato down with the garlic for 25 minutes, until only a brick-red paste remains.
Crush the aubergines into the tomato with a fork, add the spices and oil, and cool. Eaten cold, preferably the next day.

msemen.d: A square layered pancake, hand-stretched then folded with semolina and butter, cooked on a griddle. The layers come not from turning but from stretching: the dough is pulled until transparent, which is only possible with a heavily oiled dough.
s: Knead the flour, fine semolina, warm water and salt for fifteen minutes: the dough must become very supple, almost pourable.
Divide into balls, oil them generously and rest them 30 minutes under the oil — it is what will allow the stretching.
Spread each ball flat on an oiled surface, pulling from the centre outward, until you can see your hand through it.
Scatter melted butter and semolina, then fold in three one way and three the other to make a square of nine layers.
Flatten slightly and cook on a dry griddle 3 minutes a side, pressing with a spatula. Serve with honey and butter.

the-a-la-menthe.d: Gunpowder green tea infused with mint and heavily sweetened, poured from a height into small glasses. The height is no flourish: it aerates the tea, raises the expected foam and cools the liquid enough for the glass to be held.
s: Scald the tea once and throw the water away after thirty seconds: that rinse removes the bitterness and dust from the rolled leaves.
Keep that first liquor in a separate glass — Moroccans set it aside and return it at the end, as it holds the essence of the tea.
Pour boiling water over the rinsed leaves and infuse three minutes only, without mint: the tea infuses alone.
Then add the whole mint, stems and all, and the sugar, and give it two minutes more — boiled mint turns bitter.
Pour back and forth three times between pot and glass to mix, then serve holding the pot fifty centimetres up.

chorba-frik.d: A lamb soup with cracked green wheat, tomato and coriander, served every evening of Ramadan. Frik is durum wheat harvested green then burned over straw: that scorching gives it a smoky taste ripe wheat lacks, and it thickens without disintegrating.
s: Fry the small-diced lamb in smen with grated onion and cinnamon for ten minutes, without deep colour.
Add the tomato purée and grated tomato and let them cook down fifteen minutes before adding liquid: what Algerian cooks call sweating the sauce.
Moisten with hot water, add the soaked chickpeas and cook 45 minutes.
Rinse the freekeh in plenty of water and rub it between your hands: it carries a dust of burnt chaff that would make the soup harsh.
Add it for 25 minutes only, stirring often as it catches. Finish with coriander, mint and a squeeze of lemon.

rechta.d: Fresh noodles steamed and served in a white chicken broth with turnips and chickpeas. It is the dish of great occasions in Algiers and Tlemcen; the broth is deliberately pale, with no tomato and no chilli, and cinnamon takes the place of paprika.
s: Knead a firm dough, rest it an hour, then roll it very thin and roll up the sheet before cutting one-millimetre noodles.
Separate them by hand with flour, then oil them lightly and steam them three times for fifteen minutes.
Between each steaming, take them out, sprinkle with salted water and separate them with a fork — without those three cookings they stick in a block.
Make the broth with the chicken, onion, cinnamon and smen, with no tomato: rechta is known by its pale colour.
Add turnips, courgettes and chickpeas for the last half hour. Serve the noodles in a mound, the broth poured over at the table.

mhadjeb.d: A semolina pancake stretched until transparent, filled with a tomato and onion compote and folded into a square. It is Algerian street food par excellence; the stretching is done flat on an oiled table, and the dough must be so thin it tears at the least jerk.
s: Knead the fine semolina and warm salted water for twenty minutes: it is long, but semolina becomes extensible only at that price.
Oil the balls and rest them an hour under oil, never under a cloth — the oil prevents a skin and allows the stretching.
Cook the onion and tomato down for 40 minutes to a thick paste, and cool it completely.
Stretch each ball flat on the oiled table, from centre to edge, until you can see the wood through it.
Set the filling in the centre, fold the four sides into a square and cook on a dry griddle 4 minutes a side, pressing down.

mtewem.d: Garlic lamb meatballs simmered in a white sauce, with two whole heads of garlic in the pot. Mtewem means with garlic: half goes into the meatballs, half into the sauce, and it is a dish served only to people one knows well.
s: Pound a whole head of garlic with salt in a mortar to a cream — chopped by knife it would stay in hard pieces inside the meatball.
Mix it with the minced lamb, eggs, breadcrumbs, cinnamon and parsley, and rest an hour in the cold.
Fry the meat pieces with grated onion and smen, add the second head of garlic in whole cloves and the chickpeas.
Moisten to cover and simmer 45 minutes before lowering the meatballs in, one by one and without stirring.
They cook 25 minutes and must never boil hard: agitated, they fall apart. The sauce stays white, with not a trace of tomato.

kalbelouz.d: A semolina and almond cake drowned in orange blossom syrup, served during Ramadan. The name means heart of almond: the semolina is not worked but left to rest, and cold syrup is poured over a scalding cake — the reverse does not work.
s: Mix the coarse semolina, melted butter, a little sugar and orange blossom water with your fingertips, without kneading.
Rest it 2 hours: the semolina must swell of its own accord, and a worked dough gives a rubbery cake.
Press half into a dish, spread the almonds blended with sugar, cover with the rest and cut the diamonds before baking.
Bake 45 minutes at 180°C, then pour cold syrup over the scalding cake as it leaves the oven.
Hot syrup on a hot cake stays on the surface: it is the difference in temperature that drives it in. Wait six hours before serving.

makroud.d: Semolina diamonds filled with date paste, fried then dipped in honey. Kairouan made them its speciality and sells them by weight on the Great Mosque square; the dough holds no water but only olive oil, which makes it short rather than elastic.
s: Rub the semolina and warm olive oil between your hands for ten minutes, until every grain is coated, and rest it an hour.
Add water only at the very end, and as little as possible: an over-hydrated dough turns elastic and the makroud hardens.
Stone the dates, blend them with the cinnamon, zest and orange blossom water to a supple paste.
Form a rope of dough, hollow it into a channel, fill with dates and close it, then flatten and cut diamonds.
Fry at 170°C until golden, drain, then plunge them scalding into warm honey for three minutes. Drain on a rack.

ojja-merguez.d: Eggs poached in a harissa tomato sauce with merguez, served in the cooking pan. It is eaten with a spoon and bread, straight from the pan; the eggs are not beaten but broken in whole, and the yolk must stay runny.
s: Char the green peppers over a flame, peel them and cut them into strips: raw, they would stay crunchy and unbalance the sauce.
Fry the merguez, lift them out and keep the red fat — it, not the tomato purée, is what colours the sauce.
Slake the harissa and purée in that fat and fry them for a minute before adding the grated tomato.
Reduce for 20 minutes until the oil rises to the surface: the sign the sauce is ready, exactly as for a tagine.
Make wells, break the eggs into them, cover and give them three minutes only. Serve in the pan, with bread and nothing else.

kamounia.d: A stew of liver or beef dominated by cumin, cooked long into an almost black sauce. The name comes from kamoun, cumin: three spoonfuls go in, which seems excessive until you understand that long cooking removes its bitterness.
s: Sear the diced meat in olive oil until frankly brown, in small batches.
Pound the garlic with the cumin and salt in a mortar: ground dry, cumin does not release its oils and stays dusty.
Fry that paste for thirty seconds in the hot oil before adding the purée and harissa — that brief pass removes the raw taste.
Moisten to cover and simmer 2 hours covered, until the sauce darkens and thickens.
Add the diced liver in the last ten minutes only: cooked longer it turns grainy and bitter.

tajine-tunisien.d: A thick baked omelette bound with cheese and eggs, cut into squares like a frittata. Here the word does not mean the Moroccan earthenware dish but its exact opposite: the Tunisian tajine is oven-baked, eaten cold, and cut with a knife.
s: Cook the chicken with the onion and turmeric until not a drop of liquid remains, then shred it.
Any residual moisture makes the tajine collapse and stops it cutting cleanly: the only real difficulty.
Fry the diced potato separately, until tender and golden.
Beat the eggs, add the grated cheese, breadcrumbs, parsley and harissa, then all the cooled fillings.
Pour into an oiled dish 4 cm deep and bake 40 minutes at 180°C. Cool completely before cutting into squares.

bambalouni.d: A ring doughnut fried and rolled in sugar, sold scalding as it leaves the oil. It is eaten standing at the stall: it exists only at that moment, and a ten-minute-old bambalouni has nothing left of what you came for.
s: Dissolve the yeast in warm water and let it foam, then beat it into the flour and salt — no sugar in the dough, only on it.
The dough must be very soft and sticky, nearly liquid: it is worked with a wetted hand, never a floured one.
Beat it hard for ten minutes, lifting it and letting it fall back, then prove 1½ hours.
Take a handful, pierce it with a finger and stretch the ring by hand directly over the oil — a bambalouni is never shaped in advance.
Fry at 180°C, one minute a side, and roll in sugar immediately. Eaten within three minutes.

mrouzia.d: A lamb tagine with honey, raisins and ras el hanout, deeply sweet and long confited. It is made for Eid, when the sacrificial meat must keep without refrigeration: honey and salt turn it into a savoury preserve that lasts weeks.
s: Rub the lamb with ras el hanout, saffron and salt twelve hours ahead — the mixture must penetrate before any cooking.
Fry it in smen with the grated onion, then moisten to cover and simmer 2 hours covered.
Plump the raisins separately and add the honey only in the last half hour: poured in at the start it would burn on the base.
Uncover and reduce until the sauce becomes a thick syrup that coats the meat and shines.
Fry the almonds separately and scatter them as you serve, with toasted sesame seeds.

shorba-libyenne.d: A lamb soup with tomato and orzo pasta, heavily scented with dried mint. The mint is crushed between the palms over the pot just before serving: added during cooking it loses everything and the soup becomes an ordinary tomato soup.
s: Fry the small-diced lamb with the onion and dry spices for ten minutes, before the tomato goes in.
Add the tomato purée and fry it for a minute: that frying removes the metallic acidity no sugar would later correct.
Moisten with hot water, add the chickpeas and cook 1 hour at a bare simmer.
Add the orzo for the last twelve minutes only — any earlier and it drinks the broth and the soup becomes a porridge.
Crush the dried mint between your palms over the pot, off the heat, and serve with plenty of lemon.

asida-libyenne.d: A cooked flour paste mounded into a dome and hollowed into a well of honey and melted butter. It is made for the birth of a child and for the Mawlid; it is eaten by hand, pinching a piece from the edge of the dome and dipping it in the well.
s: Bring salted water to the boil and tip the flour into the centre all at once, without stirring, then leave it three minutes.
That wait without stirring is the Libyan method: the flour hydrates by itself and forms fewer lumps than any whisking.
Then work it with a wooden spoon for twenty minutes, pressing against the sides: the paste must turn smooth, elastic and come away.
It is ready when it forms a block that follows the spoon out of the pan without sticking.
Mound it on a dish, hollow a wide well in the centre with your fist and fill it with warm honey and melted butter.

mbatan.d: Two slices of potato enclosing a spiced meat filling, crumbed and fried. The potato is cut like a wallet, without going through: it needs a thin blade and a steady hand, and a slice cut all the way through spills its filling into the oil.
s: Cut the potatoes into 1 cm slices, then split each slice through its thickness keeping one side attached.
Blanch them three minutes in salted water and cool them: raw, they would not cook through during frying.
Cook the filling until dry, then cool it completely — warm, it would make the coating slide off.
Fill each wallet without overloading, close it and press with the flat of your hand to seal.
Flour, egg then crumb, and fry at 175°C, 4 minutes a side. Serve with harissa and lemon.

ghoriba-libyenne.d: A cracked shortbread biscuit, with almonds or semolina, so short it dissolves without chewing. The cracks are not decorative: they appear by themselves when the fat is in the right proportion, and a smooth top signals an over-hydrated dough.
s: Mix the ground almonds, icing sugar and oil by hand, without whisking: a ghoriba is worked with the fingertips.
Add one egg, the orange blossom water, then the flour and baking powder, and stop the moment the dough comes together.
Rest it an hour in the cold: without rest the oil weeps out during baking and the biscuits spread.
Shape balls and roll them in a thick layer of icing sugar — it is that sugar that cracks, not the dough itself.
Press an almond into the centre and bake 18 minutes at 160°C. They must stay pale: browned, they are dry.

mhalbiya.d: A rice-flour milk cream scented with rose water, served cold and scattered with pistachios. It holds neither egg nor gelatine: rice starch alone sets it, which demands slow cooking and constant stirring so it does not catch.
s: Slake the rice flour and cornstarch in a quarter of the cold milk until not a lump remains, then strain.
Bring the rest of the milk to a tremble with the sugar and pour in the cold mixture, whisking without pause.
Stir without stopping for twenty minutes over low heat: rice flour catches instantly and a burnt note carries through the whole dish.
The cream is ready when it coats the spoon and a furrow drawn with a finger holds for three seconds.
Add the rose water off the heat — heated, it evaporates and leaves nothing. Pour into cups and set 4 hours in the cold.

ruz-mufalfal.d: A spiced rice in which every grain stays separate, served with lamb and pine nuts. Mufalfal means peppered, but really names the texture: the rice must be grain by grain, achieved by rinsing it seven times and pearling it in fat before any liquid.
s: Rinse the rice seven times until the water runs perfectly clear, then soak it 30 minutes and drain it for an hour.
Fry the diced lamb with the onion and whole spices in smen, then moisten and cook 45 minutes.
Pearl the drained rice in the fat for two minutes before any liquid: that coating isolates each grain and stops it sticking.
Pour in broth at exactly one and a half volumes to one of rice, bring to the boil, cover and drop to the lowest heat.
Twelve minutes, then ten minutes off the heat without uncovering. Fluff with a fork and crown with fried pine nuts and almonds.

tamiya.d: The Egyptian falafel, made from dried broad beans rather than chickpeas, green inside and coated in sesame. Broad beans give a far lighter, moister texture than chickpeas; Egypt claims the older version, and Copts were making it during Lent.
s: Soak the skinned broad beans 12 hours and on no account cook them: falafel is made with raw pulses, and cooked beans give a mush that falls apart in the oil.
Mince them with the herbs and garlic twice, keeping some grain — a blender would reduce them to a smooth, dense paste.
Salt and add the bicarbonate only as you fry: added earlier, it makes the mixture weep.
Shape flat 5 cm patties and press one face into the sesame, not both.
Fry at 175°C, three minutes a side. The inside must stay bright green and moist; a brown centre means the mixture waited too long.

mahshi.d: Hollowed vegetables and vine leaves stuffed with herbed rice, packed tight in a pot. The rice goes in raw and swells by half: which is why they are never filled more than two-thirds, and an overfilled mahshi bursts and empties into the broth.
s: Hollow the courgettes and aubergines with a corer leaving five millimetres of wall: any thinner and the vegetable collapses.
Rinse the rice and mix it raw with grated tomato, onion, chopped herbs and melted smen, without cooking it.
Fill only two-thirds and press barely — the rice must have room to swell.
Line the base of the pot with tomato slices and pack the vegetables upright and tight, so they hold each other up.
Set a plate on top to keep them down, add liquid to half their height and simmer 1¼ hours without ever stirring. Lemon on serving.

fattah.d: Layers of fried bread, rice and meat doused with a garlic and vinegar broth. It is the dish of Eid al-Adha, made with the sacrificial meat; the stale bread at the bottom must stay crisp in places and soaked in others, and that contrast is the point.
s: Poach the lamb 2 hours with the onion, cardamom and bay, skimming, and keep the broth.
Cut the stale bread into squares and fry or toast them until brown and hard: soft bread would turn to paste.
Make a rice with vermicelli toasted in smen, moistened with the lamb broth.
Make the sauce by frying pounded garlic in smen until golden, then add the vinegar and tomato purée, and take it off the heat at once.
Build: bread at the bottom, broth poured over, rice, meat, then the garlic sauce. Serve immediately, before all the bread has softened.

rozz-bil-laban.d: A very creamy rice pudding, browned in the oven until a skin forms. The rice is first cooked in water then long in milk: cooked straight in milk it would stay hard at the centre, because milk sugars and calcium toughen the starch.
s: First cook the rice in water for 15 minutes, until tender but whole, and drain it.
Add the hot milk and cook 40 minutes over very low heat, stirring every five minutes.
Sweeten only halfway through: sugar added too early stops the starch swelling and the rice stays firm.
Thicken with cornstarch slaked in a little cold milk, add the cream and vanilla, and scent with rose water off the heat.
Pour into a dish and give it five minutes under the grill to form the brown skin. Eaten warm or cold, never scalding.

umm-ali.d: A gratin of crumbled puff pastry, milk, nuts and raisins, browned in the oven. Legend attributes it to Shajar al-Durr, a 13th-century sultana, who is said to have had it distributed to celebrate a rival's death; the story is doubtful, the pudding is not.
s: Bake the puff pastry flat until deeply golden and dry, then cool it and crumble it by hand.
Pale or soft pastry would turn to glue: it must be frankly baked before it meets the milk.
Heat the milk with the sugar and vanilla without boiling, and plump the raisins in it for ten minutes.
Mix the crumbled pastry with the chopped nuts in a dish, pour the hot milk over and let it absorb for five minutes.
Cover with unsweetened whipped cream and give it 25 minutes at 200°C, until the top is brown and blistered. Serve scalding.

mhadjeb-au-fromage.d: The melted cheese version of the Constantine mhadjeb, more recent and now the biggest street seller. The cheese replaces the tomato compote but brings a new constraint: it melts and tries to escape, which means sealing all four sides with a firm pinch.
s: Knead the fine semolina and warm salted water for twenty minutes, until the dough turns smooth and very supple.
Divide into balls, cover them with oil and rest an hour: without that immersion the stretching is impossible.
Melt the onion for 30 minutes with the paprika and harissa, cool it, then mix it with the diced cheese.
Stretch the dough flat on an oiled table until transparent, fill the centre and fold the four sides in, pinching each seam.
Cook on a dry griddle 4 minutes a side, pressing down: the cheese must melt entirely without ever escaping.

or-lam.d: A buffalo and vegetable stew with sakhan wood, which numbs the tongue like Sichuan pepper. A stick of sakhan goes into the pot and comes back out: it is not eaten, it flavours.
s: Grill the meat over coals before it goes in the pot: that smoke is what separates or lam from an ordinary stew.
Bruise the sakhan wood with a mallet to release its sap, and drop it into a litre of boiling water.
Add the meat, bruised lemongrass and shallot, and simmer for 1 hour.
Take the sakhan out before it dominates everything, then add the aubergines and long beans.
Finish with the wood ear mushrooms, dill and chilli. Serve with sticky rice, eaten by hand.

amok-trey.d: A fish mousse with kroeung paste and coconut milk, steamed in a banana leaf cup. It must set like a custard: if it stays runny, either the egg or the patience was short.
s: Pound lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, kaffir lime leaves, shallot, garlic and shrimp paste in a mortar: this is kroeung, and it takes twenty minutes of arm work.
Slice the fish thinly and work it with the kroeung in a bowl, always stirring the same way.
Add the coconut milk a spoonful at a time, then the beaten eggs: the mixture should thicken and turn silky.
Make cups from banana leaf softened over a flame, pinned at the corners.
Line them with noni leaves, fill and steam gently for 25 minutes. Decorate with coconut cream and pepper.

banh-xeo.d: A crisp turmeric rice pancake filled with prawns and bean sprouts. The name imitates the sound of batter hitting the scorching pan: xèo, the sizzle, is the only measure of the right heat.
s: Mix the rice flour, coconut milk, turmeric, water and spring onion, and rest for 2 hours.
The batter must be as thin as milk: any thicker and the pancake goes soft instead of crisp.
Steam the mung beans and fry the sliced pork with the prawns.
Heat a pan until a drop of water dances on it, oil it and pour in a thin ladleful, swirling.
Fill one half, cover for 2 minutes, then uncover so the edge crisps. Fold, and eat rolled in a lettuce leaf, dipped in nuoc cham.

gudeg.d: Green jackfruit stewed five hours in coconut milk and palm sugar, with teak leaves that stain it mahogany. Yogyakarta calls itself the gudeg city; it is eaten at breakfast as at dinner.
s: Boil the green jackfruit for 20 minutes and discard that water: it removes the latex.
Pound the shallot, garlic, candlenuts, coriander and galangal into a fine paste.
Line the base of the pot with teak leaves — they give the colour, without which gudeg stays pale.
Pack in the jackfruit, hard-boiled eggs and chicken, and pour over the paste, coconut milk and palm sugar.
Simmer for 5 hours over very low heat without stirring, until almost dry. Serve with rice and cracklings.

ayam-betutu.d: A whole chicken stuffed with spice paste, wrapped in banana bark and cooked four hours under embers. Betutu is ordered a day ahead in the warungs of Gianyar: nobody makes it to order.
s: Pound all the aromatics into a thick paste — the Balinese base genep — and fry it in oil for 20 minutes.
Rub the chicken inside and out, working under the skin, and marinate for 6 hours.
Stuff it with blanched cassava leaves mixed with a third of the paste, and sew the opening.
Wrap it in several thicknesses of flame-softened banana leaf, and tie it firmly.
Bury under embers or cook for 4 hours at 150°C: the flesh should leave the bone by itself.

nasi-kandar.d: Plain rice drowned under several curries poured together in one ladle. Kandar was the pole of the Tamil hawkers who sold this rice door to door; the mixing of sauces is called banjir, the flood.
s: Cook the rice plain, without spices: it is the white canvas on which everything will mix.
Make a chicken curry with coconut milk, spiced with cinnamon sticks and star anise.
Make a second curry, of okra and aubergine with tamarind, sharper and thinner.
Fry hard-boiled eggs until the skins crack, and keep a fish curry alongside.
Serve the rice and pour the sauces one over another: the banjir is not an accident, it is the point.

kaeng-som.d: A sour yellow curry, without coconut milk, of a strength northern Thailand considers unreasonable. Tamarind and turmeric give it body; the chilli is present in quantities that startle even regulars.
s: Poach a piece of the fish and pound it in a mortar with the chillies, shallot, fresh turmeric and shrimp paste.
This fish-based paste is the southern signature: it gives the broth a body the central curry lacks.
Slake it in a litre of boiling water and simmer for 10 minutes.
Season with tamarind, fish sauce and palm sugar: the first taste should be frankly sour.
Add the vegetables in order of firmness, then the fish and prawns for 5 minutes only.

sinigang-na-baboy.d: A pork soup soured with green tamarind, with vegetables and kangkong leaves. The sourness may come from tamarind, guava or green mango: each family defends its acid and scorns the others.
s: Blanch the ribs for 10 minutes and discard that water: the broth must stay clear.
Return them to two litres of water with the onion and tomato, and simmer for 1 hour, skimming.
Add the diced taro: it breaks down and thickens the broth naturally, which is the point.
Stir in the tamarind and taste: the soup should make you salivate, without catching the throat.
Add the vegetables in order of firmness, the water spinach last of all, and serve with rice and fish sauce.

la-paz-batchoy.d: A noodle soup in a bone and offal broth, crowned with crushed chicharrón. La Paz market claims its invention in the 1930s; the broth there simmers from opening to closing.
s: Make a broth from pork and beef bones, 3 hours at a simmer, skimming relentlessly.
Soak the kidney for 2 hours in vinegared water, then poach it and slice it thinly.
Do the same with the liver, poaching it barely: overcooked it turns grainy.
Season the broth with a spoonful of shrimp paste and soy sauce, without making it salty.
Assemble the noodles, offal, pork and a poached egg, and crown with fried garlic and crushed chicharrón at the last moment.

bun-cha-ca.d: A clear fish broth with cakes of pounded flesh, fried then poached. The fish is pounded until springy: it is that bounce under the tooth, not the taste, that judges the cake.
s: Fillet the fish, skin it and pound the flesh in a mortar with garlic, sugar, fish sauce and plenty of pepper.
Pound for 15 minutes: the paste should turn sticky and bounce when thrown against the side.
Fold in chopped dill and spring onion, shape flat cakes and fry them 3 minutes a side.
Make a clear broth from the heads and bones with pineapple and tomato, and strain it carefully.
Poach the cakes for 5 minutes in that broth and serve over vermicelli, with sprouts, herbs and lime.

lu-rou-fan.d: Fatty minced pork stewed in soy sauce and rice wine, spooned over white rice. Taiwan calls it the national dish; north and south argue over the size of the dice, to the millimetre.
s: Cut the belly by knife into 5 mm dice, fat included: the fat makes the texture, and removing it makes another dish.
Fry the sliced shallots in oil to a deep gold, then lift them out and keep the oil.
Render the pork dry in a wok until it colours and the fat runs.
Add the garlic, fried shallots, both soy sauces, rice wine, rock sugar and spices.
Cover with water and simmer uncovered for 1¼ hours: the sauce should turn syrupy and coat every dice.

o-a-tsian.d: An omelette bound with sweet potato starch, translucent and elastic, with small oysters. The starch is what matters: without it, it is merely an oyster omelette, and the night markets would not forgive.
s: Slake the sweet potato starch in twice its volume of cold water and let it stand: it should stay thin and milky.
Make the sauce by thickening ketchup, miso, sugar and a little water with the cornstarch.
Heat the wok fiercely, oil it, and toss the oysters for 30 seconds.
Pour the starch batter over them: it turns translucent and gelatinous at once. Do not stir.
Break the eggs over the top, add the greens, flip in one movement and serve under the red sauce.

thenthuk.d: A soup of dough torn by hand straight into the broth, with mutton and vegetables. Then means to pull, thuk soup: the pieces are irregular on principle, and a rolling pin would miss the point.
s: Knead the flour, water and salt into a firm dough, and rest it for an hour under a damp cloth.
Fry the diced mutton with the onion, garlic, ginger and tomato, then add two litres of water.
Simmer for 40 minutes, then add the daikon and carrot.
Roll the dough into 3 cm strips, oil them, then stretch and tear pieces straight over the simmering broth.
They rise within 3 minutes when cooked. Add the spinach and herbs, and serve scalding.

biryani-sindhi.d: A biryani with potatoes, prunes and yogurt, sharper and hotter than its cousins. Sindh adds dried plum: that sweet-sour counterpoint surprises, then quickly becomes indispensable.
s: Fry the sliced onions to a deep brown and set half aside: they perfume and colour.
Marinate the chicken for 3 hours in the yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, masala and half the fried onions.
Cook the marinade for 30 minutes with the tomato and potatoes, until the oil separates.
Par-boil the soaked rice for 6 minutes in salted water with whole spices, and drain it three-quarters cooked.
Layer meat, prunes, rice, herbs, fried onions and saffron; seal and leave 25 minutes over very low heat.

kuku-sabzi.d: An omelette so green with herbs that the egg barely shows, served at Nowruz. Green is the colour of renewal: eaten on the first day of spring so the year will be fertile.
s: Wash the herbs, spin them thoroughly dry and chop them very finely: you need an enormous volume, nearly two packed litres.
Blot them in a cloth: the least moisture would leave the kuku soft in the middle.
Beat the eggs without aerating them, add the flour, baking powder, turmeric and salt.
Fold in the herbs, crushed walnuts and barberries: the mixture should be more green than yellow.
Pour into a buttered pan and cook covered for 20 minutes over low heat, then flip for 15 more. Serve warm with yogurt.

khash.d: A cow's-foot broth cooked all night and eaten at dawn with raw garlic and lavash. Served from December to March, before sunrise, and custom requires vodka with it, never wine.
s: Soak the trotters for 24 hours under cold running water, changing it six times: this removes the smell.
Scrape them thoroughly and blanch them for 15 minutes; discard that water.
Return them to a large pot of clean water, without salt, vegetable or any spice.
Simmer for 7 to 8 hours, skimming: the broth should turn milky and set to a jelly when cold.
Serve scalding and unsalted. Each diner adds salt, pounded garlic and crumbled lavash to their own bowl.

shah-plov.d: Saffron rice and lamb sealed in a crown of lavash bread, baked golden like a crown. It comes whole to the table and is opened in front of the guests: the crisp bread is half the dish.
s: Rinse the rice seven times and soak it for 2 hours in salted water: this gives long, separate grains.
Par-boil it for 6 minutes in plenty of water and drain it half cooked.
Fry the diced lamb with the onion, apricots, chestnuts and raisins for 30 minutes.
Line a buttered pot with lavash brushed with ghee and egg yolk, leaving the edges hanging well over.
Fill with layers of rice and meat, fold the bread over, and bake for 50 minutes at 180°C. Turn out in one movement and cut like a cake.

soup-curry-sapporo.d: A thin, spiced curry in which a chicken leg and whole vegetables sit, with rice served separately. Invented in Sapporo in the 1970s, it is the exact opposite of thick Japanese curry: the broth is spooned, and the vegetables stand proud of the bowl.
s: Confit the very finely sliced onion for 40 minutes over low heat, until brown and melting: it is the base of the broth.
Add the grated garlic and ginger, then the spices off the heat — thrown into hot oil they burn in three seconds.
Add the grated tomato, reduce, then moisten with the broth and simmer 40 minutes.
On no account thicken it: a soup curry must stay as thin as consommé, and the least flour would make it an ordinary curry.
Fry the vegetables whole and separately so they hold their shape, and stand them up in the bowl with the leg. Rice on the side.

ishikari-nabe.d: A pot of salmon and vegetables in miso, simmered at the table over a burner. It comes from the mouth of the Ishikari, where fishermen cooked the unsellable trimmings; head and skin go in, for the gelatine, rather than the handsome fillets.
s: Soak the kombu an hour in cold water and lift it out as soon as the water trembles: boiled, it turns slimy and bitter.
Blanch the salmon pieces for ten seconds then rinse them cold — this removes scum and odour, and clears the broth.
Stand the vegetables upright in the pot, the slowest to cook at the bottom, and set the salmon on top.
Slake the miso in a ladle of hot broth before stirring it in, and never let it boil: above 80°C it loses its scent.
Finish with a knob of butter, the Hokkaidō signature, and set the pot in the middle of the table over its burner.

kaisendon.d: A bowl of vinegared rice covered with raw fish, sea urchin and salmon roe. It is eaten at the harbour market from seven in the morning; unlike sushi the fish is not worked but simply sliced, which demands a freshness only a port allows.
s: Season the still-warm rice with sweetened vinegar, cutting it in with a spatula and never stirring, and fan it to make it shine.
Let it cool to body temperature: ice-cold rice numbs the fish, scalding rice cooks it.
Slice each fish according to its grain: tuna across the fibres, salmon on the bias and thinner, scallop split through its thickness.
Wipe the blade between each fish so as not to carry the taste of one onto another.
Arrange without overlapping, leaving the rice visible in places, and set the sea urchin and roe last — they crush under anything else.

gyutan-sendai.d: Slices of beef tongue salted then charcoal-grilled, served with barley rice and oxtail soup. A Sendai cook put them on his menu in 1948: the occupying Americans ate neither tongue nor tail, and he took both.
s: Peel the tongue raw by slitting it with a point: at this stage the skin comes away with a knife, whereas after cooking it must be torn.
Cut it into 6 mm slices across, and score each slice in a shallow lattice on both sides.
Those cuts are not decorative: they stop the slice curling into a ball over the coals.
Dry-salt it and rest 48 hours in the cold: that long cure tenderises the tongue, which is a very firm muscle.
Grill over fierce coals 90 seconds a side, no longer. Serve with barley rice, oxtail soup and lemon.

wanko-soba.d: Tiny portions of buckwheat noodles served in small bowls that a server refills without pause. You stop only by closing the lid, and custom demands you count: fifteen bowls make one normal portion, and regulars pass a hundred.
s: Knead the buckwheat and wheat flours with warm water, working fast: buckwheat dough dries and cracks within minutes.
It has almost no gluten and is not kneaded like bread dough: you press it together, never stretching it.
Roll to 1.5 mm, fold the sheet like a concertina and cut noodles the same width as their thickness.
Cook them 90 seconds only in plenty of boiling water, then rinse in iced water to stop the cooking and wash off the starch.
Serve in small handfuls in a dashi and soy broth, with the garnishes apart. The bowls are refilled the moment they are empty.

kiritanpo.d: Rice mashed and moulded around a cedar stick, grilled then simmered in chicken broth. Akita woodsmen carried their rice into the forest this way and grilled it over the fire; the name comes from the shape, like a cut spear-tip wrapping.
s: Cook the rice wetter than usual, then pound it until half the grains are broken — not all, or it becomes a paste.
Mould it while still hot around wooden sticks in a one-centimetre layer, wetting your hands in salted water.
Grill over coals, turning, until the surface is golden and dry: that crust is what will stop the rice falling apart in the broth.
Twist out the sticks, cut into 5 cm lengths and add them to the broth for the last five minutes only.
Beyond that they collapse. Serve with the chicken, burdock shaved into slivers and maitake mushrooms.

ika-no-shiokara.d: Strips of raw squid fermented in their own salted viscera, eaten on the tips of chopsticks with sake. The fermentation is driven by enzymes from the squid's liver: a preservation method from before refrigeration, and the taste is powerfully briny.
s: Gut the squid keeping the brown-orange liver sac intact: it drives the fermentation, and a burst sac ruins the dish.
Salt the liver alone and let it drain 24 hours in the cold, then sieve it to keep only the cream.
Skin the bodies, cut them into 5 mm strips and salt them separately for two hours, then blot them.
Mix liver and squid with the sake and mirin, and ferment three to seven days at 8°C, stirring daily.
The mixture must smell of the sea and not of ammonia: at the least sharp odour it must be thrown away. Serve very cold, in very small quantities.

tempura.d: Prawns and vegetables in a barely mixed batter, fried to a pale, lacy crust. The Portuguese brought it in the 16th century with their ember-days fritters — tempora — but the Japanese made it the opposite of a coating: the batter must be nearly invisible.
s: Score the belly of the prawns in three places and stretch them: without this they curl into rings in the oil.
Beat the egg into iced water with ice cubes, then tip in the flour all at once and mix barely, eight or ten strokes with chopsticks.
The batter must stay lumpy and full of dry flour: overmixed, it develops gluten and gives a thick, soft crust.
Keep the bowl on a bed of ice throughout the frying — a batter that warms loses its lightness within two minutes.
Fry at 180°C, two or three pieces at a time. Serve with a dashi and soy broth and grated daikon.

monjayaki.d: A very thin batter cooked on the griddle until sticky, scraped up with small spatulas straight off the iron. Unlike okonomiyaki it never sets: it stays semi-liquid and is eaten in small amounts, scalding, directly from the plate.
s: Whisk the flour into cold dashi to a liquid barely thicker than water: that is the whole difference from okonomiyaki.
Strain it: a single lump stays hard in the middle of a batter that itself will never set.
First fry the shredded cabbage and the fillings on the oiled griddle, then gather them into a ring with a hole in the centre.
Pour the liquid into the hole and let it bubble for a minute before breaking the dam and mixing everything.
Scrape and press constantly with two small spatulas for five minutes, until the batter catches. Eat straight off the griddle, in small scrapes.

chanko-nabe.d: The sumo wrestlers' pot, loaded with chicken, meatballs, tofu and vegetables. Chicken goes in rather than beef for a superstitious reason: a chicken stands on two legs, like a wrestler on his feet, whereas a four-legged animal touches the ground with its hands.
s: Make a broth from chicken carcass and dashi, and skim it relentlessly for the first fifteen minutes.
Shape minced chicken balls with grated ginger and a little miso, and poach them first: they scent the whole broth.
Arrange the ingredients in sectors rather than mixed: each cooks at its own pace and is lifted out when ready.
Add the cabbage last, packing it down: it releases a great deal of water and would thin the broth if added at the start.
Eat as you go, adding more ingredients to the broth as it concentrates. Finish with udon noodles in what remains.

miso-katsu.d: A breaded pork cutlet under a thick sauce of Nagoya red miso. Hatchō miso, fermented two years in barrels under stacked stones, is almost black and far saltier than white miso: it is used sparingly, cut with sugar and dashi.
s: Score the fat of the cutlet every two centimetres so it does not curl, and flatten it slightly.
Coat in flour, egg then panko, pressing barely: the panko must stay in standing flakes, not crushed.
Fry 6 minutes at 170°C, low and long — breaded pork over fierce heat browns before the centre cooks.
Make the sauce by slaking red miso in hot dashi with the sugar, mirin and sake, and reduce for 10 minutes.
It must coat the spoon and stay glossy: over-reduced it turns bitter. Pour it at the last moment, over a sliced katsu.

hoto-nabe.d: Wide flat noodles simmered directly in a miso and pumpkin soup, never boiled separately. That is exactly what sets it apart from udon: the noodle starch thickens the broth, and rinsing them first would ruin the dish.
s: Knead the flour and salted water for 10 minutes into a firm dough and rest it 30 minutes under a cloth.
Roll it to 3 mm and cut strips a centimetre and a half wide: hōtō is far wider and thicker than udon.
On no account rinse them or precook them: their flour is what will thicken the soup, and that is the whole recipe.
Cook the pumpkin, daikon and taro in the dashi for 20 minutes, until the pumpkin begins to collapse.
Drop the raw noodles in and simmer 15 minutes, then slake the miso off the heat. The soup should be thick and yellow.

kishimen.d: Wheat noodles as flat as ribbons, served in a clear dashi broth. They are so thin they cook in three minutes against twelve for udon; they are sold on the platforms of Nagoya station, eaten standing between two trains.
s: Knead a firm dough, then tread it wrapped in a bag, as in Japan: the foot develops the gluten without warming the dough.
Rest it 2 hours: without rest it shrinks back and never reaches the required thinness.
Roll to 1.5 mm — far thinner than udon — and cut 8 mm ribbons.
Cook them 3 minutes in plenty of boiling water and rinse cold to remove the starch, then reheat them in the broth.
Nagoya broth is clear and made with light soy: a dark broth would mask the wheat flavour of the noodle, which is the whole point.

kitsune-udon.d: Udon in a clear broth, crowned with a sheet of fried tofu simmered in soy syrup. The name means fox: legend has Inari, the harvest deity, travelling with foxes, and foxes are said to love the fried tofu left at her shrines.
s: Blanch the fried tofu sheets for thirty seconds and press them between two plates: this degreasing is essential, or the broth turns oily.
Simmer them 15 minutes in a syrup of dashi, soy, mirin and sugar, until they have drunk it entirely.
Let them cool in that syrup: they keep absorbing as they cool, and that is when they take their sweet-salt flavour.
Make a kombu and bonito dashi, and season it with light Kansai soy — Osaka broth is nearly transparent, unlike Tokyo's.
Cook the udon, rinse them, reheat them in the broth and lay the tofu sheet on top, whole and uncut.

yudofu.d: Tofu warmed in barely trembling kombu water and dipped in a soy sauce. It is the cooking of Kyoto's Zen temples: nothing is added to the tofu, and the exercise is precisely to do nothing — overheated, it turns spongy and riddled with holes.
s: Use a Kyoto tofu, firm but silky, made with spring water: it is the only ingredient in the dish and nothing will hide its quality.
Soak the kombu an hour in cold water in the earthenware pot, and do not remove it — here it stays in the bottom throughout the meal.
Cut the tofu into 5 cm cubes and lower them gently into the cold water, before heating.
Bring it very slowly to 70°C and hold: the water must never tremble, only steam. At a boil, tofu holes and toughens.
Lift the cubes out with a skimmer as they rise, and dip them in a sauce of soy, mirin and bonito, with grated ginger.

kaiseki-ryori.d: A meal of some ten courses following a fixed order of techniques: raw, grilled, simmered, steamed, fried. It descends from the light meal served before the tea ceremony; its first rule is seasonal — an ingredient outside its fortnight cannot appear.
s: Choose every ingredient within its fortnight of perfection: kaiseki has no fixed recipe, only a calendar.
Make a first-extraction dashi — kombu lifted out at 60°C, bonito infused thirty seconds — and never let a drop of it boil.
Serve in the order of techniques: raw sakizuke, wanmono in clear broth, grilled yakimono, simmered takiawase, fried agemono.
Each course is three or four mouthfuls and comes in a different vessel, chosen for the season and the colour of the food.
Finish with rice, miso soup and pickles served together: that is the signal of the end, and nothing follows.

hiroshima-tsukemen.d: Cold noodles dipped in a chilli sauce, with raw cabbage and cucumber. Unlike Tokyo tsukemen, served with a scalding broth, the Hiroshima version is eaten entirely cold: the sauce is sour, fiercely hot, and ordered by strength level.
s: Make the sauce the day before: soy, vinegar, sugar, grated garlic, sesame oil and Korean chilli, rested overnight in the cold.
The chilli must infuse rather than be added at the last moment: a same-day sauce is aggressive and unbalanced.
Cook the noodles, rinse them at length in iced water and drain thoroughly — residual water would thin the sauce.
Shred the cabbage and cucumber very finely and leave them ten minutes in iced water so they snap.
Serve noodles, vegetables and sauce in three separate vessels. You dip mouthful by mouthful, and the sauce is never poured over the noodles.

kaki-no-dotenabe.d: Oysters simmered in a pot whose rim has been lined with a wall of miso. Dote means dyke: the miso is smeared as a bank around the inner wall, and pushed into the broth little by little to adjust the seasoning as the meal goes on.
s: Wash the shucked oysters in salted water with a little starch, which traps the grit without damaging them, then rinse and blot.
Mix the miso with the sugar, mirin and sake to a supple paste, and smear it as a bank around the inner wall of the pot, above the liquid line.
Pour in the dashi and arrange the vegetables, without the liquid reaching the miso.
Bring to a tremble and push a little miso into the broth with chopsticks: the seasoning is adjusted gradually, on demand.
Add the oysters last and count three minutes: beyond that they shrink and toughen beyond recovery.

miyajima-manju.d: Small maple-leaf-shaped cakes filled with red bean paste. They were created around 1906 for pilgrims to the Itsukushima shrine; the shape recalls the maples of the Momijidani valley, and the island sells several million a year.
s: Whisk the eggs and sugar for 8 minutes to the ribbon, then add the warm honey, milk and flour sifted with the baking powder.
Rest the batter an hour in the cold: it must relax, and a rested batter flows better into the mould's cavities.
Heat the mould over low heat and brush it with butter for every batch, without exception.
Fill each cavity halfway, set a ball of bean paste in the centre and cover with the remaining batter.
Close the mould and cook 3 minutes a side, turning once. The cakes must stay pale and soft, never browned like a biscuit.

sanuki-udon.d: Thick, square-sectioned udon famous for their elastic chew, served with very little dressing. Kagawa eats three times the Japanese average and has eight hundred shops for a million people; the dough there is kneaded underfoot, wrapped in a bag.
s: Dissolve the salt in the water before adding it: the proportion varies with the season, higher in winter, and it governs the elasticity.
Knead, then wrap the dough in a bag and tread it for twenty minutes, folding as you go: the foot develops gluten without warming the dough as a hand would.
Rest 3 hours covered, then tread it again briefly before rolling.
Roll to 3 mm and cut noodles 3 mm wide: the section must be square, the sanuki signature.
Cook 12 minutes in a great deal of unsalted water, rinse cold while rubbing, and serve with a plain dashi, a raw egg or grated ginger.

katsuo-no-tataki.d: A loin of bonito seared for seconds over a rice-straw flame, raw at the centre, cut in thick slices. Straw burns very fast and very hot: it seizes the surface without cooking the flesh, and leaves a smokiness charcoal does not give.
s: Fillet the fish keeping the skin: it takes the flame and shields the flesh during the operation.
Salt the surface generously and leave it ten minutes — the salt forms a crust that helps the searing.
Skewer the loin on a fan of chopsticks and pass it through the straw flame, ten seconds a side, turning constantly.
Plunge it immediately into iced water to stop the cooking dead, then blot it thoroughly: without that shock the heat travels on toward the centre.
Cut thick slices, a centimetre, and serve with plenty of raw sliced garlic, ginger, spring onion and ponzu.

tokushima-ramen.d: A ramen in a dark, sweet pork broth, crowned with simmered belly and a raw egg cracked on top. The egg is not soft-boiled but entirely raw: it is broken and stirred into the scalding broth, which thickens it and softens the soy, very forward here.
s: Blanch the pork bones five minutes, throw the water away and rinse them: that is what gives a clean broth rather than a grey, scummy one.
Return them to cold water with the garlic and ginger, and simmer 3 hours without ever boiling hard.
Simmer the belly separately in a syrup of soy, sugar, mirin and sake for 90 minutes, then cut it into strips.
Season the broth with that cooking syrup: it gives Tokushima ramen its brown colour and its sweetness.
Assemble the noodles, belly and bean sprouts, and crack a raw egg in the centre. It blends into the broth from the first mouthful.

mentaiko.d: Pollock roe sacs salted then marinated in chilli, eaten with rice or tossed through pasta. A Japanese repatriate from Korea developed them in Fukuoka in 1949, adapting Korean myeongnan-jeot to local taste, less salty and less fiercely hot.
s: Choose intact, firm sacs: a pierced membrane lets the eggs escape during salting and the whole batch is lost.
Dry-salt them between two layers of salt and leave 12 hours in the cold, tilting the dish so the brine runs off.
Rinse with sake and let them soak in it for two hours: the alcohol removes bitterness and firms the membrane.
Make the marinade with mirin, Korean chilli, kombu and garlic, and rest it overnight before laying the sacs in.
Marinate five days in the fridge, turning daily. Slice and serve on hot rice, or mix with butter for pasta.

champon.d: Noodles in a white pork and seafood broth, under a mountain of stir-fried vegetables. Chen Ping-shun, a Chinese restaurateur in Nagasaki, invented it around 1899 to feed Chinese students cheaply: the noodles cook in the broth itself, which turns it milky.
s: Boil the pork bones and chicken hard for 3 hours — unlike other Japanese broths this one must boil vigorously to emulsify the fat and turn white.
Stir-fry the meats, seafood and vegetables over fierce heat in sesame oil, in that order, within three minutes.
Pour the scalding broth over the vegetables in the wok and bring it to the boil.
Tip the raw noodles straight in: their starch finishes thickening and whitening the broth, and that is the whole difference from ramen.
Give it three minutes, adjust the salt and serve at once, vegetables on top. A champon that waits has its noodles drink the broth.

castella.d: A dense, moist honey cake with no fat, baked in a wooden frame. Portuguese traders brought it to Nagasaki in the 16th century as pão de Castela; it holds neither butter nor leaven, and all its lightness comes from beating the eggs.
s: Use a high-gluten flour and sift it three times: with no fat, the structure holds only by gluten and air.
Whisk whole eggs and sugar over a warm bain-marie for 12 minutes, until the mixture ribbons and takes five seconds to settle.
Add the honey slaked in warm milk, then the flour in three additions, folding with a spatula without breaking the foam.
Pour into a paper-lined frame, rap the tin to bring the large bubbles up, and drag a chopstick across the surface to burst them.
Bake 50 minutes at 160°C, turn out warm and wrap in film at once: that overnight rest in its own moisture gives castella its texture.

rafute.d: Pork belly simmered three hours in awamori, black sugar and soy, until it melts. It was a dish of the Ryūkyū royal court; Okinawa eats the whole pig, from snout to trotters, and says only the squeal is wasted.
s: Poach the whole belly 1 hour in water with the ginger, then throw that water away: it carries off most of the fat and the strong smell.
Let the meat cool before cutting it into 5 cm cubes: hot, it collapses under the knife.
Simmer it in awamori and dashi for 1 hour, with no soy or sugar — salt added too early firms the fibres and blocks the tenderising.
Then add the black sugar, and twenty minutes later the soy: sugar penetrates before salt, the Japanese order, and it is not arbitrary.
Reduce for another hour uncovered, basting, until the sauce coats and shines. Serve with rice and a touch of mustard.

sata-andagi.d: Okinawan doughnuts that split into three as they fry, like a flower opening. The name means fried sugar in Okinawan; the split is the sign of good frying, and a ball left smooth means the oil was too hot.
s: Beat the eggs and sugar without aerating them: an airy batter would swell too fast and burst rather than split cleanly.
Add the flour sifted with the baking powder and mix as little as possible; the batter should be thick and sticky, almost impossible to shape.
Rest it 30 minutes then scoop balls with an oiled hand, without smoothing them.
Lower them into oil at 160°C only — no hotter: it is the low temperature that lets the ball swell slowly and split in three.
Allow 8 minutes, turning them: they should be brown outside and dry within. At 180°C they would burn before opening.

okinawa-soba.d: Thick wheat noodles in a pork and bonito broth, with a pork rib and pickled ginger. Despite the name there is not a gram of buckwheat in it: the Japanese soba federation objected in 1976, and Okinawa won a dispensation to keep the word.
s: Dissolve the bicarbonate in the water before kneading: it gives the noodles their yellow colour and their chew in place of kansui.
Knead firmly, rest 2 hours, then roll to 2 mm and cut noodles 3 mm wide.
Make a pork and bonito broth, skimmed relentlessly: in Okinawa it stays clear, unlike the tonkotsu of Kyūshū.
Braise the pork ribs 2 hours in a syrup of soy, brown sugar and awamori until the meat leaves the bone.
Cook the noodles, rinse them, oil them lightly and rest them an hour — in Okinawa they are cooked ahead, and they are the better for waiting.

jiaozi.d: Pork and cabbage dumplings, poached or pan-fried, made as a family on New Year's Eve. Their shape recalls imperial silver ingots, and they are eaten at midnight to call in prosperity; one is sometimes hidden with a coin inside.
s: Salt the chopped cabbage and let it drain 30 minutes, then press it thoroughly: its water is the enemy of a jiaozi, piercing the wrapper from inside.
Work the filling always in the same direction for five minutes, adding ginger water a spoonful at a time until it turns sticky.
That emulsion is what gives the juice: a filling merely mixed stays dry and solid.
Roll discs thicker at the centre than at the edge, fill them and pleat only the upper edge against the smooth lower one.
Poach three times, adding a glass of cold water at each return to the boil — the northern method, and it stops the wrappers bursting.

zhajiangmian.d: Wheat noodles under a very thick sauce of pork and fermented soybean paste, ringed with raw vegetables cut into batons. The sauce is nearly black and so salty that only a spoonful goes in: it is the raw vegetables, in quantity, that balance the bowl.
s: Slake both soybean pastes in a little water and rest them ten minutes: dry, they burn instantly in the wok.
Fry the minced pork letting it render all its fat and begin to crisp — that fat will carry the sauce.
Tip in the slaked pastes and fry them slowly for 20 minutes over low heat, stirring: they must darken and the oil rise to the surface.
That separation of oil is the sign the sauce is ready; before it, the sauce keeps a raw fermented taste.
Cut every raw vegetable into fine batons and ring them around the noodles. Each person mixes their own bowl.

guo-bao-rou.d: Slices of pork loin fried twice and lacquered with a vinegar caramel, crisp and sharp. A Harbin cook created them around 1907 for Russian diplomats who found Chinese food too salty: he sweetened and soured it, and the dish stayed.
s: Cut the loin into 3 mm slices across the grain and marinate them twenty minutes in sake and salt.
Soak the potato starch in water for an hour, then pour off the clear water and keep the paste at the bottom: it is that wet starch, not dry powder, that gives the blistered crust.
Coat each slice in the paste and fry once at 160°C for 2 minutes, until they whiten.
Raise the oil to 190°C and fry them again for 40 seconds: the second bath gives the crispness that survives the sauce.
Make a pale caramel with sugar and vinegar, tip in the slices and toss for ten seconds only, off the heat. Serve immediately.

clay-pot-rice.d: Rice cooked in an earthenware pot with Chinese sausage, served straight from the pot. The whole point is at the bottom: a crust of toasted rice scraped up at the end, which a cook achieves by tilting the pot over the flame in the last minutes.
s: Soak the rice 30 minutes and drain it: soaked, it cooks faster and the base crusts before the top burns.
Oil the inside of the cold pot generously, sides included — without that the crust sticks and tears.
Add the rice and water at one and a quarter volumes, bring to the boil uncovered then cover and drop to the lowest heat.
After ten minutes, lay the sausages and marinated chicken on the rice, close it and give it twelve minutes.
Tilt the pot over the flame and turn it a quarter turn every thirty seconds for three minutes: that is how the crust forms. Pour over the sauce and mix at the table.

wonton-noodles.d: Fine egg noodles and shrimp dumplings in a clear broth of dried shrimp. Cantonese noodles are kneaded with a long bamboo pole the cook straddles and rides: the only way to compress so dry a dough.
s: Make a broth from pork bones and dry-toasted dried shrimp: they, not fish, give a Cantonese broth its flavour.
Salt the raw prawns for twenty minutes, rinse them and cut them into large pieces — never minced, they must snap.
Mix them with the pork and sesame oil, working in one direction only, and rest an hour in the cold.
Fold the wontons without seeking perfection: the floating tail of wrapper is part of the dish, and it gives the cloud texture.
Cook the noodles 20 seconds only, rinse them cold then return them to boiling water for five seconds: that double pass gives the Cantonese chew.

shuang-pi-nai.d: A buffalo milk custard with two skins, steamed in its own bowl. The first skin forms as the milk cools, the milk is poured out from under it, then a second forms during steaming: hence the name, and the operation fails with milk below eight per cent fat.
s: Bring the buffalo milk to a tremble then pour it into the bowls and let it cool twenty minutes: a thick skin forms on the surface.
Pierce that skin gently at the edge and pour the milk out from beneath into another vessel, leaving the skin stuck to the bottom of the bowl.
This is the decisive gesture: a torn skin, or one carried off with the milk, and the dish has one skin instead of two.
Mix that milk with the beaten whites and sugar, strain, then pour it back very gently down the side so the skin lifts and rises.
Steam 12 minutes over gentle heat, covered with film: condensation falling on it would pierce the second skin.

hong-shao-rou.d: Cubes of pork belly braised in a caramel of cane sugar, soy and rice wine, lacquered and glossy. Red braising is a technique rather than a recipe: it is the caramel, made dry before any liquid, that gives the colour, not the soy sauce.
s: Poach the whole belly 10 minutes with ginger, throw the water away and rinse: that blanching removes scum and odour.
Cut it into 4 cm cubes keeping the rind — without it the piece falls apart and the sauce gains no gelatine.
Melt the rock sugar dry in a little oil to a dark amber, then tip in the pork cubes and coat them.
That caramel is the heart of the technique: too pale and the colour is missing; burnt and the whole dish turns bitter and must be started again.
Deglaze with Shaoxing wine, add the soys, spices and water to cover, and simmer 1½ hours then reduce uncovered for twenty minutes.

chou-doufu.d: Tofu fermented in a brine of vegetables and shrimp, fried and served with a chilli sauce. The smell is legendary and carries fifty metres; the taste is mild and milky, which disconcerts anyone who knew only the smell.
s: The brine is made weeks ahead by fermenting vegetables, dried shrimp and salt in water, until it smells frankly.
Press the tofu between two boards for two hours to drive out the water — waterlogged tofu will not take up brine.
Submerge it completely and ferment it six to forty-eight hours according to the strength wanted, in the cold.
Rinse it quickly and blot it, then fry at 180°C for four minutes: the outside must be brown and crackling, the inside stay creamy.
Serve scalding, split at the centre, with fermented cabbage and a sauce of chilli, garlic, soy and vinegar poured into the cut.

nian-gao.d: A glutinous rice cake with brown sugar, steamed then sliced and fried. Its name is a pun: nian gao means year cake, but sounds like higher year, and it is eaten at New Year so that the coming one may rise above the last.
s: Dissolve the brown sugar in hot water and let it cool: poured boiling onto glutinous rice flour it cooks it into unrecoverable lumps.
Pour the warm syrup onto the flour, whisking, to a smooth batter the consistency of thick pancake batter.
Strain it: glutinous rice flour forms lumps that stay hard after cooking and never break down.
Pour into an oiled tin, set the red dates on top and steam 1 hour, covered with film against condensation.
Cool twelve hours — a warm nian gao is impossible to slice. Cut slices, dip in beaten egg and fry until golden.

zui-ji.d: Chicken poached then marinated overnight in Shaoxing wine, served cold as a starter. The flesh must stay barely pink at the bone: in Shanghai a chicken white right through is held to be overcooked, and the marinade never rescues dry meat.
s: Rub the chicken with salt and leave it an hour, then lower it into simmering water with the ginger and spring onion.
Kill the heat as soon as it returns to a tremble, cover, and let the chicken poach in the cooling water for 40 minutes.
That carry-over cooking is what keeps the flesh juicy: water held at a boil would dry it out within twenty minutes.
Plunge it at once into iced water: the shock contracts the skin and gives it its characteristic gelatinous texture.
Joint it, lay the pieces in the Shaoxing wine with the goji berries and star anise, and marinate 24 hours in the cold. Served chilled.

dandan-mian.d: Noodles over a broth-free sauce of crisp pork, sesame and Sichuan pepper. The name comes from the dan dan, the carrying pole the seller balanced on his shoulder with his baskets: the original has no broth precisely because it would have had to be carried.
s: Fry the minced pork dry until it crisps and separates into grains — a good ten minutes, until it stops sizzling.
Add the chopped preserved greens and stir-fry two minutes: their acidity is what stops the dish being merely fatty and hot.
Toast the Sichuan pepper dry then grind it in a mortar: ground in advance, it loses its numbing effect within days.
Build the sauce in the bottom of the bowl — sesame paste, chilli oil, soy, vinegar, garlic, pepper — without a drop of broth.
Set the scalding noodles on top with two spoonfuls of their cooking water, and mix at the table. Crown with the pork and crushed peanuts.

gong-bao-ji-ding.d: Diced chicken stir-fried with dried chillies, peanuts and a sweet-sour black vinegar sauce. It carries the title of Ding Baozhen, governor of Sichuan in the 19th century; it was renamed during the Cultural Revolution to erase the imperial reference, then took its name back.
s: Cut the chicken into 1.5 cm dice and marinate them twenty minutes in Shaoxing wine, soy and starch: that coating holds the water in the flesh.
Make the sauce entirely in advance in a bowl — black vinegar, sugar, soy, starch: the stir-fry takes ninety seconds and nothing can be improvised.
Toast the dried chillies and Sichuan pepper in warm oil until they darken, and lift them out if you prefer it mild.
Sear the chicken over maximum heat without stirring for the first thirty seconds: that is how it colours instead of boiling.
Pour in the sauce and stir ten seconds only: it thickens instantly. Add the peanuts off the heat, so they stay crisp.

tang-yuan.d: Glutinous rice balls filled with black sesame, served in their sweetened cooking water. They are eaten at the Lantern Festival that closes New Year: their round shape and their name, close to tuányuán, reunion, make them the symbol of the family gathered.
s: Toast the black sesame dry until it crackles, then grind it while still warm: cold, it will not release its oil.
Mix it with the sugar and lard, and chill until firm before shaping balls — a soft filling pierces the dough as you work.
Pour boiling water onto a fifth of the flour to make a cooked paste, then mix it with the rest and warm water: that blend of cooked and raw dough is what makes the ball extensible.
Enclose each ball in a disc of dough, drawing it up by hand, and roll it smooth with not the least crack left.
Poach in trembling — never boiling — water until they rise, then two minutes more. Serve in a syrup of ginger and rock sugar.

bulgogi.d: Beef sliced thin, marinated in soy, pear and sesame, seared on a plate. The Korean pear is not there for flavour: it contains an enzyme, calpain, that cuts muscle fibres and tenderises the meat within hours.
s: Firm the meat an hour in the freezer before slicing: at room temperature you will not get two-millimetre slices.
Grate the pear and onion and mix them with the soy, sugar, crushed garlic and sesame oil.
Do not exceed four hours of marinating: the pear enzyme keeps working and the meat eventually turns mealy.
Sear on a very hot plate in a single layer, never crowded — crowded, the meat gives up its juice and boils.
Serve with rice and lettuce leaves in which the meat is wrapped, by hand.

samgyeopsal.d: Pork belly grilled at the table, unmarinated, eaten in a lettuce leaf. The name means three layers of flesh: fat, lean, fat — and it is never marinated, precisely so those layers stay distinct on the palate.
s: Ask for belly cut one centimetre thick, no more and no less: thinner it dries out, thicker the fat does not render.
Heat the plate empty and lay the slices on with no added fat — the pork gives up enough to cook the vegetables afterwards.
Turn only once, when the underside is well browned, after four or five minutes.
Grill sliced garlic and kimchi in the rendered fat at the edge of the plate.
Cut the meat with scissors, lay it on lettuce with ssamjang, garlic and a perilla leaf, close it and eat in one mouthful.

tteokbokki.d: Cylinders of rice cake simmered in a red gochujang sauce. The spicy version dates from the 1950s: a Sindang-dong restaurateur is said to have dropped a tteok into chilli sauce and served the accident, which made her fortune.
s: Soak the tteok thirty minutes in cold water if dry or refrigerated — otherwise they stay hard in the middle.
Make a stock of dried anchovies and kombu, twenty minutes at a tremble, then strain it.
Slake the gochujang, gochugaru, sugar and soy in that stock before bringing it to the boil.
Add the tteok and cook fifteen minutes, stirring often: the starch they release thickens the sauce, the only thickener there is.
Add the fish cakes and hard-boiled eggs at the end. Serve scalding, with the sauce coating.

sundubu-jjigae.d: A scalding stew of unpressed tofu, served bubbling in its earthenware pot. The village of Chodang has made its tofu with seawater rather than nigari since the sixteenth century: sea salt sets the soy into a softer, meltier mass.
s: Heat the earthenware pot empty over medium heat: heated too fast, or empty over a fierce flame, it cracks.
Fry the pork in sesame oil, add the gochugaru and let it sizzle twenty seconds to release its colour.
That sizzle is what gives the red oil on the surface; added to liquid, the chilli stays dull and powdery.
Moisten with stock, add the clams and vegetables, and bring to a hard boil.
Spoon in the tofu in large curds without crushing it, break an egg on top and serve at once, still bubbling.

japchae.d: Sweet potato noodles stir-fried with julienned vegetables and beef. The dish was invented around 1600 for a royal banquet and then contained no noodles at all: they entered only in the twentieth century, and ended up giving it its name.
s: Cook the noodles six minutes in boiling water, rinse them cold and cut them in two with scissors.
Season them at once with soy and sesame oil while warm: cold, they clump into a block and absorb nothing.
Stir-fry each vegetable separately, hot and briefly — cooked together they give up their water and the japchae goes soggy.
Blanch the spinach for ten seconds only, and press it out thoroughly between your hands.
Combine everything off the heat, mixing by hand so nothing breaks, and serve warm or at room temperature.

gimbap.d: A seaweed roll filled with sesame-seasoned rice and strips of vegetables and meat. It is often confused with Japanese maki, but its rice is never vinegared: it is seasoned with sesame oil and salt, which changes the whole flavour.
s: Cook the rice slightly firmer than usual and season it warm with sesame oil and salt, never vinegar.
Prepare each filling separately in long strips of the same section, and cool them completely.
A warm filling gives off steam that softens the seaweed and bursts the roll when cut.
Spread the rice over two-thirds of the sheet in a thin layer, line up the fillings and roll tightly on the mat.
Oil the knife blade before each cut and slice in one movement, without sawing.

dakgangjeong.d: Twice-fried chicken coated in a sticky chilli and rice-syrup sauce. Double frying is a Korean invention: the first bath cooks, the second dehydrates the crust, and the chicken stays crisp even drowned in sauce.
s: Dry the chicken thoroughly and coat it in cornflour alone, no egg and no wheat flour: that is what gives the fine, dry crust.
Rest it twenty minutes so the starch hydrates and adheres — put in dry, it falls off in the oil.
First fry at 160°C for ten minutes, until cooked but still pale. Drain and cool ten minutes.
Second fry at 190°C for three minutes: the crust hardens and turns amber.
Reduce the sauce separately until it coats, and toss the chicken off the heat, at the last moment.

bingsu.d: A mountain of shaved ice, topped with sweet red beans and condensed milk. The ice is not crushed but shaved into flakes a tenth of a millimetre thick: the resulting texture melts in the mouth without ever crunching.
s: Freeze milk rather than water: the fat prevents large crystals forming and gives supple flakes.
Cook the red beans two hours, discarding the first water after ten minutes' boiling to remove bitterness.
Sweeten them only once tender — sugar added too early hardens the skins and they will never cook.
Shave the ice just before serving, piled high and unpacked.
Cover with beans, tteok, fruit and roasted soybean powder, and pour the condensed milk on at the last moment.

tteokguk.d: A soup of rice-cake coins in clear beef broth, eaten at New Year. In Korea one does not age a year at one's birthday but at Lunar New Year: eating tteokguk is taking a year, and children ask for two bowls.
s: Soak the brisket an hour in cold water, changing it: that is what gives a clear rather than cloudy broth.
Cook it two hours at a tremble, skimming regularly, never at a hard boil.
Soak the rice-cake coins thirty minutes if dry, and rinse them to remove surface starch.
Cook them six minutes in the strained broth; they are ready when they rise and turn translucent at the edges.
Separate the eggs, make two thin omelettes, one yellow and one white, and cut them into diamonds as garnish.

budae-jjigae.d: A spicy stew combining kimchi, sausages, tinned ham and instant noodles. Born near the American bases after the Korean War, it used military surplus; its name means army stew and it fully owns its origin in scarcity.
s: Use a well-fermented kimchi, sour and faintly fizzy: a young kimchi will not give the depth that holds the whole dish together.
Arrange the ingredients in sectors in a wide pan rather than mixing them — that is the customary presentation, and each diner picks.
Mix the gochujang, gochugaru and crushed garlic into the stock before pouring, never as a paste in the bottom of the pan.
Bring to the boil and give it fifteen minutes, until the kimchi softens and the sausages flavour the broth.
Add the noodles and cheese in the last three minutes only. Earlier, the noodles disintegrate and thicken everything.

sannakji.d: Octopus cut live and served at once, the tentacles still moving. The movement is not that of a living animal but a nerve reflex: the neurons in the tentacle keep commanding the suckers for several minutes after cutting.
s: Use only very small octopus, alive, bought from a tank and prepared within the hour.
Rub them with coarse salt to remove the mucus, then rinse thoroughly in cold water.
Cut the tentacles into two-centimetre lengths and dress at once with sesame oil and seeds.
The sesame oil is not merely a dressing: it coats the suckers and reduces their grip.
Chew very thoroughly before swallowing. Active suckers can grip the throat, and the choking risk is real.

hobakjuk.d: A sweet pumpkin porridge thickened with glutinous rice flour. It is what is served to convalescents and to women after childbirth: easy to digest, warming, and held to be restorative for centuries.
