s: Use a dense, dry-fleshed squash such as red kuri: watery pumpkins give a thin porridge that cannot be rescued.
Steam it rather than boil it, forty minutes, until a knife passes through without resistance.
Pass it through a sieve or a food mill — a blender works in air and the porridge turns foamy instead of silky.
Slake the glutinous rice flour in cold water before adding it: tipped in dry it lumps instantly.
Cook ten minutes, stirring without pause, add a pinch of salt to lift the sugar, and garnish with pine nuts.

haejangguk.d: A soup of beef bones, congealed blood and cabbage, eaten the morning after. Its name means literally soup to chase the hangover; some houses in Cheongjin-dong have served it since the 1930s without ever closing at night.
s: Soak the bones six hours in cold water, changing it three times, then blanch them ten minutes and discard that water.
This double cleaning is what gives a clean broth: without it the soup stays grey and smells of tallow.
Boil the bones at least three hours at a gentle roll, until the broth turns milky.
Blanch the cabbage and press it out, then season it with fermented soybean paste and garlic before adding it.
Add the blood curd in large dice in the last ten minutes, at a tremble — boiled, it disintegrates into powder.

sundae-coreen.d: A pork blood sausage stuffed with sweet potato noodles and glutinous rice. Unlike European blood sausages it contains far more starch than blood: the blood binds and colours, and the noodles make the body.
s: Turn the casings inside out and rub them with coarse salt and flour, then rinse at length — a badly cleaned casing ruins everything.
Soak the glutinous rice four hours and cook the noodles before cutting them short.
Mix the strained blood, noodles, rice, blanched and pressed cabbage and aromatics, and taste by frying a spoonful.
Fill loosely, only two-thirds full: the stuffing swells as it cooks and a packed casing will certainly burst.
Poach at 80°C for forty minutes, pricking the sausages with a needle after ten minutes to let the steam out.

bossam.d: Pork belly poached with aromatics, sliced and eaten wrapped in brined cabbage. Bossam is traditionally the meal of kimjang, the great November kimchi-making: it is eaten with freshly salted cabbage, before it ferments.
s: Poach the whole belly for an hour and a half in water scented with soybean paste, ginger and leeks.
Add a spoonful of instant coffee to the water: a modern habit but an effective one, it neutralises the pork smell and colours the rind.
Cool ten minutes out of the broth before slicing — hot, the meat collapses under the knife.
Salt the cabbage two hours in coarse salt, rinse it and press it: it should bend without snapping.
Make a radish salad with gochugaru and salted shrimp, and serve the three elements to be assembled at table.

makgeolli.d: A cloudy, faintly sparkling rice alcohol, coarsely filtered. It ferments thanks to nuruk, a wheat ferment carrying moulds and wild yeasts: the fungus first turns starch into sugar, then the yeast turns sugar into alcohol.
s: Wash the rice until the water runs clear, soak it two hours then steam it to firm, separate grains.
Spread it and cool it to exactly 30°C: hotter kills the yeasts, colder and fermentation will not start.
Crumble the nuruk and mix it with the rice and water in a sterilised vessel, leaving a third empty.
Cover with a cloth and ferment seven days at 22-25°C, stirring with a wooden spoon daily.
Strain through wide muslin, pressing lightly: makgeolli must stay cloudy, that is its very definition.

bori-cha.d: An infusion of roasted barley, drunk cold in summer and hot in winter, in place of water. It holds no caffeine and is served to children and adults alike; nearly every Korean household keeps a jug of it in the refrigerator all year.
s: Toast the barley dry in a heavy pan, stirring without pause, until the grains brown and become fragrant, a good ten minutes.
Stop before they blacken: a single burnt grain makes the whole infusion bitter.
Bring the water to the boil, tip in the barley and lower the heat at once.
Infuse at a tremble for ten to fifteen minutes depending on the strength wanted, then strain without pressing.
Drunk hot or iced. Cooled, it keeps three days in the refrigerator but no longer.

sikhye.d: A sweet rice drink in which the grains float whole on the surface. Barley malt turns the rice starch into maltose: exactly the beginning of brewing beer, halted before any alcoholic fermentation.
s: Slake the malt powder in warm water and let it settle an hour, then draw off the clear liquid, leaving the sediment.
Cook the rice to firm grains and mix it into the malt liquid at exactly 60°C.
That temperature is decisive: above 65°C the enzyme is destroyed, below 55°C it works too slowly.
Hold at 60°C for five hours, until a couple of dozen grains rise to the surface — that is the signal.
Remove the floating grains, boil the liquid ten minutes with the sugar and ginger, and return the grains as you serve, iced.

shoyu-ramen-tokyo.d: The original ramen: a clear poultry broth with soy, wavy noodles and chashu. It was born in 1910 at the Rairaiken in Asakusa, run by a Japanese owner with twelve Cantonese cooks — ramen is thus Chinese in origin and Tokyo-born.
s: Soak the carcasses an hour in cold water, blanch them ten minutes and discard that water.
Simmer three hours with ginger and leek, never boiling: a shoyu broth must stay translucent, and boiling emulsifies it cloudy.
Make the tare separately — soy, mirin and sake reduced — and the dashi with kombu and bonito: the three elements meet only in the bowl.
Braise the rolled, tied belly two hours in the tare, then cool it before slicing.
Two spoonfuls of tare in the bottom of the bowl, scalding broth over it, then the noodles drained with a sharp shake.

fukagawa-meshi.d: Rice with clams and miso, the dish of the Edo bay fishermen. Fukagawa was a fishing quarter built on clam beds; the dish was made aboard the boats, and the version with broth poured over rice is the older one.
s: Purge the clams three hours in 3% salt water, in the dark: they spit out their sand, and darkness encourages it.
Open them in sake, covered, for two minutes, and take them out as soon as they gape.
Strain the released juice through muslin — it always holds sand, and it carries all the flavour.
Slake the miso in a little warm broth before adding it, and never boil it: heat destroys its aroma.
Pour the broth over hot rice, add the shelled clams and grated ginger, and serve at once.

anmitsu.d: Cubes of agar jelly, red bean paste, fruit and a black syrup. Agar is drawn from seaweed and sets at room temperature, which allowed this dessert to be served in summer long before refrigeration.
s: Soak the powdered agar in cold water for ten minutes, then boil for exactly one minute.
One minute is enough: agar activates at 90°C, and longer cooking degrades it so the jelly will not set.
Pour into a flat mould two centimetres deep and let it set at room temperature, an hour.
Make the kuromitsu by reducing brown sugar and water for twenty minutes, until it coats the spoon.
Cut the jelly into one-centimetre cubes, arrange with the fruit, anko and mochi, and pour the syrup at the table.

yakitori.d: Chicken skewers grilled over binchotan charcoal, glazed with tare or simply salted. Binchotan burns very hot with no flame and no smoke: it cooks by radiant heat, which is why yakitori never tastes scorched.
s: Make the tare by reducing soy, mirin, sake and sugar with grilled bones, for forty minutes.
A house's tare is never thrown out: it is topped up and skewers are dipped in it, and it deepens year on year.
Cut the meat into even pieces and thread them tightly, alternating with leek.
Grill dry first, without sauce, until the surface firms — glazed too early, the sauce burns before the meat cooks.
Then dip in the tare and return to the fire three times, letting it caramelise between each pass.

ningyo-yaki.d: Small moulded cakes in the shape of figures, filled with red bean paste. Ningyocho was Edo's puppet theatre district; the moulds reproduced the characters played on stage, and some are unchanged since 1907.
s: Whisk the eggs and sugar over a warm water bath until the ribbon holds three seconds on the surface.
Fold in the sifted flour in three additions with a spatula, never whisking: developed gluten would make the cake rubbery.
Rest the batter thirty minutes in the cold, so the bubbles stabilise.
Heat the cast-iron mould, brush it with oil and fill the cavities only halfway.
Set a ball of anko in, cover with batter and close the mould. Two minutes a side, over medium heat.

taiyaki.d: A cake shaped like a sea bream, filled with red bean paste. The tai is Japan's celebration fish, too dear for most: taiyaki gives its shape to a penny cake, and that has been the whole idea since 1909.
s: Make a loose batter, barely thicker than pancake batter, and rest it an hour in the cold.
Resting removes the air bubbles that would leave holes in the fish's fins and tail.
Heat the taiyaki mould well and oil it for every batch, edges included.
Fill one half of the mould 60% full, lay the anko in a bar down the centre, cover with batter and close.
Three minutes a side, turning the mould. The batter that escapes forms a frill: it is broken off by hand, and it is the best part.

melon-pan.d: A brioche topped with a crosshatched biscuit crust. It contains no melon: the name comes from the lattice, which recalls the rind of a netted melon, and the classic version never had any fruit flavour at all.
s: Make a soft brioche dough and prove it an hour and a half, until doubled.
Separately make a soft creamed biscuit dough, and firm it in the cold for thirty minutes.
Roll the biscuit into thin discs and wrap each brioche ball, leaving the base bare — fully covered, the brioche cannot rise.
Roll in granulated sugar and score the lattice with a scraper, without cutting through.
Prove an hour, then bake 15 minutes at 180°C. The crust should stay pale and crack along the lines.

yuba.d: The skin that forms on the surface of heated soy milk, lifted off with a chopstick. It came with the Zen monastery cooking of Kyoto, which forbids meat: yuba supplied the protein, and making it demands a monk's attention.
s: Use a thick unsweetened soy milk, at least 10% dry matter: a diluted milk forms no skin at all.
Heat it in a wide shallow vessel at exactly 80°C, never letting it tremble.
The skin forms in five to seven minutes. Slide a chopstick underneath and lift in one movement, without hesitating.
A hesitation tears the sheet; it must be lifted in one continuous motion, from the edge to the centre.
Reckon about ten sheets per litre, each thicker than the last. Serve with soy, wasabi and a light dashi.

kushikatsu.d: Skewers crumbed in fine panko and fried, dipped in a communal sauce. Shinsekai's absolute rule: dip once only. The sauce tray is shared by the whole room, and returning a bitten skewer to it is the one unforgivable offence.
s: Thread each ingredient on its own short skewer, unmixed: each has its own cooking time.
Make a thin batter of flour, egg and water rather than a dry coating — that gives Osaka's fine crust.
Sieve the panko and keep only the fine crumb; coarse panko drinks too much oil.
Fry at 170°C for two to three minutes depending on the ingredient, and drain upright on paper.
Serve with raw cabbage in large pieces, which is both a side dish and a spoon for taking more sauce.

butaman.d: A steamed bun filled with pork and onion, an Osaka speciality. It descends from the Chinese baozi that came through Nagasaki, but the Osaka version is larger, sweeter and eaten standing on the station platform.
s: Chop the onion very finely, salt it ten minutes and press it out: otherwise it weeps into the filling and soaks the dough.
Work the minced pork in one direction only, five minutes, until it turns tacky and elastic.
That one-way mixing aligns the proteins and gives a filling that holds; stirred at random, it crumbles.
Knead the dough, let it double, then divide and roll discs thicker at the centre than at the edge.
Pleat the closure upwards, prove twenty minutes and steam 15 minutes over a fierce boil.

nishin-soba.d: Buckwheat noodles in a clear dashi with a long-simmered dried herring. Kyoto is landlocked: fish reached it only dried, and migaki nishin, dried herring from Hokkaido, travelled a month without spoiling.
s: Soak the dried herring twenty-four hours in rice water or weak green tea, changing it twice.
The tea is not an affectation: its tannins neutralise the strong smell of dried fish, which plain water leaves untouched.
Then simmer it two hours in soy, mirin, sake and sugar, until the bones crush under a finger.
Make a kombu and bonito dashi and season it lightly — it must not compete with the herring.
Cook the soba in unsalted water, rinse them cold to remove the starch, and reheat them in the broth.

zangi.d: Marinated fried chicken, cousin to karaage but more heavily seasoned. The distinction is debated in Hokkaido: some say zangi marinates longer, others that it is dipped in sauce after frying — and Kushiro claims the 1960 invention.
s: Cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces, keeping the skin — that is what crisps.
Marinate an hour in soy, sake, grated ginger and garlic, then beat the egg straight into the marinade.
Coat in potato starch just before frying: starch gives a finer, drier crust than flour.
Fry once at 160°C for four minutes, then rest three minutes out of the oil.
Second fry at 190°C for one minute. That rest between baths lets the heat reach the centre without drying the surface.

ika-meshi.d: Squid stuffed with rice and simmered in sweet soy. The dish was born in 1941 at Mori station: rice was scarce, squid abundant, and the platform bento ended up the most famous in Japan.
s: Gut the squid without slitting them: pull the head and the innards come with it, leaving the body an intact tube.
Remove the transparent quill and rinse the inside, then blot thoroughly.
Fill only two-thirds full with raw rice: rice doubles in volume and an overfilled squid bursts every time.
Close the opening with a cocktail stick, pinching without tightening.
Simmer an hour covered in the soy and mirin broth, over very low heat. Cool in the liquid before slicing.

chan-chan-yaki.d: Salmon and vegetables cooked on a plate with a miso and butter sauce. It was born on the fishing boats of the Sea of Okhotsk: everything was cooked on a cast-iron plate on deck, and the name is said to imitate the noise of the spatulas.
s: Mix miso, mirin, sake, sugar and grated garlic into a soft paste and rest it an hour.
Lay the salmon skin down on the scalding plate and leave it a good minute untouched.
Arrange the vegetables all around, never on top: the fish must stay in contact with the iron for the skin to crisp.
Spread the miso paste over the fish, cover and cook ten minutes in the vegetables' own steam.
Add the butter at the end and toss everything at once with the spatula, straight on the plate.

miso-ramen-sapporo.d: A rich, fatty miso ramen crowned with butter and sweetcorn. It was invented in 1955 when a customer asked to add noodles to his miso soup; the fat layer on top is no excess but a thermal lid, essential at -15°C.
s: Boil the pork bones three hours at a hard rolling boil — here, unlike shoyu, cloudiness and emulsion are the aim.
Fry the minced pork, garlic and ginger in lard over fierce heat in a wok.
Add the miso and toast it thirty seconds in the fat before moistening: that gives its roasted flavour.
Pour the scalding broth into the wok and boil twenty seconds to emulsify the fat — a whisk alone will not do it.
Throw in the bean sprouts for ten seconds only. Butter and sweetcorn on top as you serve.

morioka-reimen.d: Very elastic cold noodles in an iced broth, with a slice of watermelon. It was created in 1954 by a Korean restaurateur in Morioka who adapted naengmyeon to Japanese taste; the watermelon is his addition, and it caused an outcry.
s: Knead the starch and flour with boiling water: scalding water gelatinises the starch and gives the characteristic elasticity.
Work the dough fifteen minutes, until it bounces back under your palm, then extrude it straight into boiling water.
Cook three minutes and plunge at once into iced water, rubbing the noodles between your hands to remove the starch.
That rinsing is decisive: badly rinsed, the noodles clump into a block and lose their bite.
Make a degreased beef broth, seasoned and chilled until ice crystals form in it.

morioka-jajamen.d: Flat warm noodles topped with a miso and pork paste, mixed at the table. At the end you crack a raw egg into the empty bowl and hand it back to the cook, who pours in scalding noodle water: this chîtantan is the obligatory second half of the meal.
s: Fry the pork dry until it renders its fat and starts to crisp.
Add the miso, sesame paste, sugar and sake, and reduce twenty minutes over low heat.
The paste should turn nearly black and pull from the base in one mass; too pale, it lacks power.
Cook the flat noodles and drain without rinsing — here the surface starch helps the sauce cling.
Serve warm, never scalding, with cucumber and spring onion. Keep some cooking water for the final chîtantan.

harako-meshi.d: Rice cooked in salmon broth, topped with the fish and its own roe. The name means rice of the belly's child: mother and offspring are served in one bowl, and it is made only in autumn, when the salmon run up the Abukuma.
s: Poach the salmon in a soy, sake and mirin broth for ten minutes only, and remove it.
Cook the rice in that strained broth made up with water: this is where the dish is decided, the rice must take all the fish's colour.
Free the roe from its membrane in warm salted water, rolling it with your fingertips.
Warm water, counterintuitively, relaxes the membrane; cold water contracts it and the eggs tear.
Flake the salmon over the rice, add the roe off the heat and cover five minutes without cooking — heated roe hardens and turns white.

imoni.d: A taro and beef soup with soy, cooked in great pots on the riverbank. Every autumn thousands gather on the banks of the Mamigasaki; in Yamagata the soup is beef and soy, in Sendai pork and miso, and the quarrel is taken seriously.
s: Peel the taro wearing gloves: its sap causes severe itching on bare skin.
Rub it with salt then rinse: the mucilage comes away and the broth stays clear instead of turning gluey.
Cook the taro alone for twenty minutes in the dashi, before anything else — it takes the longest.
Add the blanched konjac, burdock and mushrooms, then the thinly sliced beef last.
The beef should cook two minutes only. Season with soy and serve with plenty of raw spring onion.

senbei-jiru.d: A soup into which hard wheat crackers are broken, softening without disintegrating. The nanbu senbei used here is baked specially for soup: thicker and unleavened, it holds twenty minutes in broth where an ordinary biscuit would dissolve in three.
s: Use kayaki-type senbei, sold for soup: snacking senbei dissolves and thickens everything to porridge.
Fry the chicken, then moisten with dashi and add the sliced roots.
Cook thirty minutes uncovered, until the burdock loses its bitterness.
Break the crackers into quarters and drop them into the simmering broth ten minutes before the end.
Do not stir once the crackers are in: they break up and the broth turns cloudy.

hitsumabushi.d: Lacquered eel served on rice, eaten in three successive ways. The first quarter plain, the second with condiments, the third with broth poured over; the fourth in whichever way you preferred, and that order is not negotiable in Nagoya.
s: Grill the eel dry over coals, without sauce, until the fat begins to drip.
In Nagoya it is not steamed, unlike Tokyo: it stays firm and crisp, and that is the whole regional difference.
Then dip it in the tare and return it to the fire four times, letting it dry between passes.
Cut it into fine strips and mix some into the rice, keeping the rest on top.
Serve a light green-tea dashi in a teapot, for the third stage.

tebasaki.d: Chicken wings fried without batter, glazed with sweet soy and heavily peppered. They are fried twice and never floured: the skin alone makes the crust, and that sets them apart from every other wing in the world.
s: Dry the wings thoroughly, uncovered in the refrigerator overnight if possible: the skin must feel dry to the touch.
Fry them bare at 160°C for eight minutes, with no flour and no starch at all.
Rest them five minutes, then return them to 190°C for two minutes to harden the skin.
Reduce the sauce separately until it coats, and toss the wings off the heat, in a bowl.
Pepper very generously, far beyond what instinct suggests, and finish with toasted sesame.

miso-nikomi-udon.d: Udon simmered directly in a red miso broth, served in the clay pot. Nagoya's hatcho miso ferments two years in wooden vats weighted with stones, with no rice or barley: the darkest and saltiest miso in Japan.
s: Use raw, not pre-cooked udon: they are simmered in the broth and the starch they release thickens it, which is the point.
Do not rinse the noodles — the whole dish rests on that starch.
Slake the red miso in cold dashi, then bring gently to a tremble.
Add the chicken and mushrooms, then the noodles, and simmer fifteen minutes in the clay pot.
Crack the egg on top two minutes before serving and bring the pot to the table still bubbling.

hoba-miso.d: Miso grilled on a dried magnolia leaf set directly on the coals. The hoba leaf is fire-resistant once dried and scents the miso as it heats; Hida farmers used it as a disposable plate in winter, when the dishes froze.
s: Soak the dried leaves twenty minutes in water, then blot them: damp, they will not catch fire on the coals.
Mix the miso with mirin, sake and sugar, working to a soft but not runny paste.
Spread it in the centre of the leaf leaving a three-centimetre margin all round.
Lay the mushrooms and beef on top, and set the leaf on gentle coals or a griddle.
The miso should bubble and brown at the edges without ever burning. Eaten with a spoon, over rice.

masu-sushi.d: Marinated trout pressed onto vinegared rice in a round mould, between bamboo leaves. It is a keeping sushi, older than the fresh kind: pressure and vinegar preserved it for days, and it has been sold at Toyama station since 1912.
s: Fillet the trout, salt it in coarse salt for two hours then rinse and blot it.
Marinate it two hours in sweetened rice vinegar, until the flesh pales on the surface but stays pink at the centre.
Line a round mould with bamboo leaves overhanging generously, then lay the trout skin down.
Pack the vinegared rice on top, firmly, and fold the leaves over.
Press under a two-kilo weight for six hours in the cold. Without that prolonged pressing, the sushi falls apart when cut.

sauce-katsudon.d: A breaded cutlet dipped in brown sauce and set on rice, with no egg. Ordinary katsudon is bound with beaten egg; the Komagane version does without entirely, and Komagane and Fukui both claim its paternity.
s: Nick the sinew between fat and lean every two centimetres: without that, the cutlet curls as it cooks.
Flatten it with a mallet to a centimetre, then salt it and rest it ten minutes.
Crumb it in the standard way, pressing the panko on firmly, and rest a quarter of an hour so the coating adheres.
Fry at 170°C for six minutes, then drain upright for three — laid flat, the underside coating goes soft.
Dip the whole cutlet in the hot sauce for two seconds only, and set it on the rice with raw cabbage.

sasa-dango.d: Glutinous rice dumplings with mugwort, filled with anko and wrapped in dwarf bamboo leaves. Sasa leaves carry antibacterial compounds: they kept dango for days in summer, long before any refrigeration.
s: Blanch the mugwort with a pinch of bicarbonate for two minutes: the bicarbonate fixes the green, without it the dough turns olive brown.
Rinse it in iced water, press it hard and chop it very finely before pounding.
Knead the flours with hot water, work in the mugwort and continue until the dough turns smooth and supple as an earlobe.
Enclose the anko, shape into ovals and wrap in three sasa leaves tied with straw.
Steam twenty minutes. Eaten warm or cold, and they keep three days at room temperature.

onomichi-ramen.d: A soy ramen whose broth marries small dried fish with pork bones, topped with cubes of back fat. The floating lard cubes, called seabura, are no excess: they melt slowly and keep the soup scalding to the last mouthful.
s: Simmer the pork bones two hours, then add the small dried fish for the last twenty minutes only.
Boiled longer, niboshi turn frankly bitter: the mistake that ruins the most Onomichi ramen.
Render the diced back fat over very low heat for forty minutes, until the cubes turn translucent without colouring.
Use flat straight noodles, not wavy: that is the local shape, and they hold the fat better.
Two spoonfuls of tare in the bottom, the broth, the noodles, and a good spoonful of seabura on top.

fugu-sashimi.d: Pufferfish sliced so thin the plate shows through, arranged in petals. The liver and ovaries hold tetrodotoxin, a thousand times deadlier than cyanide and with no antidote: only cooks holding a state licence may prepare it.
s: Never attempt to prepare fugu yourself: the butchery requires a licence earned through three years' apprenticeship and a state examination.
Buy it already trimmed from a licensed fishmonger, with liver and gonads removed and destroyed as regulations require.
The flesh is very firm and has almost no taste: the whole point is the texture and the fineness of the cut.
Slice with a long thin knife in one drawn movement, to transparency — the chrysanthemum pattern is the customary presentation.
Serve with ponzu, grated radish and chilli, and spring onion. Eaten two or three petals at a time.

izumo-soba.d: Very dark buckwheat noodles served stacked in three round bowls. The buckwheat is milled with its black husk, which no other region does: the noodle is darker, more fragrant and rougher, and the cooking water is drunk at the end.
s: Use wholemeal buckwheat flour, milled with the husk: that gives Izumo its colour and flavour.
Add the water in three stages, mixing with your fingertips, never all at once — buckwheat absorbs very unevenly.
Knead ten minutes then roll to two millimetres and fold before cutting with a wide blade.
Cook forty seconds in plenty of boiling water and rinse at once in iced water.
Serve stacked in three round bowls, the sauce poured over rather than alongside. Keep the cooking water to drink afterwards.

uwajima-tai-meshi.d: Raw sea bream marinated in egg and soy, poured over hot rice. It should not be confused with Matsuyama's tai meshi, where the fish is cooked with the rice: in Uwajima the fish stays raw, and the two towns do not agree on this.
s: Fillet the sea bream and slice it on the bias, a little thicker than ordinary sashimi.
Make the sauce with soy, mirin, sake and dashi, and cool it completely before beating in the raw eggs.
Added warm, it would coagulate the eggs and the marinade would turn to omelette.
Marinate the fish exactly ten minutes: beyond that the soy salts it through and the flesh hardens.
Pour everything over scalding rice and mix at the table. The rice's heat barely thickens the egg, which is all that is wanted.

jakoten.d: Cakes of small fish ground whole and fried, bones included. Unlike kamaboko the flesh is neither washed nor whitened: bones, skin and innards are ground in with it, which gives the grey colour and the strong flavour.
s: Use very small fish — smelt, anchovy, hotarujako — headed and gutted but not filleted.
Grind them whole through a fine plate, passing twice: the bones must become imperceptible.
Work the paste ten minutes with the salt until it turns tacky and elastic: that is the myosin developing, and without it the cake crumbles in the fryer.
Shape flat half-centimetre ovals between wetted palms.
Fry at 170°C, three minutes a side. Eaten hot with grated ginger, or cold in an udon soup.

mizutaki-hakata.d: A chicken hotpot whose broth turns white and milky from long boiling. The name means cooked in water: no dashi and no seasoning at the start, only chicken and water, and all the flavour comes from collagen drawn out of the bones.
s: Boil the carcasses hard for two hours, uncovered: here a rolling boil is wanted, it emulsifies the collagen.
This is the exact opposite of a clear broth — a mizutaki that stays transparent has failed.
Add the jointed chicken and cook forty minutes more, with no salt and no soy.
Bring the pot to the table and cook the vegetables in it as you go, dipping each mouthful in ponzu.
At the end, tip rice into the remaining broth and bind with beaten egg: this zosui closes the meal.

karashi-renkon.d: Lotus root with its holes packed with mustard miso, battered and fried. It was created in the seventeenth century for a sickly lord of Kumamoto; the recipe stayed a family secret until the end of the Meiji era.
s: Boil the lotus lengths in acidulated water for twenty minutes, so they stay white and slightly crisp.
The vinegar prevents oxidation: without it, lotus browns within minutes in the air.
Mix the miso, mustard and honey, and rest an hour — mustard needs time to develop its heat.
Pack the holes by pressing the miso in with your thumb, from both ends, until they are full.
Coat in a flour and turmeric batter, and fry at 170°C. Serve cold, thinly sliced.

chicken-nanban.d: Fried chicken dipped in sweet vinegar then covered with a thick tartare sauce. Nanban in Japan means anything from the southern barbarians, that is the Portuguese: the technique of vinegar-marinating fried fish is borrowed directly from them.
s: Coat the chicken in flour then beaten egg, with no breadcrumbs: a Portuguese-style coating, light and supple.
Fry at 170°C for eight minutes, until the crust colours without hardening.
Plunge the scalding pieces into the warm sweet vinegar, ten seconds only.
Hot meat draws in the vinegar by capillary action; cooled, it takes up nothing and the dish falls flat.
Make the tartare with chopped hard-boiled egg, onion and gherkins, and spoon it on generously as you serve.

basashi.d: Raw horse sliced thin, served with garlic, ginger and sweet soy. Kumamoto has been its capital since the sixteenth century, when a lord besieged in Korea is said to have had to eat his mounts; horsemeat carries few parasites, which makes eating it raw safer than pork.
s: Use only horsemeat expressly sold for raw consumption, previously frozen at -20°C for 48 hours.
That freezing has been a legal requirement in Japan since 2011: it neutralises sarcocystis, the only parasite genuinely found in horses.
Thaw slowly in the refrigerator, never in water, and slice the meat while still very cold.
Cut across the grain at three millimetres with a perfectly sharp knife, wiped between each slice.
Serve with grated garlic and ginger, sliced onion and soy sweetened with mirin.

sara-udon.d: Fine crisp noodles under a sauced stir-fry of vegetables and seafood. Despite the name it contains no udon: the noodles are fine fried vermicelli, and the dish was invented around 1900 by the same Chinese restaurateur as champon.
s: Stir-fry the pork then the seafood over fierce heat, separately, and set them aside.
Add the vegetables in order of firmness: carrot, cabbage, then bean sprouts last, for ten seconds only.
Moisten with broth and thicken with cornflour slaked in cold water, never tipped in dry.
The sauce must be thick and glossy: too thin, it soaks the noodles before the plate reaches the table.
Lay the fried noodles on the plate and pour the stir-fry over at the last moment. Eaten within five minutes.

toriten.d: Chicken in tempura batter, marinated before coating, served with ponzu. It differs from karaage in the coating: a light tempura batter rather than starch, and the batter stays pale and supple instead of drily crisp.
s: Marinate the chicken thirty minutes in soy, sake, garlic and ginger, then blot it thoroughly.
Make the tempura batter with iced water and barely mix, leaving visible lumps.
Overworked batter develops gluten and turns heavy, drinking up oil.
Use the batter within ten minutes: after that it warms and loses its lightness.
Fry at 175°C for three minutes. Serve with ponzu and Japanese mustard, never the usual tempura sauce.

taco-rice.d: Spiced taco meat, cheese and salad served over Japanese rice. Invented in 1984 by a restaurateur in Kin, near the American base: the soldiers wanted tacos, the locals ate rice, and the compromise became Okinawa's emblematic dish.
s: Fry the minced beef with the onion until it loses all its water and begins to catch.
Add the spices and toast them thirty seconds in the fat before moistening with ketchup and Worcestershire.
Reduce until the meat is dry and glossy: meat in sauce would soak the rice.
Serve on short-grain Japanese rice, never long grain — that is what holds it together on a spoon.
Build in order: rice, meat, grated cheese that melts on contact, then raw lettuce and tomato on top.

jimami-tofu.d: A peanut tofu containing no soy at all, set with sweet potato starch. Its texture is that of a very firm custard rather than tofu: it does not coagulate, it gelatinises, making the name a confusion rather than a kinship of technique.
s: Soak raw peanuts eight hours, then rub them between your hands to remove every red skin.
Those skins give a stubborn bitterness and speckle the preparation brown.
Blend with the water and strain through muslin, pressing very hard: this is the peanut milk, and it must be perfectly smooth.
Slake the starch in that cold milk, then heat gently, stirring without pause for twenty minutes.
The mixture thickens abruptly then turns elastic and pulls from the base. Pour into a mould and set three hours in the cold.

umibudo.d: A seaweed in clusters of small beads that burst under the tooth. Each bead is a vesicle full of seawater; that salty burst is the whole point, and it is lost irretrievably on contact with cold.
s: Never refrigerate umibudo: cold deflates the vesicles, and they never plump again.
Keep them at room temperature in their salt water, and eat them within three days.
Rinse them in seawater or heavily salted water, never fresh water — osmosis would burst them instantly.
Dip them thirty seconds in iced water just before serving, which firms them without deflating them.
Do not pour the sauce over: serve it alongside and dip each mouthful, or the soy's salt empties them.

dorayaki.d: Two soft pancakes joined around red bean paste. The name means grilled on a gong: legend has a wounded samurai leaving his gong with a farmer, who used it as a griddle.
s: Whisk the eggs, sugar, honey and mirin until the mixture pales and doubles in volume.
Fold in the sifted flour without working it, then rest the batter thirty minutes in the cold.
Slake the bicarbonate in the water and add it just before cooking: added early, it loses all its lift.
Cook in a non-stick pan with no fat, over low heat, until bubbles break the surface.
Wipe the pan between each pancake: the least trace of fat marks the surface and the dorayaki loses its even colour.

nikujaga.d: A beef and potato stew in sweet soy, the family dish par excellence. It is said to have been born in the imperial navy around 1870: an admiral trained in England wanted a beef stew, and the cook, lacking wine and brown sauce, used soy and sugar.
s: Use very thinly sliced beef, almost translucent: the stew cooks forty minutes and a thick piece would toughen.
Fry it first, briefly, then add the vegetables in large pieces and the dashi.
Add the sugar before the soy, always: large sugar molecules penetrate more slowly, and the reverse order shuts them out.
Set an otoshibuta, a lid smaller than the pan resting on the liquid itself, which spreads the broth without reducing it too fast.
Simmer thirty minutes, then turn off the heat and let it cool: it is in cooling that the flavour enters the potatoes.

tandoori-chicken.d: Chicken marinated in yoghurt and spices, roasted in a vertical clay oven. It was developed in Peshawar before Partition then brought to Delhi in 1947 by Kundan Lal Gujral, who also invented butter chicken to use up the leftovers.
s: Remove all the skin and score the flesh to the bone every two centimetres.
Skin stops the marinade entering and burns before the flesh cooks: that is why tandoori is always skinless.
Make a first short marinade of lemon, salt and chilli, one hour, to open the fibres.
Drain the yoghurt overnight in muslin before the second marinade: runny yoghurt slides off instead of clinging.
Cook six hours later at 250°C, on a rack and uncovered, brushing with mustard oil twice.

chole-bhature.d: A spiced chickpea curry with a puffed fried bread. The chole's very dark colour comes not from any colouring but from black tea: the chickpeas are cooked with a tea bag, which stains them without affecting the flavour.
s: Soak the chickpeas overnight with a pinch of bicarbonate, then cook them with the tea bag.
Take out the tea after twenty minutes: longer, and its tannins turn the chickpeas bitter and slightly astringent.
Brown the onions at length, fifteen minutes at least, until they melt into a dark paste.
For the bhature, use a yoghurt and semolina dough left to ferment three hours — that is what makes them puff.
Fry at 190°C, holding the bread under the oil for two seconds: it balloons at once.

aloo-paratha.d: A flatbread stuffed with spiced potato, cooked in ghee on a griddle. It is the Punjabi breakfast, served with yoghurt, white butter and pickles; the filling must be cold and perfectly dry, or the bread tears.
s: Steam the potatoes, never boil them: boiled, they take on water and the filling turns wet.
Rice them and cool them completely, uncovered, for a good half hour.
Knead a soft wholemeal dough and rest it thirty minutes under a damp cloth.
Form a cup in your palm, fill generously and close by drawing up the edges, then flatten by hand before using the pin.
Cook on a hot griddle, brushing with ghee, until brown spots appear on both sides.

naan-beurre.d: A leavened flatbread slapped onto the wall of the tandoor and brushed with ghee. Unlike chapati, naan contains leavening and white flour: it was a court bread, confined to Mughal royal kitchens until the twentieth century.
s: Knead a soft dough and prove it two hours: it should stay slightly tacky to the finger.
A firm dough gives a brittle naan; it is the moisture that creates the steam and the big bubbles.
Shape into a teardrop, by hand as far as possible, and wet one face with water before slapping it into the oven.
With no tandoor, heat a cast-iron pan white hot, lay the naan wet side down and cover.
Invert the pan towards the flame to colour the top, then brush with melted ghee as it comes off.

yakhni-pulao.d: Rice cooked in a scented lamb broth, pale and unspiced with chilli. It differs from biryani on one decisive point: here rice and meat cook together in one broth, whereas biryani layers two separately cooked preparations.
s: Boil the lamb with the whole spices tied in muslin for forty minutes, and strain the broth.
The muslin lets you remove every spice at once: in a pulao one should never bite into a clove.
Soak the basmati for thirty minutes only, then drain it half an hour uncovered.
Fry the onions to deep brown, set half aside, and brown the meat in the rest.
Moisten with measured broth, one and a half parts to one of rice, and cook fifteen minutes covered then ten off the heat.

laal-maas.d: An intensely red lamb curry with mathania chillies and garlic. It was the hunting dish of the Rajput kings: chilli in quantity masked the strong taste of game, and the absence of tomato or onion makes it a curry of disconcerting simplicity.
s: Use mathania chillies or failing that Kashmiri: they colour intensely without burning as much as they look.
Soak them twenty minutes in hot water then blend them to a smooth paste with the garlic.
Brown the meat in ghee over fierce heat, until coloured on all sides.
Add the beaten yoghurt off the heat, a spoonful at a time, stirring: poured in at once into a hot pan it splits without fail.
Simmer an hour and a half covered. The ghee should rise to the surface, the sign the curry is ready.

rajma-chawal.d: Stewed red kidney beans served over white rice, the family dish of North India. The kidney bean is American: it came with the Portuguese in the sixteenth century and naturalised so thoroughly that it now passes for immemorially Indian.
s: Soak the beans twelve hours: without soaking they never cook properly and stay toxic.
Raw kidney beans contain phytohaemagglutinin: a hard boil of at least ten minutes is essential, a gentle simmer will not do.
Boil hard for ten minutes, then simmer an hour and a half until they crush easily.
Crush a quarter of them against the side and stir them back in: that gives the silky sauce, with no flour and no cream.
Make the masala separately — browned onions, tomato, spices — and bring it to the beans for twenty minutes.

amritsari-kulcha.d: A potato-stuffed bread, crisp and layered, crushed by hand as it leaves the oven. Crushing it is not decorative: it bursts the layers and releases the steam, without which the kulcha goes soft within two minutes.
s: Use dried pomegranate seeds, anardana: their sourness is what sets the Amritsari kulcha apart from every other.
Mash the steamed potatoes and cool them completely before seasoning.
Laminate the dough: roll it out, brush with ghee, roll into a rope, coil it into a spiral, and rest twenty minutes.
That lamination gives the layers; without it you get an ordinary paratha.
Bake in a tandoor or at 250°C, then crush the bread between your palms and douse it with melted ghee.

pakora.d: Vegetable fritters in chickpea flour, fried and served with chutney. Chickpea flour has no gluten: the batter has nothing to make it rise, and it is the vegetable's own steam alone that creates the wanted ragged texture.
s: Salt the sliced onions and leave them ten minutes: they release the water that hydrates the batter, so less plain water is needed.
Work in the chickpea flour gradually, to a batter that coats without running.
Add the ajwain: it is there for digestion as much as flavour, and its absence is noticed at once.
Fry at 170°C first, four minutes, then drain and rest.
Return them to 190°C for one minute before serving. That double fry keeps them crisp for half an hour.

jalebi.d: Spirals of fermented batter fried then steeped in sugar syrup. The fermentation sets them apart from imarti and zulbia: it gives a faint sourness that cuts the syrup, and without it a jalebi is merely cloying.
s: Mix flour, yoghurt and water and ferment twelve hours at room temperature: the batter should smell sour and bubble.
The syrup must be at one-thread stage, 105°C: thicker, it will not penetrate; thinner, the jalebi goes soggy.
Add lemon juice to the syrup to stop it crystallising as it cools.
Pipe the batter into the ghee at 175°C in spirals, through a pierced squeeze bottle, starting from the centre.
Steep them scalding in the warm syrup, thirty seconds exactly. The temperature contrast draws the syrup in.

chaat-de-delhi.d: A street snack combining crisp elements, yoghurt, chutneys and sour spices. Chaat rests on a precise principle: it must bring six tastes together at once — sweet, salty, sour, hot, bitter and astringent — and the balance between them makes a vendor's name.
s: Make both chutneys the day before: the green with mint and coriander, the brown with tamarind and palm sugar.
Whisk the yoghurt with a little water and a pinch of sugar until it falls from the spoon without being runny.
Build the chaat in order: crisp elements at the bottom, potato and chickpeas, yoghurt, then the chutneys.
The sev and pomegranate go on at the very last moment, as you serve.
Put on in advance, they soften within two minutes, and a chaat without crunch is no longer a chaat.

kulfi.d: A dense ice of reduced milk, set in conical moulds without churning. It is precisely the absence of churning that makes kulfi: with no air worked in, it melts very slowly and its texture is dense, almost waxy, the opposite of a Western ice cream.
s: Reduce the milk by half over medium heat, a good hour, scraping the sides regularly.
The skin that forms at the edges is not discarded: it is scraped back in, and it gives kulfi its characteristic grain.
Add the sugar only once the reduction is done, then the cardamom and infused saffron.
Cool completely before moulding: poured warm, kulfi forms large crystals as it freezes.
Freeze six hours in conical moulds. Unmould by running the mould under warm water for two seconds.

awadhi-biryani.d: A pale, fragrant biryani cooked sealed under a crust of dough. It opposes Hyderabad's in every respect: here the meat is pre-cooked in broth rather than marinated raw, and the spices are infused then removed, giving an aromatic dish that is not hot.
s: Cook the lamb in broth with the spices tied in muslin for an hour, until nearly tender.
Parboil the rice for five minutes only in plenty of salted water: it should snap cleanly between the nails.
Layer meat, rice, fried onions and saffron milk, then seal the pot with a rope of dough all round the lid.
That seal, the dum, traps every bit of steam: it is what cooks the rice and makes the biryani, and a badly sealed pot fails it.
Cook thirty minutes over very low heat on a diffuser. Open at the table, breaking the crust of dough.

petha.d: Candied ash gourd, translucent and crisp. Legend has them born in Shah Jahan's kitchens during the building of the Taj Mahal; their transparency comes from a lime treatment that firms the fruit's cell walls.
s: Peel the gourd, remove the seeds and cut it into cubes, then prick each piece twenty times with a fork.
Soak twelve hours in limewater: the calcium binds to the pectins and makes the flesh crisp and translucent.
Then rinse at great length, five or six changes of water, until every trace of lime is gone.
Blanch with a pinch of alum, then poach in sugar syrup in three stages, resting overnight between each.
Those successive steepings replace the fruit's water with sugar without bursting it. Finally air-dry twelve hours.

banarasi-dum-aloo.d: Small potatoes fried then simmered in a sauce with no onion or garlic. The absence is deliberate: the temple cooking of Varanasi excludes onion and garlic as stimulants, and the sauce rests on yoghurt, tomato and asafoetida.
s: Steam the potatoes, peel them and prick them all over with a fork.
Those holes let the sauce in: without them the potato stays bland at the centre however long it cooks.
Fry them in ghee until golden and slightly wrinkled, then set aside.
Toast the asafoetida a few seconds in the hot ghee: it stands in for garlic, but burnt it turns frankly unpleasant.
Add the beaten yoghurt off the heat and return the potatoes for twenty minutes, covered.

poha-jalebi.d: Sautéed flattened rice served with a sweet jalebi, the Indore breakfast. Pairing savoury and sweet on the same breakfast plate is peculiar to Madhya Pradesh; the two are eaten together, mouthful by mouthful, not one after the other.
s: Use thick poha, never thin: thin poha collapses into paste the moment it is wetted.
Rinse it in a sieve under a thin stream of water for ten seconds only, then drain it ten minutes.
It should crush under a finger without stickiness. Over-soaked, nothing will save it.
Pop the mustard seeds in hot oil before anything else: they must jump, that is the signal.
Add the poha off the heat and fold gently with a fork, never a spoon, which would crush it.

bhutte-ka-kees.d: Fresh corn grated and cooked in milk with spices and coconut. It is sold in the evening in Indore's Sarafa lane, a jewellers' market by day and a food night market from eight in the evening to two in the morning.
s: Grate the fresh corn on the medium blade, straight off the cob, to get a lumpy purée and not whole kernels.
Choose ears with milky kernels: mature corn gives a floury texture and a flat taste.
Pop the mustard in ghee, add asafoetida, ginger and chilli, then the grated corn.
Stir without pause for five minutes before adding milk: raw corn catches instantly.
Add the hot milk little by little, as for a risotto, to a creamy mass. Lemon and grated coconut off the heat.

bhopali-gosht-korma.d: A lamb korma with almonds and yoghurt, mild and deeply fragrant. Bhopal was ruled by four successive women between 1819 and 1926, the Begums, whose kitchens gave the city a culinary tradition distinct from Lucknow's or Hyderabad's.
s: Soak the almonds, cashews and white poppy seeds for an hour, then blend them to a perfectly smooth paste.
White poppy seed is korma's traditional thickener: it gives body without a creamy taste, and nothing truly replaces it.
Fry the onions to deep brown, then blend them with the yoghurt into a purée.
Brown the meat, add the onion purée then the nut paste, and moisten barely.
Simmer two hours covered. A korma must never boil: at a rolling boil the yoghurt splits and the sauce goes grainy.

malaiyo.d: A milk foam so light it dissolves before it can be swallowed, made only in winter. The milk is left outdoors all night to catch the dew: without it the foam will not rise, and the season ends the moment the nights warm.
s: Boil the milk with the saffron and cardamom, then let it cool.
Leave it outside all winter night under muslin: it is the dew and the night cold that prepare the milk.
At dawn, whisk it with a bamboo whisk for an hour, skimming off the foam as it rises.
The whisking must be done in the cold: as soon as the milk warms, the foam collapses and will not rise again.
Pile the foam into small bowls, sweeten barely and scatter with pistachios. Eaten within the minute.

pav-bhaji.d: A spiced vegetable mash served with buttered griddled rolls. It was invented in the 1850s for Bombay's textile workers: a complete hot meal eaten standing during the midday break, made from the previous day's leftover vegetables.
s: Steam all the vegetables then crush them roughly with a hand masher, directly in the pan.
Never blend: bhaji must keep lumps, and a smooth purée makes it bland and pasty.
Fry the onions, ginger, garlic and tomatoes at length, until the mixture pulls from the base.
Add the masala and toast it in the butter for thirty seconds before adding the vegetables.
Do not stint on the butter: it binds everything, and a lean pav bhaji has never convinced anyone.

bhel-puri.d: Puffed rice tossed with chutneys, onion and crisp bits, assembled to order. It is the snack of Mumbai's beaches; it must be eaten within two minutes of mixing, after which the puffed rice slumps and the dish loses its point.
s: Warm the puffed rice a few minutes in a low oven before assembling: airborne moisture softens it within a day.
Make both chutneys ahead and keep them cold, but add them only at the very last moment.
Blot the cut vegetables on paper: their water is the first enemy of crispness.
Toss everything in a large bowl by hand, lifting rather than stirring.
Serve at once, without exception. A bhel puri that waits five minutes is a bhel puri lost.

bombay-duck-fry.d: A lizardfish with very soft flesh, crumbed in semolina and fried. Despite the name it is no duck: the term is said to come from the Bombay mail trains that carried the dried fish, whose powerful smell filled the carriages.
s: Use fresh fish if you can find it: the dried kind, very pungent, needs an hour's soaking and quite different handling.
The flesh is up to 90% water: press the fillets gently between two cloths for twenty minutes before crumbing.
Marinate in lemon, turmeric and chilli for half an hour, no longer — the acid eventually breaks down this fragile flesh.
Crumb in fine semolina mixed with rice flour: semolina alone falls off, rice flour makes it hold.
Fry at 180°C, two minutes a side, turning once only. The fish breaks at the least excess handling.

misal-pav.d: A sprouted bean curry topped with crisp bits, served with a soft roll. The kat, the red oil floating on top, is poured separately and to taste: it makes a misal's reputation, and some Pune houses serve it in a jug.
s: Sprout the moth beans over two days: soaked twelve hours then drained and covered with a damp cloth.
Dry-toast the grated coconut and onion to deep brown before blending them: that toasting gives the smoky taste.
Make the kat separately: a generous quantity of oil heated with the spice paste, until it splits and reddens.
The red oil is skimmed off the top with a ladle and served apart, never stirred into the curry.
Assemble at the last moment: beans, crisp farsan, raw onion, coriander, lemon. The kat is poured at the table.

puran-poli.d: A flatbread filled with a paste of split peas and palm sugar. It is made for Holi and Gudi Padwa; the pea cooking water, called katachi amti, is never discarded and is used for a spiced soup served alongside.
s: Cook the split peas until they crush, then drain them thoroughly, keeping the water for the amti.
Mix them with the palm sugar and cook dry, stirring, until the mass pulls from the base in one piece.
A filling that is too wet soaks through the dough and burns on the griddle: the one real obstacle in this recipe.
Pass the filling through a food mill while hot, to make it perfectly smooth.
Enclose it in a soft, heavily oiled dough, roll it out carefully and cook in ghee on a gentle griddle.

pani-puri.d: Small hollow spheres filled with stuffing and spiced water, eaten in one mouthful. They carry six different names across the country — golgappa in Delhi, puchka in Kolkata, gup chup in Odisha — and each city holds its version to be the only true one.
s: Knead a very firm dough of fine semolina, almost unworkable, and rest it an hour under a damp cloth.
Roll it paper-thin and cut small four-centimetre discs.
Fry at 190°C, pressing each disc under the oil with a skimmer: the violent steam balloons it into a hollow sphere.
Oil that is too cool gives flat greasy discs: the one point where this recipe genuinely fails.
Make the green mint water the day before and keep it iced. Pierce, fill, top up and eat in one go.

dhokla.d: A savoury steamed cake of fermented chickpea, light as a sponge. The batter's natural fermentation produces carbon dioxide: that is what raises a dhokla, and quick versions with bicarbonate have neither its tang nor its texture.
s: Mix chickpea flour, yoghurt and water and ferment eight hours somewhere warm.
The batter should have visibly risen and smell frankly sour: under-fermented, it gives a dense cake.
Add the eno or bicarbonate at the very last second, stir three times and steam immediately.
The gas escapes within a minute: any hesitation at this stage is paid for with a flat dhokla.
Steam fifteen minutes over a fierce boil, then pour over a tempering of mustard, curry leaf and sesame in scalding oil.

thepla.d: A soft, spiced flatbread with fresh fenugreek that keeps for days. It is the Gujarati travelling bread: it holds a week without refrigeration, and turns up in the luggage of almost any Gujarati on the move.
s: Chop the fresh fenugreek very finely and salt it ten minutes: it releases water that will hydrate the dough.
That bitter water is what gives the flavour: throwing it out and adding plain water makes an ordinary bread.
Knead with the flours and yoghurt without adding water until the dough has come together.
Rest twenty minutes only — a long rest turns the fenugreek bitter.
Cook on a griddle, brushing with oil, until brown spots appear. Keeps a week wrapped in a cloth.

fafda-jalebi.d: Crisp chickpea strips served with sweet jalebis and grated papaya. It is the Gujarati Sunday breakfast and the ritual dish of Dussehra; combining salty, sweet and sour in one mouthful is the very principle of it.
s: Knead a very firm chickpea dough, slapping it against the worktop rather than kneading it.
Spread each portion with your palm in a single sliding movement towards you, forming a long even strip.
It is a gesture that takes practice: the dough must stretch without tearing, in one pull.
Fry at 180°C until the sizzling stops — the noise ends when all the water has gone.
Serve with hot jalebis, fried chillies and a salad of grated green papaya with salt and mustard.

khakhra.d: A flatbread cooked until brittle as a biscuit, pressed throughout the cooking. Continuous pressure with a cloth pad is what drives out every trace of moisture: it is what takes the bread from supple to brittle, and nothing replaces it.
s: Knead a firm dough and rest it thirty minutes, then roll it as thin as possible, to transparency.
A thick khakhra stays supple at the centre however long it cooks: thinness is the first condition.
Cook on a griddle over very low heat, never fierce — over high heat the surface burns before the inside dries.
Press continuously with a folded cloth pad, turning the bread, for three to four minutes a side.
The khakhra is ready when evenly pale brown and sounding hollow. Keeps a month in an airtight tin.

handvo.d: A savoury cake of fermented rice and lentils with grated vegetables, baked with a crust. The thick golden bottom crust is the part people compete for; the handvo is turned halfway through to get two rather than one.
s: Soak the rice and lentils six hours, then grind them to a coarse paste — handvo must keep some grain.
Mix with the yoghurt and ferment twelve hours: the batter should rise and smell sour.
Grate the bottle gourd and press it: its water would make a soggy cake, but do not throw it away, it serves to adjust the batter.
Add the eno just before baking and pour the batter onto a tempering of mustard and sesame already hot in the tin.
Cook covered twenty minutes, turn it over in one piece, then twenty minutes on the other side. Two crusts beat one.

xacuti.d: A very dark Goan curry with toasted coconut and a dozen spices. The name is pronounced shakuti: the spelling is Portuguese, the x standing in sixteenth-century Portuguese for a sound Konkani wrote otherwise.
s: Dry-toast the grated coconut over low heat, stirring without pause, until it turns deep brown.
That hard toasting gives xacuti its almost black colour and nutty taste; pale coconut gives a pale, flat curry.
Toast each spice separately for a few seconds, then grind them with the coconut and a little water to a smooth paste.
Brown the chicken, add the softened onions then the paste, and cook it ten minutes in the fat before moistening.
Simmer forty minutes, adding tamarind at the end. Xacuti should be thick and nearly black.

goan-fish-curry.d: A fish curry with coconut milk, chilli and kokum, bright orange and frankly sour. Kokum, a dried black fruit, brings a fruity acidity that neither tamarind nor lemon reproduces; it is the signature of the Konkan coast.
s: Blend fresh grated coconut with the spices and a little hot water to a perfectly smooth paste, then press out the milk.
Do not use toasted coconut here: unlike xacuti, a Goan fish curry must stay bright and clear.
Soak the kokum ten minutes in warm water and add it with its liquid.
Cook the sauce twenty minutes uncovered before laying in the fish, never letting it boil.
Poach the fish eight minutes at a tremble, without stirring. Shake the pan, do not stir.

bebinca.d: A cake of sixteen layers baked one at a time, with coconut milk and egg yolk. Each layer is baked separately and must colour before the next: it takes three hours, and the number of layers was once a marker of wealth.
s: Beat the yolks, sugar and coconut milk, then fold in the sifted flour: the batter should be as loose as pancake batter.
Strain it: the least lump shows in a three-millimetre layer.
Butter the tin generously with ghee, pour a ladleful and put it under the grill until the surface browns.
Brush with ghee between every layer, without exception: the ghee separates the layers and is what makes them visible when cut.
Repeat sixteen times. Cool twelve hours before turning out: warm, the cake tears between layers.

prawn-balchao.d: Prawns preserved in a chilli and vinegar paste, halfway between pickle and curry. Balchão descends from Macanese balichão, itself from Malacca: a recipe that went twice round the Portuguese empire before settling in Goa.
s: Grind the spices and garlic in palm vinegar, never in water: the vinegar is the preservative, and water would turn the preparation.
Fry the prawns very briefly, one minute, and remove them before making the sauce.
Cook the paste in oil for twenty minutes over low heat, until the oil splits and rises to the surface.
That separation is the sign the paste is cooked: without it the balchão tastes of raw vinegar and will not keep.
Return the prawns for five minutes only. Balchão keeps a fortnight in the cold and improves over the first days.

rasgulla.d: Balls of fresh cheese poached in a light syrup, spongy and saturated with sugar. West Bengal and Odisha fought over its origin in the courts for years; both were finally granted separate geographical indications.
s: Curdle the boiling milk with lemon juice, then strain and rinse the curd in cold water to remove the acidity.
Press it thirty minutes only: too dry and it will not swell; too wet and the balls disintegrate in the syrup.
Knead the paneer with your palm for ten minutes, until perfectly smooth and slightly greasy to the touch.
That kneading is the whole secret: it breaks the grains and gives the elasticity that lets the ball double in size.
Poach in a light syrup, covered, fifteen minutes at a rolling boil. The balls must double; if they stay small, the kneading was not enough.

mishti-doi.d: A yoghurt sweetened with caramelised palm sugar, set in an earthenware pot. The porous clay is not decorative: it absorbs whey through its walls, concentrating the yoghurt and giving it a firmness no sealed vessel allows.
s: Reduce the milk by a third, a good hour, scraping the sides to return the skin to the pan.
Melt the palm sugar separately until it frankly caramelises, then stir it into the hot milk.
Cool to exactly 45°C before adding the yoghurt: hotter kills the cultures, colder and they will not start.
Pour into unglazed clay pots that have been soaked in water for an hour.
Ferment eight hours somewhere warm, untouched, then chill six hours before serving.

shorshe-ilish.d: Hilsa shad poached in a pungent mustard paste with mustard oil. Hilsa is an extremely rich fish but riddled with fine Y-shaped bones; Bengalis eat them without removing them, separating them in the mouth by a technique learnt in childhood.
s: Soak the mustard seeds twenty minutes in warm salted water with a green chilli.
Salt and chilli during grinding prevent bitterness: ground alone, mustard turns frankly bitter and the dish is lost.
Grind slowly in a mortar or a blender on low speed, adding the water little by little.
Heat the mustard oil to smoking then let it fall back before using it: raw, it is acrid and aggressive.
Lay the fish steaks in the paste, cover and poach twelve minutes over very low heat, never stirring or turning.

kathi-roll.d: A paratha rolled around grilled meat with egg, eaten walking. It was invented at Nizam's in Kolkata in the 1930s: office workers wanted to take their kebab away without dirtying their hands, so the skewer was rolled into the bread.
s: Marinate the chicken two hours in drained yoghurt, garlic, ginger and spices.
Grill it on a very hot plate in a thin layer, until the edges caramelise.
Make layered parathas and keep them supple under a cloth, stacked — a dry paratha cracks when rolled.
Beat an egg and pour it onto the paratha lying flat in the pan: it bonds to the bread, which is what makes a kathi roll leakproof.
Fill with meat, raw onion with lemon and chaat masala, roll tightly and wrap in paper.

sandesh.d: A confection of barely sweetened fresh cheese, pressed into small shapes. Unlike rasgulla, sandesh is not poached: the curd is cooked dry with sugar, very briefly, and the whole difficulty is stopping before it turns grainy.
s: Curdle the milk, strain and rinse in iced water, then press under a weight for a full hour.
The curd must be frankly dry: any residual moisture will make the sandesh melt as it cooks.
Knead it with your palm for ten minutes until smooth, then work in the icing sugar.
Cook over very low heat for five to seven minutes only, stirring without pause: the mass should pull away but stay supple.
One minute too long and sandesh turns sandy and brittle. Mould it warm, decorate and set in the cold.

luchi-alur-dom.d: White puffed fried breads served with a potato curry. Luchi differs from puri in the flour: refined white here, wholemeal for puri, giving a paler, softer bread that stays white in the fryer.
s: Rub the ghee into the flour before adding water: that rubbing stops the gluten developing and gives a tender luchi.
Knead briefly to a firm dough and rest it thirty minutes under a damp cloth.
Do not use flour for rolling but a little oil: flour burns in the bath and blackens the oil.
Fry at 180°C, holding the disc under the oil for two seconds. It puffs at once and must stay white.
Oil that is too hot colours it before it puffs; that is the only mistake possible with luchi.

kosha-mangsho.d: An almost dry mutton curry, very dark brown, got by prolonged sautéing. Kosha means rubbed, worked: the meat is stirred in its sauce for over an hour, with no water added, until everything has reduced and browned.
s: Marinate the mutton two hours in yoghurt with crushed garlic and ginger.
Caramelise a spoonful of sugar in the hot mustard oil before anything else: that burnt sugar gives the dark colour.
Add the meat and stir it without pause over medium heat for forty minutes, without adding a drop of water.
That prolonged sautéing makes the dish: each time the sauce catches, you scrape and continue, and the colour deepens.
Then add a little hot water and simmer an hour covered. Kosha is ready when the oil frankly separates.

masor-tenga.d: A light, sour Assamese fish curry with no hot spices. The acidity comes from thekera, a dried mangosteen, or from lemon; it is a summer dish meant to cool, and the absence of chilli and heavy oil sets it apart from every neighbouring curry.
s: Rub the fish steaks with turmeric and salt and leave them twenty minutes before browning them in mustard oil.
Fry the fish first and set it aside: added raw to the broth it flakes apart and clouds the soup.
Crackle the fenugreek seeds in the oil for a few seconds only — burnt, they turn bitter.
Add tomatoes and gourd, moisten and cook fifteen minutes, then add the soaked thekera.
Return the fish for five minutes. The broth should stay clear and frankly sour, never thick.

pitha-assam.d: Glutinous rice cakes filled with coconut and palm sugar, griddled or fried. They are made for Bihu, the Assamese harvest festival; the rice must be soaked, pounded and sieved the same day, since bought flour lacks the same plasticity.
s: Soak the glutinous rice six hours, drain it an hour then pound it while still damp and sieve it finely.
The flour must stay slightly damp to the touch: dry, it will not bind and the pitha splits as it cooks.
Dry-toast the sesame and coconut, then mix them with melted palm sugar and cool.
Spread a thin layer of flour on the hot griddle, let it set for thirty seconds, fill and fold.
Pitha binds through the rice's own steam alone: there is no egg and no binder, and too hot a griddle stops it sticking.

haleem.d: A porridge of wheat and meat pounded for hours until it turns stringy. Hyderabadi haleem has held a protected geographical indication since 2010; it is made only during Ramadan, and restaurants close that counter the rest of the year.
s: Soak the cracked wheat and lentils overnight, then cook them separately until they collapse completely.
Cook the meat separately with the spices for three hours, until it falls from the bones.
Bring everything together and pound with a wooden pestle, without pause, for two hours.
That pounding is the dish itself: it breaks the meat fibres and blends them into the wheat starch, which no blender reproduces.
Haleem is ready when it pulls into long strands and no piece is identifiable. Serve with melted ghee and lemon.

double-ka-meetha.d: Sliced bread fried then steeped in saffron milk with dried fruit. Double is Hyderabadi slang for sliced bread, because it doubles in size as it bakes; the dessert has been served at the city's Muslim weddings since the time of the Nizams.
s: Cut off the crusts and cut the bread into triangles, then let it dry two hours in the air.
Fresh bread drinks ghee like a sponge and the dessert turns greasy and heavy.
Fry in ghee to golden brown, then drain on a rack rather than paper, so both faces stay crisp.
Reduce the milk by a third with the saffron and cardamom, then sweeten.
Pour the hot milk over the bread just before serving, not in advance: the bread should be soaked but keep its shape.

osmania-irani-chai.d: A sweet-salty butter biscuit dunked in heavily reduced milk tea. The biscuit is named after the last Nizam, Osman Ali Khan; Hyderabad's Irani cafés, run by Zoroastrians who came from Persia in the nineteenth century, have served it for over a century.
s: The biscuit must be as frankly salty as it is sweet: that unusual balance makes an Osmania, and a timid hand with salt makes it ordinary.
Cream the butter and icing sugar at length, then fold in flour, milk powder and cardamom without kneading.
Rest the dough an hour in the cold, roll to seven millimetres and cut discs.
Bake 15 minutes at 170°C: the biscuits should stay pale and barely colour at the edges.
For the chai, boil the tea in the milk for twenty minutes, pouring it from height between two vessels to aerate it.

idli-sambar.d: Steamed cakes of fermented rice and lentils with a sour lentil stew. The fermentation relies on a bacterium naturally present on the skin of urad lentils: which is why they are never washed too much, and why the batter rises with no added yeast.
s: Soak rice and lentils separately for six hours, with the fenugreek among the lentils.
Grind the lentils first, with iced water and in bursts: the batter must stay cold, the grinder's heat would kill the cultures.
Then grind the rice more coarsely and mix by hand — the hand carries the cultures, it is said, and the practice is universal.
Ferment ten hours at 28-30°C: the batter should double and smell frankly sour.
Do not stir the risen batter before pouring it into the moulds: every turn of the spoon drives out gas and weighs the idli down.

meen-curry-kerala.d: A deep red fish curry with kudampuli, cooked in an earthenware pot. Kudampuli, or Malabar tamarind, darkens the curry and gives a smoky sourness; the unglazed clay manchatti absorbs and returns the flavour from one day to the next.
s: Soak the kudampuli twenty minutes in warm water; do not substitute ordinary tamarind, the acidity is not the same.
Use coconut oil and nothing else: it gives the recognisable smell of a Kerala curry.
Crackle the mustard and fenugreek, then fry the shallots, garlic, ginger and curry leaves at length.
Add the chilli paste and cook it in the oil until it splits, before any liquid goes in.
Lay in the fish, cover and simmer fifteen minutes without stirring. The curry is better the next day.

avial.d: A mixture of vegetables cut into batons bound with coconut and yoghurt, barely spiced. Legend credits it to Bhima of the Mahabharata, who improvised a dish from every leftover vegetable; it is the centrepiece of the sadya, the banquet served on a banana leaf.
s: Cut all the vegetables into batons of the same size, five centimetres by one: the shape is canonical and part of the dish.
Add them in order of firmness, a few minutes apart, in very little water.
The vegetables must stay whole and recognisable: a puréed avial has failed.
Grind the fresh coconut with the cumin and green chilli, coarsely, without making a smooth paste.
Add the coconut then the yoghurt off the heat, and finish with a thread of raw coconut oil and curry leaves.

ven-pongal.d: A porridge of rice and mung lentils with pepper, cumin and ghee. Ven means white: it is the savoury version of pongal, as against the sweet sakkarai pongal, and black pepper entirely replaces chilli.
s: Dry-toast the mung lentils until fragrant before rinsing them: that toasting gives the nutty flavour.
Cook rice and lentils together in plenty of water, until everything collapses into porridge.
Pongal must be frankly soft and loose; firm, it hardens as it cools and becomes inedible.
Crack the pepper roughly in a mortar rather than grinding it: you should bite into pieces.
Fry the cashews, pepper, cumin and curry leaves in ghee and pour the lot over the pongal.

mysore-pak.d: A confection of chickpea flour, ghee and sugar, porous and melting. It was created around 1935 in the kitchens of Mysore Palace by the cook Kakasura Madappa; the original used a quantity of ghee most modern recipes no longer dare.
s: Sift the chickpea flour three times and dry-toast it two minutes: without that the raw taste dominates.
Bring the sugar and water to 118°C on a thermometer, the soft ball stage, before working in the flour.
Pour in boiling ghee in a stream, ladle by ladle, without ever stopping stirring.
It is the gradual addition of ghee that creates the honeycomb: poured in at once it splits and the mysore pak turns dense and greasy.
Stop when the mass foams and pulls from the base. Pour at once and cut after three minutes, no later.

bisi-bele-bath.d: A one-pot dish of rice, lentils and vegetables bound by a coconut masala. The name means literally hot lentil rice in Kannada: it is never eaten cold, and its texture tightens as it cools to the point of becoming a block.
s: Toast each masala spice separately, dry and over low heat: together, some burn while others stay raw.
Toast the coconut last and cool everything before grinding — ground hot, the spices release their oil and form a paste.
Cook the rice and lentils together, longer than usual: they must collapse, unlike a pulao.
Add the tamarind, vegetables and masala, and cook twenty minutes more.
The dish must be frankly loose as it leaves the heat: it thickens enormously within ten minutes. Serve scalding with ghee.

rasam.d: A clear broth of tamarind, pepper and tomato, drunk or poured over rice. It is never boiled once seasoned: the moment it boils, rasam loses its perfume and goes flat, and knowing when to cut the heat is the whole art of it.
s: Crack the pepper, cumin and garlic roughly in a mortar just before use: ground ahead, they lose most of their perfume.
Cook the tamarind water with the tomatoes and turmeric for ten minutes, until the raw tamarind smell goes.
Add the lentil cooking water and the cracked powder, and watch the pan.
Cut the heat the moment white foam rises to the surface, before a proper boil: that is the signal.
Pour over a tempering of mustard, chilli and curry leaves fried in ghee, and cover at once.

puttu-kadala.d: A cylinder of rice flour and coconut steamed and served with a black chickpea curry. Puttu is cooked in a bamboo or brass tube; the word comes from Tamil and means portioned, from the way it breaks into sections.
s: Dry-toast the rice flour five minutes, then cool it before moistening.
Moisten it with salted water using your fingertips, until it barely clumps under pressure without forming a paste.
This is the most delicate point: too dry and the puttu crumbles; too wet and it turns dense and heavy.
Sieve it, then fill the tube alternating layers of flour and grated coconut, never pressing.
Ten minutes' steaming is enough. Push the cylinder out of the tube with a stick and serve with the chickpea curry.

thayir-sadam.d: Rice mixed with yoghurt and milk, tempered with spices, eaten at the end of a meal. It closes every Tamil meal and acts as a buffer after sour and spicy dishes; it also travels well, and is the South Indian train meal par excellence.
s: Cook the rice longer than usual, until frankly soft, then half-crush it with a spoon.
Let it cool to warm before adding the yoghurt: hot, it would curdle the yoghurt into whey.
Add milk as well as yoghurt: it tempers the acidity and stops the dish turning too sour within hours.
Crackle mustard and urad lentils in hot oil with the chilli and curry leaves, and pour over the rice.
Salt at the last moment: salted ahead, the yoghurt weeps and the rice goes runny.

hui-guo-rou.d: Pork belly poached then stir-fried with fermented chilli bean paste. The Chinese name means meat returned to the wok: it was first boiled as an offering to the ancestors, then re-fried to be eaten, and the ritual made the recipe.
s: Poach the whole belly thirty minutes with ginger and leek, until a chopstick passes through without resistance.
Cool it completely, two hours in the refrigerator: warm, it cannot be sliced thin.
Cut two-millimetre slices, as wide as possible — the thinness makes the dish.
Stir-fry them dry in the wok until they curl into cups and the fat turns translucent.
Only then add the doubanjiang and let it toast in the rendered fat, until the oil reddens.

fuqi-feipian.d: Thin slices of cold beef offal drowned in chilli oil with peanuts. The name means husband-and-wife lung slices: it comes from a couple of vendors in the 1930s whose slices were reckoned the thinnest in Chengdu, and there has never been any lung in it.
s: Soak the offal three hours in cold water, changing it, then blanch it ten minutes.
Cook it two hours in a heavily spiced broth, then let it cool in that broth overnight.
It is cooling in the broth that flavours it through; taken out hot, it stays bland at the centre.
Slice it ice-cold at one millimetre with a perfectly sharp knife — thinness is the dish's very name.
Coat with chilli oil and reduced broth, and scatter crushed peanuts and raw celery.

yuxiang-rousi.d: Slivers of pork stir-fried in a sweet, sour and spicy sauce, with no fish at all. The name comes from the seasoning traditionally used for fish in Sichuan; there has never been any in the dish, a permanent source of confusion outside China.
s: Cut the pork into fine slivers with the grain and velvet it with cornflour and wine.
Use pickled chilli, paojiao, not doubanjiang: its sourness defines the yuxiang flavour.
Make the sauce ahead, balancing sugar and vinegar in almost equal parts, and taste it raw.
The sweet-sour balance is the whole dish: too much sugar dulls it, too much vinegar makes it aggressive.
Stir-fry over maximum heat, ninety seconds in all, and add the sauce last, all at once.

zhong-shui-jiao.d: Poached pork dumplings served in a sweetened garlic chilli oil. They carry the name of Zhong Xiesen, who opened his stall in 1893; the sweet garlic sauce is his signature, and it sets these dumplings apart from every other in China.
s: Work the minced pork in one direction with ginger water for ten minutes, until it turns tacky.
Add the water in small additions while mixing: the filling must absorb its own weight in liquid to stay juicy.
Roll discs thicker at the centre than the edge and pinch shut without pleating, in a simple half-moon.
Poach in trembling water, adding a glass of cold water each time it boils, three times over.
That repeated thermal shock cooks the filling without bursting the wrapper. Coat with chilli oil and sweet garlic soy.

mayi-shangshu.d: Sweet potato noodles stir-fried with crumbled minced pork. The name describes the look: grains of meat clinging to translucent noodles suggest ants climbing branches, an image at least as old as the thirteenth century.
s: Soak the noodles twenty minutes in warm, not hot, water: in boiling water they go gluey and clump into a block.
