Drain them and cut them with scissors into twenty-centimetre lengths, or they are impossible to eat.
Fry the pork until crisp, then add the doubanjiang and let the oil redden.
Moisten with broth and drop in the noodles: they must absorb all the liquid, which is how they take the flavour.
Toss with chopsticks rather than a spatula, lifting: they break at the least excess force.

bangbang-ji.d: Poached chicken shredded with a stick, served cold under a sesame and chilli sauce. Bang means stick: the flesh was beaten with a wooden mallet to separate into even fibres, and the vendors' rhythmic knocking announced them in the street.
s: Poach the chicken twenty minutes at a tremble with ginger and spring onion, then cut the heat and let it cool in the water.
Cooling in the broth keeps the flesh juicy; taken out hot, it dries within ten minutes.
Beat the cooled breast with a rolling pin, without crushing it, until the fibres separate.
Shred them by hand along the grain: a knife gives pieces the sauce will not cling to.
Loosen the sesame paste with cold broth before adding anything else — poured straight into oil, it seizes.

mao-xuewang.d: A scalding stew of congealed duck blood, offal and vegetables in a chilli broth. It was born on the Yangtze wharves, where boatmen bought cheap the offal butchers did not want; mao means rough or coarse, and the name owns it.
s: Cut the blood curd into large dice and poach them in salted trembling water for five minutes before anything else.
That prior poaching firms the blood: dropped raw into the broth, it disintegrates into powder.
Toast the doubanjiang in oil until it reddens, then moisten with stock and infuse ten minutes.
Add the ingredients in order of firmness, finishing with the blood and bean sprouts.
Pour a ladle of scalding chilli oil over the lot as you serve, as for shui zhu yu.

liangfen.d: A jelly of mung bean starch cut into strips, served cold and heavily spiced. It is the summer street food of Sichuan: the jelly neutral and cold, the dressing burning, and the contrast between them is the whole point.
s: Slake the starch in a third of the cold water, perfectly, before bringing the rest to the boil.
Pour the cold mixture into the boiling water, whisking without pause: the reverse gives irrecoverable lumps.
Cook five minutes, stirring, until the mixture turns translucent and very thick.
Pour into an oiled mould and set three hours at room temperature, never in the refrigerator — cold makes it brittle.
Cut into thick strips with a wetted knife and dress as you serve.

zhangcha-ya.d: A duck cured, smoked over tea leaves and camphor, then steamed and fried. The four successive stages — cure, smoke, steam, fry — take two days, and each does something the others cannot.
s: Toast the Sichuan pepper with the coarse salt and rub the duck inside and out, then cure twenty-four hours in the cold.
Smoke it twenty minutes over a mixture of tea, rice and brown sugar heated in the bottom of a covered wok.
The rice and sugar are the fuel; tea alone burns too fast and gives acrid smoke.
Then steam it an hour and a half: that stage tenderises the flesh and renders the fat.
Finally deep-fry the whole duck three minutes at 190°C to crisp the skin. Serve with steamed buns.

lazi-ji.d: Fried chicken cubes buried under a mountain of dried chillies. The chillies are not eaten: they are there to scent the oil and the chicken, and the meat is hunted out among them with chopsticks, which is part of the pleasure.
s: Cut the chicken into small cubes on the bone, with a cleaver: the bone keeps the flesh juicy through the double fry.
Marinate thirty minutes in wine, soy and ginger, then coat in cornflour.
Fry once at 160°C for four minutes, then again at 190°C for one minute, to harden the crust.
Cut the chillies into lengths and shake out the seeds, or the dish becomes genuinely inedible.
Toast them thirty seconds in a little oil with the pepper, add the chicken and toss dry.

char-siu-bao.d: Steamed buns split into three, filled with sauced barbecued pork. The star split at the top is not decorative: it proves the dough has risen properly, and a bun that stays closed is judged a failure in dim sum houses.
s: Use a low-protein flour, or cut it with cornflour: whiteness and fineness make the Cantonese bao.
Add baking powder as well as yeast, at the final kneading only.
It causes the violent lift in the steamer and bursts the top into three points.
Cool the cornflour-thickened filling completely: warm, it soaks through the dough during the second prove.
Steam twelve minutes over a fierce boil and do not open the basket for two minutes — the cold air makes them collapse.

oie-rotie-cantonaise.d: A lacquered goose roasted on a spit, with a glassy crisp skin. The skin is separated from the flesh by blowing air between them: that separation lets the fat render and the skin crisp without the meat drying.
s: Separate the skin from the flesh by blowing air in at the neck, without piercing it: the decisive gesture of the recipe.
Then scald the whole goose thirty seconds, which contracts the skin and closes the pores.
Brush with a mixture of maltose and vinegar, then dry twelve hours hung in front of a fan.
That drying is what gives the glaze: damp skin never lacquers, it blisters and greys.
Roast an hour and a half at 200°C, starting back upwards. Serve with plum sauce.

wonton-crevettes.d: Dumplings with a whole prawn in a dried fish broth. The prawn must snap under the tooth: it is treated with salt and bicarbonate then rinsed, which alters its texture and gives the crunch Cantonese call shuang.
s: Rub the shelled prawns with salt and bicarbonate, leave twenty minutes, then rinse at length in iced water.
Dry them thoroughly between two cloths: that treatment gives the snap, and nothing replaces it.
Toast the dried flounder in the oven before adding it to the broth — it is the signature of Cantonese wonton soup.
Fold the wontons keeping plenty of loose wrapper: the floating tail is intended, it gives the silky texture.
Poach them separately in clear water, never in the broth: they would cloud it with starch.

poisson-vapeur-cantonais.d: A whole fish steamed and doused with soy and scalding oil. It is the dish that measures a fish's freshness as no other does: with no spices or sauce to mask, the least approximation of freshness shows at once.
s: Set the fish on two crossed chopsticks in the dish, so steam circulates underneath.
Without that, the underside sits in its own juices and cooks twice as fast as the top.
Allow eight minutes for eight hundred grams, over the fiercest steam possible, and not a second more.
Throw away the liquid in the bottom of the dish without fail: it is bitter and would spoil the whole sauce.
Pour over warm soy, then smoking oil onto the raw ginger and spring onion laid on top.

cheung-fun.d: Wide sheets of rice steamed and rolled around a filling. The batter must be stirred just before each ladleful: rice starch settles within a minute, and unstirred batter gives an uneven, brittle sheet.
s: Mix the three starches with cold water and rest an hour: rice flour alone gives a sheet that cracks.
Oil the tray very lightly, then pour a thin ladleful, tilting to spread it in one movement.
Stir the batter for every ladleful, without exception: that is where the sheet's evenness is decided.
Steam three minutes at maximum, covered. The sheet is ready when it blisters and turns translucent.
Lift it with an oiled scraper starting at one corner, fill and roll while the sheet is scalding and supple.

poulet-blanc-coupe.d: A chicken poached until barely set, served cold with a ginger sauce. The flesh must stay pink near the bone: Cantonese hold that a chicken cooked white through to the bone is a chicken ruined, and the juices should still run faintly red.
s: Plunge the whole chicken into a large pan of trembling water, lift it out after thirty seconds, and repeat three times.
That in-and-out evens the temperature between skin and centre, and stops the skin splitting.
Then poach it twenty-five minutes at 85°C, never letting it boil.
Plunge it straight into iced water: the shock contracts the skin and separates it from the flesh in a gelatinous film.
That jelly under the skin is the mark of a good chicken. Serve cold, chopped with a cleaver, with a ginger and spring onion paste in scalding oil.

crevettes-sel-poivre.d: Whole prawns fried in their shells and tossed with salt, pepper and garlic. The shell is eaten: fried at high temperature it turns brittle and concentrates most of the flavour, and peeling them means throwing half the dish away.
s: Snip off the antennae and legs but keep the shell and head, and split the back to remove the vein.
Dry them thoroughly: a wet prawn makes the oil erupt and its shell never turns brittle.
Coat in cornflour alone and fry at 190°C for ninety seconds, until the shell cracks under tongs.
Dry-toast the salt and peppercorns beforehand, then grind them coarsely.
Pour off the oil, return the prawns to the scalding wok with the garlic and spices, and toss dry for thirty seconds.

dun-tang.d: A broth cooked four hours in a sealed pot itself set inside a steamer. The liquid never boils and stays perfectly clear; it is a tonic cooking, associated in Chinese medicine with restoring strength after illness.
s: Blanch the meats and bones five minutes and rinse them cold, until no scum remains.
Double steaming allows no skimming during cooking: everything must be clean at the start.
Put it all in a porcelain pot, cover with cold water and seal the lid with wet paper or heatproof film.
Set the pot in a steamer with water halfway up, and leave four hours at a gentle boil.
The resulting broth must be perfectly translucent. Salt only at the end, in the bowl.

poulet-braise-dezhou.d: A chicken fried then braised for hours, so tender it bones itself with a shake. It has been sold since 1692 on the platform at Dezhou station to travellers on the Beijing-Shanghai line; it is called the chicken whose bones fall out when shaken.
s: Truss the chicken by folding the wings and tucking the legs inside: it must stay compact through five hours' cooking.
Brush it with diluted maltose and let it dry an hour before frying.
Deep-fry it whole for two minutes at 200°C: the skin takes an amber colour and firms, which stops it splitting during the braise.
Then braise five hours at a tremble in the spiced broth, never letting it boil.
Cool it in the broth. The chicken is ready when a shake is enough to part the flesh from the bones.

tangcu-liyu.d: A Yellow River carp fried whole and coated in a glossy sweet-sour sauce. The fish is served arched with the tail raised: it is held in that position during frying, and the posture stands for the carp leaping the rapids.
s: Score the carp diagonally on each side, down to the bone, in five or six even cuts.
Those cuts open the flesh into a fan in the fryer and let the sauce penetrate.
Coat in cornflour, spreading the cuts open by hand so each one is covered.
Hold the fish by the tail and lower it in arched for thirty seconds before letting go: it will keep that shape.
Make the sauce separately and pour it scalding over the fish at the table, so the sizzle is heard.

cong-shao-haishen.d: Sea cucumber braised in a brown scallion sauce, a Shandong banquet dish. The dried animal must soak three to five days with the water changed morning and evening; it swells to five times its volume, and any contact with fat stops it rehydrating.
s: Soak the sea cucumbers three days in cold water, changing it twice a day.
Use only perfectly degreased vessels: a trace of fat prevents rehydration and the cucumber dissolves.
Open them, remove the innards and the white internal tendons, then poach twenty minutes before rinsing.
Fry the scallion whites in oil until browned, then remove them and keep the scented oil.
Braise the cucumbers in that oil and the stock for twenty minutes, thicken with cornflour and return the scallions on top.

jiuzhuan-dachang.d: Pork intestines nested inside one another and braised in a sweet-sour sauce. The name comes from a scholarly customer of the nineteenth century who compared the nine nested layers to the nine levels of the Taoist heaven; the dish actually has three.
s: Turn the intestines inside out and scrub them with coarse salt and flour, then rinse; repeat at least four times.
Inadequate cleaning is noticed at once and no sauce will cover it: that is the whole challenge of the dish.
Nest the segments inside one another, three thicknesses, to make a thick roll.
Poach an hour, then fry briefly to firm them, before braising an hour in the sweet-sour sauce.
Slice into one-centimetre rounds: the three layers should show clearly in cross-section.

hongshao-baoyu.d: Abalone long braised in a reduced brown broth and served whole. Dried abalone costs more than fresh and rehydrates over three days; its texture after braising, at once firm and yielding, is held impossible to achieve with the fresh animal.
s: Soak the dried abalone three days in cold water, changing it morning and evening.
Then brush them to remove sand from the folds, and poach them an hour before braising.
Make a superior stock with chicken, pork ribs and Jinhua ham, simmered four hours and degreased.
Braise the abalone in that stock eight hours at a tremble, or three hours under pressure.
Reduce the liquid until it coats, thicken barely with cornflour and nap the whole abalone. Never slice them.

liangban-haizhe.d: Strips of salted jellyfish, crunchy and translucent, dressed with vinegar. Jellyfish has almost no flavour: the whole point is its texture, a particular crunch lost irretrievably if heated more than a few seconds.
s: Rinse the salted jellyfish under running water, then desalt it two hours, changing the water three times.
Scald it for exactly five seconds, no longer: it contracts and turns crunchy.
Beyond ten seconds it literally melts and shrinks to a quarter of its volume, with no way back.
Plunge it straight into iced water, which fixes the texture, and leave it twenty minutes.
Drain thoroughly, cut into strips and dress just before serving — dressed ahead, it weeps.

songshu-guiyu.d: A boned fish scored in diamonds and fried until it bristles like a squirrel's tail. The cuts must pass through the flesh without cutting the skin: it is the skin contracting in the fryer that spreads the diamonds and makes the shape.
s: Fillet both sides keeping the skin and the tail attached to the head, then remove every bone.
Score each fillet in diamonds a centimetre apart, stopping just short of the skin.
This is the decisive point: a cut too deep goes through the skin and the fish falls apart in the oil.
Coat each diamond in cornflour, spreading them by hand, then shake off the excess.
Hold the fish by the tail and lower it head first into 190°C oil, holding it raised for thirty seconds.

shizi-tou.d: Enormous pork meatballs simmered two hours, so tender they are eaten with a spoon. The name comes from their size and their rough surface, likened to a lion's mane; the meat is cut by knife and never machine-minced.
s: Cut the pork by knife into tiny dice, half fat and half lean: that proportion makes the tenderness.
A mincer crushes the fibres and makes a dense ball; knife cutting leaves them whole and the ball stays open.
Work the mixture in one direction with ginger water, then throw it against the bowl twenty times.
That throwing drives out trapped air and stops the ball bursting; without it, it splits during poaching.
Shape four enormous balls and poach them two hours at 80°C in the broth with the cabbage. Never boiling.

yanshui-ya.d: A duck brined then poached and served cold, its flesh white and firm. Nanjing is nicknamed the duck-eating city; a hundred thousand a day are said to be eaten there, and salted duck is marked by pale unlacquered flesh, the opposite of Peking duck.
s: Toast the salt with the Sichuan pepper until fragrant, then rub the duck inside and out.
Dry-cure six hours, then rinse and soak two hours in clear water to desalt the surface.
That desalting is essential: without it the skin is inedible while the centre stays bland.
Poach at 80°C for forty minutes, filling and emptying the cavity with hot water three times to even the cooking.
Cool in the broth, then chill twelve hours before carving. Eaten cold.

wuxi-paigu.d: Spare ribs braised in a very sweet red sauce, glossy and sticky. Wuxi is known for its cooks' heavy hand with sugar: Jiangsu cooking is sweet in general, but Wuxi's is sweet enough to surprise Chinese diners themselves.
s: Blanch the ribs ten minutes and rinse them in hot water, never cold — cold water contracts the meat.
Use red yeast rice for the colour: it is a natural colouring, and dark soy never gives that bright red.
Caramelise the rock sugar in oil first, to an amber colour, then drop in the ribs.
Braise an hour and a half covered, then uncover and reduce twenty minutes, basting without pause.
The sauce must coat the ribs in a glossy film. Reduced too far, it crystallises and turns bitter.

yaxue-fensi-tang.d: A clear duck broth with vermicelli, blood curd and offal. It is the Nanjing breakfast: it uses everything salted duck leaves behind, and the city alone counts several thousand stalls.
s: Boil the duck carcass two hours with ginger and spring onion, skimming, to a clear light broth.
Poach the diced blood curd in salted trembling water before adding it to the broth: raw, it disintegrates.
Clean the intestines with salt and flour, then poach each offal separately according to its own time.
The vermicelli are poached apart and rinsed: in the broth their starch would cloud it at once.
Assemble in the bowl at the last moment and pour over the scalding broth. White pepper and chilli oil to taste.

wensi-doufu.d: A block of silken tofu cut into thousands of threads finer than a hair, served in soup. It bears the name of an eighteenth-century monk; an accomplished cook draws more than five thousand threads from a single block, and the dish serves as a knife test in Chinese schools.
s: Use a firm silken tofu and chill it an hour: cold, it holds better under the blade.
First remove the outer skin from all six faces, or the threads will stay joined.
Slice horizontally as thinly as possible without spreading the block, then turn it a quarter and cut across.
Slide the whole thing into a bowl of cold water: the threads separate by themselves and float.
Pour the scalding broth over. Never stir with a spoon: the bowl is swirled to mix.

xihu-cuyu.d: A grass carp poached and coated in a clear Zhenjiang vinegar sauce. The fish must fast two days in clean water before cooking: this purges the mud from its flesh, and without it the taste of lake bottom dominates everything.
s: Split the fish lengthways keeping the back attached, so it cooks flat and evenly.
Poach it exactly three minutes in trembling, never boiling water — this is a very fragile-fleshed fish.
Take it out as soon as the eye whitens and the dorsal fin pulls away with a light tug.
Make the sauce in the poaching liquid: vinegar, sugar, grated ginger, thickened with a little cornflour.
The sauce must stay clear and transparent. Nap the fish and serve within the minute, or the flesh falls apart.

longjing-xiaren.d: Small river shrimp stir-fried with Longjing green tea leaves. It is made only in April, with the first flush; the infusion water is used too, and the leaves are eaten with the shrimp.
s: Shell the shrimp by hand and velvet them with egg white, cornflour and salt, then rest them an hour in the cold.
Steep the tea at 80°C for three minutes only: hotter or longer and it turns bitter and spoils the dish.
Separate the leaves from the infusion and keep both; the leaves go in at the end, the water is the liquid.
Stir-fry the shrimp thirty seconds over high heat in barely warm oil — they should whiten without colouring.
Add the leaves and two spoonfuls of infusion, toss ten seconds more and serve. The whole dish takes a minute.

jiaohua-ji.d: A stuffed chicken wrapped in lotus leaves and baked sealed in a clay shell. Legend has a beggar who stole a chicken burying it under a fire to hide it; the shell is cracked with a mallet at the table, and the trapped steam escapes all at once.
s: Marinate the chicken twelve hours in Shaoxing wine, soy and spices, massaging it several times.
Stuff it with pork, mushrooms and pickled greens fried together and cooled.
Wrap it in soaked lotus leaves, three crossed layers, then in parchment.
Coat with a three-centimetre layer of clay, leaving not the smallest opening: the seal is everything.
Bake four hours at 200°C. Crack the shell with a mallet in front of the guests, and the lotus scent escapes in one breath.

meicai-kourou.d: Pork belly steamed on a bed of dried fermented mustard greens. The vegetable absorbs the rendered fat and gives it back as it cooks: it is an exchange, and why the dish is never greasy despite the quantity of belly used.
s: Soak the dried mustard greens an hour and rinse them five times: they are very salty and hold a lot of grit.
Poach the whole belly forty minutes, then prick the rind all over and brush it with dark soy.
Fry it rind down, covered and at arm's length: it spits violently for the first few seconds.
Plunge it straight into cold water for ten minutes: that shock blisters the rind, which turns porous and melting.
Slice, pack the slices rind down in a bowl, cover with the greens and steam three hours. Invert onto the plate.

wenzhou-yuwan.d: Strips of fish rolled by hand in starch and poached in a sour vinegar soup. They are not round despite the name: the fish is cut into strips rather than ground, and the fibrous texture that results is peculiar to Wenzhou.
s: Fillet the fish and cut it into strips five centimetres by one, across the grain.
Do not grind it: the texture of a Wenzhou fish ball comes precisely from those intact fibres.
Work the strips with salt and ginger water for ten minutes, until they turn tacky.
Coat each strip in sweet potato starch, rolling by hand, leaving no bare patch.
Poach at a tremble for three minutes; they rise when ready. Serve in a heavily vinegared and peppered broth.

runbing-quanzhou.d: Large translucent pancakes rolled cold around braised vegetables and sweetened peanuts. Unlike the fried roll, runbing is eaten uncooked and rolled at the table; the pancake is made by dabbing a ball of sticky dough onto a scalding plate.
s: Work the dough by hand for fifteen minutes, until very elastic and sticky, then rest it an hour.
Take a handful and dab it onto the scalding plate in a circular motion: a thin film is left behind.
The gesture takes practice — too firm and the pancake is thick, too light and it has holes.
Braise the vegetables separately according to their own times, then combine them and drain thoroughly for an hour.
Crush the toasted peanuts with sugar. Rolling happens at the table: pancake, toasted seaweed, vegetables, sweet peanuts.

lizhi-rou.d: Pork scored so that it opens into a bristling ball in the fryer, in a red sweet-sour sauce. It contains no lychee: the pieces, once fried, take the shape and colour of the fruit, and that is where the name comes from.
s: Cut the pork into three-centimetre squares and score each in a tight lattice on both faces, without cutting through.
Those cuts are what make the piece open into a ball in the fryer: the finer they are, the sharper the effect.
Marinate in wine and red yeast rice, which gives the colour without artificial colouring.
Coat in sweet potato starch and fry at 190°C for ninety seconds: the pieces bristle at once.
Toss them in the sweet-sour sauce for ten seconds only, so they keep their crispness.

shacha-mian.d: Noodles in a broth of shacha paste, with peanuts and dried fish. Shacha is the Chinese version of Malay satay, brought back by Fujianese emigrants returning from Southeast Asia: the name comes from sate, said in Hokkien.
s: Toast the shacha paste in hot oil for a minute before moistening: that wakes the dried fish aromas.
Add the broth little by little, whisking, so the paste dissolves without lumping.
A thread of coconut milk rounds the broth: the direct inheritance from Southeast Asian satay.
Poach each topping separately in the broth according to its own time, and set it aside.
Cook the noodles apart and rinse them. Assemble in the bowl and pour the scalding broth over.

sibao-tang.d: A chilled dessert combining four elements in a light syrup, served in summer. The four are not fixed: each stall composes its own from a dozen possible ingredients, and the name describes the structure rather than a set recipe.
s: Cook each element separately: they do not share a cooking time, and together some collapse while others stay hard.
Soak the mung beans overnight and cook them until they crush without dissolving.
Remove the green germ at the centre of the lotus seeds: it is frankly bitter and spoils the whole.
Make the light syrup separately and chill it completely before assembling.
Build in the bowl at the last moment, with the crushed ice last. Eaten within five minutes.

fuzhou-yuwan.d: White, perfectly smooth fish balls filled with minced pork. They differ from Wenzhou's in every respect: here the flesh is ground to an elastic paste, and the ball is round, smooth and hollowed around a filling.
s: Use sea eel for preference, or a very firm white fish, perfectly free of sinew.
Grind the flesh with salt and iced water in several stages, keeping the paste below 10°C.
Temperature is decisive: above 12°C the proteins coagulate and the paste loses its elasticity for good.
Beat the paste against the bowl fifty times, until a test ball dropped in cold water floats.
Shape the balls in your palm around the pork filling and poach at 80°C, never boiling.

duojiao-yutou.d: A split carp head covered with chopped fermented chillies and steamed. Duojiao is chilli chopped and salt-fermented for months; it is as sour as it is hot, and that sourness is what distinguishes Hunan chilli from Sichuan's.
s: Split the head from underneath, leaving the top skin attached, so it opens out flat.
Rub it with wine and salt and leave twenty minutes, then blot off the released liquid.
Spread the fermented chilli in a thick even layer over the whole surface, leaving no bare patch.
Steam twelve minutes over the fiercest steam, no longer: the cheek is cooked well before the rest.
Pour smoking oil over the raw spring onions and serve with noodles to soak in the juices, as is the custom in Changsha.

dongan-ji.d: Chicken poached then stir-fried with vinegar, ginger and Sichuan pepper. It goes back to the Tang dynasty and has featured at Chinese state banquets since 1949; it is a sour rather than hot dish, which is rare in Hunan.
s: Poach the whole chicken twenty minutes at 85°C, then let it cool in its broth.
Bone it warm and cut the flesh into strips with the skin attached: it brings fat that would otherwise be missing.
Use far more ginger than instinct suggests — in julienne it acts almost as a vegetable.
Stir-fry over high heat for a minute, adding the vinegar down the sides of the wok so part of it flashes off.
Poured into the centre, vinegar stays raw and aggressive; poured onto scalding metal, it loses its bite and keeps its scent.

xiaochao-huangniurou.d: Beef stir-fried very fast with fresh green chillies and fermented chilli. Hunan cooking uses fresh chilli where Sichuan uses dried: the result is sharper, greener, and burns the throat more than the tongue.
s: Slice the beef very thinly across the grain and velvet it with cornflour and wine for fifteen minutes.
Use long fleshy green chillies, split in two rather than chopped: they must stay pieces you eat.
Heat the wok until it smokes before adding the oil — that is wok hei, and without it the dish lacks its characteristic scorched note.
Stir-fry the beef forty seconds, remove it, then do the chillies separately before bringing everything together.
The whole dish takes no more than two minutes' cooking. Beyond that the beef toughens and the chillies collapse.

yongzhou-xueya.d: Duck stir-fried then bound with its own blood, which coats every piece. The blood is collected onto vinegar to stop it clotting, then poured in raw at the end: it makes no sauce but a dark glossy film on the meat.
s: Beat the blood with the vinegar as soon as it is collected, or it clots into lumps and will no longer coat the meat.
Chop the duck into small pieces on the bone with a cleaver, so they cook fast and present plenty of surface.
Stir-fry over high heat until they render their fat and brown, a good fifteen minutes.
Add chillies and aromatics, moisten barely and cook twenty minutes covered.
Cut the heat, then pour in the blood, stirring without pause. It sets in the residual heat: over the flame it would go grainy.

kouwei-xia.d: Crayfish braised in a heavily spiced sauce, eaten with the hands in summer. In the 2000s they became the night ritual of Chinese cities: eaten at midnight, with plastic gloves, alongside iced beer.
s: Scrub the live crayfish one by one under water, working the belly, then pull out the vein by twisting the central tail fin.
This cleaning is slow but not optional: crayfish live in mud and a badly scrubbed batch is inedible.
Snip off the tip of the rostrum with scissors, which lets the sauce into the head.
Toss them in scalding oil until they redden, then remove them before making the sauce.
Braise twenty minutes in beer and spices, then let them cool in it for an hour — cooling is when they take the flavour.

chou-guiyu.d: A fish fermented a week under a weight, powerfully smelling and flaky-fleshed. The fermentation was discovered by accident: merchants carrying salted fish into the mountains found it smelling on arrival, and cooked it rather than throw it away.
s: Salt the gutted fish and stack it under a stone in a wooden vessel, at 20-25°C.
Allow six or seven days in summer, longer in winter; turn it daily and replace the stone.
The smell turns frankly strong, but the flesh must stay firm and white: if it softens or greys, throw it all away.
Rinse, blot and brown the fish in a pan on both sides before braising.
Braise twenty minutes with the pork and bamboo shoots. The flesh then parts into petals, like leaves.

li-hongzhang-zahui.d: A stew of dried seafood and meats brought together in a thick broth. It is named for the diplomat Li Hongzhang, who in 1896, entertaining American guests with no dish left ready, is said to have had all the kitchen's leftovers combined.
s: Rehydrate each dried item separately and to its own timetable: sea cucumber needs three days, squid one night.
Pre-cook each meat apart, then cut everything into pieces of the same size so nothing dominates.
Build the stew in order of firmness, adding elements five minutes apart.
Thicken the broth with cornflour at the end: this dish should coat, halfway between soup and stew.
Do not stir when serving: the elements are arranged in a ring and each diner takes what they want.

wenzheng-shansun.d: Spring bamboo shoots braised with dry-cured ham and chicken. They must be cooked within hours of harvest: after a day the shoot lignifies and develops a bitterness nothing removes.
s: Split the shoot lengthways before peeling: the sheaths then come away in one, instead of being torn off one by one.
Blanch ten minutes in salted water to remove the oxalic acid, which gives a rasping feel in the mouth.
Cut on a very open bias: this increases the surface and lets the broth into the fibre.
Braise with the ham and chicken for forty minutes, covered, in a lightly salted broth — the ham already brings plenty of salt.
It is done when the shoot is translucent at the edges. Serve it alone, the ham having served only to flavour.

mao-doufu.d: Tofu covered with a white bloom of mould, pan-fried until the skin colours. The mould is a Mucor, the same genus as on cheeses: it breaks down the soy proteins and gives the tofu a flavour recalling a ripened cheese.
s: Cut firm tofu into cubes and set them spaced on a bamboo rack, not touching.
Leave them three days at 20°C somewhere humid and out of draughts.
The white bloom should be even and smell of fresh mushroom. Any black, green or pink patch means contamination: throw it all away.
Pan-fry over medium heat in a little oil, without turning until the face is frankly golden — the bloom forms a crust.
Serve with a chilli sauce. The taste is close to a bloomy-rind cheese, which always surprises.

wuwei-xunya.d: A duck smoked over tea and camphor wood, then steamed. It differs from the Chengdu duck in being cold-smoked: the smoke penetrates over several hours without cooking the bird, and the flesh keeps a pink tone to the bone.
s: Dry-cure the duck with toasted salt and pepper for twenty-four hours, turning it twice.
Then hang it four hours in a draught so the skin dries and becomes tacky to the touch.
That tacky film, the pellicle, is what the smoke clings to: without it, smoking does not take.
Cold-smoke below 30°C for two hours: the duck must not cook at this stage.
Finally steam it an hour and a half. The flesh stays pink near the bone, which is normal for this dish.

jingjiang-rousi.d: Pork slivers stir-fried in sweet soybean paste and rolled in tofu skin. The dish descends directly from Peking duck: same sauce, same spring onions, same rolling gesture, but with pork instead of duck and at a tenth of the price.
s: Cut the pork into fine slivers and velvet them with egg white and cornflour for twenty minutes.
Cook the sweet soybean paste separately in oil for five minutes, until it shines and loses its raw taste.
Stir-fry the pork thirty seconds in warm oil, then drain it before folding it into the sauce.
That low-temperature pre-cooking is what keeps the slivers tender: seared over high heat, they toughen.
Plate on a bed of raw julienned spring onion and serve with tofu skins for rolling at the table.

douzhi-jiaoquan.n: Fermented mung bean juice with fried ring
douzhi-jiaoquan.d: A sour-smelling fermented mung bean juice drunk with a fried ring. It is the Beijing breakfast hardest on outsiders: the smell suggests soured milk, and Beijingers say that liking douzhi proves you are truly of the city.
s: Soak the mung beans overnight, grind them with plenty of water and let them settle six hours.
Separate the starch that sinks from the cloudy liquid above: that liquid becomes the douzhi.
Let it ferment two days at room temperature, until it smells frankly sour.
Heat it without boiling, stirring: boiled, it splits and separates beyond recovery.
Serve scalding with a fried dough ring and pickled vegetables, which cut the acidity.

shuan-yangrou.d: Lamb sliced very thin and dipped a few seconds in a clear water broth. The broth holds almost nothing — water, ginger, a few jujubes: the Beijing hotpot stakes everything on the quality of the meat, the opposite of the Sichuan version.
s: Firm the leg two hours in the freezer, then slice it at a millimetre and a half, across the grain.
The slices must be thin enough to see the plate's pattern through: that is the test Beijing houses use.
The broth is not seasoned: water, ginger, jujubes and whole spring onions, nothing more.
Dip each slice ten seconds holding it with chopsticks, until it changes colour, and no longer.
All the flavour comes from the sesame and fermented tofu sauce, mixed in each diner's own bowl.

shengjian-bao.d: Filled pork buns browned at the base and steamed above, full of broth. The broth comes from a pork skin jelly mixed into the filling: it melts as it cooks and fills the bun, so the first bite must be cautious.
s: Cook the pork skin three hours with ginger, strain and set it to a jelly in the cold.
Chop the cold jelly into small dice and mix it into the filling, one part jelly to two of meat.
Prove the dough only halfway: over-proved, the bun swells and the broth pierces the base.
Pack the buns close, seam up, in an oiled pan and brown them three minutes dry.
Then pour in water to a centimetre, cover at once and let the steam cook them ten minutes.

congyou-banmian.d: Noodles tossed with confited scallion oil and sweetened soy. There is nothing else: four ingredients in all, and success rests entirely on the patience with which the scallions are browned without ever burning.
s: Cut the scallions into five-centimetre lengths and separate whites from greens: they do not cook at the same rate.
Confit them in the oil over very low heat, whites first, for thirty to forty minutes.
Over high heat the scallions blacken in three minutes and the oil turns bitter: the only way to fail this dish.
They are ready when deep brown, shrivelled and brittle; lift them out and keep the oil.
Stir the soy and sugar into the hot oil, pour over the drained noodles and return the fried scallions on top.

cifantuan.d: Glutinous rice pressed by hand around a fried dough stick, dried pork and pickled vegetables. It is the breakfast Shanghainese eat walking to the metro; the dough stick should be a day old and refried, so it stays crisp under the damp rice.
s: Soak the glutinous rice at least six hours, then steam it forty minutes on a cloth.
Boiled, it turns sticky and shapeless; steamed, each grain stays distinct while clinging to the others.
Spread the scalding rice on a damp cloth in a one-centimetre layer, and let it cool two minutes.
Lay the filling in a line down the centre, close it using the cloth and press firmly into a cylinder.
The rice must still be hot to bind: cooled, it no longer sticks and the roll falls apart.

yangrou-chuan.d: Lamb skewers with cumin and chilli, grilled over a long narrow brazier. Alternating lean and fat on the skewer is not decorative: the fat renders and bastes the lean throughout, and a skewer without fat dries in three minutes.
s: Cut the meat and fat into two-centimetre cubes and thread them alternately, four lean to one fat.
Marinate two hours with grated onion alone: the spices go on at the grill, never before.
Cumin burns on the coals if put in the marinade; it is dusted on during cooking, in three stages.
Use a narrow brazier on which the skewers rest by their ends, the meat suspended above the coals.
Turn every thirty seconds, eight minutes in all, dusting with cumin and chilli at each turn.

laghman.d: Hand-pulled noodles under a stir-fry of lamb and vegetables. The noodles are neither cut nor extruded: the dough is oiled, coiled and rested for hours, then pulled into a single strand that can run several metres.
s: Knead a soft salted dough, rest it an hour, then roll it into ropes and oil them generously.
Coil the ropes in an oiled dish and rest them at least three hours, covered.
That long rest relaxes the gluten to the point where the dough stretches without ever breaking: without it, it snaps at the first pull.
Pull each rope, slapping it on the worktop and folding it back on itself at each pass.
Cook two minutes in boiling water and top with the lamb and vegetable stir-fry, made separately in the wok.

polo-xinjiang.d: Rice with lamb, yellow carrots and raisins, cooked in one pot. Xinjiang's yellow carrots are sweeter and less watery than orange ones; they melt away giving the rice its colour, and substituting changes the dish.
s: Render the lamb fat first and lift out the cracklings: everything else will cook in that fat.
Brown the meat, then the onions, then the carrots in thick batons, never stirring once they are in.
The carrots form a layer that insulates the rice from the meat: stirred, they collapse and the rice turns to porridge.
Pour the rinsed rice over without mixing, add boiling water two centimetres above, and push in the whole garlic heads.
Cook thirty minutes covered, then mix only as you serve, turning from the bottom upwards.

nang-xinjiang.d: A large flatbread baked against the wall of a clay oven, dimpled at the centre. The pattern stamped with a nail tool is not decorative: the dimples stop the centre puffing, so the bread bakes evenly from centre to rim.
s: Knead a firm dough with melted lamb fat and prove it two hours.
Roll into thirty-centimetre discs leaving the rim twice as thick as the centre.
Stamp the centre with a nail tool, or failing that a fork, pricking right through to the worktop.
Brush with salted onion water and scatter sesame and nigella, pressing them to make them stick.
Slap the disc onto the scalding wall of a 250°C oven. Five minutes is enough; the rim puffs, the centre stays flat.

tsampa.d: Roasted barley flour kneaded by hand into butter tea and shaped into balls. It has been the staple of the Tibetan plateau for centuries: barley is the only grain that ripens at four thousand metres, and the prior roasting allows it to be eaten uncooked.
s: Roast the barley grains in hot sand until they pop, then sieve and mill: roasting is what makes it edible uncooked.
Make the butter tea by churning strong black tea, yak butter and salt in a churn for several minutes.
Churning emulsifies the butter into the tea: merely stirred, it rises in a pool and the drink is undrinkable.
Pour hot tea into the bowl, add the flour little by little and knead with your fingertips, in the bowl itself.
Form a firm ball that holds in the palm. The proportion is judged by hand, never measured.

shou-zhua-rou.d: Mutton boiled in salted water with no spices, eaten by hand with a knife. The total absence of seasoning is the principle: Mongolian cooking holds that good mutton needs nothing, and spices there pass for an admission of weakness.
s: Use lamb under a year old, in pieces on the bone: the dish rests entirely on the quality of the animal.
Start in cold water and bring slowly to a tremble, skimming relentlessly for the first half hour.
Add nothing but salt, and only halfway through. No bay, no star anise, no pepper.
Allow an hour and a half to two hours, until the flesh leaves the bone under a light pull.
Serve the pieces whole, with a knife. Each diner cuts their own and dips it in a garlic and chilli sauce.

poutine-rapee.d: A ball of grated potato stuffed with salt pork, boiled for three hours. Nothing to do with Quebec poutine; in Acadia it is the Christmas dish, and grating twenty pounds of potatoes is a family affair.
s: Grate two thirds of the potatoes very finely and press them in a cloth until nothing more runs out.
Collect the pressing liquid and let it settle: the starch falls to the bottom; discard the clear water and keep the starch.
Boil the remaining third, mash it, and mix it with the pressed gratings and the recovered starch.
Shape balls around a cube of salt pork and onion, sealing them well: one leak and the ball falls apart.
Poach for 3 hours in barely simmering salted water, never at a hard boil. Serve with butter, brown sugar or molasses.

bannock-des-prairies.d: A flat unleavened bread cooked in a pan or on a stick over the fire. First Nations adopted it in the 19th century with trading-post flour; it has become an ambiguous symbol, both food and memory.
s: Mix the flour, baking powder and salt, then rub in the lard with your fingertips.
Pour in the warm water all at once and bring the dough together in a few movements: overworked, it turns elastic and hard.
Fold in the saskatoon berries without crushing them, if you have them.
Flatten the dough to 2 cm and cook it in a pan in a little fat, 8 minutes a side over medium heat.
It is ready when it sounds hollow. Serve hot, broken by hand, with maple syrup.

hangtown-fry.d: An omelette of fried oysters and bacon, born in 1849 in the gold camps. A newly rich miner is said to have asked for the most expensive dish on the menu: oysters came by mule from San Francisco, and eggs cost a fortune.
s: Shuck the oysters and pat them thoroughly dry: a wet oyster refuses the crumb.
Flour them, dip in beaten egg then breadcrumbs, and fry 90 seconds a side in butter.
Grill the bacon until crisp, and keep the fat in the pan.
Beat the remaining eggs with the cream, without aerating them, and pour them onto the hot fat.
Arrange the oysters and bacon over the top, let it set for 4 minutes over low heat, and serve with lemon.

green-chile-stew.d: A pork stew with roasted Hatch green chiles, thick and green. Every autumn New Mexico roasts its chiles in rotating drums in car parks: the smell announces the season better than a calendar.
s: Roast the green chiles until the skins blister and blacken, then shut them in a bag for 15 minutes.
Peel, seed and chop them roughly: they should stay in visible pieces.
Sear the cubed pork in lard, dust with flour and let it turn golden.
Add the onion, garlic, cumin and oregano, then the stock, and simmer for 45 minutes.
Add the chiles, tomato and potatoes for 30 minutes. Serve with flour tortillas.

frogmore-stew.d: Shrimp, smoked sausage, corn and potatoes boiled together and tipped onto a table covered in newspaper. You eat standing, without plate or fork, and throw the shells into the middle.
s: Bring a very large pot of water to the boil with the seasoning, cut lemons and whole garlic.
The broth should taste frankly too salty and too spiced: the ingredients will absorb it.
Add the potatoes for 12 minutes, then the sausage in lengths for 5 minutes.
Add the corn in lengths for 5 minutes, then the whole shrimp for 3 minutes only.
Drain in one movement and tip the pot into the middle of the table. Melted butter and lemon to taste.

kalua-pig.d: A whole pig cooked seven hours in an imu, an earth oven lined with lava stones and banana leaves. Hawaiian red sea salt is the only seasoning; the smoke does the rest.
s: Dig a pit and heat lava stones in it on a hardwood fire for three hours.
Score the pork deeply and rub it with red salt, working into the cuts.
Slip hot stones into the cavity: the animal then cooks from within as well as without.
Wrap it in ti leaves then banana leaves, set it on the stones and cover with damp earth.
Leave for 7 hours without opening. The flesh shreds at a fork; toss it with a little steamed cabbage.

burgoo-kentucky.d: A stew of several meats and every vegetable, simmered half a day in a cauldron. It is made for horse races and political rallies; the rule is that the spoon must stand up in it.
s: Cook the meats together for 2 hours in the beef stock, until they leave the bone.
Lift them out, bone them and shred them by hand; return the meat to the broth.
Add the tomato, onion and potatoes, and simmer for 1 hour, stirring regularly.
Add the corn, lima beans, okra and cabbage, and continue for 2 hours over very low heat.
Stir the bottom often: at this stage burgoo catches in an instant. Finish with Worcestershire and bourbon.

haluski-pittsburgh.d: Noodles with butter-melted cabbage, the dish of Slovak steelworkers. The cabbage must cook forty minutes until sweet and brown: rushed, it stays a vegetable and misses the point.
s: Slice the cabbage very finely, salt it and let it drain for 30 minutes, then squeeze it.
Fry the bacon, lift it out, and melt the onion in the rendered fat and butter.
Add the cabbage and cook it for 40 minutes over medium heat, stirring now and then.
It should go from white to golden brown and turn frankly sweet: that is the only moment that matters.
Toss in the cooked noodles, caraway and bacon, season generously with pepper, and serve with soured cream.

rice-and-beans-belize.d: Rice cooked in coconut milk with red beans, served with chicken stewed in recado. Belize distinguishes rice and beans, cooked together, from beans and rice, cooked apart: they are not the same dish.
s: Soak the beans overnight, then cook them for 1 hour with the garlic, thyme and whole chilli.
Marinate the chicken in recado rojo, vinegar and garlic for 3 hours.
Caramelise the brown sugar in the oil until it smokes, and drop in the chicken: it takes a mahogany colour.
Barely moisten and simmer covered for 45 minutes.
Pour the rice into the beans with the coconut milk — two parts liquid to one of rice — and cook covered for 25 minutes.

nacatamal.d: A very large maize tamal filled with pork, rice, potato and olive, cooked five hours. Eaten on Sunday morning at breakfast, with coffee and bread: one is ample for two.
s: Marinate the pork for 12 hours in sour orange, garlic and annatto.
Work the masa with melted lard and a little broth, at length, until a small ball floats in water.
Soften the banana leaves over a flame and lay them crosswise, two thicknesses deep.
Spread a large ladle of masa, then the pork, raw rice, sliced potato, olive, prune and mint.
Fold into a large square parcel, tie it, and steam for 5 hours. It is opened on the plate, never before.

sancocho-de-gallina-panama.d: A hen broth with yam and culantro, drunk scalding even in great heat. In Panama it is served at daybreak after a night out, and it is sworn to set a man right.
s: Marinate the jointed hen in pounded garlic, oregano and lime for an hour.
Put it in three litres of cold water and bring slowly to a simmer, skimming relentlessly.
Cook for 1 hour: a farm hen needs that long, a battery chicken far less.
Add the yam in large pieces and the corn, and continue for 30 minutes.
Add the culantro only at the end, whole, and lift it out before serving. White rice alongside.

gallo-en-chicha.d: A cockerel stewed in chicha, fermented maize beer, with dried fruit and panela. It is made for the patron saint's day; the chicha needs eight days to ferment, so nobody starts the day before.
s: Marinate the jointed cockerel for 12 hours in the chicha with garlic, bay and spices.
Drain it keeping the marinade, pat it dry and colour it in the oil.
Dry-toast the relajo spices and grind them: this Salvadoran blend is what perfumes the dish.
Add onion, tomato, marinade, panela and dried fruit, and simmer covered for 2½ hours.
The sauce should turn dark and syrupy, frankly sweet-sour. Serve with rice and bread.

run-down.d: Fish stewed in coconut milk reduced until the oil separates. The name describes the method: the coconut milk is 'run down' until it breaks into custard, before the fish even goes in.
s: Boil the coconut milk uncovered for 25 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and the oil beads: that is the run down.
Add nothing before this step: put in too early, aromatics stop the milk separating.
Add the onion, garlic, spring onion, thyme and crushed allspice.
Add the tomato and the whole scotch bonnet — unsplit — and give it 10 minutes.
Slide in the fish in lengths and poach for 12 minutes without stirring. Serve with boiled green plantain.

conch-fritters.d: Fritters of chopped conch, served with a pink lime sauce. The conch is beaten with a mallet before chopping: without that it stays rubbery whatever the cooking.
s: Beat the conch with a mallet to tenderise it, then chop it finely by knife.
Marinate it for 20 minutes in lime: the acid continues what the mallet began.
Mix the flour, baking powder, eggs and milk into a thick batter, denser than a pancake batter.
Fold in the drained conch, the finely diced vegetables and the chilli.
Drop spoonfuls into oil at 175°C and fry for 4 minutes, turning. Serve with mayonnaise, ketchup and lime.

fungee-and-pepperpot.d: A maize polenta with okra alongside a stew of greens and salted meats. Antigua's national dish is eaten on Wednesdays, the day schools historically served pepperpot.
s: Soak the salted meats for 8 hours, blanch them, then cook them for 1 hour in clean water.
Add the squash, aubergine and okra, and give them 25 minutes: the vegetables should collapse and thicken the stew.
Add the spinach and the whole chilli for the last 10 minutes.
For the fungee, cook the sliced okra in salted water, lift it out, and rain in the maize flour.
Work it for 20 minutes with a flat stick, return the okra, beat in butter, and mould it in a wetted bowl.

callaloo-chicken-dominique.d: Chicken stewed in a purée of dasheen leaves with coconut milk, thick and dark green. The dasheen leaf scratches the throat if undercooked: forty minutes is a minimum, not a suggestion.
s: Wash the chicken with lime as Caribbean custom requires, then marinate it in garlic, thyme and spring onion.
Strip the ribs from the dasheen leaves and chop them roughly: the rib stays tough and irritant.
Colour the chicken in coconut oil, then add the onion and garlic.
Add the leaves, okra and half a litre of water, cover and cook for 40 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk, break down the leaves with a whisk to thicken, and give it 15 minutes without boiling. Serve with rice.

pepperpot-guyana.d: A black stew with cassareep, the bitter cassava syrup that preserves meat without refrigeration. Some family pepperpots have been reheated for generations: cassareep is a natural antiseptic, and the dish does not spoil.
s: Blanch all the meats for 15 minutes and discard that water: pepperpot must stay clean despite its colour.
Return them to the pot with the cassareep, cinnamon, cloves and orange peel.
Add water only to the level of the meat: cassareep must not be diluted, it is the sauce.
Simmer for 3 to 4 hours over very low heat, until the meat falls away and the sauce coats.
Add the whole wiri wiri peppers at the end. Serve with plait bread; reheat every day.

bouillon-d-awara.d: A stew of awara palm paste, smoked meats and fish, made at Easter. Guianese belief holds that whoever eats it will return to Guiana: it takes two days and gathers the whole family.
s: Slake the awara paste in two litres of water and reduce it for 4 hours uncovered, stirring regularly.
It should go from bright orange to dark brown and halve in volume: that long cooking is everything.
Soak and blanch the smoked meats, and cook them separately for 40 minutes.
Add them to the paste with the smoked fish and the vegetables, in order of firmness.
Simmer for another hour, add the prawns at the end, and serve with white rice.

pato-no-tucupi.d: Duck poached in tucupi with jambu, served at the Círio de Nazaré. The duck is first roasted then boiled: that double treatment, contrary to all European culinary logic, is what makes the dish.
s: Rub the duck with pounded garlic, lime and salt, and leave it 12 hours in the cold.
Roast it for 1 hour at 200°C, until the skin is well coloured and the fat has rendered.
Boil the tucupi for 2 hours with the garlic, chicory and basil, uncovered.
Joint the roast duck and lower the pieces into the boiling tucupi for 40 minutes.
Blanch the jambu and add it at the end. Serve with rice and farofa.

guatita.d: Tripe stewed in a peanut and potato sauce, yellow with annatto. The name means 'little belly'; it is Guayaquil's street dish, served at all hours and never on a smart restaurant menu.
s: Scrub the tripe with coarse salt and lemon, rinse it at length, then blanch it for 15 minutes.
Cook it for 2 hours at a bare simmer until a fork slides in easily, and cut it into strips.
Make a refrito of onion, garlic, tomato, cumin and annatto for 20 minutes.
Slake the peanut butter in warm milk and stir it into the refrito, with the diced potatoes.
Add the tripe and simmer for 30 minutes: the potatoes collapse and thicken the sauce. Coriander at the end.

chairo-paceno.d: A soup of chuño, potato freeze-dried by Andean nights, with lamb and wheat. Chuño is made by letting tubers freeze overnight and treading them by day: the technique is a thousand years old.
s: Soak the chuño overnight, then rub it between your hands to remove the skins and rinse it in several changes of water.
Soak the wheat overnight too, and cook it separately for 1 hour: it does not soften at the same rate.
Cook the meats for 1 hour in three litres of water with the onion and garlic.
Make a refrito of ají amarillo, cumin and oregano, and stir it into the broth.
Add the roughly crushed chuño, the wheat and the vegetables, and give them 45 minutes. Huacatay off the heat.

silpancho.d: A breaded steak flattened until it covers the whole plate, over rice and potatoes. Cochabamba judges a silpancho by its size: if it does not overhang the plate, it was not beaten enough.
s: Beat the beef slices between two sheets into a 3 mm disc, 25 cm across.
Season, and press them firmly into the breadcrumbs on both sides, without egg wash: that is the local peculiarity.
Cook the rice, and fry the sliced potatoes until golden.
Fry the meat for 90 seconds a side in very hot oil: any longer and it dries out.
Plate rice, potatoes and meat, then two fried eggs, and crown with a raw salad of tomato, onion and locoto.

mbeju.d: A cake of cassava starch and cheese cooked in a pan, without flour or leavening. It is not kneaded: the mixture stays as dry crumbs and welds together in the heat, which disconcerts the first time.
s: Cream the lard with the salt, then work in the grated cheese and the eggs.
Add the cassava starch and rub it in with your fingertips: the mixture must stay crumbly, never form a ball.
Add the milk a spoonful at a time, just enough that a crumb holds when squeezed in the hand.
Tip a 1 cm layer into a hot pan and press it only lightly with the back of a spoon.
Let it weld for 8 minutes over medium heat, flip it in one movement and cook 6 minutes. Serve scalding.

boston-baked-beans.d: White beans baked seven hours in a stoneware pot with molasses and salt pork. Boston was nicknamed Beantown because of them: the city refined Caribbean sugar, and molasses, a worthless by-product, cost less than sugar.
s: Soak the beans overnight, then simmer them 40 minutes until the skins split when you blow on them.
Never salt the soaking or parboiling water: salt hardens the skin and seven hours of oven will not undo it.
Score the salt pork in a lattice without cutting through the rind, and bury it in the centre of the pot with the whole onion.
Mix the molasses, brown sugar and dry mustard into a litre of hot water, and pour to cover the beans by a centimetre.
Bake covered 6 hours at 130°C, topping up with hot water if the level drops, then uncover for the last hour to let the top crust.

blueberry-pie-du-maine.d: A wild blueberry pie, the state's official dessert since 2011. Maine grows nearly all of North America's wild blueberries: half the size of cultivated ones, twice as sharp, and gathered only with a hand rake.
s: Mix the blueberries with the sugar, cornstarch, zest and lemon juice, and macerate 30 minutes so they give up their juice.
Drain that juice, reduce it by half in a pan and pour it back over the fruit: without this the pie floods its base.
Line the tin, fill it in a dome and dot with butter.
Cover with a second disc, seal, glaze and cut five wide vents — the steam must escape fast, one chimney is not enough.
Bake 15 minutes at 220°C then 40 minutes at 190°C, until juice bubbles through the vents. Cool 4 hours before cutting.

whoopie-pie.d: Two cocoa cake domes enclosing a marshmallow cream, neither pie nor cake. Maine, the Pennsylvania Amish and Massachusetts all claim the invention; the name is said to come from the cry of farmers finding one in their lunch pail.
s: Cream 60 g of the butter with the brown sugar, add the egg, then alternate the cocoa flour and buttermilk in three additions.
The sour buttermilk activates the bicarbonate: the batter rises at once and must be piped without delay.
Drop generous spoonfuls onto the tray, well spaced — they spread by half as they bake.
Bake 11 minutes at 180°C: they must stay soft and matt, an overbaked whoopie crisps and is no longer one.
Whisk the remaining butter with the icing sugar, marshmallow and vanilla, fill generously and press without squashing.

louis-lunch-hamburger.d: A beef patty cooked upright in a vertical cast-iron broiler, served between two slices of toasted white bread. Louis Lassen improvised it in 1900 for a customer in a hurry; the shop still uses the same 1898 broilers, and flatly refuses ketchup.
s: Choose mince at twenty per cent fat and do not work it: shape the patties with your fingertips, without packing.
Compressed meat turns dense as it cooks; it is the one gesture that separates a good burger from a bad one.
Salt and pepper the surface only, just before cooking: salted ahead, mince weeps and welds together.
Cook upright in a vertical broiler, or failing that on a scalding cast-iron pan, 4 minutes a side, never pressing with a spatula.
Toast the bread, set the patty on it, a slice of cheese melted by the meat's heat, onion and tomato. Nothing else — certainly not ketchup.

toll-house-cookies.d: The first chocolate chip cookies, invented in 1938 by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn. Out of nuts, she chopped up a Nestlé bar expecting it to melt: it did not, and she sold the recipe to Nestlé for a dollar and a lifetime supply of chocolate.
s: Cream the softened butter with both sugars for 5 minutes, until it pales: that aeration gives the crisp edge.
Add the eggs one at a time then the vanilla, and finally the flour and bicarbonate, mixing as little as possible.
Chop the chocolate with a knife rather than using chips: irregular shards make seams, chips stay beads.
Chill the dough 24 hours: the flour hydrates, the sugar caramelises better, and the cookie keeps its thickness in the oven.
Bake 11 minutes at 190°C. Take them out while the centre still looks raw — they finish setting on the hot tray.

fluffernutter.d: A peanut butter and marshmallow cream sandwich, on white bread. Marshmallow Fluff was invented in Somerville in 1917; a Massachusetts senator proposed making it the official state sandwich, which the legislature is still debating.
s: Take the peanut butter out half an hour ahead: cold, it tears the crumb instead of spreading.
Spread it on one slice in a thick, even layer, right to the edges.
Spread the marshmallow cream on the other slice, never on the same one: layered together they merge and the contrast of textures is lost.
Close the sandwich without pressing — marshmallow escapes under the least pressure.
Cut on the diagonal with a knife run under hot water and wiped. Eaten within the hour, before the bread goes damp.

pancakes-au-sirop-derable.d: Thick buttermilk pancakes drowned in Vermont maple syrup. The Abenaki were tapping maples before the settlers arrived; forty litres of sap make one of syrup, which explains the price and rules out flavoured imitations.
s: Mix the dry ingredients on one side, the wet on the other, then combine in ten turns only.
The batter must stay lumpy: a smooth batter has developed its gluten and gives flat, rubbery pancakes.
Rest it 15 minutes, while the bicarbonate reacts with the buttermilk and bubbles rise to the surface.
Heat a pan over medium heat and grease it with a buttered cloth. Pour a ladleful and wait for the bubbles to burst and the edges to dry before turning — once only.
Warm the maple syrup before serving: cold, it sets the butter and slides off instead of soaking in.

apple-pie-nouvelle-angleterre.d: A double-crust apple pie, served warm with a slice of sharp Vermont cheddar. The pairing startles outside New England; a local saying has it that apple pie without cheese is like a kiss without a squeeze.
s: Use two varieties: one that holds, one that collapses. The first gives the pieces, the second the purée that binds them.
Cut the apples into thick wedges, squeeze lemon over and mix with the sugar, flour and spices.
Let them drain 45 minutes in a colander and reduce the collected juice to a syrup before pouring it back: that is what stops the gap forming under the crust.
Fill in a high dome, dot with butter, cover, seal by pinching and cut four vents.
Bake 20 minutes at 220°C then 40 minutes at 190°C. Serve warm, with aged cheddar cut in thick slices.

bagel-lox-schmear.p: Lower East Side, New York, United States
bagel-lox-schmear.d: A split bagel spread with cream cheese and covered with cured salmon, red onion and capers. The bagel came from Poland with Ashkenazi Jews around 1880; lox is not smoked but brined, and the word comes from Yiddish laks, salmon.
s: Choose a bagel baked that day, with a glossy crust: a bagel boiled before baking shines, one merely baked does not.
Split it and toast it only if it is a day old — toasting a fresh bagel destroys its characteristic chew.
Take the cream cheese out twenty minutes ahead and work it with a spatula until smooth.
Spread it thickly, almost as thick as the crumb: the schmear is not a thin layer, it is one of the two main ingredients.
Lay the salmon in loose folds, add very thin onion rings, capers, dill and pepper. Close and eat at once.

dirty-water-hot-dog.d: A beef frankfurter kept hot in the simmering water of a cart, served with sauerkraut and onion sauce. New Yorkers call it a dirty water dog: the water in the tank is never changed all day, and that is reckoned to make the flavour.
s: Make the onion sauce: sliced onions melted for 25 minutes, then tomato purée, vinegar, sugar and a pinch of cinnamon, let down with water.
Reduce it 20 minutes until it coats: it is what separates a New York hot dog from every other.
Heat water to 85°C and hold the frankfurters in it at least 15 minutes, never boiling — a boil splits the skin.
Warm the buns in the steam above the tank, never in a toaster: the bread must be soft and damp.
Dress in this order: yellow mustard, frankfurter, pressed sauerkraut, onion sauce. Eaten standing, within two minutes.

black-and-white-cookie.d: A large soft cookie iced half vanilla, half chocolate, on its flat side. Born around 1902 in a German bakery in Yorkville, it became a New York emblem of coexistence — and is always eaten starting from the dark side.
s: Cream the butter and sugar, add the eggs then alternate flour and milk: this is a cake batter, not a biscuit dough.
Drop large spoonfuls well apart and smooth them into 10 cm discs with the back of a wet spoon.
Bake 14 minutes at 190°C until the edges barely colour, and cool completely upside down, flat side up.
It is the flat side that is iced, never the domed one: that is the New York rule and it admits no exception.
Make a thick icing of icing sugar, hot water and lemon; ice one half white, add cocoa to the rest and ice the other, drawing the border with a straight edge.

pork-roll-taylor-ham.d: Slices of cured pork griddled with an egg and cheese in an English muffin. New Jersey is split over the name: Taylor ham in the north, pork roll in the south, with the border crossing the state at Trenton — the argument has never been settled.
s: Cut the pork roll into 6 mm slices and make four cuts in each from the edge toward the centre.
Those cuts are not decorative: without them the slice domes as it cooks and touches the griddle only at the edges.
Griddle them 3 minutes a side on a dry plate, until the edges brown and crisp.
Cook the eggs on the griddle in the rendered fat, yolk firm or runny to taste, and lay the cheese on so it melts in the heat.
Toast the muffin, stack pork roll, egg and cheese, and close. Ketchup, salt, pepper — the only combination New Jersey allows.

biscuits-and-gravy.d: Savoury buttermilk scones drowned in a white sausage gravy. It has been the Appalachian breakfast since the early 19th century: two cheap ingredients, flour and milk, kept a man going until evening in the mines.
s: Freeze the butter for half an hour and grate it into the flour: the frozen shreds melt in the oven and create the leaves that lift the biscuit.
Pour in the cold buttermilk and bring the dough together in a few movements, without kneading — a worked biscuit turns to stone.
Fold the dough in three twice, like puff pastry, then cut with a cutter pressed straight down in one clean movement.
A cutter that is twisted seals the layers and the biscuit rises lopsided. Bake 14 minutes at 220°C with the biscuits touching.
Fry the crumbled sausage meat, dust with two spoonfuls of flour, moisten with hot milk and pepper very generously: pepper is the gravy's third ingredient, not a seasoning.

pulled-pork-caroline-du-nord.d: A pork shoulder smoked for ten hours then pulled, dressed with a cider vinegar sauce. North Carolina divides into two schools: the East smokes the whole hog with pure vinegar sauce, the West takes only the shoulder and tolerates a touch of tomato.
s: Rub the shoulder with a mix of salt, pepper, paprika and brown sugar, and leave it twelve hours in the cold, uncovered.
Uncovered drying forms a tacky film on the surface: that film holds the smoke, and wet meat takes none.
Smoke at 110°C over hickory or oak for ten hours, to 95°C at the centre — temperature, not the clock, decides.
Around 70°C the temperature stops rising for two hours: that is the stall, collagen melting. Do not raise the heat, wait.
Rest it an hour wrapped, then pull it by hand with two forks. Dress with the vinegar sauce and serve in a bun with coleslaw.

southern-mac-and-cheese.d: Macaroni bound with egg and evaporated milk, baked until it can be cut in squares. Thomas Jefferson brought the recipe back from France in 1790, but it was James Hemings, his enslaved cook trained in Paris, who worked it out in America.
s: Cook the macaroni two minutes less than the packet says: it finishes in the oven and drinks the custard.
Grate the cheese yourself: pre-grated cheese is coated in anti-caking starch, which makes the bake grainy.
Beat the eggs with the evaporated milk, mustard and cayenne — this is a custard, not a béchamel, and it is what lets you cut it.
Layer pasta and cheese in three tiers in a buttered dish, keeping a third of the cheddar for the top.
Pour over the custard, rest ten minutes so it seeps through, and bake 45 minutes at 180°C. Cool 20 minutes before cutting.

fried-green-tomatoes.d: Slices of unripe tomato crumbed in cornmeal and fried, served with a remoulade. The recipe appears in northern books as early as 1877; the South adopted it during the Depression, when waiting for a tomato to ripen was a luxury.
s: Choose frankly green, hard tomatoes, never blushing: one that has begun to ripen collapses in the fryer.
Cut them into 8 mm rounds, salt them and drain them 20 minutes on paper, then blot them.
Flour, dip in buttermilk beaten with egg, then cornmeal: cornmeal alone, without flour beneath, will not cling to a wet tomato.
Fry 3 minutes a side in two centimetres of oil at 180°C, without crowding the pan.
Drain upright and salt at once. Serve with a remoulade of mayonnaise, chopped gherkin, paprika and cayenne.

pimento-cheese.d: A spread of orange cheddar, sweet peppers and mayonnaise, called the caviar of the South. It was born in New York around 1910, from newly made cream cheese meeting tinned Spanish sweet peppers, but the South has claimed it beyond recall.
s: Grate the cheddar on the coarse holes, not in a processor: the shreds must stay distinct, a cheese purée is no longer pimento cheese.
Choose a well-aged orange cheddar: the annatto colouring changes nothing in the taste but gives the expected colour.
Drain the sweet peppers and chop them by knife, keeping visible pieces.
Mix with a fork with the mayonnaise, cream cheese, grated onion, cayenne and plenty of pepper.
Rest it overnight in the fridge: the cheese absorbs the mayonnaise and the spread firms up. Take it out an hour before serving.

skillet-cornbread.d: A cornbread baked in a scalding cast-iron skillet, with a dark, crackling crust. The South puts no sugar in it and says so firmly: a sweetened cornbread is cake, and a sure sign of a northern recipe.
s: Put the cast-iron skillet with the lard in a 230°C oven twenty minutes ahead: it must be smoking when the batter arrives.
It is the shock of cold batter on scalding iron that forms the crust: in a warm pan you get a pale, soft cake.
Mix the cornmeal, flour, bicarbonate, baking powder and salt, then the buttermilk and eggs, in twenty turns only.
Take out the skillet, swirl the smoking fat up the sides, and pour the batter in at once: it must sizzle immediately.
Bake 22 minutes. Turn out onto a board and serve warm with butter — or crumbled into a glass of buttermilk, as in the South.

etouffee-aux-ecrevisses.d: Crawfish tails smothered in a blond roux and served over rice. Étouffer, in Acadian French, means to cook covered in little liquid; Breaux Bridge has proclaimed itself the crawfish capital of the world since 1959 and holds a festival for it.
s: Make a butter and flour roux and cook it to the colour of peanut butter, stirring without pause for 10 minutes.
An étouffée roux is blond, not brown: the dark roux belongs to gumbo, and confusing the two changes the dish entirely.
Throw in the trinity — onion, celery, green pepper — all at once into the scalding roux: the shock stops the roux cooking dead.
Add the garlic, broth and cayenne, and let it thicken 15 minutes uncovered.
Fold in the crawfish tails and cover: they cook in 5 minutes and turn rubbery beyond eight. Add parsley and serve over rice.

muffuletta.d: A round sesame loaf filled with cured meats, provolone and a marinated olive salad. Salvatore Lupo invented it in 1906 for the Sicilian dockers of the French Market; it is eaten cold and is better for being pressed for hours before cutting.
s: Make the olive salad the day before: green and black olives chopped, giardiniera, garlic, capers, oregano, drowned in olive oil.
It must macerate at least twenty-four hours — it is the dish, the cured meats are only a support.
Split the round loaf horizontally and hollow the crumb of the lid slightly to make room.
Moisten both faces with oil from the salad, then build: olives, provolone, meats, provolone, olives.
Close, wrap tightly and press under a weight for at least 3 hours. Cut in quarters at the moment of serving, never before.

boudin-cajun.d: A sausage of pork, liver and cooked rice, inherited from French boudin blanc by the deported Acadians. It is bought at the butcher's and eaten standing in the car park, squeezing the casing between the teeth to take only the filling — the casing is thrown away.
s: Poach the pork, liver and trinity 1 hour in salted water, and keep the broth carefully.
Mince the meat and liver on the medium plate, keeping some grain: a Cajun boudin is not a mousse.
Mix with the rice cooked in that broth, the spring onion, parsley, cayenne and plenty of black pepper.
The proportion is roughly half rice, half meat: more rice and the boudin turns pasty, less and it falls apart.
Fill the casings loosely and poach 20 minutes at 75°C, never boiling — beyond that the casing splits and all the rice escapes.

king-cake.d: A cinnamon brioche crown iced in the three Mardi Gras colours — purple, gold and green. The French bean has become a plastic baby hidden underneath: whoever finds it must provide the next king cake, which keeps the custom going until Lent.
s: Knead a brioche dough with the flour, warm milk, yeast, eggs, sugar and salt, then work in the softened butter.
Prove 1½ hours, roll into a large rectangle and cover with butter, brown sugar, cinnamon and beaten cream cheese.
Roll it up tightly lengthwise, then join the two ends into a crown, pinching the join firmly.
Cut the top of the crown on the bias every five centimetres, to let the spiral of filling show.
Prove for an hour and bake 30 minutes at 180°C. Ice with sugar and lemon, and sprinkle in three bands of purple, gold and green.

chili-con-carne-texas.d: A stew of beef cubes in a purée of dried chillies, without a single bean. The Chili Queens sold it on San Antonio's Plaza from 1880; in Texas, putting beans in a chili is an offence no competition admits.
s: Seed the dried chillies, toast them 30 seconds a side in a dry pan, then soak them 30 minutes in hot water.
That brief toasting wakes the oils; burnt a second too long, they make the whole chili bitter and nothing rescues it.
Blend them with the soaking water into a smooth purée and pass it through a sieve to hold back the skins.
Cut the beef into 2 cm cubes — never minced — and sear them in lard in small batches.
Add the chilli purée, garlic, cumin, oregano and broth, and simmer 2½ hours. Thicken with slaked masa harina in the last twenty minutes.

breakfast-tacos.d: Flour tortillas filled with scrambled egg, chorizo and potato, eaten at the wheel. Austin and San Antonio dispute the invention with equal bad faith; the one point of agreement is that the tortilla must be flour and made that morning.
s: Dice the potatoes small and fry them 12 minutes, until golden and tender.
Fry the crumbled Mexican chorizo separately and keep its red fat: it is what will colour the eggs.
Beat the eggs with no milk or cream and cook them in that fat over low heat, stirring without pause — they must stay creamy and underdone.
Warm the tortillas thirty seconds a side on a dry griddle: microwaved, they turn rubbery.
Fill, add cheese to melt in the heat, the tomato and jalapeño salsa, coriander and a squeeze of lime. Fold and eat at once.

kolaches-texan.d: A soft brioche wrapped around a smoked sausage, sold on the highway between Dallas and Austin. Moravian Czechs settled in West in 1880; a true koláč is sweet and open, and the savoury sausage version is properly called a klobasnek.
s: Make a starter with the yeast, warm milk and a little flour, and wait for it to double before going further.
Knead with the rest, then work in the softened butter: Czech dough is richer than bread dough and lighter than brioche.
Prove 1½ hours, then flatten 60 g pieces into rectangles.
Blot the sausages carefully: a wet sausage makes the dough lift as it bakes and the klobasnek opens.
Roll the sausage up with a strip of cheese and jalapeño, seam underneath, prove 40 minutes and bake 18 minutes at 190°C.

chicken-fried-steak.d: A tenderised steak, crumbed and fried like chicken, drowned in a white pepper gravy. It is the Viennese schnitzel filtered through Texas's German and Czech immigrants; Lamesa claims the invention in 1911 and holds an annual festival for it.
s: Tenderise the steaks with a toothed mallet to 8 mm: the connective tissue must be broken, or the meat shrinks in the oil.
Flour them, dip in egg beaten with milk, then in flour mixed with baking powder and paprika.
The baking powder in the coating is the Texan trick: it puffs the crust and gives it its blistered look.
Rest the crumbed steaks 15 minutes on a rack: the coating hydrates and grips, instead of peeling off in sheets.
Fry 4 minutes a side at 175°C, set aside, and make the gravy in three spoonfuls of the frying fat with flour, hot milk and plenty of black pepper.

chile-con-queso.d: A melted cheese dip with chillies and tomato, served scalding with corn chips. Born in San Antonio in the 1920s, it owes its fluidity to the emulsifying salts of processed cheese: a farmhouse cheddar would split into oil and strings.
s: Roast the green chillies until the skin blackens, shut them in a bag for 15 minutes, peel and chop them.
Fry the onion and crumbled chorizo, then add the crushed tomato and reduce for 10 minutes.
Dice the cheese and melt it over a bain-marie with the milk, never over direct heat: above 70°C it splits.
Fold the garnish into the melted cheese off the heat, and add the cumin and coriander.
Serve at once in a warmed dish: queso sets within five minutes, and reheating it a second time turns it grainy.

kansas-city-ribs.d: Pork ribs smoked five hours and lacquered with a thick molasses sauce. Henry Perry, born in Tennessee, opened his first stand in 1908 and founded the Kansas City school; the city now counts over a hundred barbecue houses.
s: Remove the white membrane from the back of the rack by lifting it with a knife then pulling with a cloth: it never melts and blocks the smoke.
Rub with a mix of brown sugar, paprika, salt and pepper, and leave twelve hours in the cold.
Smoke at 110°C over applewood, three hours uncovered, spraying apple juice every hour.
Wrap in foil with a little juice and continue two hours: that stage tenderises without drying.
Unwrap, brush with sauce and return for thirty minutes to lacquer it. The meat should give under the tooth, but not fall off the bone.
