cincinnati-chili.d: A beef sauce with cinnamon and cocoa served over spaghetti, under a mountain of grated cheddar. The Kiradjieff brothers, Macedonian immigrants, created it in 1922 by adapting a Balkan stew; you order it three, four or five ways depending on the toppings.
s: Never brown the meat: whisk the raw minced beef into cold water with a fork, until not a lump remains.
That is what sets Cincinnati chili apart from every other: boiled meat stays in fine grains and the sauce is not greasy.
Bring to the boil, add the grated onion, tomato purée and every spice, and simmer 2½ hours uncovered.
Rest it overnight in the cold and lift off the set fat: it is the only way to reach the expected texture.
Serve over spaghetti, with grated cheddar piled high, kidney beans and raw onion according to how many ways you want it.

toasted-ravioli.p: The Hill, St. Louis, Missouri, United States
toasted-ravioli.d: Breaded, fried ravioli dipped in tomato sauce, the speciality of St. Louis's Italian quarter. Legend has a cook dropping ravioli into the fryer instead of the pot around 1940; they are called toasted although they are fried, which nobody explains.
s: Use fresh uncooked ravioli: pre-poached ones tear during crumbing and let the filling escape.
Beat the eggs with the milk and pass the ravioli first through that, then through breadcrumbs mixed with parmesan.
Let them dry 15 minutes on a rack before frying: the coating grips and does not peel off in the oil.
Fry 2 minutes a side at 180°C, six at a time, so the temperature does not fall.
Drain, salt and scatter parmesan while they are scalding. Serve with hot tomato sauce, for dipping.

corn-dog.d: A sausage on a stick, dipped in cornbread batter and fried. Patented in 1929 in Springfield as the crusty cur, it found its public at Midwest state fairs; it is the stick, more than the batter, that made it the first American meal eaten walking.
s: Blot the sausages and roll them in a film of dry flour: without it the batter slides off and bares the sausage in the oil.
Skewer them on wooden sticks, pushing them in only two-thirds of the way.
Mix the batter and pour it into a tall narrow glass: the only way to dip a corn dog in one vertical movement.
The batter should be as thick as waffle batter — too thin it runs, too thick it stays raw in the centre.
Dip, drain for two seconds and lower into oil at 180°C, holding the stick for ten seconds before letting go, so the crust sets.

brownies-palmer-house.d: The first known brownie, created in 1893 at the Palmer House hotel for the World's Fair. Bertha Palmer wanted a dessert ladies could carry in a lunch box: smaller than a slice of cake, sturdier than a tart, apricot-glazed to keep.
s: Melt the chocolate and butter over a bain-marie, never above 45°C, and let it cool before the eggs go in.
Whisk the eggs and sugar separately for 5 minutes to the ribbon: that foam gives the thin shiny crust on top.
Fold in the warm chocolate, then the flour and salt in ten turns — overmixed, the batter gives a cake and not a brownie.
Pour into a lined tin and cover with whole walnut halves, generously, as at the Palmer House.
Bake 35 minutes at 175°C: the centre should still tremble. Coat with apricot glaze let down with hot water as it leaves the oven.

navajo-taco.d: A round of fried bread topped with beans, meat and raw vegetables. Fry bread was born in 1864 during the Long Walk, when the army issued deported Navajos flour and lard in place of their crops: a dish born of a deportation, now both emblem and subject of argument.
s: Mix the flour, baking powder and salt, pour in the warm water and bring the dough together without kneading: fry bread needs no developed gluten.
Rest it 30 minutes under a cloth — it is the rest, not the working, that makes it supple to stretch.
Stretch each ball by hand to 20 cm and pierce a hole at the centre with a fingertip: without it the round balloons and cooks unevenly.
Fry in two centimetres of lard at 190°C, 90 seconds a side, until it blisters and browns.
Drain and top it scalding with crushed pinto beans, spiced meat, lettuce, tomato, cheese and sour cream. Eaten by hand, folded in two.

chimichanga.d: A burrito fried until crisp, coated with sauce and melted cheese. Monica Flin of El Charro in Tucson is said to have dropped a burrito in the fryer in 1922 and swallowed a curse in front of her nephews: chimichanga is the word she invented instead.
s: Braise the chuck 3 hours with the onion, cumin and green chillies, then shred it and let it cool.
A warm filling softens the tortilla and the chimichanga opens in the oil: the commonest failure.
Warm the tortillas to make them pliable, fill the lower third, fold the sides in then roll very tightly.
Fix the flap with a wooden pick or a smear of bean paste, which glues as it cooks.
Fry 3 minutes at 190°C, spooning oil over the top, then coat with sauce and cheese and pass under the grill. Remove the pick before serving.

carne-adovada.d: Pork marinated overnight in a purée of New Mexico red chillies, then braised until it shreds. Adovada comes from adobado, marinated: the chilli marinade was first a preservation, before refrigeration, and the dish is traditionally served at Christmas.
s: Remove the stems and seeds from the dried red chillies, then soak them 30 minutes in boiling water.
Do not toast them as you would for a Texas chili: New Mexico chilli is sweet and fruity, and toasting turns it bitter.
Blend them with the soaking water, garlic, oregano, cumin, vinegar and honey, and pass through a sieve.
Cut the pork into 4 cm cubes and marinate it overnight in that purée, in the cold.
Braise covered 3 hours at 160°C, adding nothing but broth if the sauce tightens too far. Serve with flour tortillas.

salsa-verde-du-desert.p: Santa Fe, New Mexico, United States
salsa-verde-du-desert.d: A green sauce of roasted tomatillos, jalapeños and coriander. The tomatillo is not a green tomato but a husked fruit, grown by the Aztecs long before it; its acidity, not the lime's, is what gives the sauce its bite.
s: Remove the papery husks from the tomatillos and wash them in hot water: they are covered in a sticky, bitter film.
Roast them whole on a dry scalding griddle with the onion, unpeeled garlic and jalapeños, turning them.
They are ready when the skin blackens in patches and the flesh slumps — allow 12 minutes, no more.
Blend barely, in pulses: a salsa verde blended too long turns foamy and pale instead of staying dark green.
Add the coriander, lime juice and salt outside the blender, with a fork. Rest an hour before serving.

california-roll.p: Little Tokyo, Los Angeles, California, United States
california-roll.d: An inside-out maki, rice outside, filled with crab, avocado and cucumber. Ichiro Mashita invented it in the sixties at the Tokyo Kaikan for Americans put off by raw fish and by visible seaweed: rice on the outside hid the nori.
s: Wash the rice seven times until the water runs clear, cook it and season it with sweetened vinegar, cutting it in with a spatula and never stirring.
Spread the cold rice over the whole nori sheet, then turn the lot over: the nori ends up underneath and the rice against the mat.
Cover the mat with cling film before turning, otherwise the rice sticks to it and the roll tears.
Line up the crab, avocado and cucumber along the lower third, and roll pressing evenly, without crushing.
Roll the log in sesame seeds and cut into eight with a wetted knife, wiping the blade between each slice.

avocado-toast.p: Venice, Los Angeles, California, United States
avocado-toast.d: A slice of sourdough covered with crushed avocado, lemon and chilli flakes. Popularised in Sydney in the 1990s, it exploded in Venice around 2010; California grows nearly all American avocados, and crushing rather than blending is the one rule that matters.
s: Choose a Hass avocado that yields under the thumb near the stem but stays firm in the middle: overripe, it turns stringy and grey.
Toast the sourdough until frankly brown: pale bread goes soggy under avocado within two minutes.
Crush the avocado with a fork in a bowl, with lemon juice and coarse salt, leaving pieces — never in a blender.
The lemon is not there for flavour but against oxidation: without it the avocado browns before it reaches the table.
Spread on the still-warm bread, trickle olive oil, pepper, add the chilli flakes and, if you like, a poached egg.

sourdough-san-francisco.p: Fisherman’s Wharf, San Francisco, California, United States
sourdough-san-francisco.d: A wild-leavened bread with a thick crust and a frankly sour crumb. The starter arrived with the gold rushers of 1849; a bacterium peculiar to the bay, named Lactobacillus sanfranciscensis, gives it its acidity, and the same starters have run since the 1906 earthquake.
s: Refresh the starter twelve hours ahead: it must triple and just begin to fall, the sign it is at peak activity.
Mix the flours and water alone and leave them an hour to autolyse — hydration before salt makes the dough extensible without kneading.
Add the starter then the salt, and give it six sets of folds thirty minutes apart instead of kneading.
Ferment 4 hours at 24°C, shape into a tight round and chill overnight: it is the cold that develops the acidity.
Bake in a pot preheated to 250°C, 20 minutes covered then 25 uncovered at 230°C. Wait two hours before cutting.

in-n-out-double-double.d: Two thin patties and two slices of cheese in a soft bun, with a pink sauce. Harry and Esther Snyder opened California's first drive-through in Baldwin Park in 1948; animal style, with caramelised onions and a mustard-cooked patty, has never appeared on a menu in sixty years.
s: Make the sauce: mayonnaise, ketchup, very finely chopped gherkins and a spoonful of their vinegar, mixed and chilled an hour.
Shape two 60 g patties and press them between films to 12 cm across: they must be wider than the bun, because they shrink by a quarter.
Griddle the cut faces of the bun in butter until brown: that toasted layer is what keeps it from going soggy.
Sear the patties on a scalding griddle, 90 seconds a side, brushing the raw face with mustard before turning them.
Stack: sauce, lettuce, tomato, onion, patty, cheese, patty, cheese. Serve within the minute.

mission-burrito.p: Mission District, San Francisco, California, United States
mission-burrito.d: A giant burrito holding rice, beans, meat, cheese, guacamole and sour cream, wrapped in foil. It was born in 1961 in the Mission District: the innovation was the steamed tortilla, supple enough to wrap a whole meal in one piece.
s: Marinate the steak in lime, garlic and cumin for an hour, then grill it over high heat and rest it before dicing.
Steam the large tortilla for ten seconds, or thirty in a damp cloth in the microwave: it must go soft and elastic.
A dry tortilla cracks when folded, and a burrito that cracks loses everything; it is simple mechanics.
Fill it in a thick band down the centre, rice and beans at the bottom to absorb the juices, meat and wet items above.
Fold both sides inward, then roll, tightening firmly at every turn. Wrap in foil immediately: the foil is what holds it together.

cobb-salad.p: Hollywood, Los Angeles, California, United States
cobb-salad.d: A salad composed in parallel stripes of chicken, bacon, egg, avocado and Roquefort. Bob Cobb, who ran the Brown Derby, improvised it one night in 1937 from what was left in the fridge; the next day Sid Grauman ordered one, and it stayed on the menu for thirty years.
s: Chop all the greens very finely — this is a chopped salad, not a leaf salad, and that is what lets it be eaten with a spoon.
Grill the bacon until it snaps, drain it on paper and chop it once cold, otherwise it squashes.
Boil the eggs 9 minutes, refresh them in iced water and chop them separately.
Lay each element in a parallel stripe over the bed of greens, without mixing: the arrangement in rows is the definition of the dish.
Whisk a red wine vinegar and mustard dressing, and pour it at the table, in front of your guests, before tossing.

french-dip.d: A roast beef sandwich in a bun dipped in the roasting juices, served with a bowl of jus on the side. Two Los Angeles houses have disputed the invention since 1908; one says a roll fell into the dripping pan, the other that a customer with sore gums asked for it that way.
s: Sear the joint on every face, then braise it 2 hours with the onion, garlic and herbs in the broth.
Cool it completely in its juices: the only way to slice it thinly enough, a hot joint shreds under the blade.
Strain the juices, skim them and keep them scalding: they are the dish, and lukewarm jus ruins everything.
Slice the beef with a long knife, almost translucent, and warm it thirty seconds in the jus before filling.
Dip the cut face of the roll in the jus — the top stays dry so the sandwich can be held — fill it and serve a bowl of jus alongside.

donuts-glazed-la.p: Inglewood, Los Angeles, California, United States
donuts-glazed-la.d: A ring of yeasted dough fried and sugar-glazed, still warm. Los Angeles has more donut shops than any other American city, largely run by Cambodian refugees who arrived after 1975; the glaze must go onto a hot donut, so that it turns transparent.
s: Knead a soft yeasted dough with warm milk, yeast, eggs, sugar and salt, then work in the softened butter.
Prove for an hour, roll to 1 cm and cut the rings; re-roll the trimmings once only.
Prove 45 minutes on squares of oiled paper, uncovered: an over-proved donut collapses in the oil.
Fry at 175°C, 60 seconds a side, sliding them into the oil off their paper so as not to distort them.
Dip them in a glaze of icing sugar and milk as they come out, still scalding: on a cold donut the glaze stays white and opaque.

cedar-plank-salmon.p: Pike Place, Seattle, Washington, United States
cedar-plank-salmon.d: A sockeye salmon fillet cooked on a red cedar plank set over coals. The peoples of Puget Sound have cooked this way for a thousand years: the wet plank smoulders without burning and the wood gives a resin no marinade or smoker reproduces.
s: Soak the cedar plank at least 2 hours in water, weighted with a plate: a dry plank catches fire within three minutes.
Use only untreated red cedar sold for cooking — hardware-store boards are impregnated with chemicals.
Salt the salmon half an hour ahead, blot it, then brush it with mustard and brown sugar.
Set the plank alone on the coals until it crackles and smokes, then turn it over and lay the salmon on the hot face.
Cover and allow 20 minutes without ever turning the fish: it is ready when the flesh parts into flakes under a point. Serve on the plank.

dungeness-crab.d: A whole crab boiled in seawater, served with clarified butter and lemon. It takes its name from a hamlet in Washington State where it was fished from 1848; it became the state crustacean in 2009, and its season runs November to June.
s: Buy them alive and lively: a crab dead more than an hour develops a bitterness cooking does not remove.
Bring a large pot of water salted to 35 g per litre — the salinity of the sea — to a rolling boil with the bay.
Drop the crabs in head first and allow 12 minutes for eight hundred grams, from the return to the boil.
Chill them at once in iced water: without that shock they keep cooking inside the shell and the meat turns stringy.
Pull off the apron, lift the carapace, remove the gills and crack the claws with the back of a knife. Garlic clarified butter and lemon, nothing else.

smoked-salmon-chowder.d: A creamy soup of alder-smoked salmon, potato and corn. It is the Pacific Northwest version of the New England chowder: salmon replaces the clam, and alder replaces southern hickory, which gives a gentler smoke.
s: Render the diced bacon, lift it out and sweat the onion and celery in its fat, without colour.
Dust with flour, cook it two minutes then whisk in the hot fish broth.
Add the diced potatoes and cook 15 minutes, until they crush against the side of the pot under a spoon.
Crush a quarter of the potatoes into the soup to bind it: a chowder is thickened with neither starch nor cream alone.
Add the cream, corn and flaked smoked salmon off the heat, and do not boil again — smoked salmon shrinks and dries within a minute.

marionberry-pie.d: A pie of marionberry, a blackberry bred in 1956 in Marion County. It is Oregon's unofficial berry, and the state grows nearly the world's entire crop: juicier and sharper than a common blackberry, it needs more thickener than any other.
s: Mix the berries with the sugar, tapioca and lemon juice, and macerate 30 minutes so the tapioca hydrates.
Tapioca beats cornstarch for this berry: it survives long acidic cooking without breaking down, which cornstarch does not.
Fill the pastry case in a dome, dot with butter and cover with a lattice of strips rather than a solid disc.
The lattice is not decorative: this berry gives up so much juice that it must be allowed to evaporate as it bakes.
Bake 15 minutes at 220°C then 40 minutes at 190°C, until the juice bubbles at the centre and not only at the edges. Cool 4 hours.

seattle-teriyaki.d: Grilled, lacquered chicken thighs served on rice with a cabbage salad. Toshihiro Nakae opened Toshi's in 1976 and created the format: the city now has several hundred teriyaki shops, a Seattle dish more than a Japanese one.
s: Use boneless thighs with the skin: breast dries out and Seattle teriyaki is not made otherwise.
Reduce the soy, sugar, mirin, garlic and ginger by half: the sauce must coat the back of a spoon, or it slides off the meat.
Marinate the chicken an hour in a third of that sauce, and keep the rest for lacquering.
Grill skin down first over medium heat for ten minutes, without basting: the sugar would burn before the flesh cooked.
Lacquer only in the last three minutes, in two coats. Serve on rice, with cabbage shredded and dressed with rice vinegar.

spam-musubi.d: A lacquered slice of Spam on a block of rice, belted with nori. Spam arrived with army rations during the Pacific war and never left: Hawaii eats more of it per head than any other state, and Barbara Funamura settled this format around 1980.
s: Cook the sushi rice and let it cool without vinegar: in Hawaii the musubi rice is plain, only the Spam is seasoned.
Cut the Spam into eight one-centimetre slices and griddle them dry until the edges brown and crisp.
Deglaze the pan with soy, sugar and mirin, and let the syrup coat each slice 2 minutes a side.
Use the empty Spam tin as a mould: press the rice into the bottom, set the slice on top, and push it out in one movement.
Belt it with a strip of nori, damping the end to stick it. Eaten by hand, warm or cold, within six hours.

loco-moco.d: A bowl of rice topped with a beef patty, a fried egg and brown onion gravy. Invented in 1949 at the Lincoln Grill in Hilo for hungry teenagers coming off the surf, who wanted something other than a sandwich and could not afford a proper meal.
s: Cook a short, sticky white rice, wetter than a pilaf: it must hold a dome in the bowl and drink the gravy.
Shape thick 150 g patties without packing, and press a hollow in the centre with your thumb so they do not dome as they cook.
Sear them 4 minutes a side, lift them out and soften the onion in the rendered fat for 15 minutes.
Dust with flour, moisten with broth, add soy and Worcestershire, and let it thicken to a coating consistency.
Build: rice, patty, gravy, then the fried egg at the last moment, yolk runny. It is the yolk that binds everything in the bowl.

shave-ice-hawaienne.d: Ice shaved into flakes, doused with tropical fruit syrups, over a scoop of ice cream and azuki beans. Japanese plantation workers brought it around 1900 as kakigori; the ice is shaved, never crushed, and that is the whole difference.
s: Make a simple syrup of equal sugar and water, divide it in three and flavour each part with a different fruit, blended and strained.
Cool the syrups completely: poured warm over the ice they melt it before it reaches the table.
Freeze a block of water rather than cubes: it is a block that is shaved, and cubes give shards instead of flakes.
Shave the ice in very thin layers and pile it without pressing, into a high dome: the snow must stay airy and melt on the tongue.
Set the scoop of ice cream and the azuki beans at the bottom of the cup, under the snow, and pour the syrups in three sectors. Condensed milk over the top.

malasada-hawaienne.d: A Portuguese doughnut with no hole and no filling, rolled in sugar. Madeiran and Azorean workers brought it to the plantations from 1878; it was eaten on Shrove Tuesday to use up the lard, and Honolulu still calls that day Malasada Day.
s: Dissolve the yeast in warm milk with a spoonful of sugar and wait until it foams properly.
Knead with the flour, eggs, 60 g of the sugar, the zest and salt for 15 minutes, then work in the softened butter.
The dough must stay very soft and sticky: that is what gives the stringy crumb, and it is handled with oiled hands.
Prove 1½ hours, scoop out balls with an oiled spoon without shaping them — a malasada is irregular by definition.
Fry 90 seconds a side at 175°C and roll them in the remaining sugar while scalding. Eaten within the hour.

huli-huli-chicken.d: A chicken marinated in soy, pineapple and ginger, grilled between two racks turned over and over. Ernest Morgado created it in 1955 for a farm fundraiser; huli means turn in Hawaiian, and the cook shouted it so the helpers flipped the racks together.
s: Spatchcock the chicken by removing the backbone: laid flat, it cooks evenly between two racks.
Mix the soy, ketchup, brown sugar, pineapple juice, grated ginger and garlic, and set aside a third for glazing.
Marinate three hours at most: pineapple holds an enzyme that dissolves protein, and a whole night would turn the flesh to mush.
Grill over indirect heat, bone side down first, turning every five minutes for forty minutes.
Baste only in the last ten minutes, in three coats, turning each time: applied earlier, the sugar carbonises.

saimin.d: A noodle soup in dashi and pork broth, topped with char siu, egg and kamaboko. It was born in the plantation camps where Japanese, Chinese, Filipinos and Portuguese shared kitchens: nobody can claim its origin, which is precisely what it says.
s: Blanch the pork bones five minutes, throw the water away and rinse them: that is what gives a clear broth instead of a grey one.
Return them to cold water with the ginger and simmer 2½ hours without ever boiling.
Meanwhile soak the kombu and dried shrimp cold, and heat them only to 60°C at the end.
Kombu brought to the boil turns slimy and bitter: it is lifted out the moment the water trembles, the rule of dashi.
Combine both broths, season with soy, and pour over noodles cooked separately. Top with char siu, egg, kamaboko and spring onion.

japadog.d: A hot dog dressed the Japanese way: Japanese mayonnaise, teriyaki sauce, grated daikon and shredded nori. A Japanese couple opened their cart on Burrard Street in 2005; the queue they created has spawned half a dozen imitators in the city.
s: Reduce the soy, sugar and mirin by half to a teriyaki that coats: too thin and it runs to the bottom of the bun.
Grate the daikon at the last moment and press it lightly — undrained, it soaks the bread within two minutes.
Griddle the sausages rather than boiling them: a japadog is known by its crisp skin, unlike the classic North American hot dog.
Steam the buns, then dress in this order: mayonnaise, sausage, teriyaki, daikon.
Finish with nori cut into fine threads and sesame seeds. The seaweed must stay dry: put under the sauce, it goes limp.

bison-burger.d: A burger of prairie bison, a lean and faintly sweet meat. Bison fed the First Nations for millennia before being wiped out in the late 19th century; Alberta's rebuilt herds now supply it, and its leanness demands short cooking.
s: Bison holds only two or three per cent fat: mix a spoonful of cold melted butter into each patty, or it will be dry.
Shape the patties without packing and press a hollow in the centre so they do not dome.
Sear them on a scalding griddle 3 minutes a side, no longer: medium, bison is still good; well done, it is beyond saving.
Never press with a spatula — the little juice it holds would go at once.
Rest 3 minutes before assembling, while the juices redistribute, and build the burger on a butter-toasted bun.

green-onion-cake.d: A layered spring onion pancake, pan-fried and cut into wedges. Siu To introduced it to Edmonton in 1979; the city adopted it so completely that it became its unofficial dish, and it has been sold at every Alberta festival for forty years.
s: Pour boiling water onto the flour and work it with a spoon: this is a scalded dough, which turns extensible and will not tear when stretched.
Knead five minutes once cool enough, then rest an hour under a damp cloth.
Roll very thin, brush with oil and cover with sliced spring onion, then roll it up tightly lengthwise.
Coil the rope into a spiral and press it gently flat: that spiral, not butter lamination, is what creates the layers.
Fry in oil 4 minutes a side over medium heat, then crush the cake between two spatulas to separate the leaves. Serve with a soy and vinegar dip.

fat-boy-winnipeg.d: A burger drowned in a chilli meat sauce, with shredded cabbage and mayonnaise. It came out of Winnipeg's Greek cafés in the sixties; the sauce, thick and cumin-scented, is ladled on and the sandwich wrapped in paper at once so it holds together.
s: For the sauce, whisk half the raw minced beef into cold broth before heating: the meat stays in fine grains and the sauce is not greasy.
Add the grated onion, tomato purée, chilli and cumin, and simmer 45 minutes until it coats the ladle.
Shape flat patties from the remaining beef and sear them on a scalding griddle, 3 minutes a side.
Shred the cabbage very finely and mix it with the mayonnaise just before serving — made ahead, it weeps.
Build: toasted bun, mayonnaise, patty, cheese, a good ladle of sauce, cabbage. Wrap in paper and wait a minute before biting.

honey-dill-sauce.d: A sauce of mayonnaise, honey and dill, served with chicken fingers and chips. It is so particular to Manitoba as to be unknown two provinces away: Manitobans often discover while travelling that it exists nowhere else.
s: Use fresh dill and not dried: dried, it brings only a grassy bitterness and no freshness at all.
Chop it very finely by knife, without the tough stems, and leave it a minute on the board to release its oil.
Warm the honey barely so it blends without lumps — heated above 40°C it loses its scent.
Mix into the mayonnaise with the garlic powder, a touch of vinegar and the lemon juice, whisking with a fork.
Rest 4 hours in the cold: the sauce is flat for the first quarter of an hour and right afterwards. It keeps a week.

pickered-fish.d: Walleye or pike from Lake Winnipeg pickled in sweetened vinegar with onions and juniper. Gimli was founded in 1875 by Icelanders fleeing a volcanic eruption; they recreated their fish curing there, and the settlement remains the largest Icelandic community outside Iceland.
s: Fillet the fish and pull every pin bone with tweezers: pike has whole rows of them, and one spoils the dish.
Dry-salt them 12 hours in the cold, then rinse and soak them 2 hours in clear water.
Boil the vinegar, water, sugar and spices, then cool completely — a warm marinade would cook the fish white and leave it woolly.
Cut the fillets into 4 cm pieces and layer them in a jar with onion rings.
Cover with the cold marinade and refrigerate at least five days. It keeps a month and goes with rye bread.

tarte-au-sucre.d: A tart of brown sugar and cream, set like a soft caramel. It descends from the sugar tarts of northern France, adapted first to maple sugar then to imported brown sugar; it must not be baked until firm, it sets as it cools.
s: Line the tin and blind-bake the pastry 12 minutes: without that pre-baking the very liquid filling would soak the base.
Mix the brown sugar and flour dry before adding any liquid — the only way to avoid lumps.
Add the cream, melted butter, egg and vanilla, and whisk just enough to combine, without aerating.
Pour into the pre-baked case and bake 30 minutes at 180°C: the centre must still tremble frankly when it comes out.
A tart baked until firm turns grainy as it cools. Let it set 4 hours at room temperature.

cretons.d: A pork spread cooked in milk with cinnamon and clove, eaten on toast at breakfast. Despite the name they are nothing like French cretons, which are fried fat residues: the milk and the sweet spices make this a Quebec pâté of its own.
s: Sweat the very finely chopped onion and garlic, then add the minced pork, crushing it with a fork so it does not clump.
Moisten with milk and simmer 1½ hours uncovered over very low heat, stirring every ten minutes.
The milk must evaporate almost entirely and the fat separate: the sign the cretons are ready.
Add the breadcrumbs in the last ten minutes — they absorb the remaining fat and give the spreadable texture.
Pot them, press down and set 12 hours in the cold. The spices only come through on the second day.

pouding-chomeur.d: A plain cake over which hot syrup is poured before baking: the cake rises, the syrup sinks, and a sauce forms beneath the sponge. It was created by Montreal factory women during the 1929 slump, with brown sugar — the maple syrup came later.
s: Cream the butter and sugar, add the eggs then alternate flour and milk, and pour the batter into a deep dish.
The dish must be tall: the syrup nearly doubles as it boils and overflows a tart tin.
Bring the maple syrup, cream and brown sugar to the boil and let them bubble for two minutes.
Pour it scalding over the raw batter, without mixing: that difference in temperature is what sends the syrup to the bottom.
Bake 40 minutes at 180°C without opening the door. Serve warm, digging down to the sauce beneath.

cipate.d: A layered pie of game, pork and potato separated by sheets of pastry, baked for six hours. The name comes from sea pie, the English sailors' dish, reshaped by French ears; in Abitibi it is made with hare and moose, elsewhere with chicken.
s: Cut all the meats into 3 cm cubes and marinate them overnight with the onion, savory and spices.
Line a cast-iron pot with a thick sheet of pastry taken up the sides — a cipâte bakes in its dish and is never turned out.
Alternate meat, potato and pastry sheets in three tiers, salting each layer.
Pour in hot broth to cover the top tier, cover with a sheet of pastry and cut a wide chimney.
Bake 45 minutes at 200°C then 5 hours at 140°C. Top up with broth through the chimney if the level drops: a dry cipâte is a failure.

oreilles-de-crisse.d: Strips of salt pork belly fried until they curl into crisp horns. They accompany the sugar shack meal in spring; the name, a disguised oath, comes from the shape they take in the fryer — an ear folded on itself.
s: Soak the salt pork belly 2 hours in cold water, changing it twice, or the oreilles will be inedible.
Cut it into 5 mm strips across the grain, keeping the rind: it is the rind that makes them curl.
Poach them 10 minutes in simmering water and blot them thoroughly — that pre-cooking renders some fat and stops them burning.
Fry them in their own fat over medium heat for 8 minutes, adding nothing: they fold themselves.
Drain on paper, pepper and trickle over maple syrup. Eaten scalding, they soften within a quarter of an hour.

grands-peres-au-sirop.d: Balls of dough poached straight in boiling maple syrup, swollen and soaked through. They are never fried: they steam under the lid, above the syrup as much as in it, which is why the pan must not be opened.
s: Bring the maple syrup, water and sugar to the boil in a wide, deep pan: the liquid should be three centimetres deep.
Rub the cold butter into the flour, baking powder and salt, then bind with the milk without working the dough.
Scoop balls with a spoon and set them on the surface of the boiling syrup, without pushing them under and without touching.
Cover immediately and give them 20 minutes over low heat, never lifting the lid: the trapped steam doubles them in size.
They are done when a needle comes out dry. Serve scalding, in the syrup, with cold cream.

partridgeberry-pie.p: St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
partridgeberry-pie.d: A pie of tundra lingonberries, very sharp, sweetened and thickened with starch. Newfoundlanders call them partridgeberries and pick them in September on the wind-scoured barrens; the berries freeze on the plant and keep all winter.
s: Sort the berries by hand and pick out leaves and stems — washing them makes them burst and lose their juice.
Mix them with the sugar and cornstarch, but taste first: lingonberry is far sharper than blueberry and takes twice the sugar.
Heat a third of them in a pan for five minutes to burst them, then mix with the raw ones: the first give the sauce, the second hold their shape.
Fill, dot with butter and cover with a solid disc — this berry gives little juice, and a lattice would dry it out.
Glaze, cut three vents and bake 50 minutes at 190°C. Cool completely: warm, the filling runs.

malpeque-oysters.d: Oysters from Malpeque Bay, served raw on ice with lemon. They grow four to seven years in colder water than farther south, which slows growth and concentrates flavour; they took the grand prize at the St. Louis Exposition in 1900.
s: Keep the oysters flat, cupped side down, in a damp cloth: laid on their side they lose their liquor.
Open them with a short knife going in at the hinge and not the side: the hinge gives with a quarter turn, the side needs force.
Discard the first liquor and wait two minutes: the oyster makes a second, clearer and far better.
Free the oyster from the lower muscle so nobody has to do it, and return it to its shell.
Serve on crushed ice with a shallot vinegar and lemon. A few may go two minutes under the grill, buttered with garlic.

hodgepodge.d: A creamy stew of the season's first garden vegetables, barely cooked and bound with butter. It is not a winter dish but a late July one: awaited all year, made once or twice when the new potatoes and beans arrive together, and then the season is over.
s: Use new potatoes with thin skins, unpeeled but scrubbed: at this season the skin is the best of the vegetable.
Cook each vegetable in the same pot but one after another, longest first, lifting each out as it is done.
Keep very little water in the base — two centimetres — because with the cream it will make the sauce.
Return everything to the pot, add the cream and butter and let it tremble for three minutes only, never boiling.
The vegetables must stay crisp: an overcooked hodgepodge becomes a soup and loses what made it worth waiting for.

rapure-acadienne.d: A bake of grated, pressed potato in which the extracted water is replaced by chicken broth. It is an operation of substitution: every drop of liquid is removed from the potato and exactly the same volume given back as broth, producing a translucent, gelatinous texture.
s: Poach the chicken 1½ hours with the onion and bay, bone it and keep all the broth, strained and scalding.
Grate the potatoes very finely and press them by handfuls in a cloth, until not another drop comes out.
Measure the extracted water: exactly that volume of boiling broth must go back into the gratings, no more and no less.
Pour the very hot broth in, whisking: the gratings whiten, thicken and turn translucent within seconds.
Build in two layers with the chicken in the middle, scatter bacon and bake 2½ hours at 200°C to a brown, crackling crust.

blueberry-grunt.d: Wild blueberries stewed under steamed dumplings, all in one pan. The name comes from the sound: the fruit grunts as it bubbles under the lid. It dates from when kitchens had no oven and everything was done over the fire.
s: Stew the blueberries with the sugar, water, zest and cinnamon for 8 minutes, until they burst and give up their juice.
The liquid must stay generous: it is the steam rising from it that cooks the dumplings, and a dry base leaves them raw.
Rub the butter into the flour, baking powder and salt, then bind with the milk without working the dough.
Drop spoonfuls of dough onto the bubbling fruit, without pushing them under and well spaced — they double.
Cover and give them 15 minutes without ever lifting the lid. Serve scalding, with cold cream poured over.

caribou-steak.d: A caribou steak seared in butter, served rare with lingonberries. Caribou has been hunted by the Dene and Inuvialuit for millennia; the meat holds almost no fat and the animal feeds on lichen in winter, which gives it a taste of moss and resin.
s: Take the meat out two hours ahead: a steak frozen at the centre would cook outside before the middle was even warm.
Crush the juniper in a mortar with the pepper and rub it into the meat, but salt only as it goes into the pan.
Sear over fierce heat in foaming butter, 2 minutes a side, spooning it over with the garlic and thyme.
Caribou has no fat to protect it: past rare it turns dry and livery, with no way back.
Rest it as long as it cooked, then deglaze with red wine and lingonberry jam. Serve with potatoes.

muktuk.d: Skin and blubber of narwhal or bowhead whale, eaten raw in cubes. It is one of the few sources of vitamin C in the Arctic: the skin holds as much as an orange, and without it scurvy would have been unavoidable in a diet with no plants.
s: Muktuk is taken from a freshly hunted animal and eaten within hours, or frozen immediately.
It is not cooked: heating destroys the vitamin C that justifies its use, and turns the skin rubbery.
Cut it into two-centimetre cubes with an ulu, keeping the black skin and white blubber together: those two layers are what make muktuk.
The skin should crack under the tooth and the blubber melt: if the skin is soft, the animal was old or the keeping too long.
Serve raw, with salt, raw onion or a touch of soy. It is also eaten lightly fermented under moss, but that preparation needs local knowledge.

boston-cream-pie.d: A sponge filled with pastry cream and glazed with chocolate, despite being called a pie. It was created in 1856 at Boston's Parker House hotel; it was called a pie because it was baked in pie tins, cake tins then being scarce.
s: Make the pastry cream first and chill it at least four hours, covered on the surface.
A warm cream melts the sponge and the cake slides apart the moment it is cut.
Bake two sponge discs rather than one to be split: cutting gives an uneven surface the cream soaks through.
Spread the cold cream on the first disc leaving a centimetre margin, then set the second on without pressing.
Coat with a warm ganache and let it run naturally down the sides. Chill two hours before serving.

apple-cider-donuts.d: Doughnuts made with reduced sweet cider, rolled in cinnamon sugar. They belong to the New England autumn: sold at orchards during picking season, and the cider reduction is what separates the good ones from the rest.
s: Reduce the sweet cider by three-quarters, to under 200 ml of thick dark syrup.
Without that reduction the apple flavour disappears entirely in the fryer: the step everyone cuts short and the reason the recipe fails.
Cool the syrup before working it in, then handle the dough as little as possible.
Chill it an hour: soft and sticky, it cannot be cut cleanly.
Fry at 180°C, ninety seconds a side, and roll in cinnamon sugar while still scalding.

new-england-boiled-dinner.d: Corned beef boiled with cabbage, beetroot and root vegetables, served on one plate. The leftovers gave rise to a second dish, red flannel hash, where the beetroot turns everything red: half the point of the meal is the next day.
s: Rinse the corned beef in cold water and soak it an hour if the brine is strong.
Bring to a tremble, never a boil: at a rolling boil the fibres contract and the meat goes dry and stringy.
Allow three hours covered, skimming for the first half hour.
Cook the beetroot separately, always: in the same pot it would dye the whole dish pink within the first hour.
Add the roots an hour before the end, the cabbage in wedges for the last twenty minutes. Serve with mustard and horseradish.

new-york-pizza.d: A large pizza with a thin, pliable crust, sold by the slice and folded in half to eat. The fold is not a joke: the slice is twenty-five centimetres long and would droop without it, and folding is the only way to eat it standing.
s: Knead a dough at 63% hydration and ferment it twenty-four hours in the cold.
That long ferment gives the pliability: a dough proved in two hours is brittle and snaps when folded.
Do not use cooked tomato — New York sauce is crushed raw tomato, barely salted and scented with oregano.
Stretch by hand to forty centimetres, leaving a two-centimetre rim, and never use a rolling pin.
Bake at 290°C on a scalding stone, eight to ten minutes, until the underside is spotted brown.

pecan-pie.d: A pie of syrup and egg custard topped with pecans. The pecan is the only major nut tree native to North America; the pie spread in the 1920s through a campaign by the corn syrup maker Karo.
s: Blind bake the shell fifteen minutes with weights: the filling is very liquid and would soak a raw base.
Toast the pecans dry for ten minutes and cool them: raw, they stay soft under the filling.
Beat the eggs without frothing — foam rises and forms a spongy crust on the surface.
Lay the pecans rounded side up in the shell, then pour the filling gently over: they float up and arrange themselves.
Bake 50 minutes at 175°C. The centre should still tremble; it sets as it cools.

collard-greens-sud.d: Collard leaves simmered for hours with smoked pork. The cooking liquid is called pot likker and is never thrown out: it concentrates the vitamins leached into the water, and is drunk or soaked up with cornbread.
s: Wash the leaves three times in plenty of water: collards hold a great deal of grit between their ribs.
Strip the central rib from every leaf — it stays tough after two hours' cooking and spoils the texture.
Simmer the ham hock alone for an hour first, to flavour the broth before the greens go in.
Add the greens in batches: they shrink by three-quarters and would not fit the pot at once.
Allow another hour. Add the vinegar at the very end, off the heat: added early it fixes the green but toughens the leaf.

hushpuppies.d: Fried cornmeal balls served alongside fried fish. The name is said to come from fishermen throwing scraps of batter to the dogs to quiet them; the etymology is uncertain, but the pairing with a fish fry is constant since the nineteenth century.
s: Use medium-grind cornmeal: too fine and the ball is dense, too coarse and it stays sandy.
Combine dry and wet barely, for fifteen seconds, leaving the batter lumpy.
Rest ten minutes for the meal to hydrate, but no longer: the baking powder starts working and waiting wastes its lift.
Scoop with a small ice cream scoop and drop into oil at 180°C, without shaping by hand.
They turn themselves over when one side is cooked. Allow three minutes in all.

reuben-sandwich.d: A grilled sandwich of corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese and Russian dressing on rye. Omaha and New York have disputed its invention for a century; the Omaha version has it born around 1925 at a poker game in the Blackstone Hotel.
s: Press the sauerkraut out thoroughly in a cloth: its water soaks the bread and ruins the sandwich.
Warm the corned beef by steaming rather than in a pan, so it stays supple and moist.
Build in this order: bread, cheese, beef, sauerkraut, dressing, cheese, bread. Cheese on both sides walls off the moisture.
Butter the outside of the bread, not the pan: the butter melts evenly and browns the crumb without scorching it.
Grill under a weight over medium heat, four minutes a side, until the cheese runs at the edges.

goetta.d: A preparation of pork and steel-cut oats, moulded then sliced and pan-fried. It was brought by Lower Rhine German immigrants in the nineteenth century: the oats stretched a little meat across several meals, and Cincinnati still eats hundreds of tonnes a year.
s: Boil the whole pork with the aromatics for two hours until it falls apart, then shred it and keep the broth.
Use steel-cut oats, never rolled: rolled oats dissolve into porridge and the goetta will not slice.
Cook the oats in the broth an hour and a half over very low heat, stirring often — they catch easily.
Fold in the meat and cook another thirty minutes, until a spoon stands up in the mass.
Pour into loaf tins and chill twelve hours. Slice at a centimetre and fry in butter to a brown crust.

fajitas.p: Rio Grande Valley, Texas, United States
fajitas.d: Grilled skirt steak sliced thin, served with peppers and flour tortillas. The word names the beef skirt, a cut ranch owners left to the Mexican vaqueros as part payment; they made it into the dish that now carries its name.
s: Remove the silverskin from the skirt: it contracts in the heat and buckles the meat.
Marinate four hours in lime, garlic and spices, and no more than six — the acid eventually turns the flesh mealy.
Grill on a scalding cast-iron plate, three minutes a side, aiming for a good crust and a rare centre.
Rest ten minutes, then slice across the grain on the bias, at half a centimetre.
Slicing with the grain makes this cut inedible however it was cooked: the direction of the cut is everything.

queso-fundido.d: Cheese melted in the oven with chorizo and peppers, served bubbling. It needs a pasta filata cheese that melts without splitting; cheddar, tempting as it is, releases its oil and sets to rubber within a few degrees of cooling.
s: Char the poblanos over a flame until the skin blisters, seal them ten minutes and peel them.
Fry the crumbled chorizo and drain the rendered fat: left in the dish it separates from the cheese and floats on top.
Grate the cheese rather than dicing it: grated, it melts evenly and without lumps.
Bake at 200°C for ten minutes only, just long enough for the cheese to stretch.
Serve at once, in the baking dish. Two minutes cold and it hardens beyond recovery.

sopapillas.p: Santa Fe, New Mexico, United States
sopapillas.d: Fried pillows of dough, hollow inside, served with honey. In New Mexico they accompany the savoury course rather than dessert: a corner is torn open and honey poured in, which cools the mouth between mouthfuls of chilli.
s: Knead briefly and rest an hour: an overworked dough stays flat and will not hollow.
Roll to exactly five millimetres and cut triangles or squares, without re-rolling the trimmings.
The dough must be handled as little as possible; re-rolled, it loses its power to puff.
Heat the oil to 195°C, hotter than for most frying: it is the violent steam that lifts the two faces apart.
Submerge the dough and hold it under with a skimmer for three seconds. It balloons at once.

pulled-pork-sandwich.d: Pork shoulder smoked for ten hours, pulled and served in a bun with slaw. In Memphis the slaw goes in the sandwich, not beside it: that is the local rule, and serving it on the side marks you as an outsider.
s: Rub the shoulder with the spice mix twelve hours ahead, and leave it uncovered in the refrigerator.
Smoke at 110°C over hickory or apple wood for ten hours, aiming for 95°C at the centre.
Around 70°C the temperature stops rising for hours: that is the stall, caused by evaporation, and you simply wait it out.
Wrap in butcher's paper at that point if you want to shorten it, never in foil, which softens the bark.
Pull by hand, mixing the dark bark through the pale meat, douse with vinegar sauce and serve with the slaw inside the bun.

hoppin-john.d: Rice with black-eyed peas and smoked pork, eaten on New Year's Day for luck. Each pea stands for a coin and the greens served alongside for banknotes: the superstition is taken seriously enough that the dish is unfindable on 2 January.
s: Soak the peas overnight: they then cook in forty minutes instead of two hours.
Simmer the ham hock alone for an hour first, then add the soaked peas to that broth.
Salt only at the end — smoked pork is already salty, and early salt hardens the pea skins.
Measure the remaining broth and cook the rice in it, two parts to one, set on the peas without stirring.
Twenty minutes covered, then rest ten minutes. Serve with stewed collard greens alongside.

haupia.d: A coconut milk pudding set with arrowroot and cut into firm squares. It was once set with pia starch, a now scarce Hawaiian plant; cornflour has replaced it, but the original texture was more translucent and firmer.
s: Slake the starch in cold water to a perfectly smooth milk, without a single lump.
Heat the coconut milk and sugar without boiling, then pour in the slaked starch in a stream, whisking.
Boil for one full minute, stirring: starch reaches its thickening power only after a proper boil.
Taken off before that, the mixture looks set but returns to liquid as it cools and will never cut.
Pour into a square dish two centimetres deep and set three hours in the cold. Cut with a wetted knife.

whitebait-fritters.d: Whole whitebait held in a plain egg batter, barely bound. On the West Coast neither flour nor onion goes in: that would hide a fish that sells for the price of white gold.
s: Rinse the whitebait in iced water and drain them thoroughly, without pressing: they are fragile.
Beat the eggs barely, with a fork, with salt and pepper — nothing else.
Fold in the whitebait gently: the mixture should hold far more fish than egg.
Foam butter in a pan and pour a ladleful per fritter, without spreading it.
Give them 90 seconds a side, no more: overcooked, whitebait falls apart and loses its sweetness. Serve with lemon, on buttered bread.

rewena-paraoa.d: A Māori bread raised on a potato starter, dense and faintly sour. The starter, the bug, is handed down through generations and fed on potato and sugar: some are over a hundred years old.
s: Three days ahead, boil the potatoes and mash them with their water, a spoonful of flour and one of sugar.
Ferment covered in a glass jar, stirring daily: the starter should bubble and smell sweet-sour.
If it smells frankly of vinegar it has gone too far; if it does nothing by the third day, start again.
Knead the flour, salt, starter and warm water for 12 minutes, and prove for 2 hours.
Add the bicarbonate when shaping, prove for 40 minutes, and bake for 45 minutes at 190°C. Always keep back a spoonful of starter for next time.

barramundi-au-paperbark.d: A whole barramundi wrapped in melaleuca bark and cooked over coals. Top End peoples have used this bark for millennia: soaked, it does not burn and lends the fish a eucalypt note.
s: Soak the melaleuca bark for 30 minutes in water: dry, it catches fire within seconds.
Scale and gut the fish, and score it three times on each side.
Rub it with lemon myrtle, ground bush tomato and salt, and fill the belly with lemon and spring onion.
Wrap it in two thicknesses of wet bark and tie it with fibre string.
Set the parcel on moderate coals for 15 minutes a side. The bark blackens on the surface without the fish burning.

lamingtons.d: Cubes of sponge dipped in chocolate icing then rolled in coconut. Named after Lord Lamington, governor of Queensland, who reportedly called them 'those bloody poofy woolly biscuits'.
s: Make a butter sponge, bake it in a tray for 30 minutes at 180°C, and let it cool completely.
Wrap it and rest it overnight: fresh sponge crumbles when dipped, day-old sponge holds.
Cut 4 cm cubes, wiping the blade between cuts.
Make a fluid icing with the cocoa, icing sugar, melted butter and a little hot milk.
Dip each cube on a fork, let it drip, then roll it at once in the coconut. Dry for 2 hours on a rack.

lu-sipi.d: Lamb and taro leaves cooked in coconut milk, in parcels, under the earth. Tonga has bought frozen mutton flaps from New Zealand since the 1970s: the dish is old, the ingredient recent.
s: Cut the lamb into large dice with its fat: lean, it dries out under the earth.
Strip the ribs from the taro leaves and stack them into cups, five or six per parcel.
Fill with meat, onion and coconut cream, salt, and close them carefully.
Wrap each cup in a banana leaf and tie it with fibre.
Cook for 2½ hours in the umu on hot stones, or covered in a 160°C oven. Serve with boiled taro.

coconut-crab-vanuatu.d: The largest land crustacean in the world, grilled then stewed in its own coconut milk. It feeds on coconuts and its flesh keeps that taste; its scarcity now makes it an occasional dish.
s: Boil the crab for 15 minutes in salted water, then split it and detach the claws.
Save the yellow fat from the abdomen: it is the prized part, and it flavours the sauce.
Grill the pieces briefly over coals to fix the aroma.
Fry the onion, garlic and ginger, add the coconut cream and the reserved fat.
Simmer for 15 minutes without boiling, return the crab, and serve with taro and island cabbage.

sup-sup.d: A soup of root vegetables and greens in coconut milk, thick and mild. The name is Tok Pisin: sup sup, the soup of soups, made with whatever the garden gives that day.
s: Peel the roots and cut them into large even cubes: they must cook together.
Boil them for 20 minutes in a litre of water with the onion, garlic and flaked smoked fish.
Add the squash and green plantain, and give them another 15 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and bring to a bare simmer, never boiling.
Add the aibika leaves last, for 5 minutes only: overcooked, they turn grey.

poulet-au-lait-de-coco-salomon.n: Chicken with coconut and green pawpaw
poulet-au-lait-de-coco-salomon.d: Chicken stewed in coconut milk with green pawpaw, which behaves here as a vegetable. Green pawpaw holds an enzyme that tenderises meat: it does a marinade's work without being one.
s: Peel the green pawpaw and remove the seeds; cut it into large cubes.
Colour the jointed chicken in the oil, then add the onion, garlic and ginger.
Add a glass of water and the pawpaw, and simmer covered for 30 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and continue for 20 minutes without boiling: the pawpaw turns translucent and soft.
Add the island cabbage leaves at the end. Serve with boiled sweet potato and lime.

fafaru.d: Raw tuna marinated in lime and drowned in coconut milk, the everyday dish of Polynesia. It is made at the lagoon's edge with the morning's fish: beyond a few hours it loses all interest.
s: Choose tuna caught the same day and keep it on ice until the last moment.
Cut it into 2 cm cubes, salt with coarse salt for 5 minutes, then rinse and pat dry.
Pour over the lime juice and leave 10 minutes only: the flesh must stay red at the centre.
Drain and discard the juice, which would curdle the coconut milk.
Add the fresh coconut milk, julienned cucumber and carrot, tomato and spring onion. Serve immediately.

rukau.d: Taro leaves long-melted in coconut milk and onion, served as an accompaniment. In the Cooks a cook is judged on her rukau: undercooked it scratches the throat, overcooked it is a characterless purée.
s: Strip the ribs from the taro leaves: they carry most of the irritant crystals.
Boil them for 30 minutes in plenty of water, then drain and discard that water.
Squeeze them between your hands and chop them roughly.
Soften the onion in butter, add the leaves and cook covered for 15 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk and continue for 15 minutes over low heat. Serve with boiled taro or a roast.

ika-mata-niue.d: A gratin of thinly sliced green pawpaw and taro, drowned in coconut cream. Niue serves it at village feasts; the pairing of root and fruit, both barely sweet, surprises then quickly convinces.
s: Peel the green pawpaw and taro, and cut them into 3 mm slices, as even as you can.
Rinse the taro in cold water to remove surface starch, which would make the gratin gluey.
Line a dish with banana leaves and alternate layers of taro and pawpaw.
Salt lightly between the layers and pour in coconut cream to just below the surface.
Cover with leaves and bake for 1 hour at 180°C. Rest for 15 minutes before cutting into portions.

palolo.d: A dense coconut bread, baked in leaves, somewhere between cake and flatbread. Coconut cream keeps it soft for days, and it is cut into thick slices for travelling.
s: Grate the fresh coconut and press half of it for cream; keep the pulp.
Mix the flour, baking powder, sugar, salt and grated pulp.
Add the coconut cream and melted butter, and work just enough to bring it together: overworked, the dough goes hard.
Spread it 2 cm thick on softened banana leaves, and fold into a flat parcel.
Bake for 30 minutes at 190°C or on hot stones. The top should brown and the centre stay soft.

maori-boil-up-pork.d: A green soup of giant clams, thickened with cream, once served at state banquets. Toheroa has been protected since 1971: its green colour comes from the phytoplankton it feeds on, and nothing replaces it.
s: Purge the clams for 4 hours in seawater or heavily salted water, changing it twice.
Steam them open and strain their liquor carefully through a cloth: sand always hides in it.
Chop the flesh finely by knife — blended, it turns elastic and loses its grain.
Make a pale roux in butter, moisten with the strained liquor and the milk, and cook for 15 minutes.
Add the flesh and the cream and simmer for 5 minutes without boiling. Lemon and parsley at the last moment.

anzac-biscuits.d: Oat biscuits with golden syrup, eggless, posted to soldiers in the Great War. The absence of egg is no accident: without it the biscuit survives two months at sea without spoiling.
s: Combine the oats, flour, coconut, sugar and salt dry.
Melt the butter with the golden syrup, without letting them boil.
Slake the bicarbonate in the boiling water and pour it into the butter: the mixture foams at once and doubles.
Pour over the dry ingredients and work quickly, then shape flattened balls, well spaced.
Bake 15 minutes at 160°C for a chewy biscuit, 20 for a crisp one. Both camps have their partisans.
